Chapter 64: Old Baldy

← Chapter 63 · Guide Home · Chapter 65 →

Research notes: Chapter 64

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Lorena · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Decay and Ruin · Motherhood, Pregnancy, and Birth

Symbols: Hair, Wig, and Baldness · Pregnancy, Birth, and Children

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Ecclesiastes · Greek Mythology · Music and Composers · Suicide in History and Literature · The Bible

Chapter 63 gave you the moment the wig came off. Chapter 64 is what comes after: Miss MacIntosh, still bald-headed, still in the fog, telling Vera the story of her entire life. And Vera, for once, listening, and beginning to understand something Miss MacIntosh cannot see about herself.

This is one of the most tender chapters in the novel.

What actually happens

Miss MacIntosh talks. She tells Vera about her childhood baldness, her wigs made from stolen horsehairs, the barber who told her nothing could be done, the boys who tried to hook her wig with fishing lines, the phrenologist who praised the magnificent shape of her skull, the Gaelic prince she claims as an ancestor, and the two orphans from her years as a matron: a forger who sent her Christmas cards from Alcatraz, and Lorena, the dancing girl she loved.

Vera listens. And somewhere in the listening, she realizes she can see Miss MacIntosh in a way that Miss MacIntosh cannot see herself. She begins, quietly, to compose an elegy for her.

At the end of the chapter, they are in the last month they will have together.

Bald from birth

Miss MacIntosh was born without hair and has never grown any. As a child, she wore a toupee. Later she stole hairs from horses to make her own wig. Boys knew about it and taunted her: fishing lines thrown at her head to hook the hairpiece. She was afraid of animals and people both. She wandered.

She tells Vera about the barber she visited, the barber pole that once meant bloodletting and leeches, the barber's eloquent helplessness in the face of her condition: there was nothing to be done, not one hair to be grown. She accepted it. She had to.

And then she traces her baldness back into legend: she is descended, she says, “from a Gaelic prince who was” also bald, who lost his golden crown at sea, who was “cast up on the bleak shores of Scotland” with nothing. His crown floated on the waves. His hair was gone. She claims this man as her ancestor and his loss as her inheritance.

This is not delusion. It is dignity. Miss MacIntosh is doing what humans have always done with their pain: finding it a lineage, giving it a history, refusing to let it be merely random. If she is bald, then she is bald like a prince. If she has no crown, then neither did he, and he survived it.

Lorena

Of all the orphans Miss MacIntosh cared for in her years as a matron, she loved only two well enough to keep in contact: a forger imprisoned at Alcatraz, who sent her beautifully decorated Christmas cards every year with signatures ranging “from Abraham Lincoln to William Jennings Bryan”; and Lorena.

Lorena was a dancing girl: dark, beautiful, with long hair like "the midnight curtain concealing the star until the star was revealed." She laughed at Miss MacIntosh when they first met, and then ran away, and eventually became a strip-tease dancer. Years later she was paroled into Miss MacIntosh's care, and she ran away again, and Miss MacIntosh could not pursue her because pursuing was not what a parole officer could do.

Lorena lived in the spotlight. Miss MacIntosh lived in the shadow. Between them, every possible trajectory of womanhood: the one who displayed herself and the one who concealed herself, the one who slept with many men and the one who learned to live without protection, the one who danced in the light and the one who saved on electric lights because she hated what they stood for.

Miss MacIntosh reflects that Lorena once invited her to join the strip-tease act, believing she would have made a sensational performer. The image is almost unbearably poignant: bald Miss MacIntosh, in a spotlight. The woman who spent her life keeping her wig on, imagined as the woman who takes everything off.

She says they were "very dear friends" for a time.

Vera sees what Miss MacIntosh cannot

This is the chapter's turning point, and Young handles it with great delicacy. As Miss MacIntosh speaks, Vera begins to perceive something: she can see Miss MacIntosh, in a way that Miss MacIntosh cannot see herself. She sees the courage inside the practicality, the loneliness inside the sternness, the love inside the woman who said love is "a system of mutual deception."

She sees the pale narcissus: that image appears here: a flower breaking through rock, fragile and improbable, insisting on blooming in barren ground. That is what Vera sees when she looks at Miss MacIntosh with her wig off. Not the exposure. The persistence.

And she begins composing her elegy. Not out loud. Internally. The way Mr. Spitzer composes music that no one hears. The way everything in this novel that matters most happens in the interior, where only the composer knows it exists.

"I wandered. I wandered on and on. I broke my nose. I lost my breast."

Miss MacIntosh compresses her life into a few spare sentences that Young gives her without decoration. She wandered from job to job, from city to city. She broke her nose: how, she doesn't fully explain. She lost her breast to a mastectomy. She had no place. She walked into the traffic flow.

That last detail: walking into traffic. Your notes suggest this may have been her first attempt at suicide. Young doesn't say so directly. She leaves it open, the way she leaves everything open: as something that might have been accident, might have been intention, might have been the moment between them that she survived without understanding why. Miss MacIntosh, who stood for reality against illusion, for life against dream, for the practical against the imagined; she also walked into traffic once, and did not die.

She learned, after all that, to live without protection. For a woman of her era, this is no small statement. Without a father's household and without a husband's, a woman of Miss MacIntosh's time had nothing in a very literal sense: no social standing, no legal protection, no safety net of any kind. She built her own shelter out of practicality and an umbrella and a wig made from stolen horsehair. She carried herself through the world with the one thing she could control: her willingness to face it.

"Vanity, vanity, all is vanity"

Miss MacIntosh reaches for Ecclesiastes in this chapter: the Preacher's great cry that everything under the sun is empty, fleeting, futile. Wealth, wisdom, pleasure, effort: all passes. All comes to nothing.

In Miss MacIntosh's mouth this is not despair. It is realism. She has never needed illusions to sustain her; she has sustained herself on reality alone. If reality is ultimately vanity, that is not a reason to stop. You knit your bones together even though they unravel faster than you can knit. You carry your umbrella. You go.

The last month

The chapter closes with the knowledge that this is Vera and Miss MacIntosh's last month together. Everything that has just been said (the baldness, Lorena, the wandering, the traffic) has been said in the shadow of ending. Miss MacIntosh knew, when she removed her wig in Chapter 63, that she was running out of time for pretense. Now the time itself is visibly running out.

Vera will lose the only person who ever told her the truth. And she is already, silently, beginning to mourn.

What to hold onto

Miss MacIntosh, bald-headed, telling Vera the story of the Gaelic prince who lost his crown at sea, and the dancing girl who ran away, and the forger who sent Christmas cards from Alcatraz. And Vera, listening, seeing her clearly for the first time, and beginning to understand that this is an elegy she is composing, even now, even while Miss MacIntosh is still speaking.

guide-56-the-funeral-and-the-dispersal:
Chapter 56: The Funeral and the Dispersal

← Chapter 55 · Guide Home · Chapter 57 →

Research notes: Chapter 56

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer

Themes: Fate and Chance · Madness and Sanity

Symbols: Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · Clouds and Storms · Keys, Doors, and Locks · Weddings and Funerals

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology

Allusions: Gambling and Playing Cards · Napoleon and Wellington

Peron is buried with his poker chips, his dice, and a playing card.

Joachim arranges the funeral with the care and precision he brings to everything: the corpse dressed with sartorial elegance, the best suits, the formal correctness that Peron in life would have found hilarious. A violinist with an empty sleeve plays. An official track bugler performs: someone who has played at Pimlico and Suffolk Downs, at the great racetracks where Peron spent much of his life. The ceremony is perfect. Joachim leaves only the red rose in the grave, the recognition at “the portals of the great city.”

And then, over the years that follow, he gives away everything else. Peron's wardrobe (the extraordinary, bewildering accumulation of a man who could be anything and dressed accordingly) goes to the homeless, the poor, the tramps on the street. Homburgs. Stetsons. “Trilbys, pork-pies, brown bowler derbies.” Jockeys' silks. Cantons and merinos and astrakhans and Irish cambrics and paisleys. All of Peron's identity, all the costumes of the chameleon, scattered into the city. Joachim, keeping only his own threadbare suit, watches the dispersal and wonders which of them is still alive.

What actually happens in Chapter 56

Chapter 56 is a chapter of aftermath: the aftermath of Peron's death that Joachim has been living inside for all these years, rendered now in its most direct and least oblique form. He describes the funeral. He describes the dispersal of the wardrobe. He describes his own philosophical collapse: the inability to believe in reality as a stable foundation, the sense of being a puppet controlled by unknown forces, the question of who tailored him in this strange life, the mad tailor who cut his existence from this particular cloth.

His grief is not personal grief only. Young has always given Mr. Spitzer a grief larger than any individual loss: he mourns flowers, moths, tides, stars, moments. He mourns the impermanence of all things. This chapter gives that grief its most explicit form: the cosmic mourning of a sentimentalist who cannot stop noticing what passes. The funeral is for Peron. The mourning extends, in concentric rings outward, to everything that will not last.

The chapter closes with Joachim lamenting the absence of a guiding author or architect of being. He carries “the golden key to the door that” is no more. The door is gone. The key remains, perfectly made, opening nothing. The dead musician who lives despite attempts to silence him, that last image, encapsulates what Mr. Spitzer has been all along: a persistence that continues past the point where persistence makes obvious sense, because the alternative is the silence that no one should choose for themselves.

The funeral rites for the gambler

Poker chips, dice, and a playing card in the grave.

This is Joachim's version of love: knowing his brother well enough to bury him with the tools of his trade, the instruments of the life he actually lived rather than the life the conventional ceremony would prefer to acknowledge. Most funerals pretend that the dead person was better behaved than they were. Joachim buries Peron as Peron was: a gambler, a man of chance, a person whose relationship to fate was always a wager rather than a plan.

The red rose he leaves is the recognition, at “the portals of the great city,” the entrance to wherever Peron has gone. The red rose for Peron, the white rose worn by Joachim himself: life passing beyond life. The two brothers each assigned their color at the threshold. Peron's red is vitality, passion, the gambler's flush. Joachim's white is the pale replica, the mourner, the one who remains behind in the register of the barely living.

Young presents this funeral as a performance of love: an act of witness and recognition that required Joachim to know Peron completely and to honor that knowledge rather than correct it. He gave Peron the funeral Peron would have wanted, not the funeral convention prescribed. This is the most intimate thing he has ever done. He does it alone.

The wardrobe dispersed

Peron's wardrobe was a collection of identities: every hat and suit a different version of the chameleon's display, a different costume for a different occasion in a life organized around becoming whatever the moment required. The homburgs for the formal occasions. The Stetsons for the Western affect. The trilbys for jazz clubs and Hollywood glamour. The jockeys' silks for the racetracks. The elaborate layers of fabric (canton flannels, merinos, astrakhans, paisleys) each one the costume of a different Peron.

Joachim gives all of it away. To the poor. To tramps. He scatters Peron's identity through the city the way the wind scattered the elegy in the previous chapter. He keeps only his own threadbare suit. He keeps being himself, in the suit that is too thin and too worn and too obviously the suit of a man who values his dignity more than his comfort, because the suit is what he has and the suit is what he is.

The dispersal is grief and it is liberation and it is the opposite of accumulation. Peron accumulated. He collected identities the way Joachim collected stamps, except that Peron wore his collection rather than filing it. When Joachim gives the wardrobe away, he is undoing the collection: sending the identities back into circulation, letting them become the clothing of whoever needs them next. The tramp in Peron's homburg is wearing a piece of Peron. The tramp does not know this. The homburg does not care. The identity disperses into the city like everything else.

The mad tailor

Who tailored him in this strange life?

Mr. Spitzer's question (who is the author or architect of his existence, who cut and stitched him into this particular shape) is the philosophical question of theodicy rendered as a sartorial complaint. If there is a God who designed the universe, why did this God design it as it is? If there is a principle of order underlying existence, why does the order keep failing? Who made Mr. Spitzer the pale replica of his brother, the man who arrives a minute late, the cautious chess player who cannot take the final action?

The mad tailor is the answer Young provides, not as theology but as image. The creator of this particular existence was mad. The stitching is wrong. The basting stitches (the temporary stitches meant to hold the garment together until the real work is done, the stitches that are supposed to be removed) have never been removed. Mr. Spitzer is being held together by temporary fastenings that were never meant to be permanent. He is, in this sense, perpetually provisional: a garment that was not finished, assembled from pieces that do not quite match, basted into the shape of a person and then left to wear the basting.

Puppet, dummy, cloud with unraveling seams

Young gives Mr. Spitzer three self-images in rapid succession: puppet, tailor's dummy, and cloud with seams unraveling.

The puppet has no agency; it moves when the strings move it. The tailor's dummy has no self; it exists only to display the garments placed upon it. The cloud with unraveling seams has no coherence; it is a shape that is actively losing the stitching that held it together, becoming formless as it moves. Three versions of a self that has been emptied of what makes a self: agency, interiority, coherence.

And yet Mr. Spitzer is not simply these things. He is also the person who arranged Peron's funeral with love. Who gave the wardrobe to the poor with intention. Who wanders the city finding the lost heirs and the forgotten legacies. Who keeps the great secret. Who carries the alpenhorn. Who composes the elegy in fragments and watches it scatter in the wind. The puppet moves when the strings move it and also writes music. The dummy displays the garments and also loves. The cloud is unraveling and is also still a cloud, still holding its shape against the dispersal.

The golden key to the door that is no more

The chapter's final image: Joachim carries “the golden key to the door that was no more.”

He has the key. The key is perfectly made: golden, precise, the right instrument for the right lock. The door it was made for no longer exists. The house that held the door was lost in the bankruptcy. The life organized around the door (the twin house, the music as tomb, the careful conservative investments) is gone. The key remains, opening nothing, carried in his pocket through every chapter of his wandering, in the silk hat and the threadbare suit, through the fog-bound city and the wrong carriage and the missed connection and the beachcomber's house.

Young's key that opens nothing is among her most exact images for Mr. Spitzer's condition. He is perfectly equipped for a life that no longer exists. He has the instrument for the situation he prepared for, and the situation has been dismantled. He carries the key anyway because the key is his. Because having it is the only form of relation to the lost house that remains available. Because you do not throw away a golden key simply because the door is gone. The door may come back. The door may appear somewhere else. He is still looking.

What to hold onto

Chapter 56 is the most direct account of Peron's actual funeral and its aftermath that the novel offers, and it is organized around the central paradox of Joachim's grief: he mourned his brother better than his brother ever mourned him. He gave Peron the perfect burial. He dispersed the perfect wardrobe. He kept the single suit and the golden key and the threadbare dignity and went on.

What to carry forward: the poker chips in the grave, the intimate act of honoring a person as they were rather than as convention required them to be. The wardrobe scattered through the city as Peron's identity dissolving into general circulation. The mad tailor who basted instead of sewing and left the temporary stitches in place. And the golden key, carried through every chapter, opening nothing, never thrown away.

For the Curious

  • On Beau Brummell and the philosophy of dress
  • On the history of Peron's hats
  • On basting stitches and the provisional self
  • On the red rose and white rose
guide-72-esther-longtree:
Chapter 72: Esther Longtree

← Chapter 71 · Guide Home · Chapter 73 →

Content note: The Esther Longtree chapters (72 to 81) deal with stillbirth and pregnancy loss, rape, infanticide, racist violence including lynching, and cruelty to children. This chapter centers on pregnancy and stillbirth.

Research notes: Chapter 72

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Esther Longtree · Jacqueline White · Justice O’Leary · The Chicago Detective · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Identity and the Self · Motherhood, Pregnancy, and Birth

Symbols: Birds · Pregnancy, Birth, and Children · Shadows

Philosophy: Hinduism

Allusions: Judaism · Pregnancy, Abortion, and Midwifery · The Bible

She is the one Dr. O’Leary told you about through the wall in Chapter 69: the woman who believes herself always pregnant, who suffers miscarriage after miscarriage, whose condition baffled him and broke him and whose name, if he ever said it, you may have missed in the dark.

Her name is Esther Longtree. She is the waitress at the Greasy Spoon. She has “a bald spot shaped like a large coin” on her head, long black hair that flows loose at whatever cost to sanitation, ponderous red lips, a deformed foot, and a belly that has been swollen for as long as anyone in town can remember. She is perpetually pregnant. She has never carried a living child to term.

She is one of the great figures in this novel, and this chapter is hers entirely.

If you have been reading along, you already know something about what Esther represents: the woman always waiting, always gestating, always on the verge of the thing that never arrives. She was introduced as a rumor: a medical curiosity, the doctor’s strangest case, the woman no one quite understands. Now you meet her in full, and she turns out to be something larger than a case history. She is vast with grief and hope and philosophy and humor, enormous with the children she has lost and the one she still believes is coming. Chapter 72 is Esther’s monologue, Esther’s meditation, Esther’s world. Read it slowly.

The Setting: The Greasy Spoon

It is early spring, foggy, the morning after Vera’s sleepless night at the Tavern. The town is described in its morning configuration: an undertaker’s hearse, ghostly old automobiles, a grey wagon pulled by a bony mule. Between the undertaker and the beauty parlor, between death’s preparation and beauty’s, stands the Greasy Spoon, where Esther works.

She took the job from Jacqueline White, the previous waitress, who got sick. She is the passive policeman’s only daughter. Her parents think she is an old maid, a failure, a puzzle they cannot read. They tease her. They do not know what she carries. The Greasy Spoon is both a restaurant and a symbol. It is where ordinary life gets fed (truck drivers, salesmen, travelers) and where Esther has spent years standing between the living and the dead, serving food, carrying children no one ever sees born. The hollyhocks painted on the cracked walls reach toward the ceiling, straining upward against the decay around them. Young gives Esther exactly this setting: life insisting on itself in a place given over to grease and impermanence.

Esther Herself

She is described with a physicality Young lavishes on very few characters: plum-colored and square, ponderous red lips, breasts like milky breakers, hair she tosses freely. She has morning sickness and evening sickness. Her belly is enormous. She has a bald spot, a deformed foot, and she laughs uproariously at things others find distressing. She talks to herself. She talks to the unborn child. She talks to the stillborn children who haunt her, the ones she has buried under leaves and snow and in rivers and who come back to her in whispers. She is “brilliant but dumb,” “ugly outside but beautiful inside,” “experienced and sought after” yet also an old maid in her parents’ estimation. She keeps lovebirds. She knits without thread: a gesture of preparation for a child that may not come, or of faith in the act of preparation itself, regardless of outcome. She has made “a little black suit for the” child she believes will survive. She has prepared layettes. She is ready. She is not deluded in the way Catherine is deluded, or Dr. O’Leary. Her mind, Young tells us, is clear and luminous. She knows exactly what has happened to her: she has carried as many children as autumn leaves, and none of them lived, and she is pregnant again, and she believes this one might be different. This is not confusion. This is hope maintained in the full knowledge of its own history. It is one of the bravest things in the novel.

The Little Shadow Boxer

This is what Esther calls the child she is carrying now: “the little shadow boxer who in the waters of her womb” has grown and grown and has warded off every blow. She can feel the little shadow foot playing against her side. She can feel the heartbeat accelerating under her heart. Two hearts, she says: mine and his.

A shadow boxer fights an opponent who is not there. The fight is real; the opponent is invisible. This is precisely Esther’s situation: she is fighting for a life against the force that has taken every other life she has carried, a force she cannot see or name or locate. The child is fighting too, from inside, against the same invisible opponent. The image is also tender in a way Young rarely allows herself to be this directly. The little shadow foot against Esther’s side. The heartbeat. Two hearts. For all the novel’s philosophical and mythological weight, this is simply a woman feeling her baby move and loving it with the particular love of someone who knows she may lose it.

The Fathers

Esther has had many fathers for her children. They are almost all salesmen, which in this era means traveling men, men who pass through: the piano-tuner, the “horn-blower, the tin roofer, the soap salesman,” the rubber salesman, the featherweight boxer, the Chicago detective. They come through town, they stay a night or two at the diner or the hotel, and then they are gone. They are, almost without exception, sterile. Not always in the clinical sense (the pregnancies are real, the children are real) but in some deeper way that Young does not quite medicalize: the children of these men do not survive. They are born still. They haunt Esther. Some of the fathers write years later “asking if the child was ever born,” unaware or unwilling to accept that it was not, that it never will be. There is one exception in this chapter: a sad, stout drummer, a Fuller Brush salesman, who comes in crying. His grief is not about Esther’s children. His wife’s sister’s little girl died of scarlet fever, and he cannot recover from it. He abandoned his business, his family, his life, and now he wanders the roads selling brushes and carrying a bag of candy for a child who is dead and will never eat it. He sits at the counter, weeping. Esther serves him. He is the saddest man in the chapter, and possibly the most honest: he knows exactly what he has lost and cannot stop carrying it. The traveling salesmen collectively are one of Young’s sharpest observations about American masculinity: men in motion, men who sell things, men who pass through women’s lives and disappear before the consequences arrive. They represent, in aggregate, the absent father writ American: not villainous, not deliberate, simply gone.

Dr. O’Leary’s Verdict

Dr. O’Leary, whom you met in Chapters 69 and 71 in his dissolving state, turns out to have encountered Esther before his mind gave way. He came into the diner to get a drink (a nickel, which dates the encounter to sometime between 1930 and 1959) and Esther asked him about her condition. He told her she was “the immortal medical case.” He told her she would never die in childbirth; her labor would be easy, like passing a seed. He told her the problem was atmospheric: the unusual pressure, the thinning ether, the whirling stars. He told her the problem would end with her and would “not be seen again upon the earth.”

This is both the most and least helpful medical opinion Esther has ever received. It offers her everlasting hope. It explains nothing. It attributes her condition to forces beyond anyone’s control or comprehension and then reassures her that she will survive what it will not explain. This is Dr. O’Leary at his most compassionate and his most useless, which is to say, at his most human.

His attribution of Esther’s condition to “atmospheric pressure” and “thinning ether” is also, in its way, Young’s. The novel treats Esther’s pregnancy as operating on a cosmic scale: stars, moon, wind, the Milky Way. She is not merely a woman with a medical condition. She is a woman whose body is in conversation with forces so large they dwarf medicine.

Who Killed Cock Robin?

Near the chapter’s end, Esther poses the question from the old English nursery rhyme: “Who killed Cock Robin?” The rhyme is ancient, probably older than its first written records, and no one is certain what it originally meant; it may involve Celtic sun gods, may involve real historical figures, may be simply the nursery-rhyme recording of a universal truth about death. In the rhyme, everyone takes responsibility and no one is wholly to blame: I, said the sparrow, with my bow and arrow; I, said the fly, with my little eye.

Esther’s answer: nobody. The child “was killed by the death that was in him from the time of his birth,” by “the wind, the night, the day, the” atmospheric pressure. No one is solely responsible. Death is a universal and impersonal force that operates through all things simultaneously. This is not consolation exactly, it does not bring the children back, but it is a kind of philosophical peace: she did not kill them. The sterile fathers did not kill them. The cold cosmos killed them, impartially, as it kills everything eventually. She also says: “she was soon to have a sweet, sweet little baby that would cry in her arms and that would kill them all.” The living child (if it comes, when it comes) will supersede the dead. Will put to rest the haunting whispers of the stillborn. Will end the reign of ghosts with a cry. This is Esther’s defiant hope, stated simply, as fact. She is preparing for it. She has knitted the little black suit. She is ready.

The Stillborn

They are “as many as the autumn leaves.” They are under leaves, under snow, in rivers, in the earth. They whisper to her. They cry. They are not gone in any simple sense: they persist in Esther’s consciousness the way the dead persist throughout this novel, as presences that refuse to complete their departure. Young treats them with extraordinary delicacy. They are real, Esther has buried them with her own hands, and they are also luminous abstractions: snowflakes, stars, shadows. The novel refuses to let them be merely medical events, failures of physiology. They are children who existed and were lost, and their mother remembers every one of them, and they have come back to haunt her not with malice but with the simple fact of their having been.

This is one of the places where Young’s insistence that everything real is real, “even the unreal things were real”, carries its full weight. The stillborn are not real in the way the living are real. But they are not nothing. Esther has carried them, buried them, grieved them, and is still pregnant with all of them in the only sense that counts: she has not stopped loving them or waiting for the one who will live.

What to Hold Onto

“The little shadow boxer, the little” shadow foot against Esther’s side. Two hearts: mine and his. Keep this.

The bag of candy the sad Fuller Brush salesman carries for a child who is dead. He wanders the roads with it. He cannot put it down.

Esther knitting without thread. The act of preparation as an act of faith, regardless of outcome.

Dr. O’Leary’s diagnosis: atmospheric. The thinning ether. The whirling stars. The problem will end with her and will “not be seen again upon the earth.” And Esther’s answer to “Who killed Cock Robin?”: nobody. And: soon there will be “a sweet, sweet little baby that” will cry in her arms and kill them all.

She is the passive policeman’s only daughter. She is the immortal medical case. She is always pregnant. She is luminous. She is ready.

guide-44-false-modesty-killed-my-love:
Chapter 44: False Modesty Killed My Love

← Chapter 43 · Guide Home · Chapter 45 →

Research notes: Chapter 44

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Peron Spitzer · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Death and Mortality · Fear and Courage · Love · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Clothing, Hats, and Skirts

Philosophy: Astrology, Alchemy, and Esoterica · Heraclitus and Flux · Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · Women's Suffrage

Chapter 44 is the last chapter of Volume 1, and it is the chapter where Young finally gives us what Mr. Spitzer has been unable to give Catherine across all these chapters: the truth of Cousin Hannah's private life, pieced together from the papers of a dead woman, secret letters, unintelligible languages, evidence of a double existence that was hidden from everyone, including perhaps from herself.

The suffrage captain led two lives. One was public, legible, heroic: the campaigns, the border crossings, the iron keys, the masculine virtues. The other was private, guarded, full of a grief and a longing and a love that she could not bring into the open without dismantling the self she had constructed.

“False modesty killed my love.”

She says it in the delirium. Mr. Spitzer hears it. Young offers it to you as the chapter's central confession, the thing that was never said while it might have mattered. And then the chapter, and the volume, turns toward the question this sentence opens: what does it mean to know about love without having lived it fully? What does it mean to be the confidante of everyone's secrets while keeping your own most carefully?

What actually happens in Chapter 44

Mr. Spitzer, as Cousin Hannah's lawyer, must go through her personal effects and papers after her death. What he finds is a life beneath the life: secret letters, correspondence in languages he cannot read, evidence of relationships and intimacies she never disclosed to the world. The public figure and the private person are separated by a gap as wide as the novel has been suggesting, and wider.

The chapter circles back through the deathbed (her call for her skirt, the snowdrops melting in her hand, the cry of false modesty killed my love) and reads these moments now not as mere delirium but as confession. She is naming, at last, the thing she refused to name in life. The cause she gave everything to was also, the chapter suggests, a place to put a grief that had nowhere else to go. Her suffrage activism was not separate from her private heartbreak. It was sustained by it, or ran parallel to it, or was the form her unexpressed love took when it could not be expressed.

Mr. Spitzer reflects on heroism. He wonders whether the greatest heroes might be driven by a secret cowardice: an inner failure that propels them toward greater and greater external battles because the inner battle cannot be faced. He is not certain. He is, as always, observing without arriving at conclusions. But he is asking.

And then, at the close of the chapter and the volume, the reflection “that all who lived had already died” in some sense, and that death increases the mystery of every life rather than resolving it. We know more about Cousin Hannah now than we did before. We understand her less.

The skirt, and what it was really asking for

The dying cry for her skirt, which began in Chapter 43 and continues here, is the chapter's governing paradox. Here is a woman who spent decades fighting against the constraints placed on women through dress, who would have been familiar with the bloomer controversy, who rejected the feminine decorations of her era as instruments of control. And at the end she is crying for her skirt.

Young means this to be felt on multiple levels simultaneously. On the simplest: she wants her skirt. She is cold. She is dying. She wants the comfort of familiar fabric. On another: the skirt represents the femininity she suppressed in service of the cause, the woman she might have been if she had not become the captain, the private self beneath the public armor. She is calling for something she gave away.

The suffragettes had navigated this territory literally. Lucy Stone wore bloomers, the reformist divided skirt, for years, and then abandoned them when they became a distraction from the argument. Elizabeth Cady Stanton persuaded her to follow suit. The dress was always political. To wear it was a statement. To discard it was a statement. Cousin Hannah, who had no time for feminine wiles, had been making a statement with her clothing her entire life. The deathbed cry for the skirt is the statement's final reversal: give it back.

False modesty killed my love

This is the confession. Everything else in these three chapters of deathbed has been the approach to it.

False modesty: not genuine humility, not appropriate restraint, but the performance of smallness in the service of fear. The refusal to say what you feel because the saying of it might cost you something, might make you vulnerable, might require you to be seen in a way that the armor of public purpose was designed to prevent. False modesty killed my love: I did not say what I felt. I performed the self that could not be hurt by not saying. And the love died in the silence.

Young gives this line to the woman who had no time for intimate revelations. The woman who refused self-pity and courtly graces and the apparatus of feminine sentimentality. Who had, apparently, felt exactly what that apparatus was designed to express, and been unable to express it, and paid the cost.

The folk song echo in To All My Darlings is precise: “for false was my true love’s heart.” The ballad tradition knew this grief. The person who loved faithfully and was not loved back, or loved and could not say so, or was deceived by love's appearance into trusting something that did not hold. Cousin Hannah's version is her own: the false modesty was not in the love but in herself. She failed her love by being too proud to be seen wanting it.

The confidante who never confided

One of the chapter's most philosophically interesting passages concerns Cousin Hannah's role as a keeper of other people's secrets. She received whispered confessions. She knew the hidden loves and sorrows of others. She was the person people came to when they had something they could not say anywhere else.

And yet she herself, as Mr. Spitzer discovers in the papers, had never fully experienced love or marriage or death in a conventional sense: had known about them with great intimacy from the outside, had held the evidence of other people's experiences of them, without having lived them in the forms available to most people.

Young poses this as a genuine philosophical question rather than a simple irony. Is there a kind of knowing that is deeper than experience? A person who has heard a thousand confessions about love without being consumed by any single one of them: do they know love more fully or less fully than the person who has been devastated by it? Is the confidante's knowledge more accurate, because it is not distorted by the perspective of the person inside the experience? Or does it remain fundamentally hollow, a knowing-about rather than a knowing?

The novel does not decide. But it takes the question seriously. Cousin Hannah's knowledge of human feeling was vast and real. Her experience of it was partial and suppressed. Both of these things are true, and they do not cancel each other.

Heroism and its secret engine

Mr. Spitzer's meditation on what drives great heroes is one of the volume's final philosophical gifts. He wonders whether the greatest battles are undertaken by people fleeing a private failure, whether heroism is, at least sometimes, the external expression of a courage the hero could not find for the inner battle.

This is not debunking. Young is not suggesting that Cousin Hannah's suffrage work was fraudulent because it was also driven by private grief. She is suggesting something more complex: that the inner life and the outer life are not separate domains, that the fire that fuels the public cause is often kindled in the private wound, and that this does not make the cause less real or the sacrifice less genuine. It makes the person more fully human.

The moth desiring a star: Mr. Spitzer offers this image as the definition of a heroism available to the smallest creatures. The moth that flies toward a light it cannot reach and will die trying to reach is not stupid. It is doing the only thing that makes sense given what it is. Cousin Hannah flew toward the star of women's freedom for her entire life. That the flight was also, in some part, a flight from or toward a private grief that could not be named does not make the star less real. The star was real. The flight was real. The moth was real.

Death as eternal transmutation

The chapter offers one of Young's most direct statements about what death is, in the novel's cosmology: “flowers turning into birds, birds turning into flowers,” death as this eternal transmutation. Not an end. Not a destination. A change of form.

Transmutation is the alchemical word: the transformation of one substance into another, the turning of lead into gold, the elevation of base matter into something refined. Young knows the alchemical tradition, and she knows its metaphorical weight: the process is not the destruction of what was there before but its elevation into another form. Cousin Hannah does not end. She transmutes.

Heraclitus and Thales are here too, in the background: everything is in flux, everything is transformation, nothing is static. The river is never the same river twice. The fire burns and does not stay. Cousin Hannah, who was never static, who crossed every border she encountered, who refused every fixed definition of herself; she belongs to this cosmology. She was always already in motion. Death is not the end of that motion. It is another step in it.

The dedication: for all dead loves

This is the chapter where Young's dedication to the novel surfaces: “For all dead loves and all remembered things. I have travelled through many seas.”

Read it again. For all dead loves: not for the living, not for the triumphant, not for the loves that were reciprocated and fulfilled and survived. For the ones that died. For the bridegroom at the door. For false modesty's victim. For the love Catherine constructed out of Peron's silence. For the love Mr. Spitzer could not receive because Catherine could not give it. For every love in this novel that was genuine and went unexpressed and died in the unexpression.

And all remembered things: not all things, not all facts, but the things that have been held in memory, that are still present somewhere, at their temporal coordinates, in the infinite house of what has existed. The remembered things are real. They persist. The remembering is itself a form of love.

“I have travelled through many seas.” Young is speaking directly now, in her own voice, through the dedication. This is not Catherine's journey or Vera's journey or Cousin Hannah's journey. It is Young's. She travelled through many seas to write this book. Seventeen years, a million words, the seas of research and imagination and grief and American mythology and the long question of what is real and what is dream. She arrived here: forty-four chapters into the first volume, at the deathbed of the suffrage captain, with the papers of a double life spread on the table and a lawyer who does not know what he has found.

The end of Volume 1

You have read forty-four chapters. You are halfway through the novel: technically, since Volume 2 covers chapters 45 through 82. But in another sense you are much further than halfway, because the architecture of the first half has been laying foundations: establishing the characters, their relationships, the philosophical questions, the texture of the world Young is creating. Volume 2 will use all of this.

“There was no such thing as safety—not even for her—certainly none for him.” This is one of the chapter's closing lines, and it echoes Helen Keller: security is mostly a superstition. It does not exist in nature. Life is either a daring adventure or nothing.

Cousin Hannah knew this. She lived it. She died in the knowledge of it, screaming in a desert tent with snowdrops melting in her hand, calling for her skirt and her love and the thing that false modesty killed. She is gone now, in the novel's present. She will keep returning in memory, in Catherine's dreams, in the long aftermath of a life that was genuinely large.

The bus is still moving. Vera is still on it. What Cheer, Iowa is still ahead. Miss MacIntosh is still the absent center of the wheel, and all the spokes still radiate outward from her. You have Volume 2 ahead of you, and it is magnificent.

guide-66-the-last-month:
Chapter 66: The Last Month

← Chapter 65 · Guide Home · Chapter 67 →

Research notes: Chapter 66

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Mr. Titus Bonebreaker · Old Friday · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Faith, God, and the Supernatural

Symbols: Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · Clouds and Storms

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Exploration and the Poles · Gambling and Playing Cards · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · Shakespeare · Suicide in History and Literature

We are in the final weeks. Miss MacIntosh is still alive, still talking, but everything she says now carries the weight of what Vera knows, looking back: that this is the last month they will have together, that the stories are being told because there won't be another chance to tell them. The chapter opens with Miss MacIntosh dressed for a long voyage she insists they are not going on, and it ends with her clothes strewn on the beach and her red wig torn in the sand.

Chapter 66 is the month, and the disappearance, and everything between.

What actually happens

Miss MacIntosh teaches Vera during a storm (geography, history, the heart, biology, socialism, finance) questions she fires out whether or not Vera can answer them, which Vera usually cannot. She tells Vera about her imaginary dealings on the Stock Exchange, which she calls "a palace of evil" she visits to level the rich. She tells her about the Arctic Explorer she met there. She tells her about her removed ovaries, her physical amputations, her rival love. She prepares Vera, in her eccentric and relentless way, for a world she is about to enter alone.

And then, one cold September morning, she walks into the ocean.

Miss MacIntosh in a storm

The image Young gives us at the chapter's opening is one of her great portraits: Miss MacIntosh in her whaler's hat and sea boots, black umbrella billowing, teaching Vera lessons by hurricane lamp while a storm batters the windows. She is dressed for a voyage she claims is not happening. She is prepared for an ocean she says she is not entering.

She asks questions she doesn't wait for answers to. She lectures on socialism while walking in the surf with her skirts pinned up. She decries the unequal distribution of wealth, the rich throwing dollar bills out of windows while the poor don't catch them, and she goes to the Stock Exchange to make imaginary money, she says, to level them all so they should be poor together. She invests in anthracite and tin but refuses to invest in zippers because in What Cheer, Iowa, zippers are against the will of God.

She is, as she has always been, magnificent and impossible and entirely herself.

The Arctic Explorer

At the Stock Exchange, that palace of evil she visits with her imaginary portfolio, Miss MacIntosh meets a wooden-legged explorer from Denmark, born near Elsinore Castle (yes, Hamlet's castle, and yes, Young knows exactly what she is doing with that detail). He has swept his broom, as he says, through all the great squares of the world: Trafalgar, the Kremlin, St. Mark's. He has seen things in the Arctic that have stripped him of whatever ordinary life he might have had.

He asks Miss MacIntosh, repeatedly, to come with him to the North Pole. He wants to leave everything behind (the Stock Exchange, the cities, all of it) and go north into the silence and the ice, where, he says, there is nothing unknown because nothing is known, and therefore nothing to fear.

She is drawn to him. They have “something in common—their differences from others,” their amputations (his leg, her breast and baldness) and their shared “sense of having killed something young and helpless” in themselves somewhere along the way. He reminds her of her father, who also lost a leg. Young does not make this explicit as psychology; she offers it plainly, as one of the facts of Miss MacIntosh's interior life.

But she doesn't go north with him. She has Vera to attend to. She has her imaginary stocks. She has her socialism and her umbrella and her What Cheer prejudices against zippers. She stays.

"That old religion"

Miss MacIntosh reflects on Mr. Bonebreaker in this chapter with the clarity of retrospect: he belonged to "that old religion where women must kneel before men." She couldn't kneel. She was bald and had no breast and had nothing of what that religion required of women: no seductive hair to wash a man's feet with, no performed femininity, no willingness to submit. She rejected this not defiantly but practically: it simply was not available to her, and she was not sorry.

Young makes here one of the novel's most direct feminist arguments, and she makes it through Miss MacIntosh's characteristic combination of practicality and dark humor. The "old religion" is patriarchy (the system that entitles men to women's submission, bodies, and labor) and Miss MacIntosh has spent her whole life outside it, not by choice exactly, but by condition. Her baldness, her missing breast, her removed ovaries made her unintelligible to the system. And so she went her own way.

Her hopes for the world

Among the things Miss MacIntosh tells Vera she hopes for before she dies: an end to the British Empire, an end to colonialism, the King of England losing his crown, the Tong wars ending, China the Sleeping Dragon awakening, the world reformed so that by the time Vera grows up there will be no rich people. She teaches Vera "the beauty of deprivation." She hopes for simple humanity.

These are not small hopes. They are the hopes of a woman who has lived entirely outside privilege and power, who has seen what wealth does and what empire does and what patriarchy does, and who has concluded that the structure needs to come down. She has no illusions that it will. But she teaches Vera to see it clearly, because seeing clearly is what she has always done.

The amputations she carries

In this chapter we learn the full accounting of what Miss MacIntosh's body has lost: her hair, her breast, her ovaries. She carries these losses the way she carries everything, without sentimentality, with full acknowledgment. She mentions "a rival love": suggesting her romantic life was more complicated than even Chapter 65's story of Mr. Bonebreaker conveyed. She does not elaborate. She moves on.

What she says instead is this: her death, when it comes, will be a natural death. Not a suicide; she is not like the gamblers on the Stock Exchange, she says, frenzied by losses, jumping from high windows after the crash of 1929. She will just go. Quietly, without forwarding address, into the sea.

The clothes on the beach

Young gives us the disappearance with devastating simplicity. The clothes strewn on the beach. The red wig torn in the sand. The waves returning with everything but her. Old Friday, the dog, barking by the sea: still barking, afterward, as if she might be “a moving shadow, a shadow of a black umbrella moving over water and sand—as if perhaps she had never gone or had returned.”

Vera asks: had the dog “not known the denudation and the dream, the reality and the illusion, how each must live by some pretense?” Old Friday barks at the waves. The waves come back swollen with wind, “like sheep with a thousand bells.” She is not in them.

She walked in. She did not come back. That is all.

What Vera understood, long years after

This chapter is told in retrospect: Vera looking back from long years after the disappearance, seeing the lessons in a new light. As a child, she took Miss MacIntosh's eccentricities for granted. The whaler's hat during arithmetic. The umbrella in the surf. The imaginary stocks. She absorbed all of it without fully understanding it, as children do: taking on every color except her own, she says, because she had no color yet to claim.

Now she understands. The lessons were not orthodox. The questions were not about answers. The month of stories was a bequest: Miss MacIntosh giving away everything she knew before she went into the water. She was making her will, the way Mr. Spitzer made his will with his music: leaving what she had to someone who might receive it, even if reception was uncertain.

What to hold onto

Old Friday, at the edge of the sea, barking. The red wig in the sand. The waves coming back without her. A dog who perceives something the living cannot quite see (a moving shadow, a black umbrella's shadow over water) and who refuses to stop barking at it.

She kept the rain out for as long as she could. Then she walked into the rain.

guide-51-the-trumpeter-or-the-trumpeters:
Chapter 51: The Trumpeter or the Trumpeter's Cry

← Chapter 50 · Guide Home · Chapter 52 →

Research notes: Chapter 51

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Mr. Mouse

Themes: Dreams and Imagination

Philosophy: Freud and Jung · Hinduism · Marguerite Young on Her Craft · Plato and Platonism · Time, Physics, and Chaos Theory

Allusions: Astronomy · Deafness and Sign Language · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · Music and Composers · Women's Suffrage

There is a mouse in Mr. Spitzer's papers.

His name is Mr. Mouse, and he has been busy. He has jumbled symphonies. He has eaten all Mr. Spitzer's chords. He has torn the music to ribbons and made a bed from scraps of old lawsuits and is currently wearing the paper lining of Mr. Spitzer's hat. He has also, in a moment of accidental grandeur, taken the Great Dipper of stars and shaken it like a rattle, pouring out new and unintended constellations across the sky.

Mr. Mouse is chaos. Mr. Mouse is the principle of disorder that is also, because Young always insists on this, the principle of creation. You cannot have new constellations without the shaking of the old ones. You cannot have the ribbons without the torn music. The order that Mr. Spitzer has spent his life defending (law, music, the careful preservation of documents) is being gnawed through from the inside, and the thing doing the gnawing is making something beautiful by accident.

Chapter 51 is the longest and most sweeping of Mr. Spitzer's interior chapters, and it gives him, at last, his fullest expression of what he is and is not. He does not know whether he is “the trumpeter or the trumpeter’s cry, the cry or the echo.” He is the lawyer to starfish. He is twelve cloaks. He is “the sail stalled in the mist, or the sail broke into flame.” He is a legal fiction. He is, at the very bottom of it all, the dream that is dreaming itself, even when there is no counterpart, even when there is nothing to dream about.

What actually happens in Chapter 51

Mr. Spitzer continues his long meditation in the borderland, but Chapter 51 extends that meditation into a catalogue, almost a complete inventory of every role, every form, every self he might be or have been or is not. He is the conductor lifting the baton, or perhaps only the lamplighter, or perhaps only the oarsman striking waves of darkness. He is the musician of silence: music “ever of the silence flowing under the sound of accidental or incidental music.” He is “the spectre dreaming upon the spectre.”

He is the lawyer to the dead: a lawyer to starfish, a lawyer to a dead coachman, a musician who “struck two chords together with one motion of his dead, jeweled hand.” He has stamped documents with the wrong seal by mistake: the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad instead of the President's seal, the “seal of the New England Lighthouse Underwriters” instead of the Grand Union Army. The errors compound. The paperwork of the dead is full of mistakes. Mr. Spitzer, the executor of estates and keeper of wills, has been certifying things incorrectly for longer than anyone has noticed.

The chapter catalogues the people Mr. Spitzer encounters in his wandering: seldom does he meet with anyone who does “not suffer from some form of complex illusion beyond necessity.” The old woman who believes she is a birdcage. The piano tuner who declares all foreheads hollow. The blind portrait painter. The deaf music critic who hears errors without hearing music. The old woman found with a golden arrow through her breast, who believed she was a reindeer. The chapter people these margins of normal consciousness with figures who are, in their particular delusions, only slightly more transparent than everyone else.

It closes on the one great dream: perhaps there was “only one great dream informing all dreamers and all dreams, one great dreamer dreaming through” us all. And the recognition that there is “no threshold between world and world.”

Mr. Mouse and the new constellations

Young's Mr. Mouse is not a metaphor for anything simple. He is not merely entropy, not merely the passage of time, not merely the chaos that undoes careful human work. He is the impresario, the one who produces the show, even while he destroys the score.

Young understood something about the relationship between destruction and creation that runs through her novel's entire structure. The novel itself is a kind of Mr. Mouse operation: it takes the careful categories of realism (chronological narrative, reliable narrators, settled boundaries between what is real and what is dreamed) and gnaws through them, and in doing so creates something that those categories never could have contained. The new constellations Mr. Mouse makes by shaking the Great Dipper are not planned. They are not what anyone would have designed. They are what happens when the old arrangements are released.

Mr. Spitzer opposes Mr. Mouse's will with his will. This is the contest that has defined his life: the lawyer against the mouse, order against chaos, the carefully filed document against the creature who eats documents and builds nests from them. He cannot win. Mr. Mouse will always eat faster than Mr. Spitzer can file. But the opposition itself is the music, Young suggests. The contest between them produces, in its friction, something that neither pure order nor pure chaos could generate alone.

The trumpeter or the trumpeter's cry

“He did not know whether he was the trumpeter or the trumpeter’s cry, the cry or the echo.”

This is the chapter's central question, and it is not rhetorical. Young means it as a genuine puzzle about the nature of identity: are you the source of what you produce, or are you what is produced? Is the musician the player or the music? Is the self the generator of experience or the experience itself?

For Mr. Spitzer, who has spent his existence at a second remove from everything (hearing sounds a minute late, living by other people's dreams, possibly inhabiting his dead brother's identity) the question of whether he is the trumpeter or the cry is especially acute. He has never been certain he was the original. He has always suspected he was a consequence of something that came before him, a sound that arose from a source he cannot locate. If he is the cry, then he disperses when the air stops vibrating. If he is the echo, then he exists only in relation to something that has already happened, and he will fade as the surfaces that reflect him fade.

The trumpeter would be the self that produces. The cry would be the self that is produced. Mr. Spitzer cannot determine which he is. Neither can Young. This is honest.

The lawyer to starfish

He is a lawyer to starfish. A lawyer to a dead coachman.

These are not jokes exactly, though they have the structure of jokes: the absurdist juxtaposition of a legal profession with creatures and figures that cannot benefit from legal representation. But Young means them seriously as a description of what Mr. Spitzer actually does. He is the executor of estates whose owners cannot dispute the terms. He is the keeper of wills whose testators are unavailable for consultation. He handles the legal affairs of the departed, which means he handles the formal arrangements of a world that no longer has a living stakeholder.

The starfish cannot engage with Mr. Spitzer's services. The dead coachman has no interest in the outcome of his estate. But Mr. Spitzer continues to process the paperwork, file the documents, press the wrong seals by mistake. The law continues regardless of whether the parties it serves are present or capable of benefiting. This is what law does. It persists past the point of usefulness as an act of form: a form that Mr. Spitzer maintains because the form is what he has, and without it there is only “the void where he would not be at least this shadow.”

Life as a legal fiction

“Was life a legal fiction, a realm which could never be proved, disproved, an imaginary house with its intricate ivory porches no waves should ever reach, its lights already lost?”

A legal fiction is a fact that is assumed to be true for the purposes of the law, regardless of whether it is actually true. Courts use legal fictions all the time: the fiction that corporations are persons, the fiction that certain presumptions hold unless disproved, the fiction that jurisdiction is established when it technically is not. Legal fictions are useful lies; they allow the law to function in situations where strict adherence to factual reality would prevent any decision from being made.

Young asks: what if life itself is this kind of fiction? What if the assumption that we are alive, that experience is real, that identity is stable: what if all of this is the legal fiction that allows the proceeding to continue? Mr. Spitzer, the executor of impossible estates, the lawyer to starfish, is perfectly positioned to recognize this. He has been processing legal fictions his entire career. He knows how they work. He knows how to proceed as though they are true even when they are clearly not. His life is an instance of proceeding as though the fiction holds.

The old woman who believed she was a reindeer

Young peoples Chapter 51's margins with figures of elaborate and particular delusion: the old woman who believed she was a birdcage, the piano tuner who declared all foreheads hollow, “the blind portrait painter, the deaf” music critic. And then the one that Young lingers on longest: the old woman found dead with a golden arrow through her breast, who had believed she was a reindeer.

She is not played for comedy. She is played for the full weight of what Young means by illusion: the old woman lived in a world where she was a reindeer. That world was as vivid and as internally coherent as any other world. The golden arrow was real: real enough to kill her. The delusion was complex and sustained and particular enough to generate a death that made sense only within its own terms.

Young is not saying all perceptions are equally valid. She is saying that the boundary between the old woman's world and the ordinary world is not as firm as it might appear. Mr. Spitzer, who struggles to distinguish which chair is real and which is its dream, who is “agonized by attributing consciousness to everything,” who cannot tell whether he is alive or dead; he is several degrees away from the old woman who was a reindeer, not infinitely far from her. The novel has been insisting, since Chapter 1, that the borders between these states are thinner than convention requires.

One great dream informing all dreamers

Perhaps there was “only one great dream informing all dreamers and all dreams, one great dreamer dreaming through” us all.

This is the chapter's philosophical summit, and it has a long history. The Upanishads describe Brahman as the universal consciousness in which all individual minds participate. Jung's collective unconscious is the reservoir of shared archetypes and images that every individual psyche draws from. Plato's theory of Forms proposes a realm of perfect Ideas from which all individual instances are imperfect copies. Young arrives at this convergence point not through any of these traditions specifically but through the logic of Mr. Spitzer's particular condition: a man who may be dreaming someone else's dream, who may be an image within an image, who has experienced enough of the world's multiplicity to wonder whether what looks like infinite individual consciousness is actually one thing manifesting in many temporary forms.

Young does not endorse this as doctrine. She gives it to Mr. Spitzer as a possibility that arrives in the borderland between life and death, where the usual distinctions have worn thin enough to let the light through. If he is only dreaming, he notes, then he is accompanied by a great deal of company. All the other dreamers. The one great dream.

No threshold between world and world

“There was no threshold between world and world.”

Young has been approaching this formulation since the novel's first chapter: the grey bus moving through the grey Midwest, the fog that dissolves borders, the household where Catherine has made the distinction between waking and dreaming so permeable that it no longer functions as a distinction. But Mr. Spitzer's version is harder and more absolute than Catherine's: not that the threshold is blurred or difficult to find, but that it does not exist.

We live “by an imperfect concatenation, even as we died—by echoes, tremblings, reverberations, sourceless thoughts.” The threshold we imagine between the living and the dead, between this world and whatever comes after, between the self and the dream of the self; these are the legal fictions that allow the proceeding to continue. They are useful. They may even be necessary. But they are not features of the territory. They are features of our maps.

For Mr. Spitzer, who has no reliable map, who has been stamping documents with the wrong seals for decades, this is not a consolation. It is simply what he has found. “There was no threshold between world and world.” He moves through the rooms of the dead and finds them continuous with the rooms of the living. The mouse eats the music and makes new stars. The legal fictions continue to be processed. And somewhere in all of this, barely visible, the dream keeps dreaming itself.

What to hold onto

Chapter 51 is the novel's most comprehensive portrait of Mr. Spitzer, not as a character in a story but as a form of consciousness, one of the novel's possible answers to the question of what a person is when the usual scaffolding of identity, continuity, and the reliable boundary between states has been removed.

What to carry forward: Mr. Mouse and the new constellations, chaos as the engine of unexpected creation. The trumpeter-or-cry question, which is not resolved and should not be. The lawyer to starfish, keeping the forms of law alive past the point where any living stakeholder can benefit. The old woman who was a reindeer. And the one great dream, dreaming through all the smaller dreams simultaneously, with no threshold between them.

The dream continues. The mouse continues. The music continues in its silence. Mr. Spitzer continues, a supernumerary star, beyond the normal count, giving off a light that may or may not be his own.

guide-19-the-morning-after:
Chapter 19: The Morning After

← Chapter 18 · Guide Home · Chapter 20 →

Research notes: Chapter 19

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: The Search for Meaning

Symbols: Eyes and Blindness · The House

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Angels and Archangels · Gambling and Playing Cards · The Bible

After the long, overwhelming night of Chapter 18, Chapter 19 is very short. It is one of the most carefully constructed chapters in the novel precisely because of that brevity. Young has spent two chapters giving you the shock and the darkness and the voice. Now she gives you daylight.

Read it slowly. Every object in this room has been chosen. Nothing here is accidental.

What actually happens in Chapter 19

Vera wakes in Miss MacIntosh’s bed at dawn, uncertain whether the night was real or a dream. The light comes in. She keeps her eyes closed at first, already beginning to reconsider, in the safety of not-quite-looking, certain small things about Miss MacIntosh she had never examined before. The baseball cap. The ribbons worn in the evening. The acres of veiling over the whaler’s hat. The umbrella carried indoors in fair weather. Why had none of it seemed important before?

She opens her eyes.

Miss MacIntosh’s bald head is on the pillow next to hers, cold as marble. The red wig is on the hat rack within easy reach. The room’s contents are laid out in full inventory: the corset, the false teeth in the jeweled glass, the grey fedora on the floor, the ivory-boned knitting needles, the Moody’s hotel Bible chained to the table, the deuce of clubs face up on the marble slab, the playing cards with Dutch windmills on their backs. The chapter ends on a single sentence, delivered with the same plainness Miss MacIntosh herself would have used: “I observed what I must surely have always known, the fact that one breast had been amputated. What was left was no bigger than a baby’s.”

The inventory of the room

Young spends most of this short chapter on a meticulous inventory of Miss MacIntosh’s possessions, and it rewards the same attention Miss MacIntosh brought to geography lessons and bowling scores. Every object is a small biography.

The wig on the hat rack “within easy reach of her gnarled hand.” “Death should never catch her napping,” she had always said, and the wig is positioned exactly for that: grab it in a moment, be ready. The salmon-colored corset draped over the rocking chair, its metallic supporters still staring like lost eyes. The grey fedora kicked to the floor. The convict’s striped undershirt. The shirtwaist still bristling with its rusted needles and pins.

The false teeth in a jeweled water glass. The contrast is exquisite and purely Young: the teeth themselves functional, replaceable, slightly absurd; the glass ornamented and fine, perhaps the last luxury object in an otherwise stripped-down room. She saved what she saved.

The Moody’s hotel Bible chained to the table. She had always said “she was a Christian woman with an honest mind.” She chained the Bible down.

The broken ship’s compass she intended to repair. She had always “known the directions of the winds.” She had always meant to fix the instrument that finds them.

The deuce of clubs face up on the marble slab. In Chapter 14, Catherine told us the deuce of clubs portends death and is the trifoliate club that may be transformed into the cross, the cross into the rose, the rose into the snail. Here it is, the card that was always present, now visible in morning light.

The questions Vera asks before opening her eyes

The early paragraphs of the chapter give us something quietly remarkable: Vera lying with her eyes closed, already beginning to reread the past in light of what she now knows.

Why no eyebrows, and the evasive answer when asked? Why the face so sensitive to light, blushing for no reason, the colors of her skin changing so fast? Why always the baseball cap in the morning, the ribbon around her hair in the evenings, acres of veiling over the whaler’s hat in the wind? Why the umbrella carried like a shield even indoors where there was no rain?

All of it was always visible. None of it was ever assembled into a picture. Vera, like the rider over Lake Constance, was crossing ice she never knew was there, carried safely by not knowing. Now she is on the other shore. The same details that meant nothing before (the cap, the veiling, the umbrella, the blush) resolve into a portrait she can finally see.

Young is showing you something important about how knowledge works: it doesn’t create the evidence, it illuminates what was always present. The clues were never hidden. They were simply not yet read.

The last sentence

Young ends the chapter with one of the most controlled sentences in the novel: “I observed what I must surely have always known, the fact that one breast had been amputated. What was left was no bigger than a baby’s.”

Two things to hold here. First, the phrase “I must surely have always known.” Vera is extending the logic of the night (the older shock beneath the newer one, the recognition that feels like memory rather than discovery) to the body itself. She must have known. At some level, in some chamber of the mind she never entered, she knew.

Second, the measurement: no bigger than a baby’s. Young does not write this for pathos. She writes it with Miss MacIntosh’s own precision: plain, factual, “the shortest distance between two points.” It is the most tender sentence in the chapter and the most devastating, and it achieves both effects through exactness rather than elaboration. Miss MacIntosh would have approved of the sentence. She would have recognized herself in it.

What to watch for as you keep reading

Light spoilers: This section hints at what happens later in the novel. Skip it if you want to meet the story fresh.

Miss MacIntosh will reassemble herself. The wig will go back on, the corset will be laced, the umbrella will go up. The question the novel now carries is whether Vera can unknow what she knows, whether the plain, practical nursemaid of the daylight hours can coexist with the bald head on the pillow. Young’s answer, delivered slowly across many chapters, is that they must coexist. There is no version of Miss MacIntosh that erases the other.

The room’s objects will scatter. The broken compass will not be repaired. The Bible will remain chained. These are the possessions of someone who is almost done with this life, and Young has laid them out for you here like evidence at an inquest, or like the belongings of someone you will soon be asked to grieve.

Notice the bust of Martin Luther. It is the only decoration Miss MacIntosh permitted in her room, the one ornament she would not put outdoors. Luther, the reformer who nailed his theses to a church door and refused to recant. The only image she kept was a man who said: here I stand, I can do no other.
