Chapter 29: Butterflies of Resurrection

← Chapter 28 · Guide Home · Chapter 30 →

Research notes: Chapter 29

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Peron Spitzer

Themes: The Search for Meaning

Symbols: Butterflies and Moths · Weddings and Funerals

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Exploration and the Poles · Gambling and Playing Cards · Homer's Epics

Chapter 29 is the longest in the Spitzer sequence and one of the most ambitious chapters in the novel. Young gives Mr. Spitzer the floor entirely, and what he does with it is extraordinary: he speaks about butterflies for the length of a short novella, and in doing so, speaks about everything, death, resurrection, the soul, God, his brother, his grief, the question of whether any life is truly one’s own.

This is the chapter where Young earns Mr. Spitzer’s full stature as a character. He arrives here as the novel’s most profound thinker, its secret philosopher, its dark atheist who knows more about the life beyond the grave than anyone, because he has been living in the aftermath of death for so long that the two worlds have merged.

The chapter is long and the prose is dense. Let it wash over you. You will not catch every butterfly name or classical allusion on a first reading. You are not supposed to. Let the accumulation do its work.

What actually happens in Chapter 29

Mr. Spitzer speaks about butterflies. He speaks about the difficulty of distinguishing butterfly from moth, and how this mirrors the difficulty of distinguishing happiness from sorrow, brother from brother. He speaks about the butterfly as psyche, the Greek word for soul, and about butterflies observed far out at sea, wandering far off their course, perhaps blown by hurricanes between stars.

He describes everything he knows: the mourning cloak “hibernating in a hollow tree trunk” through a frozen winter, the chrysalis like a mummy in its shroud, the birth of the butterfly from the caterpillar’s silken cocoon. He catalogs hundreds of species by name: pearl crescents, painted ladies, red admirals, purple emperors, old monarchs, Arctic satyrs, Homeric butterflies, “butterflies with Latin messages written on their wings.”

He describes Peron’s funeral: “the merriest mourners who ever were,” “merry andrews and fat aldermen and” ruined gamblers and dice shooters, a crowd his brother had loved and Joachim had never understood. He describes his own grief afterward, betrayed only to an old lamp-lighter on a windy street corner “whose face was also streaked with tears,” who said of Peron: “he will never light another lamp.”

He meditates on the sock question: a sock so many times darned and patched, are these new socks or old? When the last original thread has gone, what remains? He concludes the chapter asking whether his butterflies, still glowing in his cavernous mind after all these years, are more beautiful than anything Catherine dreams.

The butterfly as the argument

Chapter 29 is structured as a philosophical argument delivered through natural history, and the argument is this: the butterfly is the proof, or at least the best available evidence, that transformation is real.

Mr. Spitzer watched the caterpillar wrap itself in silk and sleep and emerge. He has “seen the preparations of the caterpillar for a future life,” he says, and watched it achieve “immortality within the logic of mortality.” The chrysalis is like a mummy. The butterfly that emerges is the same being and a completely different one. You cannot tell, at the crucial moment of emergence, whether you are witnessing a birth or a death. Both are true simultaneously.

This is why he began collecting butterflies in the first place. Not as a hobby. As an investigation into the single question his life has been organized around: is transformation possible? Is it possible to come out the other side of a catastrophic change (his brother’s death, his own stopped life) as something new and whole, rather than simply as what remained after everything was taken?

He has no answer. But he has the butterflies, which at least demonstrate that the thing happens (somewhere, in some other kingdom) even if he has never managed it himself.

The oceanic butterflies

One of the chapter’s most beautiful passages is about butterflies observed far out at sea, miles from any shore, travelling through day and night, buffeted by winds. Some believe they were blown off course by hurricanes. Others believe they sail by “their own dreams, being these wandering psyches,” “seeking reunion with immortal love.

Mr.” Spitzer holds both explanations without resolving them. Were they blown, or did they choose to go? Is there a difference? He has seen the caterpillar sea, “wings of butterflies like sails of ships gleaming through distant clouds.” He believes these oceanic migrations may be intentional, not merely an accident or monsoon.

This is Mr. Spitzer’s life in miniature: a being far off its course, in conditions that should not support its survival, moving through the dark either because of forces beyond its control or because it is a wandering soul seeking reunion with something it has lost. He cannot say which. Neither can we.

Peron’s funeral

Young gives us the full account of Peron’s funeral here, and it is one of the most affecting passages in the novel. The crowd was “the merriest mourners who ever were”: merry andrews “and broken-down vaudeville stars, waterfront characters and cue-ball champions,” dice shooters and ruined gamblers, old fly-by-nights, mad mountebanks. A crowd that spoke in languages Joachim did not understand: “roulette wheel talk, bird cage talk,” “spirit jockeys and glass bead madames.” He has been slowly learning the translation ever since.

Everyone thought his self-containment was supernatural, his serenity almost marvelous. It was grief. Utterly devastating grief. Almost no one sensed it. Only the old lamp-lighter on the windy street corner afterward, “whose face was also streaked with tears,” who said what needed to be said: “he will never light another lamp.”

Young gives us this moment (the great lawyer and musician, his face streaked with tears in the wind, standing on a street corner with a lamp-lighter) and then moves on. She does not dwell. She trusts it to carry its own weight. And it does.

The sock question

Near the chapter’s end, Mr. Spitzer poses what he calls the philosopher’s question: his socks have been so many times darned and patched that he wonders whether the last original thread has now disappeared, making them technically new socks, albeit very fragile ones easily unravelling.

This is the Ship of Theseus, Young’s version: the famous philosophical puzzle about whether an object that has had all its parts replaced is still the same object. Mr. Spitzer applies it to himself. He has been so patched and darned over the years since his brother’s death (by grief, by impersonation, by wearing Peron’s watch, by attending Peron’s funeral as both chief mourner and the body in the coffin) that he genuinely cannot say whether what remains is Joachim or something else, made of so many replacements that the original is gone. The ghostly conformation of the old sock persists. The leg inside is still his leg. But what are these socks?

Young places this right before the final butterfly catalog because that is exactly where it belongs: the sock question is the human version of the butterfly question. The caterpillar becomes the butterfly. The old sock becomes the new sock. At what point in the transformation are you still you?

What to watch for as you keep reading

Light spoilers: This section hints at what happens later in the novel. Skip it if you want to meet the story fresh.

After Chapter 29, the novel leaves the breakfast table entirely. You have now received the full portrait of Mr. Spitzer: five chapters, from his professional life through his grief through his butterflies. He will continue to appear throughout the novel, always arriving just after the extraordinary thing has happened, always missing the party, always treading softly on the thinnest ice. You now know why.

The butterflies will keep returning. Young uses them the way she uses all her recurring images: lightly, from different angles, always adding a new facet. When you see a butterfly in the chapters ahead, carry what you know from Chapter 29: it is the soul in transit, the being mid-transformation, the creature that cannot be told from the flower it rests on until one of them moves.

The lamp-lighter who said “he will never light another lamp” is one of the novel’s most quietly charged minor figures. He mourns Peron with tears on his face. He knows what Peron was to the city’s darker corners in a way Joachim never did. He offers Joachim the only eulogy that matters, and then he goes on lighting his lamps down the dark street. Young gives us one sentence of his and moves on. That is often her method: the peripheral figure who carries more weight than the central ones.

guide-48-a-long-rehearsal-for-the-silenc:
Chapter 48: A Long Rehearsal for the Silence

← Chapter 47 · Guide Home · Chapter 49 →

Research notes: Chapter 48

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Light and Darkness

Symbols: Keys, Doors, and Locks · Lamps, Candles, and Light · Moon and Stars · The House

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology · Marguerite Young on Her Craft · Phenomenology · William James and Pragmatism · Wittgenstein

Allusions: Astronomy · Exploration and the Poles · Judaism · The Bible · Women's Suffrage

Mr. Spitzer is becoming something in Chapter 48 that he was not quite yet in the chapters before it: a figure of the threshold. Not the man who watches death from the outside (the cautious lawyer, the silk-hatted mourner, the second-remove observer) but a man who has moved so close to the border between living and dead that the border is no longer clearly visible from where he stands.

“This life was a long rehearsal of music for the silence.”

This is the chapter's governing metaphor, and it is one of the novel's most beautiful and most exact formulations. Life is not the performance. Life is the rehearsal: the practice run, the preparation, the running-through of material that will ultimately give way to the silence it was always approaching. The silence is not nothing. It is the thing the music was working toward. It is where everything unplayed finally arrives.

What actually happens in Chapter 48

Mr. Spitzer moves through an old house full of mysterious sounds, barred doors, keys that do not fit any lock, trunks and boxes whose contents he cannot fully read. He is the executor still, but the executor's work has become something stranger: he is navigating a space that feels less like a house than like a territory between states, a place where the entrance is known and the exit cannot be found.

He reflects on his brother, on the contrast between them. Peron burned brightly. Peron lit matches. Peron tempted fate and lost it and perhaps won something larger in losing it, something beyond earthly comprehension. Joachim was afraid of burning, “afraid of sudden incandescence, afraid of” the match that might light something that could not be extinguished. And now he moves through the house of the dead woman, holding the keys that open nothing, while the stars fade in the windows above him.

He imagines himself as a lamplighter: the person who goes through the city each evening lighting the gas lamps, and each morning extinguishing them. But his lamplighting is cosmic: he lights and extinguishes stars. He is angry at the idea that someone else might take his place in this duty. This is one of the chapter's strangest and most revealing moments: the revelation that Mr. Spitzer has claimed a cosmic role for himself, the role of the one who manages the lights of existence, and that the possibility of being replaced in this imagined responsibility disturbs him more than almost anything else.

The lamplighter of stars

Young's image of Mr. Spitzer as a lamplighter of stars draws on a tradition that runs from the literal lamplighters of nineteenth-century cities (the men who went through the streets at dusk with long poles, touching flame to gas mantle, and returned at dawn to extinguish them) to Saint-Exupéry's lamplighter in The Little Prince, the most faithful of all the prince's planetary inhabitants, performing his duty without question even as the planet spins faster and faster and the duty becomes increasingly absurd.

Young's version is more melancholic. Mr. Spitzer is not absurdly faithful. He is possessive. He has assigned himself the management of lights that are not his to manage (the fading stars of other people's lives, including Cousin Hannah's) and he resents the implication that this work might be taken from him or done by someone else. This is the conservative's deepest fear rendered cosmically: the world changing in ways that make his particular skill set, his particular role, his particular form of faithfulness, obsolete.

And yet. The lamplighter is also the person who makes it possible to see in the dark. He carries the light. He knows which lamps are failing and which still burn. In the long night of the novel's mourning, Mr. Spitzer is the person keeping track of what is still lit and what has gone out. That is not nothing. It is, Young suggests, the only form of love available to a man like him.

Consciousness as sporadic

“Consciousness was ever that which was sporadic, fluttering, not constant even in this life, just as sustained attention was impossible.”

This is Young's most direct statement about the nature of awareness, and it applies to Mr. Spitzer's experience with particular precision. He does not exist in a state of continuous consciousness. He is intermittent. He flickers. There are moments of acute perception (the deathbed, the papers, the alpenhorn, the skirt laid over the body) and then long stretches of the second remove, the minute-late reception of experience, the off-key singer that is his entire relationship to the present moment. The philosophical resonance here is with William James's stream of consciousness, except that James's stream is continuous even if turbulent, while Young's consciousness is more like the behavior of fireflies, or like St. Elmo's fire, appearing at the tips of pointed things and then going dark. You cannot sustain it. You cannot force it to stay lit. You can only be present when it flickers on and try to remember what you saw.

This is the experiential condition the novel has been describing in everyone (in Catherine, in Vera, in Cousin Hannah at the end) but in Mr. Spitzer it is most fully articulated. His consciousness is sporadic. His attention is intermittent. This is not a deficiency. It is the condition of being human, rendered visible in a man who has no talent for hiding it.

The stowaway

Mr. Spitzer doubts his own identity and profession in Chapter 48 with a new specificity: he feels like a stowaway. A hidden passenger. Someone who boarded under false pretenses and has been concealed in the hold, living off the ship's provisions, unseen by the proper passengers, sinking without awareness when the ship went down.

The stowaway is the perfect figure for someone who may be living another person's life, who slipped into an identity that was not assigned to him and has been riding it through decades, hoping no one checks. If Mr. Spitzer is Peron and not Joachim, then he is precisely a stowaway in Joachim's existence: the material twin in the immaterial twin's coat, the one who burned brightly borrowing the identity of the one who was afraid of matches.

And the stowaway sinks without awareness. He does not know the ship went down. He is still in the hold, still hidden, still alive in the only sense available to a person who has never fully declared themselves. Young does not deliver a verdict on this. She gives it to you as a possibility and lets it settle.

The evening star and the morning star

“Much as the evening star and the morning star.”

Venus appears twice in the sky: in the evening, low on the western horizon after sunset, and in the morning, low in the east before dawn. For centuries, observers took these to be two different stars (Vesper in the evening, Lucifer in the morning) before understanding they were the same planet seen from two positions in Earth's orbit. “The evening star and the morning star” are one.

Young uses this image for the twins, and for everything in the chapter that appears as two things and may be one: life and death, Peron and Joachim, the self that burned and the self that was afraid to burn. Two appearances, one planet. The dual name carries the full weight of the chapter's meditation on identity: the thing that sets and the thing that rises, the darkness and the dawn, may be the same thing moving through the sky. You called them different names. They were never different.

Lucifer, light-bringer, was in Roman mythology the personification of the morning star, the herald of dawn, before Christian theology absorbed him as the fallen angel. Young knows this etymology and deploys it precisely: the light-bringer is also the one who falls. The morning star rises and is also always falling toward the horizon. Every light in the chapter is provisional.

The house of barred doors

The old house Mr. Spitzer moves through in Chapter 48 (high-shouldered, full of windows and barred doors, every room opening onto another locked room, entrance known and exit impossible to find) is the chapter's governing architectural metaphor for the space between states.

He knows the entrance. He does not know the exit. This is the condition of someone who has, through the long years of his vigil, moved so close to the threshold that he is no longer clearly on either side of it. He can enter the house of the dead (the papers, the alpenhorn, the skirt, the keys) but he cannot exit through the other side to where the dead have gone. And he cannot fully return to the living world either, because the living world now contains Cousin Hannah's death and his brother's death and forty years of the second remove, and there is no version of it he can inhabit without the full weight of those absences.

“Man could not see his own end, for he passed beyond his end.” This is one of the chapter's central philosophical formulations, and it is vertiginous: you cannot witness your own death because by the time it happens, you have already gone past the point from which you could observe it. The self that would observe is the self that has ended. The observation is impossible because the observer has passed beyond. Mr. Spitzer, moving through the barred house, knows the entrance and cannot find the exit, and perhaps this is why: the exit is on the other side of the point where observation becomes impossible.

Boxes within boxes

“He who knew rhombs, circles, semicircles, boxes, boxes within boxes, parallelograms, octagons, octahedrons, ellipses, eclipses of light by darkness, darkness by light, darkness by darkness.”

Young gives Mr. Spitzer this inventory of forms, the full geometry of a trained and meticulous mind, and then immediately demonstrates that all this knowledge of shapes does not help him locate the exit. He knows every form. He cannot find the door. The legal mind, the Blackstone firm, the executor's precision with papers and keys; none of this equipment is adequate to the problem of being in a house that has no locatable exit.

The boxes within boxes are everything: legal documents containing other documents, trunks containing other trunks, lives containing other lives. Catherine's infinite house of many rooms. Cousin Hannah's double life, perhaps triple. The novel itself, which is always opening into another story inside the story, always finding another center inside the center that was supposed to be central. Young's architecture is boxes within boxes all the way down. Mr. Spitzer knows this. He has always known this. But knowing the shape of the thing does not tell you how to leave it.

It seemed better not to know

“It seemed better not to know that which was unknowable.”

This is Mr. Spitzer's accommodation with the mystery, not resolution, not transcendence, but a kind of practical peace with the limits of what can be known. He has sorted the papers. He has laid the skirt over the body. He has taken the alpenhorn into the fog-bound streets. He has asked every stranger whether they have seen her. He has found no master key that unlocks all the trunks. He has not found the exit.

And so: “it seemed better not to know.” This is not defeat. It is the acknowledgment that some rooms in the house are permanently barred, that some questions the novel asks are not questions it intends to answer, that the correct response to the truly unknowable is not more investigation but a particular kind of stillness in the face of it. Wittgenstein's silence. The suffragette's vow. The executor who stops sorting and simply sits with what cannot be sorted.

Young does not present this as wisdom exactly. She presents it as the best Mr. Spitzer can manage. In this novel, that is a form of grace.

What to hold onto

Chapter 48 is Mr. Spitzer at his most liminal: closest to the border, most uncertain which side he stands on, most fully present to the question that has been organizing his existence since his twin died. He is the lamplighter of stars. He is the stowaway who may not know the ship went down. He is “the morning star and the evening star”: the same planet appearing as two things, depending on where you stand and what time it is.

What to carry forward: this life as a long rehearsal for the silence. The house of barred doors that has an entrance but no visible exit. Consciousness as sporadic, fluttering, not constant: the firefly rather than the sustained flame. And the accommodation, provisional and honest, that “it seemed better not to know that which was unknowable.” The chapter ends without resolution because resolution is not what this chapter is for. It is for sitting with Mr. Spitzer in the house, in the dark, while the stars fade through the holes in his cape.

guide-67-move-over-doc:
Chapter 67: Move Over, Doc

← Chapter 66 · Guide Home · Chapter 68 →

Research notes: Chapter 67

Characters: Homer Capehorn · Justice O’Leary · Lorena · Madge Capehorn · Miss MacIntosh · Moses Hunnecker · Mr. Titus Bonebreaker · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Love

Symbols: Pregnancy, Birth, and Children · The Bus and the Journey

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology · Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Exploration and the Poles · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest

We are back on the bus.

After four chapters in the deep past of Miss MacIntosh's life (her baldness, Lorena, Mr. Bonebreaker, the Arctic Explorer, the last month, the clothes on the beach) Young returns us to the present tense of the novel: Vera on a bus in the grey American Midwest, searching for What Cheer, Iowa. Moses Hunnecker is still driving. Madge and Homer are still aboard. The bus has arrived in Indiana, in front of a tavern.

And Moses cannot park.

What actually happens

The bus pulls up to a tavern in Indiana and stops. Moses wants to park. He cannot park because, he insists, an old Ford belonging to someone he calls "old Doc" is blocking the space. The passengers cannot get off the bus. Moses addresses old Doc directly, at length, cursing, pleading, reasoning, and threatening, while the passengers rock in their seats with something he calls "infinite weariness." Madge laughs breathlessly. Homer daydreams about a bride. Vera sits and watches and feels tired and dreamlike.

Old Doc does not move. He may not exist. The bus does not park. Nobody gets off.

That is the entirety of Chapter 67's external event. It is also, in its way, everything.

Who is old Doc?

Moses talks to him as if he is there: an unseen presence in an old ghost buggy, a Ford without essential parts, blocking the space. Children, Moses says, shoot at him with bean-shooters. He is dead from the shoulders down. He is the undertaker in a hearse, or perhaps he is the doctor who became an undertaker, which is to say the best doctor of all.

Vera briefly contemplates this: old Doc as undertaker, death wearing a medical coat. Young leaves it open, as she always does. Old Doc might be a real person Moses knows, a former local doctor who parks badly and ignores horns. He might be a ghost. He might be death itself, parked immovably in the one spot the living need to reach.

What Moses wants, very simply, is for death to move over. To give way. To let the bus get where it's going.

Death does not move over.

Moses and the rules of traffic

Moses's frustration erupts into a lecture about traffic order: chalk lines, detour signs, slow-turn signals, the basic courtesies that keep movement possible. He is a man who believes in rules, even as he drives erratically, drinks openly, and calls on angels from behind the wheel. He believes the road should work by logic. If everyone followed the chalk lines, the traffic would flow, the buses would park, the living could get off and get on with it.

But old Doc's ghost buggy doesn't follow chalk lines. The past doesn't consult detour signs. Death is not interested in yield requirements.

This is Moses's essential predicament, and in a way it is everyone's on this bus: the laws of order and forward motion keep failing to account for what is actually blocking the road.

Madge on the ferris wheel

Madge describes their situation with a precision that cuts through Moses's noise: it is like being stalled at the top of a ferris wheel in the sky, she says. Like being trapped in a crazy house with mirrored walls and no doors.

Madge is pregnant, unhappy, returning to a place she doesn't want to return to, married to a man sleeping peacefully beside her. She knows about being stalled. She knows about mirrored walls. Her laughter (high and thin, breathless) is the laughter of someone who has given up expecting things to move.

Homer, meanwhile, daydreams about a bride. He fears his wife might never know the bride he envisions, which may simply mean he daydreams of a woman who is not Madge, or may mean something more obscure, a future self no one can reach from here. Homer is always asleep or dreaming when the important things happen. He is the person on the bus least troubled by old Doc's ghost buggy, which is the same as saying he is the person least troubled by death.

"I can't give you anything but love, baby"

Moses, draped over the steering wheel, sings this softly to himself: a 1928 song born from a couple window-shopping at Tiffany's, a man saying to his beloved: I can't buy you the sparkler. I can only give you this. Moses is a man of grandiose faith and spectacular failure, driving a bus that can't park, addressing a ghost who won't move, singing a tender song about the limits of what love can offer.

Young chooses her songs as carefully as she chooses her names. This one fits Moses exactly: all the feeling, none of the resources.

Back to the beginning

Young makes a structural move here. We have just come through four chapters of Miss MacIntosh's death: the accumulation of her life told in the last month she had, ending with clothes on a beach and a dog barking at the sea. That is the novel's emotional climax, in many ways. It is what Vera's journey is moving toward and away from simultaneously.

And now: Moses. A tavern in Indiana. A ghost buggy blocking the space.

Young returns us to the bus not to deflate what came before, but to remind us that the novel has always been both things at once: the vast interior tragedy and the small comic frustration, the philosophical abyss and the man shouting at a parking space. The bus keeps moving even when it can't park. Vera keeps searching even after the beach. The wheel turns. Moses drives on.

What to hold onto

Moses Hunnecker, slumped over the steering wheel of a bus that cannot park, singing softly to a ghost who will not move, while his passengers rock in infinite weariness and the Indiana night settles in around them. The chalk lines don't account for this. Neither does anything else. And yet the bus will move again, eventually, and they will get where they are going.

Or they won't. But Moses will keep driving regardless.

Chapter 5: A Crazy Bus-Driver Losing His Way That He Knew Too Well

← Chapter 4 · Guide Home · Chapter 6 →

Research notes: Chapter 5

Characters: Justice O’Leary · Miss MacIntosh · Moses Hunnecker · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Society, Class, and Race

Symbols: Hair, Wig, and Baldness

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Greek Mythology · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · Music and Composers · The Bible

Welcome back to the bus.

If you felt, in Chapters 3 and 4, that you had moved away from the bus and deep into Vera’s past, you were right. That is how this novel works. The bus is always there, waiting, while Vera’s memory does its long and spiraling work. And now, in Chapter 5, we return to it. Night has fallen. The roads are washed out. And Moses Hunnecker, bus driver, is holding forth.

Prepare yourself. Moses has a lot to say.

What actually happens in Chapter 5

It is nighttime on the bus. Moses Hunnecker is driving through flooded, broken roads in the dark: no stars, no signposts, the landscape dissolved into rain and mist. He is drinking. He is talking: to himself, to the old doctor, to whoever will listen.

He refuses to cut his hair. This is the chapter’s great fixed point: Moses’s hair, which has never been cut, which has grown to enormous proportions, which he treats as his last and most personal possession. He will not let anyone touch it. Not the barber. Not the Democrats. Not anyone.

He rails against the Democrats and the New Deal, against FDR, against what he sees as the government’s steady encroachment on his freedom. He is a lifelong Republican. He has never voted, he never has time, but his politics are ferocious.

He talks about the old doctor, Justice O’Leary, who sits among the passengers in a state of advanced dementia, imagining he is still making house calls, still delivering babies, his rusted forceps and broken stethoscope still tools of a living practice. Moses alternates between mockery and a kind of rough tenderness toward him.

And then, quietly, the chapter asks a question it does not answer: is Moses actually driving this bus? Or is he dreaming it? Is any of this happening?

What Vera is thinking about

Vera watches all of this with her characteristic mixture of empathy and detachment. She is the observer, the recorder, the consciousness through which we receive everything, but she does not intervene. She listens to Moses and understands, on some level, that he is caught in the same kind of loop she is: a man driving a road he knows too well, going somewhere he may never arrive, in a landscape that has stopped making sense.

There is a line Young gives us early in the chapter: “a crazy bus-driver losing his way that he knew too well.” Sit with that. You can know a road so well that you lose it, know it so well that it stops being a road and becomes something else entirely, a groove worn into habit, a dream of motion without destination.

This is Vera’s condition too. She has been circling Miss MacIntosh’s absence for so long that the circling has become its own kind of journey. Moses is her mirror in this chapter, whether he knows it or not.

Moses and his hair

The hair needs its own explanation, because Young gives it so much weight and it might otherwise seem merely eccentric.

Moses has never cut his hair. It has grown to extraordinary length and, in his telling, has taken on a life of its own, full of “burning eyes like the eyes of Argus,” twisting and growing like something alive. He talks about it the way other men talk about their souls. It is his “only virtue.” His “angel.” The one thing about himself that no one has managed to take from him.

This sounds strange until you understand the context. Moses is a man who feels that everything else has been stripped away: his country is declining, the government is encroaching, the roads are washed out, the old certainties are gone. His hair is the last thing that is purely, irreducibly his. No barber. No government. No tax on it.

There is a long tradition, across many cultures, of hair carrying the self: its strength, its identity, its spiritual power. The Biblical Samson is the most famous example: his hair was the source of his power, and when it was cut, he was undone. Moses (and Young chose this name deliberately) is a version of that story: a prophet-figure driving through the wilderness, his identity intact in his uncut hair, raging against the forces that would diminish him.

The novel also makes a quietly darkly comic point: hair and nails do not actually continue to grow after death. It only looks that way, the skin dehydrates and pulls back. If Moses is, as the chapter hints, possibly dead or dreaming rather than truly driving, his hair’s continued growth is itself a kind of illusion. The last thing he believes is real might not be real either.

The old doctor, and the ghosts he carries

Justice O’Leary has been on this bus since Chapter 1, and now we understand him better. He was once a country doctor who made house calls, who delivered babies, who was a figure of authority and care in his community. Now he is old and lost, his mind running on rails that no longer connect to the present world. He thinks he is still practicing. He sees patients who are not there. His instruments are rusted, his stethoscope broken.

Moses is not entirely wrong to mock him. But watch how Young holds both things at once: the doctor is deluded, yes, but his delusion is that he is still helping people, still bringing life into the world. Of all the delusions available to a person, this one has a certain dignity. He has not retreated into pleasure or comfort or oblivion. He has retreated into service, even if the service is imaginary.

The pregnant women he tends, his “patients”, are ghosts. Their cries and their suffering are echoes of births that may never happen, futures that may never arrive. Young is showing us a world in which the business of bringing new life into being has become spectral, uncertain, haunted.

Is any of this real?

Chapter 5 does something the earlier chapters have gestured toward but not said outright: it openly questions whether Moses is actually driving the bus or dreaming the whole thing from his four-poster bed.

Young never resolves this. She is not going to. The bus is real and the bus is a dream and the bus is a passage between worlds and all of these are true simultaneously. Moses himself wonders if he has died and is continuing out of habit, driving the same road because he doesn’t know how to stop.

This is not a puzzle you need to solve. It is a condition you need to inhabit. The novel is asking you to hold uncertainty the way its characters hold it, not as a problem to be fixed, but as the weather you’re moving through.

What matters is that Vera is on the bus. Whatever the bus is (real, dream, passage) she is in it, moving forward, searching for something that may or may not be findable.

The political weather

Moses’s tirades against the Democrats and the New Deal might seem like local color, but they are doing something more precise. Young is placing us in a specific American moment: the 1930s and ‘40s, the era of FDR, when the question of what the government owed its citizens was being fought over furiously. Moses represents one side of that argument: the man who sees government help as government control, who feels the state reaching into his last freedoms and taxing even his hair.

You do not have to agree with Moses to understand him. Young doesn’t ask you to agree. She asks you to feel the genuine fear underneath the bluster: the fear of a man who has watched his country change in ways he didn’t choose, who has no power over any of it, and who has found the one thing, his hair, his body, his self, that he can still refuse to surrender.

That fear is real. It has not gone away. Look around.

What to watch for as you keep reading

Light spoilers: This section hints at what happens later in the novel. Skip it if you want to meet the story fresh.

The four passengers named Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. Young names four passengers on the bus after the four Evangelists, the authors of the four Gospels. They appear quietly here, but they give the bus journey a spiritual dimension that will deepen as the novel continues. Moses is not just a bus driver on a midwestern road. He is a prophet-figure navigating a passage. Notice who is bearing witness to the journey.

The folk songs. Moses sings “Go Tell Aunt Rhody” (the old gray goose is dead) and “The Old Gray Mare.” Both are songs about something vital that has died or declined. Young is not being subtle here. The dead country Moses is driving through is America or a version of it, an America that has stopped being what it was supposed to be.

Wormwood, boxwood, cedar. Three woods mentioned in the chapter, each carrying Biblical weight: cedar for sacred endurance, boxwood for divine provision, wormwood for bitterness and judgment. When Young reaches for this kind of language, she is building a register of meaning that accumulates slowly. Don’t worry about tracking every reference. Just notice that the landscape has this kind of depth.

The question of whether Moses is dead. Hold it. Don’t try to answer it. Let the novel show you what it wants to show you.

What to hold onto

Chapter 5 is wild and funny and dark and a little operatic with Moses raging about his hair and his politics in the rainy dark while an old doctor tends to invisible patients. It can feel like a departure from the intimacy of Vera’s grief in earlier chapters.

But here is the thread: Vera is watching a man who, like her, has refused to let go of something. Moses will not cut his hair. Vera will not give up on Miss MacIntosh. Both of them are holding onto the one thing that still feels like themselves, in a landscape that has done its best to wash everything away.

They are more alike than either of them knows. This bus is exactly the right place for both of them.

Chapter 20: I Should Protect Her from the Knowledge of Herself

← Chapter 19 · Guide Home · Chapter 21 →

Research notes: Chapter 20

Characters: Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Faith, God, and the Supernatural

Symbols: Hair, Wig, and Baldness · The House · Weddings and Funerals

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology · Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Ancient Egypt · The Bible · The History of Opium

Chapter 20 is the last chapter of the Miss MacIntosh sequence: the four chapters that delivered the revelation and its aftermath across two nights and a dawn. After this, the novel will move on. Other stories, other characters, other rooms.

But before it moves on, Young gives us one more morning with Vera lying in the bed, eyes open now, watching Miss MacIntosh sleep. And she gives us the decision Vera makes.

It is the most important decision in the novel.

What actually happens in Chapter 20

It is full dawn. Vera lies beside the sleeping Miss MacIntosh and looks at her in the light. She sees, for the first time in daylight and without the excuse of shock or darkness, everything: the bald head, the missing breast, the deprivations that the night had revealed and that the morning confirms. She thinks about what she has seen. She thinks about God. She thinks about hair.

And then she makes her resolution: she will go on as if she never saw. She will pretend. She will iron Miss MacIntosh’s shirts with new eagerness, recite the genealogies, learn the ancient weights and measures, keep the secret locked in her own capacious heart. She will protect Miss MacIntosh from the knowledge of herself.

The chapter ends with Vera making the explicit promise that closes the sequence: “I should hold to every moment as if I lived with a dying man, and I should protect her from the knowledge of herself.”

The decision

Vera’s resolution to pretend is not cowardice. Young is careful about this. Vera is fourteen and has just had the floor taken out from under her for the second time in her life: the first being whatever happened to her father, about whom we learn only that he fell “while walking a frozen cable stretched between two snow-capped mountain peaks.” She knows what she is doing and why.

She is choosing to protect. To hold the secret in her own capacious heart and not let it surface through a flicker of an eyelid or a wandering gesture. She is choosing to give Miss MacIntosh the dignity of her own concealment. And she is choosing, at fourteen, to live with a dying person and know it and say nothing.

This is an enormous thing to choose. Young renders it plainly, without sentimentality, as the kind of moral decision that only becomes visible in retrospect as what it was: a child deciding, quietly and without fanfare, to be charitable. Which is what Miss MacIntosh asked of her, in the dark, pressing her claw-shaped hand to Vera’s forehead. There, that will teach you charity.

The teaching worked. The lesson cost everything.

Seeing her plain

Chapter 20 contains some of the most sustained and beautiful writing in the novel about what it actually means to see another person.

Young gives us Vera watching Miss MacIntosh in sleep with a clarity she has never had before: her face “sublimely peaceful even in its broken, anguished beauties such as I had hardly noticed or appreciated before.” The face that was always present, the face Vera saw every day for years, is only now being seen. The bald head, the “thin-lidded eyes closed in thin sleep,” the narrow and intolerable vacancy where the breast is missing, and in the middle of it, something that Young names as “affirmation, strong and positive, that which God Himself should tremble to see.”

Young refuses to resolve Miss MacIntosh into tragedy. She was stripped bare. She was also, in her stripping bare, something Young calls a sad masterpiece. Not a victim of her circumstances but a person who made herself, under impossible conditions, into the one authority Vera had truly known. That is the affirmation the chapter insists on finding in the wreckage.

The question Vera asks (“Whose work, I vaguely wondered, was this? Whose accomplishment, this sad masterpiece?”) does not receive an answer. It was Miss MacIntosh’s own work, built out of the materials available: proverbs, common sense, a wig, a salmon-colored corset, the courage to keep winding the alarm clock every day.

Was she deserted at the altar by her bridegroom or her bride?

Young gives Vera a list of questions about the hair: was it hair by hair “through many hesitant years, or all at one blow”? Was it her broken heart? “Was she in mourning for someone dead”? “Had some old crow plucked each hair away?” And then: “was she deserted at the altar by her bridegroom or her bride? Was she her only lover?”

Young does not answer any of these questions. She lists them as possibilities, in Vera’s wondering voice, and moves on. But the two final questions carry the weight of the sequence: the bridegroom or the bride. Both options held open simultaneously. And the last one, the strangest: was she her only lover?

A person whose inner life had no acceptable outward form, who could not find or keep a love that matched what she was, who had, perhaps, turned the capacity inward. Was she her only lover? Young asks it and does not answer it, which is the most respectful thing she could do.

Was God bald too

Near the chapter’s end, Vera’s mind drifts into a long meditation on God. Was God bald, “or bearded so that birds might hide” behind His dreaming hair? “What was God, defined in so many terms”: a fuller’s soap, a refining fire, “the light of the morning when the sun arises,” a stone of grace, “a friend that sticketh closer than a brother,” “the shadow of a great rock in a weary land?”

This passage is Young at her most formally ambitious and also her most playful, piling Biblical epithets for God one on top of another until they accumulate into something that feels less like theology and more like Vera’s mind refusing to land anywhere, floating through the possibilities the way Miss MacIntosh’s opium guests float through the alphabet.

But underneath the floating there is a serious question: if Miss MacIntosh’s baldness is a kind of nakedness before God, what does that say about God? If she is the sad masterpiece, is God the artist who made her so? Is God also somehow stripped, also somehow exposed, also bald in the sense of having nothing to hide behind? Young leaves this open. She almost always leaves this open. But she asks it, here, at dawn, over the sleeping head of the most practical woman in the novel.

What to watch for as you keep reading

Light spoilers: This section hints at what happens later in the novel. Skip it if you want to meet the story fresh.

Vera’s promise to protect Miss MacIntosh from the knowledge of herself is the emotional foundation of everything that follows in the novel. Every time Vera thinks about Miss MacIntosh (in memory, in the long search, in the chapters still to come) she is keeping that promise, or failing to keep it, or renegotiating what keeping it means. The novel is now about to expand enormously. Other characters, other histories, other geographies. You will sometimes go many chapters without returning to Vera directly. But you are now carrying what Vera carries: the knowledge of the bald head on the striped pillow, and the decision made at fourteen to go on as if she never saw.

The title of the novel appears in Chapter 20 for the first time in its full form, embedded in the prose: my plain darling. My darling. Not Miss MacIntosh, that plain nursemaid. My darling. The relationship has been named, at last, for what it always was.

guide-71-the-morning-after:
Chapter 71: The Morning After

← Chapter 70 · Guide Home · Chapter 72 →

Research notes: Chapter 71

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Justice O’Leary · Marie Weed · Miss MacIntosh · Mr. Weed · Tabitha · The Tavern Landlady · Vera Cartwheel

Symbols: Clocks and Watches · Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · Pearls and Jewels · The House

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · Judaism · Lynching and Racial Violence · Music and Composers · Pregnancy, Abortion, and Midwifery · Romantic Poets · The History of Opium

Morning comes to the Tavern. Vera has not slept.

She is stiff with wakefulness, “with ceaseless memory,” wearing her mother’s black velvet (which was meant to be Catherine’s shroud, never used) and her mother’s lace and her mother’s pearls. She is “some time past the ambiguity of dawn.” She gets up and goes out into the hotel, and what she finds there is the morning-after version of everything the night already told her: the same people, the same wreckage, now visible in grey light instead of heard through thin walls.

This chapter moves Vera through the Tavern’s spaces (Dr. O’Leary’s room, the corridor, the hotel lobby) while she thinks about Mr. Weed, remembers Catherine’s stories, encounters a woman screaming prejudice on the staircase, and finally finds the Tavern Landlady, large and goitered and speaking in a dialect thick as Indiana soil, who tells her everything she needs to know about the people in this place. Chapter 71 is a chapter of inventory: of what remains, who persists, and what the daylight reveals that the dark only suggested.

What Actually Happens

Vera wakes and thinks, first, of Mr. Weed: wondering if he has hanged himself in the night. She concludes he has not: he waits for dawn because his children play at hanging themselves, and he cannot leave them unguarded. This is his particular punishment, his particular vigil.

She thinks of her mother’s pearls, which she is wearing. Catherine believed the pearls “could not be lost or stolen”: that they were her “lost estate,” something real beyond market value. She also believed, with her characteristic defiance of arithmetic, that losing pearls made them multiply: the more that were lost, the more there were. The chauffeur James once returned thirteen pearls when twelve had been lost. Vera wears them now as an inheritance of this logic. She goes to Dr. O’Leary’s room. It is open, or she goes in: the chapter is not fastidious about how Vera arrives in places she observes. The room is a museum of disorder. Mismatched women’s shoes are scattered everywhere (“white canvas tennis shoes, green opera pumps, old” laced shoes, “buckskin shoes with buttons, gold Grecian sandals”) all without their mates, from different eras, belonging to no one currently present. Medical instruments are scattered among the shoes. His Yale diploma hangs above the bed. A calendar on the wall is stuck twenty years ago. And the books: shelves of them, a library that has lost the thread connecting one volume to the next: medical texts beside children’s primers beside political pamphlets beside obscure adventure novels beside Keats. The doctor is there, senile and leaning on his cane, his old eyes frozen, delivering imaginary babies in a barren countryside where nothing grows. There is a rumor, which the novel floats and does not confirm, of a pregnant man: a patient who perhaps is real, perhaps is the doctor’s hallucination, perhaps is both.

Sarah, the doctor’s dead sister, or the presence that haunts him by that name, is crawling on the floor. Tabitha the chambermaid moves silently through all of this, as she does every morning, hoping, the Landlady will later tell Vera, to get a baby by the doctor. She is “too crazy to be on relief.” She is here instead.

On the staircase, Vera is confronted by a woman in metallic curlers, half-dressed, her face contorted with cold rage. She accuses Vera of being a “tramp girl” who kept “a decent woman awake all night.” Then she goes further: the Jewish doctor Simeon is a dirty Jew who won’t touch her; “Hitler ran him out of Germany” and Hitler was right; Roosevelt is ruining the country; “there are no Negroes in this county” and no one wants mulattoes; the communists and the Catholics are running everything. She is a widow whose “husband died before he ever came to bed,” and her grief and her politics have hardened into each other until they are indistinguishable.

Vera descends to the lobby. The Tavern Landlady is there: large, fat, goitered, a former circus fat lady, speaking in dialect, “clombed the stairs,” “bedses,” “husbane”, with a folksy resignation that contains, nonetheless, everything Vera needs to know. The landlord is fine. Tabitha is mute and here every morning. The old watchdog who used to attend Mass is dead. The priest died in the landlord’s arms. The hotel sinks every night and comes back every morning. Outside, Tabitha kneels on the porch washing stones in the pale spring air.

Mr. Weed’s Vigil

The chapter opens with Vera still thinking about the Christian hangman, and the question she poses is quiet and precise: does he hang himself? She concludes he does not, and the reason is the children. Marie’s children (his children, the children of the woman who hanged herself from the peach tree) play at hanging themselves in the orchard. He cannot leave them. He waits for dawn to keep watch.

This is Young’s understanding of how grief actually works: not as a thing that passes but as a vigil. Mr. Weed cannot die because the people who carry his death inside them are still alive and still performing it, still rehearsing what their mother did, and someone has to be awake in case they go too far. He has made himself necessary by surviving. He is kept alive by the children’s need for a witness.

The image also completes the echo the novel has been building: Marie hanged from the peach tree, the children playing at hanging beneath it, Mr. Weed walking past on his way home with his Jew’s harp, taking the shortcut through the orchard. Everything that happened is still happening in that orchard. He still takes the shortcut.

Catherine’s Pearls

Vera wears her mother’s pearls through the chapter, and the pearls carry a philosophy. Catherine believed that real pearls, hers, “could not be lost or stolen.” They were her lost estate: what remained of a life that had otherwise dissolved into opium and illusion. She also believed, with the arithmetic of a woman who has stopped obeying mathematics, that losing pearls made them multiply. The chauffeur James returned thirteen when twelve were lost. There are now infinities of pearls, she said. Simple addition.

This is Catherine’s most compressed statement of her worldview: that loss generates abundance, that the real thing cannot be destroyed, that the shadow is more permanent than the substance. It is delusional and it is also a kind of wisdom that the novel treats seriously. Vera inherits it. She wears the pearls as a lost estate and a logical proposition simultaneously.

The pearls also carry mourning. They drip like tears. They are linked throughout the chapter to what remains of Catherine (her shroud-dress, her lace, her logic) now worn by Vera as she walks through a hotel full of people who are also, in their ways, wearing the remnants of people who are gone.

Dr. O’Leary’s Room

The shoes are the chapter’s central image. One shoe from every era, one shoe without its pair, scattered across the floor of a doctor’s office: “white canvas tennis shoes, green opera pumps, old women’s” laced shoes, “buckskin shoes with buttons, gold Grecian sandals.” They come from different times. They all lack their mates. Their wearers are nowhere.

Dr. O’Leary is an obstetrician, or was, before the “hardening of the artery of the brain” retired him from practice. The shoes are the shoes of women who came to him at their most vulnerable: pregnant, waiting, hoping. Some of those pregnancies ended well. Some did not. The shoes remain; the women are gone. The doctor, now delivering imaginary babies in a barren countryside where nothing grows, is the afterimage of a practice that has dissolved into hallucination.

His Yale diploma hangs above the bed. His calendar is twenty years out of date. His library, and Young gives us the titles with her usual care, mixing the medical and the absurd: obstetrics texts alongside children’s primers, a pamphlet on the diseases of coal miners beside Keats’ “Ode on a Grecian Urn” beside “The Causes of Ejaculatory Praecox Among the Great American Elks”, is the library of a mind that has stopped sorting by category and now holds everything together in one undifferentiated mass. It is both comic and genuinely sad. He was educated at Yale. He is now delivering imaginary babies, naked as death, in a barren field.

The rumor of the pregnant man floats through the chapter without resolution. Couvade syndrome (sympathetic pregnancy, in which an expectant father experiences some of the same symptoms as his pregnant partner) is real. Whether the doctor’s pregnant man patient is real, imaginary, or something in between is, characteristically, left open.

The Woman in Curlers

She is one of the most uncomfortable passages in the novel, and Young does not soften it. The woman confronts Vera on the staircase and delivers, in concentrated form, a litany of the prejudices that have organized a certain segment of American life: antisemitism, white supremacy, anti-communism, anti-Catholicism, xenophobia. She invokes Hitler as correct. She insists there are no Black people in the county and no one wants any. She refuses to see the Jewish doctor Simeon, who she says Hitler ran out of Germany rightly. Roosevelt is the enemy. The communists and the Catholics are running everything. This is not fringe material for its time and place; it is a reasonably accurate inventory of the views held by a significant portion of the American Midwest before the Civil Rights era. She is also a widow whose “husband died before he ever came to bed,” and she is terrified and furious and completely alone. Young gives her the prejudices and the grief simultaneously, not as explanation or excuse but as coexistence: this is what a person can contain. The hatred is real. The loneliness is real. They have grown together until she cannot separate them. Vera does not argue with her. There is nothing to argue with. She waits until the woman is done and then continues downstairs.

The Tavern Landlady

She is a new figure: the landlord’s wife, or the person who runs the hotel while the landlord manages its philosophy. She is large, fat, goitered: the Goiter Belt, the region of the upper Midwest where iodine deficiency was endemic before iodized salt, is her natural territory. She is a former circus fat lady, which means she was once spectacle, once exhibited for pay, once an American entertainment. Now she is here, behind the desk, in dialect.

Her speech is rendered phonetically: “clombed the stairs,” “bedses,” “husbane,” “weller and weller,” “axd,” “agone.” Young is giving her a voice that is entirely particular, entirely local, entirely hers: rural Indiana, working class, a woman who has watched this hotel since before it started sinking and expects to watch it after it sinks some more. She carries no illusions about the place. She simply states what is: the old watchdog attended Mass in all weathers and is now dead. The priest died in her husband’s arms. The hotel sinks every night. Tabitha washes stones every morning. Life persists.

She is, in her way, the clearest-eyed person in the Tavern. Not because she has Miss MacIntosh’s commitment to the cold surface of things, but because she has the practical intelligence of someone who has been too many kinds of things (circus exhibit, hotel keeper, widow of a community’s faith) to mistake any one version of herself for the whole truth.

Tabitha

The chambermaid. She is “too crazy to be on relief” (welfare). Relief is the Depression-era term for government assistance, later called welfare. To be too crazy for relief in the 1930s or 1940s meant to be too mentally ill to qualify for the minimal social support the state offered to the destitute. She is here instead, washing stones on the porch, caring for a mad doctor at night in the hope of getting a baby by him. She speaks one word in the chapter: “Good morning.” She says it to Vera as she kneels in the pale spring air. It is the most human sentence in the chapter.

What to Hold Onto

The mateless shoes. One from every era, every woman gone, the doctor delivering imaginary babies in a barren field while his Yale diploma watches from the wall. Catherine’s pearls and their impossible arithmetic: lose twelve, receive thirteen, multiply into infinities. Wear the loss as inheritance.

Mr. Weed’s vigil in the orchard. He does not hang himself because the children are still playing at it, and someone has to stay awake.

The woman in curlers and the full inventory of her fears. Young does not editorialize. She lets it stand: this is what some people contain.

The Landlady, ex-circus fat lady, goitered, in dialect, describing the hotel’s nightly sinking as a matter of fact. The hotel sinks. It comes back. The stones get washed. Good morning.

Chapter 34: Why No Man Had Been This Woman

← Chapter 33 · Guide Home · Chapter 35 →

Research notes: Chapter 34

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Homer Capehorn · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Mr. Chandelier · Peron Spitzer · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: The Search for Meaning

Symbols: Birds

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Suicide in History and Literature · The History of Opium · Women's Suffrage

Chapter 34 is the last of the Cousin Hannah chapters and, in some ways, the most intimate. After the grand sweep of her adventures and the epitaphs and the battle to rescue Catherine, Young brings us inside Catherine’s private experience of Hannah: what it was like to be in the room with her, what Catherine saw in her that she could not name, what Hannah’s presence revealed about both of them.

This is also the chapter where Young, writing in 1965, brings the novel as close as it will come to naming directly what has been circling since Cousin Hannah first appeared. She does not name it. She moves around it with extraordinary precision. Read with that precision in mind.

What actually happens in Chapter 34

The chapter continues the meditation on Catherine’s marriage: the wedding in white that was also in black, the dog who performed the ceremony in church Latin, the St. Bernard who gave her the Viaticum. Then it opens into a long, sustained portrait of what Cousin Hannah was like as a physical presence in Catherine’s bedroom: the iron keys jangling at her belt, the metallic sparks she gave off “at the sound of a cock crowing,” the silver scales she seemed to wear, her quick wit, her macabre retorts, her contempt for mortal men, her boundless indifference to Mr. Spitzer.

Young gives us Catherine’s most revealing admission about Hannah: Catherine “had felt both very flirtatious and very guilty, trying to resist this man who was no man.” She had imagined, when Hannah came, that she was in the presence of the love she had always wanted, not Peron’s reckless passion, not Joachim’s faithful devotion, but something that surpassed both, that seemed to dilate the heavens by its grandeur.

The chapter ends with Cousin Hannah’s final verdict on Mr. Spitzer: that he would cruelly disappoint Catherine “at the last, crucial moment, abandoning her to the furies,” even as Peron had done when he “apparently committed suicide, taking a coward’s way out—leaving Joachim to accept that vicarious responsibility which had always been the slow brother’s sense of peculiar guilt and” inestimable loss.

Why no man had been this woman

Near the chapter’s center, Catherine asks the question that gives this chapter its title: “why no man had been this woman, why no woman had been this man, why poor old Cousin Hannah, an unmarried spinster,” “was always like a traveller between two worlds.”

Young does not answer this question directly, but she surrounds it with everything needed to understand it. Hannah had seemed “to contain two people, herself and another, a secret man, even should he be only a puppet, a mere pygmy,” “or a butterfly sailing at midnight.” She had seemed voluminous enough to contain this double presence. She “had always acted as if she were about to meet” “her enemy, a timorous man, though perhaps he should be that man whom no one else should see.”

Catherine’s experience of Hannah was of someone who was perpetually between: between man and woman, between presence and absence, between the physical world of mountains and swords and the imaginary world of the bedroom. She had seemed as strange as Mr. Chandelier, “as strange as the golden cock crowing in the twilight of” Catherine’s opium dreams. She had been a threat to weakness and a dazzlement. And Catherine, “having no object for her love, had viewed her as the object of her lost romance, wondering why” this was not a man.

Young is writing about something the novel cannot name directly, and she does it by surrounding the unnamed thing with precise observation. The iron keys at Hannah’s belt, giving off dissonant music. The metallic sparks “at the sound of a cock crowing.” The silver scales she seemed to wear, shining in her own light. The quick wit, the macabre retort, the boundless indifference to Joachim. The deathbed confession that the greatest battles were domestic ones. These are the details of a particular interior life rendered from the outside, by a woman who loved Hannah and did not know how to say it.

Catherine’s most private knowledge

Young gives Catherine a moment of self-awareness that is one of the novel’s most quietly devastating: “my mother had felt both very flirtatious and very guilty, trying to resist this man who was no man.” And then: as “my mother had not wished, naturally, to show her secret agreement with her.”

Catherine knew. She had always known, at some level, that her agreement with Cousin Hannah (with her argument against men, with her contempt for mortal love, with her proposals to escape) went deeper than she ever showed. She performed flirtatiousness and dreamy inattention when Hannah came, precisely because Hannah’s presence threatened the carefully maintained architecture of Catherine’s illusions. Hannah was real in a way that the phantom bridegroom was not. And that reality was more dangerous than any dream.

Catherine’s response was to become more romantic, more nostalgic, more flirtatious exactly when Hannah appeared. As a defense. Young names this with characteristic precision: “my mother, in spite of her inclinations,” had not wished to show her secret agreement. The inclinations were there. The secret agreement was there. The performance of disagreement was the only protection available.

The cock crowing

Young places a strange, vivid image near the chapter’s center: “at the sound of a cock crowing, she had strutted, dancing a weird dance, giving off showers of metallic sparks, stretching her long neck as her cheeks twitched.” Because in certain Moroccan courtyards “she had visited, she had seen that the cock is” a “great golden sultan, lord of the morning, lord of all he surveys, that even the hens wear black veils like the secret women in purdah.”

The cock crowing is the sound of male dominion announcing itself. It is the sound that enrages Hannah more than anything else in the world. And her response is to become the cock: to dance its weird dance, to give off its metallic sparks, to stretch her neck and twitch her cheeks. She does not counter the male assertion. She embodies it, transforms it, claims it. This is what Hannah does with every force she encounters: she becomes it rather than opposing it, and in becoming it, changes what it means.

Hannah’s final verdict on the brothers

The chapter ends with Cousin Hannah’s assessment of both Spitzer brothers, delivered through Catherine’s memory: Joachim would cruelly disappoint her “at the last, crucial moment, abandoning her to the furies,” even as Peron had done when he “committed suicide, taking a coward’s way out—leaving Joachim to accept” the vicarious responsibility that “had always been the slow brother’s sense of peculiar guilt and” inestimable loss.

This is Hannah’s harshest verdict, and Young makes it her last word on the brothers. Peron was a coward who left. Joachim accepted the coward’s guilt as his own, because that is what slow brothers do. Neither chose Catherine. Neither gave her what she needed. And Joachim, Hannah predicted, would not be there at the end.

Whether Hannah is right is the question the novel will keep open. But she is right that the responsibility passed from one brother to the other, that the guilt for Peron’s death was taken on by the one who survived, and that this transference has defined Joachim’s life ever since.

What to watch for as you keep reading

Light spoilers: This section hints at what happens later in the novel. Skip it if you want to meet the story fresh.

The Cousin Hannah sequence, chapters 30 through 34, is now complete. Young has given us the full portrait: the great adventurer, the suffragette, the person who contained two selves, the one who failed to rescue Catherine, who died in her bed of her life, who left Mr. Spitzer to compose her unfinished epitaph. She will surface again in the novel’s memory, but her portrait is complete.

Catherine’s desire for “a teacher of arithmetic who would teach her to add” and subtract and divide, and then plane and solid geometry, so she might know who the geometer was) is one of the novel’s most moving passages of longing. She wants to understand the structure of reality. She wants to know whether the great illusionist who designed these “concentric circles and eccentric circles and” wandering orbs is sane or insane. She will never know. The geometer does not show his face. But the yearning for that knowledge, the desire for “one real person in the world,” is the same desire that drives Vera’s search for Miss MacIntosh. The novel turns on it.

The Irish housemaid who “polished a mirror all night long” after the golden cock crowed and thought it was morning, and eventually went stark staring mad: is a brief, perfect figure for what happens to ordinary people in Catherine’s household when the extraordinary impinges too long on the ordinary. Not the servants who adapted, who went along. The one who could not tell night from day and tried to make the mirror clear and lost her mind doing it.
