Chapter 42: The Deathbed of the Suffrage Captain

← Chapter 41 · Guide Home · Chapter 43 →

Research notes: Chapter 42

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer

Themes: Death and Mortality · The Search for Meaning

Symbols: Horses and Carriages · The House · The Sea and Water · Weddings and Funerals

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft · Nietzsche

Allusions: Fairy Tales and Folklore · Greek Mythology · Women's Suffrage

We have been circling Cousin Hannah's death for a very long time. The novel has approached it obliquely, through memory and myth, through Catherine's grief-that-looks-like-logic and Mr. Spitzer's second-remove consciousness and the long meditation on what she was and what she stood for and where she might have gone. Chapter 42 brings you to the room.

Mr. Spitzer is there. He is the last living witness, the only one who was present. And what he finds (what he has been unable to tell Catherine, what he has been obtusely, infuriatingly silent about across all these chapters) is this: the great suffrage captain died sobbing. Delirious. Calling out for things unnamed. Reduced, in her final hours, to something unrecognizable from the woman who had ridden through deserts and broken conventions and “played a mean game of cards” and never asked for pity.

Young holds this with absolute steadiness. She does not make it a diminishment. She makes it the truth.

What actually happens in Chapter 42

The chapter opens with Catherine traveling to Cousin Hannah's deathbed, not in any physical sense, since Catherine cannot walk, but in a glass carriage drawn by alabaster horses, driven by a black coachman, passing through surreal landscapes of mirrors and fountains and sleeping cities. Whether this is a dream, a hallucination, a memory, or something the novel asks us to take seriously as a real event in its own terms, Young does not specify. Farewell, she tells us, is “a matter of opinion as to the time, the place, the person.”

Mr. Spitzer, meanwhile, is preoccupied with lists: lost ships, sunken argosies, passengers whose fates are unrecorded, coordinates that no longer correspond to anything on the surface. He has spent his life cataloguing what cannot be found. This is, we understand, his way of thinking about Cousin Hannah: about all the things she was that are now unlocatable.

And then: the deathbed itself. Mr. Spitzer at the side of the woman he has observed and envied and resented and mourned for decades, watching her die. She is unrecognizable. The fiery captain, the storm king, the great warrior of the suffrage movement, is reduced to a figure who sobs and cries out in her delirium. Snow seems to fall across her face. The white tent of her death chamber suggests a desert or a pagoda: East and West collapsing together in her final room, as they collapsed together in her life.

Mr. Spitzer reflects on what all her battles actually achieved. He is not certain. He is not sure the world she fought to change has changed enough to justify the cost she paid. He keeps vigil anyway.

The glass carriage and the meaning of farewell

Catherine's journey to the deathbed in her glass carriage is one of the novel's most purely dreamlike passages.

A glass carriage is transparent: you can be seen inside it, and you can see out. It is also fragile: the fairy tale material, Cinderella's vehicle that will become a pumpkin at midnight, the conveyance that cannot last. That Catherine makes this journey in glass is Young's way of saying: this visit is real and it is not real, it is visible and it is made of something that shatters, it is a farewell and a goodbye to someone who may already be beyond farewell.

The alabaster horses turn their heads like foam. The coachman is black: Catherine's consciousness evoked in dream form, as To All My Darlings notes. The sleeping cities they pass through are every city Catherine has visited only in imagination, which is to say, every city. She arrives at a deathbed she never physically reached, says a goodbye she never physically said, and returns to her own bed where she has always been. This is what Catherine's kind of love looks like: vast, surreal, and conducted entirely in the interior. It counts. Young means it to count.

Mr. Spitzer and the lost ships

Mr. Spitzer's obsession with lost ships and unrecorded passengers is one of the chapter's quietly perfect details. He is a man who researches what cannot be recovered, who catalogs the disappeared, who tries to find coordinates for things that have no location. This is grief dressed as a profession.

Every ship on his list is Cousin Hannah. Every lost passenger is the person she was before the dying, the person she was at thirty, at forty, at the height of the campaigns when the iron keys whistled at her belt and the snow followed her indoors. He cannot find them. The ocean has no reliable records. He keeps looking.

Young gives him the detail of valuing his dignity more than his life: the conservative figure, the man victimized by routine itself. He is stuck, as all rigidly conventional thinking is stuck, between the thing that must hold and the line that must not be crossed. He cannot act, cannot speak fully, cannot tell Catherine what he saw, because to do so would be to surrender the arrangement that has kept him functional. His silence about Cousin Hannah's death is not cruelty. It is the only form of containment available to a man who has no other.

Hannah, Hamid, Al Hamid, the Great Moor

Chapter 42 gives Cousin Hannah multiple identities in a way the novel has been building toward: she is Hannah in Boston, Hamid in the East, Al Hamid, the Great Moor. These are not simply aliases. They are the different selves a person accumulates when they travel far enough and long enough and cross enough of the boundaries that were supposed to contain them.

Al Hamid is one of the Beautiful Names of Allah in Islamic tradition: the praiseworthy one, the laudable, the object of all praise. That Young weaves this into Cousin Hannah's accumulated identities, following the implication that she may have converted to Islam during her travels and eventually departed from all faith entirely, is precise. Hannah is the New England suffragette. Hamid is the traveler who crossed into other worlds. Al Hamid is the name given to the most praiseworthy. The Great Moor is the mythic figure she became in the imaginations of those who watched her go.

One person. Many names. Many selves acquired through a life lived without regard for the borders that were supposed to keep her on one side.

The unknown bridegroom

The novel surfaces here a rumor it has been keeping: there was a bridegroom. Someone left at the church door. Someone Cousin Hannah arrived for and then, at the threshold of the conventional life, turned away from. Or did not turn away from: the details are obscure, buried in the lacunae Mr. Spitzer's research keeps finding.

There are also rumors of a secret man, a caliph, someone who supported her cause from the shadows and whose relationship to her was never made legible.

Young does not resolve these rumors. She is not interested in resolving them. What she is interested in is the fact of their existence: that behind the public armor, behind the iron keys and the whistling and the suffrage campaigns and the masculine virtues and the refusal of self-pity, there was a private life that nobody fully knew. That Cousin Hannah was not only the figure she presented. That the woman who had no time for intimate revelations had intimacies she chose not to reveal.

The bridegroom left at the door is Young's sharpest emblem of this. An epithalamium, a poem written for the bride on her way to the marital chamber, was written, or deserved to be written, for someone who did not walk through that door. The poem was never delivered. The chamber was never occupied. And yet the fact of it (the door, the waiting, the choice made at the threshold) is part of who Cousin Hannah was.

What war has truly accomplished

Mr. Spitzer's meditation on war and legacy is one of the chapter's most politically charged passages, and one of the most honest.

He looks at the list of Cousin Hannah's battles: “the Peloponnesian Wars, the Siege of Rome,” Custer's Last Stand, Sherman's March, the Boer War, Paul Revere's Ride, the Siege of Atlanta, “the burning of Carthage, the taking of Venice,” the Balkan Wars (and then at her own campaign, the hundred-year war for women's suffrage) and he asks: what did it achieve? She is dying of a broken heart, forgotten by the world she fought to change. Her battles have passed into oblivion. The movement she devoted her life to has not finished its work. The rights it won are not secure. They are still being contested.

To All My Darlings notes something that lands with particular weight: suffrage for women took a hundred years, and many rights for women were not in place while Young was alive. And To All My Darlings goes on to observe that we have seen the erosion of these rights, the incompleteness of them worldwide, the organized attempts to roll them back. One can see, from this vantage, where there has to be a complete love, an obsession, for something that might never be achieved in one lifetime.

Cousin Hannah had that love. That obsession. She gave it everything. Young does not tell you it was enough. Young tells you it was what she had and she gave it and the work is not finished and she died sobbing in a tent that smelled like a desert and a pagoda, and Mr. Spitzer sat beside her and kept vigil and could not explain to Catherine what he saw.

Nietzsche's moment, and amor fati

The chapter draws on Nietzsche's concept of eternal recurrence: the thought experiment from Thus Spoke Zarathustra that asks: if you had to live this life over again, exactly as it was, with every pain and every joy, every loss and every failure and every moment of glory, for all eternity, could you love it? Would you choose it?

For Cousin Hannah, the answer implied by the novel is yes. She lived without compromise. She lived at full intensity. She gave herself entirely to the cause that claimed her. The secret wish for marriage, the bridegroom left at the door, the sobbing at the end; these are not refutations of the life. They are the life's full texture. Nietzsche called this amor fati: love of fate. Not acceptance of what happened, not resigned tolerance of what couldn't be changed, but love. Choosing it again. Saying yes to all of it.

Mr. Spitzer, watching from the bedside, cannot achieve this. He has been unable to love his fate for as long as we have known him. He survives. He does not choose.

Dying in obscurity: Hannah and Shulamith Firestone

To All My Darlings makes a connection that Young could not have made (Firestone died in 1970, and Young's novel was published in 1965) but that rings with the force of prophecy: Cousin Hannah dying in obscurity, forgotten by the world she helped create, is reminiscent of Shulamith Firestone's funeral, where mourners grappled with the idea that a whole generation of feminists had been unable to thrive in the world they had done so much to build.

This is one of the oldest and most painful patterns in the history of movements for justice: the people who do the foundational work do not live to see the harvest, and often die in conditions that bear no relationship to the magnitude of what they gave. Cousin Hannah is fictional, but she is made of real people. Her death in that white tent, reduced and sobbing and unrecognized for what she was, is a death Young knew how to write because she had seen its shape in the world.

What to hold onto

Chapter 42 is where the novel delivers what it has been holding back: the actual death of the great suffrage captain, rendered not as myth or legend but as a body in a room, failing, with one faithful if inadequate witness.

Mr. Spitzer could not tell Catherine. He could not find the words, or could not bear to say them, or knew that no description would be adequate to what he saw. The woman who had no time for self-pity died with all the self-pity her body could produce. The woman who “played a mean game of cards” showed all her cards at the end. This is not a failure. This is what dying does to even the most formidable people, and Young shows it to you without flinching because she believes you can bear the truth and that you deserve it.

Catherine made her farewell in a glass carriage, through sleeping cities, in the interior space where all her real relationships lived. It was a real farewell. It counted. Farewell is “a matter of opinion as to the time, the place, the person.” Young believes this. She means for you to believe it too.

Chapter 46: Alp Above Alp Through Consciousness

← Chapter 45 · Guide Home · Chapter 47 →

Research notes: Chapter 46

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Love · Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos

Symbols: Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · Fog and Mist · Moon and Stars · Mountains · Music and Instruments

Allusions: Romantic Poets · The History of Opium · Women's Suffrage

There is an alpenhorn in Chapter 46. It is twice Cousin Hannah's height. Mr. Spitzer, as her executor, takes it, he collects musical instruments, and carries it away from her death chamber into a flat, fog-bound city where it cannot do what it was built to do. An alpenhorn requires mountains. It requires the specific acoustic landscape of the Alps, the way its call bounces off stone walls of ice and carries across valleys that have no equivalent anywhere else on earth. In a coastal lowland, blown by one old lawyer with a silk hat and a second-remove relationship to life, it is a beautiful and useless and entirely right thing.

Chapter 46 is about what we do with the instruments of dead people. Their tools, their methods, their causes, their love: how we carry these things into landscapes where they no longer fit, because we cannot put them down.

What actually happens in Chapter 46

Mr. Spitzer, now acting as Cousin Hannah's executor, sorts through the aftermath of her life with the thoroughness and the grief that the role requires. He takes the alpenhorn. He reflects on what she was: not only a suffrage captain, not only a political figure, but a climber of mountains in the most literal and most metaphorical sense, peaks greater than peaks, Alp above Alp through consciousness, the ascent continuing even after the body gave out.

He wanders afterward through a fog-bound city asking strangers if they have seen her. People take him for mad. He is, in the specific way the novel has always used madness, more precisely sane than the people who regard him with concern. He is doing what grief requires: looking for the person who is gone in every face that isn't hers, asking the question that has no answer because asking it is the only honest response to the loss.

A steeplejack answers him. This tall figure perched high on some ecclesiastical structure, comfortable at heights where most people cannot go, speaks to Mr. Spitzer in paradoxes: “I live because I am dead.” I love because I love not. “All who have loved have died” and drowned. Time is a cloud crossing a clock face that tells no time. The chapter closes with Cousin Hannah's final cry from the deathbed, resurfacing here as the chapter's last image: “Ah, bright star of my love, find your way to the lightless star. Find your way to one who has neither wings nor light. For I am dying now, and” my love goes down.

The alpenhorn in the lowlands

Young's choice of the alpenhorn as Cousin Hannah's instrument, the thing Mr. Spitzer inherits from her death chamber, is characteristically precise.

The alpenhorn is the instrument of distance and altitude. Historically it was used to communicate across Alpine valleys, to call cattle home from high pastures, to announce arrivals and departures across distances that voices could not reach. It is five to twelve feet long. It is made of wood. It produces a sound that is part call and part echo, built for an acoustic environment that most of the world does not have.

In a flat coastal landscape, held by an old lawyer who has never climbed a mountain, it can make a sound but not the sound it was built to make. And yet Mr. Spitzer takes it. He carries the impossible instrument of Cousin Hannah's inner life into a world that cannot receive it properly, because what else do you do? You cannot leave the alpenhorn behind. The alpenhorn is the cause, the love, the aspiration that was Cousin Hannah's and is now, by the accident of survival, his to carry.

This is Young's image for every inheritance of a great life: you receive the instrument. You carry it into your own landscape. You cannot produce the original sound. You try anyway.

Mountains of consciousness

The chapter's opening description of Cousin Hannah as a climber of mountains greater than mountains (peaks of consciousness, ascent continuing Alp above Alp even past death) is one of Young's most concentrated formulations of what the novel means by greatness.

Physical mountains are the obvious correlative: the Matterhorn, Mont Blanc, the Wetterhorn, the Monch, peaks Cousin Hannah is said to have climbed, each one a formidable achievement. But Young immediately escalates: the real mountains were interior. They were the mountains of consciousness: the problems of identity and freedom and love and the nature of reality that Cousin Hannah climbed all her life, without equipment, without a guide, in weather conditions that would have turned back anyone with better judgment.

Nan Shepherd's meditation on the living mountain, the insistence that to aim for the highest point is not the only way to climb, is the counterpoint here. Cousin Hannah aimed for the highest point. Every time. That was her gift and her wound. She could not imagine walking around. She could only imagine going up, and so she fell great distances, and so the distances she fell were proportional to the heights she reached, and so the achievement and the loss were the same scale.

The steeplejack's paradoxes

The steeplejack is one of Young's most quietly extraordinary figures: a person whose profession requires living at heights others cannot reach, maintaining the structures that point upward while everyone below walks on level ground. He appears at the moment when Mr. Spitzer is wandering in grief, asking strangers about the dead woman, and he answers in the only language that the novel has been building toward: paradox.

“I live because I am dead.” I love because I love not.

These are not riddles. They are exact descriptions of states the novel has been mapping since Chapter 1. To live because you are dead: Mr. Spitzer, who has been at a second remove from life since his twin died, who has been waiting to prove that he himself died long ago, who persists without quite living; he lives in this sense, animated by the negation at his center. “I love because I love not”: Cousin Hannah, whose love was defined by its suppression, whose devotion to the cause was the form her unexpressed love took. You love most fiercely what you cannot or will not claim. The refusal is itself a form of love.

Time is a cloud crossing a clock face that tells no time. Young has been building toward this formulation for forty-six chapters. Time in this novel is never the reliable sequential progression that clock-faces propose. It is weather passing over an instrument that was built to measure something it cannot actually contain. The cloud crosses. The clock registers nothing. This is the time Catherine lives in, and Mr. Spitzer, and anyone who has been genuinely inside grief or love or the kind of consciousness that does not move in lines.

The sterility that begets all beautiful things

Mr. Spitzer's meditation on the power of dead beauty, the sterility which begets all beautiful things, is one of the chapter's most philosophically concentrated passages.

The idea has a long lineage. Keats wrote about negative capability, the capacity to remain in uncertainty without irritably reaching after fact and reason, as the condition for great art. The Romantics understood that beauty is inseparable from mortality, that what makes a thing beautiful is in part its transience, its impossibility of being held. Young takes this further: the sterility that begets. Not despite the absence of fertility, but because of it. The dead love, the love that was never consummated, the cause that was never completed; these beget things precisely because they were not finished. Completion closes. Incompletion keeps the door open.

Cousin Hannah's love, killed by false modesty, is more alive in Mr. Spitzer's consciousness than any love that was lived out and resolved and put away. The dead beauty has power that the living beauty never had, because the living beauty becomes ordinary and the dead beauty remains absolute.

Ghosts always clothed

Young offers, in Chapter 46, a curious observation: ghosts in dreams never appear naked. They are always dressed, always clothed in some form, always wearing something. This applies to the living as much as the dead. Identity is always layered. There is no unmediated self available for inspection, no moment when the mask is fully removed and the truth of a person stands bare.

This is not pessimism. It is the novel's honest accounting of what persons are: not naked truths but layered presences, the accumulated costume of a life. Cousin Hannah's iron keys and whaler's hat and rubber coat. Catherine's opium dreams and satin pillows. Mr. Spitzer's silk hat. These are not disguises over a real self; they are as real as anything underneath them. What you put on is what you are, and also more than what you are, and also less.

The ghost appears in the dream wearing the clothes of their life. This is how we know them. This is how we recognize the dead when they come back: by what they were wearing.

Prufrock in the fog

To All My Darlings notes that Mr. Spitzer's existential struggle closely parallels Eliot's The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock: the paralysis, the duality, the sense of time slipping away, the inability to act on what is felt, the awareness of mortality that makes every gesture seem both too small and too large.

Prufrock walks through the fog-bound city asking: do I dare? And in the end, he does not dare. He hears the mermaids singing each to each and does not think they sing for him. He turns back from the overwhelming question. Mr. Spitzer wandering the fog-bound streets asking strangers if they have seen Cousin Hannah is Prufrock's walk rendered without irony, not the missed opportunity of a timid man but the genuine grief of a man who loved in the only way he could manage, which was obliquely, from a distance, and too late.

Young admired Eliot. She knew her Prufrock. The fog that was so precise in that poem, the yellow fog that rubs its back upon the window-panes, is the same fog that has been moving through this novel since the first chapter. It is the atmosphere of consciousness uncertain of itself, of love that knows it cannot be received, of the person who has measured out his life in coffee spoons and is now, in the shadow of a woman's death, finally measuring it against something that was genuinely large.

Ah, bright star of my love

The chapter closes with Cousin Hannah's cry from the deathbed, restored here in its fullness: “Ah, bright star of my love, find your way to the lightless star. Find your way to one who has neither wings nor light. For I am dying now, and” my love goes down.

The echo of Keats's Bright Star sonnet is deliberate. Keats wrote to the star out of his own dying: tuberculosis at twenty-five, the bright star as an emblem of constancy that he could not himself achieve, the tension between the desire for permanence and the knowledge of the body's limits. Cousin Hannah, dying in her white tent, calls to a bright star that is also a dead star: a love that was lightless, wingless, unreachable not because it was too far but because she never allowed herself to reach for it while it could have been reached.

My love goes down. Not upward, into the mountains she climbed all her life. Down. Into the ground, into the dark, into the sea that has been lapping at the edges of this novel since Vera got on the bus. The alpenhorn cannot call it back. The steeplejack knows it. Mr. Spitzer carries the instrument into the lowland fog and tries anyway.

What to hold onto

Chapter 46 is an elegy, not for Cousin Hannah only but for every love that was not said in time, every instrument carried into the wrong landscape, every star called bright that was already going out. Mr. Spitzer collecting the alpenhorn is the novel's emblem for what we do with the lives of the people we could not save and could not fully know: we take what we can carry, we move through the fog asking questions that have no answers, and we listen when the steeplejack speaks from the heights we cannot reach.

Hold onto the steeplejack's paradoxes. “I live because I am dead.” I love because I love not. These will keep mattering. The novel is built on them.

guide-58-the-silent-violinist:
Chapter 58: The Silent Violinist

← Chapter 57 · Guide Home · Chapter 59 →

Research notes: Chapter 58

Characters: Joachim Spitzer

Themes: Music, Sound, and Silence · The Search for Meaning

Symbols: Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · Music and Instruments

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Deafness and Sign Language · Music and Composers

Here is what happens in Chapter 58, stripped to its plainest bones: Mr. Spitzer, the large, black-caped, melancholy composer we've come to know across these hundreds of pages, encounters an old man on the library steps playing an imaginary violin. That's it. That is the entire external event of the chapter.

And yet, as you've learned by now, what appears to be almost nothing in this novel is usually everything.

What actually happens

Mr. Spitzer is passing the library when he sees an old violinist (white-haired, fingers trembling) drawing an imaginary bow across imaginary strings, performing music that makes no sound at all. And here is the first astonishing thing: Mr. Spitzer knows exactly what piece he is playing. He recognizes it immediately as an obscure minor composition from childhood, something almost entirely lost to modern ears. He hears what isn't there.

This is not presented as madness. It is presented as a form of grace.

Mr. Spitzer and music

You've been traveling with Mr. Spitzer for many chapters now, and you know by this point that he is a man whose life is interior: a "silent composer," a "walking scoreboard," someone who carries music within him without ever externalizing it in a form others can easily perceive. He is deaf, or near-deaf, which Young uses not as irony but as logic: the man most attuned to music's deepest nature is the one least dependent on its physical sound.

When Mr. Spitzer watches the old violinist, he is watching a version of himself. Both men make music that exists primarily in the mind and memory. Both are artists whose work goes largely unheard. The encounter isn't just moving; it's a recognition.

The music that isn't there

Young describes the silent performance with extraordinary richness: "singings of blind moths," bird calls, sea shells buzzing like bees, sparks sparking on strings that don't exist. This isn't contradiction. It's Young's deepest argument about what music actually is, not sound waves, but something that precedes sound and survives its absence.

She calls it "pre-musical music": music that existed before human consciousness learned to organize it, and that will persist after individual hearing ceases. The old violinist isn't playing badly or playing nothing. He is playing at the source. This is the chapter's great gift to you as a reader: by the time you've spent this many pages inside Young's prose, you've been trained to hear what isn't audible. You have been practicing for exactly this moment.

The question of whether he is alive

Mr. Spitzer watches the old man's wild, convulsive movements, the intensity of the performance, and cannot determine whether what he is witnessing is music at its highest expression or a man in the process of dying. Young refuses to resolve this. The violinist is in a liminal space, and so is Mr. Spitzer, and so, by this point in the novel, are you.

This ambiguity is not evasion. It is the chapter's central claim: that the boundaries between living and dead, between sound and silence, between reality and dream, are not where we think they are. Mr. Spitzer concludes the chapter by acknowledging that he no longer clearly distinguishes between reality and dreams, between life and death, and calls this indistinction his "only wisdom." The confusion is not failure. It is what he has learned.

The surprising turn: baseball

In the middle of contemplating silent cosmic music, Mr. Spitzer starts thinking about baseball. And billiards. And polo. And fishing. And kingship.

Don't let this throw you. What he is doing is imagining the old violinist as someone else entirely: what if this man had become an athlete instead of a musician? What if the instrument in his hand had been a bat, a cue, a fishing rod, a scepter? Reality, Mr. Spitzer reflects, is "made up of just so many sticks and not one stick more." The violinist is a violinist because of the particular stick he picked up. He could have been anyone.

This is not a joke. It is Young's persistent argument about identity: that the self is not fixed, that we are each a convergence of contingencies, that another version of any one of us could be doing something entirely different with the same essential soul.

Mr. Spitzer, who prides himself on his belief that music and baseball are "fused into his psychology," is not being eccentric here. He is being consistent. Both require practice, discipline, rhythm, and the willingness to perform within a collective. Both produce beauty that disappears the moment it's made.

His brother

Woven through Mr. Spitzer's observations of the violinist is his grief for his dead brother, and his sense that the dead continue to shape us, that they do not simply vanish. The violinist's music, nearly forgotten, nearly lost, keeps pulling Mr. Spitzer back toward the people and sounds that time is trying to erase.

This is one of the chapter's quieter sadnesses: that Mr. Spitzer knows exactly how obscure that old waltz is, how few people would recognize it, and still, it is completely vivid to him. The things we love do not always survive us into the world's memory. But they survive in us, for as long as we last.

The black cape

Notice, as you've been doing, what characters wear. Mr. Spitzer's black cape has appeared throughout the novel as his signature: his boundary marker, his way of moving through a world that is too much for him. Young describes his shadow drifting, his cape as a cloak of darkness he carries. He is not morbid so much as honest: he knows he is a liminal figure, a man equally at home among the living and the dead, and he has learned to dress accordingly.

What to hold onto

An old man on library steps, playing an instrument that isn't there, performing a waltz almost no one remembers, watched by a deaf composer who hears every note. Two men making invisible music together. This is what art does, Young is telling you: it creates connection across the impossible distances, between the living and the dead, between sound and silence, between one interior world and another.

You have been learning, across the length of this novel, to hear the music that isn't audible. Chapter 58 is Young acknowledging that you've learned it.

guide-39-the-infinite-house:
Chapter 39: The Infinite House

← Chapter 38 · Guide Home · Chapter 40 →

Research notes: Chapter 39

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Lord Murdock Burdock Thrushmorton · Miss MacIntosh · Mr. Res Tacamah · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Faith, God, and the Supernatural · Madness and Sanity · Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos · The Search for Meaning

Symbols: Fog and Mist · Opium · The House · The Sea and Water

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology · Marguerite Young on Her Craft · Plato and Platonism · William James and Pragmatism

Allusions: Ancient Egypt · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · The History of Opium · Women's Suffrage

There is a sentence in Chapter 39 that stops the novel in its tracks (gently, the way a hand on a shoulder stops you, not violently) and asks you to see exactly what you are looking at.

It is “as if the perpendicular pronoun I had come to see my horizontal mother.”

Read it again. The perpendicular I. The horizontal mother. Vera, upright, moving through the world under her own locomotion. Catherine, flat, having surrendered the vertical axis entirely. Two orientations, two modes of being, meeting across the impossible geometry of love and need and the fact that one of them gave birth to the other and neither of them can fully reach across.

Chapter 39 is a portrait of Catherine's interior: her consciousness mapped as architecture, her madness examined with the patient precision of someone who has lived inside it long enough to give it a floor plan. It is one of the most sustained and searching portraits of a mind in the novel. Settle in.

What actually happens in Chapter 39

Vera describes how her mother thinks, and why. Catherine receives visitors, or imagines she receives them: Cousin Hannah's ghost, Lord Murdock Burdock Thrushmorton (whose name alone tells you the register Young is operating in), Mr. Res Tacamah, who controls his madness by dreaming rather than acting. Real visitors, imagined visitors, symbolic visitors: Catherine does not always distinguish between them, and Young does not always tell you which is which.

The chapter is also, quietly, about opium. Catherine acknowledges, with the clarity that is only available to someone deep inside a thing, that the drug has “poisoned all pleasures at their source.” She does not say this with the guilt of someone who intends to stop. She says it as a description. This is what happened. This is the swirling fog. This is how the stars got moved out of their stations.

The chapter ends at the shoreline: sea meeting land, the dead meeting the living, the fog as the habitat of absent-minded persons who walk “with their eyes hidden behind their hands.” And then a final question, one that the novel has been circling since its first page: if everything is a dream, is God dreaming too? Is religion itself the longest opium dream of all?

The infinite house

Young gives Catherine's soul the shape of a house. Not a modest house: an infinite one. Many rooms, many stairways, many heavens. Each room contains a different version of Catherine, or a different guest, or a missing element she has been looking for in all the other rooms. The floors waver like water. The walls seem to move. She has been walking through this house for decades and has not found the exit, and may not be looking for one.

This is one of the novel's great metaphors, and it rewards attention. The infinite house is not a prison exactly: Catherine is not suffering in any simple sense. She is genuinely at home in this architecture. It is the only space she knows. But it is a space from which she cannot leave, and a space in which she cannot be reliably found by anyone standing outside it.

Vera is outside it. Vera has always been outside it. The perpendicular I visits the horizontal mother in the house of the horizontal mother's mind, and they speak through the wall between their orientations, and something passes between them, and it is not nothing. But it is not the same as being in the same room.

Sanity's strange definition

Watch for the moment when Catherine offers her definition of her own sanity: her “sanity was simply this—she knew she was insane.”

This is not irony, though it sounds like it. Young means it as a genuine philosophical position, and it echoes a long tradition of thinking about madness and self-knowledge. The person who cannot see their own condition is more thoroughly lost than the person who can name it. Catherine names hers. She has given it a shape, a floor plan, a set of recurring guests. She knows the dragons in her labyrinth by name. This is a form of mastery, even if it is not a form of escape.

Troubles are cyclical, Catherine observes. They appear in different guises (dragons turning into saints, saints turning back into dragons) but the cycle itself is stable. She has learned not to be surprised. This is cold comfort, but it is comfort.

The novel is doing something careful here about the relationship between self-knowledge and cure. Catherine knows herself extraordinarily well, in the particular, partial, introspective way that opium and decades of horizontal time allow. This knowledge has not saved her. Young does not suggest it should have. Self-knowledge in this novel is not a therapeutic tool. It is a form of company: the self keeping itself company in the infinite house, learning the contours of its own labyrinth.

The multiple selves, and the cost of choosing

Catherine contemplates, in Chapter 39, the possibility of selecting one of her many selves and becoming it fully. She considers this and rejects it. To choose one self would mean losing all the fascinating false selves that have sustained her: the great courtesan, the avant-garde traveler, the woman who might have gone to Egypt, to Italy, to the land of the Kurds, to any of the other destinations her imagination has furnished with such care.

Young is working here with William James, whom she named as a major influence. James wrote that the self is not a single thing but a stream: a continuous flow of consciousness that contains many potential selves, many versions of the person we “might be or might have been.” To crystallize into one self is to foreclose the others. Catherine has refused this foreclosure. She has chosen multiplicity over coherence, and the cost is a self that cannot be pinned down, cannot be reliably located, cannot be found in the same room twice.

There is something Young admires in this, even as she shows its costs. To remain multiple is to remain open. Catherine's infinite house has more rooms than a life devoted to a single, coherent self would ever build. Young, who spent decades writing a novel as vast and various as a city, knew something about this refusal herself.

Opium and religion, religion and opium

The chapter arrives, near its end, at one of the novel's most daring juxtapositions: opium as religion, religion as opium.

Marx said it plainly: religion is the opium of the people, a drug that dulls the pain of social reality and makes the unbearable bearable, at the cost of preventing the sufferer from addressing the causes of their suffering. Young takes this analogy and turns it inside out. If religion is opium, then opium is religion: it offers transcendence, visions, a world of angels and ethereal light, an extension of experience beyond the physical. Catherine's drug-induced paradise is furnished with the same materials as any heaven.

But Young complicates both the opium and the religion. She does not simply condemn Catherine's illusions as escapism. She shows that for a person in Catherine's condition (caught in the labyrinth, unable to stand, surrounded by loss) the illusions may be what is keeping her alive. The fog is suffocating and it is also breath. The dream is a prison and it is also the only room with a window.

Miss MacIntosh's critique hovers over this passage like a weather front: face reality, face the bare face of things, refuse the comfortable lie. But Miss MacIntosh is gone. And Catherine is still here, in the infinite house, dreaming. Young leaves the argument open. She does not award the point to either position.

The visitors: real and assembled

Lord Murdock Burdock Thrushmorton and Mr. Res Tacamah deserve a moment of attention. These are not minor characters in the conventional sense; they are more like ideas Catherine has personified, given names and social manners, invited in for tea.

Lord Murdock Burdock Thrushmorton twitters like a cage of canaries. His name is a Gothic comedy: the kind of name that announces itself as excessive, as too much, as something assembled from parts that don't quite cohere. He represents the chaotic and the absurd in Catherine's world: the element that cannot be reasoned with or predicted, that arrives without warning and fills the room with incomprehensible sound.

Mr. Res Tacamah controls his madness by dreaming rather than acting, which is to say, he has chosen Catherine's strategy, the strategy of the infinite house. His drug bottle is Catherine's drug bottle. He is a self-portrait she has distributed into someone else's name, given a separate residence in the house so she can look at herself without looking.

Young learned this technique in the classroom. The note in To All My Darlings points to it directly: she would say, 'Oh, come in,' to every idea that arrived. Every voice got a chair. Every contradiction got a name and a face and a place at the table. This is how the novel is built. This is how Catherine's mind is built. The guests are ideas, the house is a philosophy, and the hostess has been receiving visitors for longer than anyone can remember.

The shore, the fog, and the question God leaves open

The chapter closes at the water's edge, which is where Young returns when she needs to mark a threshold. Sea meeting shore: the dead meeting the living, the known meeting the unknown, the boundary that moves with every wave and can never be fixed.

The fog, Young tells us, is where absent-minded persons walk “with their eyes hidden behind their hands.” Catherine is one of them. Perhaps all of us, at certain hours, are. The fog is not only fog; it is the condition of being in between, of not being able to see clearly ahead or behind, of moving through a space where the usual landmarks have dissolved.

And then the final question: if everything is a dream, is God dreaming too? Is the universe itself a hallucination generated by a consciousness larger than any individual one, and if so, does that make it more real or less?

Young does not answer. She is not being coy. She genuinely believes the question should stay open: that to close it would be to commit the error Catherine's opium commits: to insist on a particular vision of the architecture when the architecture keeps shifting. The fog has its own kind of truth. The absent-minded walkers with their eyes behind their hands are seeing something, even if it is not what the upright, perpendicular world sees.

What to hold onto

Chapter 39 is a chapter about a woman who built a world inside her mind because the outside world was not sufficient: was too thin, too narrow, too insistent on coherence. The inside world is vast and labyrinthine and costs her everything. And she has chosen it anyway.

You don't have to agree with her choice to understand it. You have to understand that it is a choice, made by a person with intelligence and imagination and a history that drove her here, and that it has its own dignity alongside its costs.

Vera stands perpendicular at the door of the infinite house, watching. She has been standing there her whole life. She came here looking for Miss MacIntosh, who once stood in this house and insisted it face reality, and was eventually swallowed by the same fog she tried to dispel. The door is still open. The mother is still horizontal. The house has no exit that anyone has found.

guide-35-she-had-been-married-to-the-suf:
Chapter 35: She Had Been Married to the Suffrage Movement

← Chapter 34 · Guide Home · Chapter 36 →

Research notes: Chapter 35

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Exploration and the Poles · Women's Suffrage

Chapter 35 is the last chapter devoted primarily to Cousin Hannah, and it is the most expansive. Young returns to Hannah’s public life (the suffrage campaigns, the foreign adventures, the iron keys and metallic presence) but now through the lens of Catherine’s longing: what it would mean if Hannah came back, what Catherine understands now that she resisted then, and what the great captain’s life finally amounted to.

This chapter is also the one where Young brings the reader closest to understanding why Cousin Hannah could not rescue Catherine. The answer, she suggests, was that Hannah’s faith in the suffrage movement (absolute, consuming, bride-like) was itself a form of the same retreat from ordinary human love that Catherine had made in the other direction. They were mirror images who could not see each other clearly.

What actually happens in Chapter 35

Catherine imagines inviting Cousin Hannah back for a long winter season, and thinks through what their relationship was and what it might now be. She would greet her without reserve now, take off her plumed hat, ask her to be seated. She would understand now what “she had not wished to understand” then.

The chapter catalogs Hannah’s suffrage career in its most complete form: the campaigns on “all fronts known and unknown, domestic and foreign and undiscovered, the” riding through distant capitals already evacuated, the triumphing over empire-makers and demoniac hordes, the refusal of a stained glass window in her memory. It also catalogs what Hannah was not: not a dancer, not a conversationalist, not a domestic figure, not someone who had time for old wounds or intimate revelations or confessions “that one had loved in secret what one” denied in public.

Young gives us the chapter’s central statement near its end: Hannah had been married “to the suffrage movement, even as if she were a bride, as if the suffrage movement were her husband, her lord and master who had carried her away.” “She had been married to no other husband.”

Married to the movement

The image of Hannah married to the suffrage movement is Young’s most complete statement of how Hannah solved, or did not solve, the problem of her own nature. The movement was “her true love, her awesome husband, the masculine dream of her life, the abundant resource of her strength.”

Young places this with characteristic precision: Hannah could not have been persuaded to confess that “she had yearned for marriage, or she had loved a man. Or she had yearned for a homunculus, a little man, a” “gentleman’s gentleman to wait on her.” The substitution of the suffrage movement for personal love is Hannah’s parallel to Catherine’s substitution of the phantom bridegroom, or Miss MacIntosh’s substitution of practical ordinariness. All three women in the novel’s inner circle have built their lives around something that stands in for what cannot be named or lived directly. Hannah’s substitute was the grandest and most public. It was also, in its way, the most complete: she was, as Young says, “this great lord, scythe sword in hand, her head reaching among the stars, this mighty captain who had rescued so many fair ladies in distress, breaking their invisible chains.”

She became the husband she could not have. She rescued the women she could not be rescued by. The suffrage movement was her marriage, and like all the marriages in this novel, it was a wedding to an absence.

Hannah’s buried life

Young gives us, near the chapter’s end, the sharpest contrast between Catherine and Hannah: Catherine is haunted by Catherine’s “buried life—by a contingent existence, the inexpressible, a way of life she had not chosen or had abandoned.” “Hannah’s life had not been haunted by” Hannah’s buried life.

This is both Hannah’s strength and her limitation. She had followed seemingly only one course, had never divided herself into opposing factions, “had forgotten herself long ago, perhaps in the great battle of the white eunuchs with the black eunuchs.” “She did not need to wage war with herself.” She had an external enemy (man, physical and present) and this meant she never had to confront the battle within.

Catherine’s many selves (“the look-out in the crow’s-nest, the negress in the belfry, the human barometer,” “the lady in the phaeton, the figurehead in the foam”) are the price of Catherine’s interior complexity, her willingness to contain contradictions. Hannah’s single-mindedness, her unity of character, was what Catherine most admired and least resembled. It was also what made Hannah unable to fully reach her.

Young adds her most cautionary note here: “the extremities of faith in anything might always beget” its opposite. Hannah’s total faith in the suffrage movement may have contained, at its extreme limit, its own negation. “Death might be the parent of love—or love” the parent of death. Catherine had always known this. Hannah, apparently, had not.

What Hannah could not do

The chapter contains one of Young’s most careful negative portraits: all the things Hannah could not do or be. She could not dance. She could not take her place in a minuet, balancing between right foot and left, shifting weight from one side to the other. She had never appeared in a ballroom. She had escorted no lady to the dance.

She had no time for intimate revelation, for the moment when one confesses that one is “the opposite of what one seemed, that all one’s life” has been a living lie, “that one had loved in secret what one” denied in public. That is the confession she could not make. That is what the loss of the skirt was about.

Young also tells us that Hannah had refused a stained glass window in her memory; “she had believed in no image, neither the living nor the dead.” After five chapters of Hannah’s life, this detail lands with unexpected weight. The woman who had ridden through every country, who had seen everything, who had known the secrets of husbands whispered to dead wives and wives whispered to dead husbands: refused to be made into an image. She would not be fixed. She would not be memorialized. “She had believed in no image,” which means she had believed in no representation of herself as a single, stable thing.

What to watch for as you keep reading

Light spoilers: This section hints at what happens later in the novel. Skip it if you want to meet the story fresh.

With Chapter 35, the Cousin Hannah sequence closes, and Volume One of the novel is drawing toward its end. We are in the last chapters of the first movement. After the break, the novel will follow Vera on her bus journey and into the wider American landscape Young has been preparing us for.

The image Catherine uses of herself (these many selves, these fragmentations of partial selves, splintered mirrors and partial images) is the novel’s self-description. Miss MacIntosh, My Darling is a novel of partial selves and splintered mirrors. Every character is an incomplete portrait of the others. Each is complete only in combination with the rest. Young has been building this from the first page.

Hannah’s observation that it was colder at home (colder than the Antarctic, colder than the glacial mountains, colder than any place the great explorers had discovered and named after their wives) is the novel’s most compressed statement about why people leave. The sleeping lady in the bed of snow, “with the snow falling on a lacy counterpane”: this is what the great Antarctic explorers were escaping. This is what Catherine has been: the cold at the center of the house. The one who cannot be warmed.

guide-69-the-room-marked-fire-escape:
Chapter 69: The Room Marked Fire Escape

← Chapter 68 · Guide Home · Chapter 70 →

Research notes: Chapter 69

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Esther Longtree · Justice O’Leary · Miss MacIntosh · Moses Hunnecker · Mr. Weed · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Freedom and Escape · Guilt, Innocence, and Justice

Symbols: Angels, Devils, and Myth · Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · Fire · The House

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology · Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Genesis · Revelation and the Apocalypse · Shakespeare · The Bible · The History of Opium

Vera has a room now. It is marked “Fire Escape.”

The bed is narrow and stuffed with corn husks. There is a warped mirror that shows only her eyes. There is a slop jar with sediment and blonde hair combings in it. On the wall, “a picture of a silver church steeple” with the words “Forget me not.” And a rocking chair that is already creaking, though no one is sitting in it.

This is where Vera will spend the night. She does not sleep. How could she? The Tavern is alive with presences: Mr. Weed’s shadow moving in the corridor, an old woman with canaries as big as turkey buzzards, a young girl named Tillie who will knit Vera a baby hood in the morning, and, through the thin wall beside her, the all-night anguish of Dr. Justice O’Leary, who is in there talking to someone named Sarah.

Sarah is dead. Or possibly not. That, as with everything in this novel, depends on your definition of real.

What Actually Happens

The landlord shows Vera to her room, taking the long way through the hotel’s corridors, pointing out the other inhabitants as he goes: Moses, who has a room here; Tillie, who lives across the hall and knits; the old woman with her terrible canaries. He tells Vera about Mr. Weed and his shadow: the shadow, apparently, being more talkative than the man himself. He is the kind of guide who tells you everything except what you actually need to know.

Once she is alone, Vera lies on her corn-husk mattress and listens. The hotel thinks out loud around her. And through the wall, Dr. Justice O’Leary begins.

He is old and failing, a physician of the old school, haunted and possibly mad. He is conducting a one-sided argument with Sarah: a woman who is dead, who may be a ghost, who arrives in his room smelling of cold breath and covered in sores, who he calls “baby” and “you old fool” and “the last disgrace of my life.” He curses her. He mourns her. He asks God why he has been abandoned. He tells her she should be ashamed. He cannot make her leave. He cannot stop talking to her. He also, in the course of the night, tells Vera (through the wall, through the strange permeability of this hotel) about his strangest case: a woman who believes she is “always pregnant with an imaginary baby” and suffers from miscarriage after miscarriage. Remember that detail. That woman will matter.

By morning, Vera is still awake. So, presumably, is Dr. O’Leary. Sarah, as always, is somewhere between.

The Room Marked Fire Escape

Vera’s room is not incidental. Young has given her a room designed for emergency egress (a room whose entire purpose is to get out, in case of catastrophe) and furnished it with the remnants of whoever was here before. The slop jar with its sediment and blonde hair combings. The rocking chair creaking on its own. The mirror that shows only eyes, not a face. The church steeple on the wall saying “Forget me not.”

Everything in this room is a trace of absence. Someone was here. They left things behind. The hotel has not cleaned them out. Forget me not: but the person who hung that picture is already forgotten, already sediment, already a combings-in-a-jar. The room is an escape and it is also a record. This is one of the novel’s recurring compressions: the thing that promises freedom is also the thing that documents everything you can’t escape from. Memory works this way. So does this hotel. So does this book.

The Landlord

He is loquacious: To All My Darlings uses that word and it is the right one. He has a tattooed chest that once had a lion on it, now faded. He has been a sailor, a soldier, a performer. He worked in intelligence during the Last War (the novel’s term for World War II, since World War I was the Great War). He has run this hotel through floods and fires. He listens to everyone. He trusts almost nothing.

He tells Vera about Mr. Weed’s shadow the way an innkeeper might pass along local legend: as information you’ll need, delivered casually, without alarm. In his telling, Mr. Weed is cautious and reserved; the shadow is the garrulous one, more forthcoming than the man himself. The shadow does his talking for him. This is the kind of doubling Young loves: the self and its unspeakable counterpart, the visible man and the part of him that moves freely in corridors at night.

He also mentions Tillie in passing: a very young girl who lives across from Vera’s room and will knit her a baby hood. Young slips this in without comment. A young girl in a decaying hotel, knitting baby hoods. We don’t know who the hoods are for. The landlord doesn’t say. He has moved on to something else.

Dr. Justice O’Leary and Sarah

This is the chapter’s heart, and it is one of the strangest and most affecting passages in the novel.

Dr. O’Leary is aging, bitter, professionally diminished, and haunted. His name is a small joke: his first name is Justice, and justice is exactly what he cannot locate, not in his own past, not in Sarah’s fate, not in the body’s failures, not in God’s apparent indifference. He has been a doctor his entire life and he does not know what Sarah is or how to treat her or how to make her stop appearing.

Sarah is described variously as a dead woman, a baby, a senile presence, something cold and covered in sores. She is not, or not only, a ghost. She is the thing Dr. O’Leary cannot stop carrying: a disgrace, a loss, a patient he failed, a person he loved and damaged, a past that will not close. Young does not explain her. You are not meant to have a resolved answer about what Sarah is. You are meant to understand what she does: she keeps him awake, keeps him talking, keeps him from the ordinary mercy of forgetting. He cries out in her voice the words of Christ on the cross: “My God! Why hast thou deserted me?” The line is from Psalm 22, spoken by Jesus in the Gospels at the moment of maximum abandonment. Dr. O’Leary uses it not for theological effect but because it is the most accurate description he has of his situation. He has been left. By Sarah, by competence, by faith, by the body’s cooperation, by whatever it is that used to make medicine feel like service rather than futility.

He also invokes “Let this cup pass from him”: Jesus in Gethsemane, asking God if there is any way to avoid what is coming. There is not. Dr. O’Leary knows there is not. He asks anyway, into the thin wall, all night.

Vera hears all of this. She doesn’t intervene. She is becoming a kind of collector of these voices (Mr. Weed last chapter, Dr. O’Leary tonight) people who are talking past their own capacity to resolve anything, who are saying the thing that cannot be said and saying it anyway because the alternative is silence and silence is worse.

The Strangest Case

Dr. O’Leary tells Vera (through the wall, in the middle of his long night of grief) about the strangest patient he ever had: a woman who believes herself “always pregnant with an imaginary baby,” who suffers miscarriage after miscarriage, who cannot stop expecting the child that is not coming.

Hold this. Young is introducing, in passing, through a physician’s corridor-monologue, the character of Esther Longtree, who will become one of the novel’s great figures in the chapters to come. You are being told about her before you meet her, in the voice of the man who failed to help her, in a hotel that already knows her by reputation. The novel prepares its characters this way: not with introductions but with rumors, with secondhand grief, with the doctor’s bafflement and the wall’s thin membrane.

A woman “always pregnant with an imaginary baby.” She is, in some sense, every character in this book: waiting for something that is perpetually expected and perpetually withheld. She is Vera, waiting for Miss MacIntosh. She is Catherine, waiting for her opium dreams to resolve into solid ground. She is the novel itself, always gestating, never quite arriving.

What the Tavern Is

By the end of this chapter you have a clearer picture of what the Tavern actually is. It is not simply a run-down hotel. It is a way station for the unresolved: people who are between things, who have not yet become what they are going to be or mourned what they have lost or finished the arguments they are having with the dead. Moses has a room here. Mr. Weed stays here. Dr. O’Leary apparently lives here. Tillie knits baby hoods here. The landlord says it is “a good enough port for a man in a storm.” He means this practically. Young means it cosmologically. Everyone in this hotel is in a storm. The port holds them without resolving anything. That is the most it can offer, and it is not nothing.

The hotel was “built in 1827 by God’s servants” and is now given over to thin walls and human-faced wasps and rocking chairs that move on their own. The faith that built it has become atmosphere. The walls remember everything. The slop jar holds what is left.

What to Hold Onto

The room marked Fire Escape. Vera’s room is for getting out, and she cannot sleep in it.

Mr. Weed’s shadow, moving in the corridor at night, more talkative than the man himself. The shadow that speaks what the body won’t. Dr. O’Leary and Sarah: a physician who cannot heal what haunts him, asking the same questions Jesus asked in the garden, all night, through a wall.

The woman “always pregnant with an imaginary baby.” She is coming.

And the picture on the wall (a silver church steeple, “Forget me not”) which is already, of course, the thing you cannot forget: that someone was here, in this bed, looking at this picture, and now they are gone. As everyone is gone. As Miss MacIntosh is gone. As the chapter ends before anything is resolved, and Vera lies awake in the dark, still listening.

guide-24-after-all-how-else-should-they-:
Chapter 24: After All, How Else Should They Keep Their Jobs?

← Chapter 23 · Guide Home · Chapter 25 →

Research notes: Chapter 24

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos

Symbols: The Sea and Water

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology · Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Ancient Egypt · Genesis · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · Napoleon and Wellington · Shakespeare · Women's Suffrage

Chapter 24 marks a shift. After nine chapters in the intense, close world of the birthday night and its aftermath, Young pulls back the camera. We are still at the breakfast table, still in the morning after, but now Vera’s mind moves away from Miss MacIntosh and out into the house, into the servants’ quarters, into Catherine’s bedroom, into the vast social machinery of imaginary guests and disconnected telephone lines.

Think of this chapter as a wide establishing shot after a long series of close-ups. It shows you the full scale of the world Vera has been living in. And it ends with Vera asking, quietly and without an answer, who on earth she is supposed to turn to.

What actually happens in Chapter 24

Vera’s mind, sitting at the breakfast table with Miss MacIntosh, moves through the household. She thinks about the servants, who have absorbed Catherine’s dream world so completely that they argue about whether it is Roman in the morning and Greek in the afternoon, polish shoes left out by imaginary guests, wait on Wellington, believe they live in forests of cuckoo clocks, drive Hannibal’s elephants over the Alps.

She thinks about Catherine: the horizontal lady who will “die in the midst of her dreams,” who discusses her own obsequies endlessly with absent social secretaries, who calls Athens on a telephone connected only to the servants’ quarters and gets Rome, who has been trying for years to reach Cousin Hannah on a number that was disconnected long ago.

She thinks about Mr. Spitzer, who is coming again in the evening, “filled with his usual euphemistic certainties” about a Heaven that will unite us all, and utterly uncertain about this earth.

The chapter ends with Vera’s question: to whom should she turn, asking the personal questions that burn in her “mind, questions as to the secret purpose of life,” love, marriage, reproduction, death? Her imagination wanders “like a dark and formless cloud, seeking” a certitude it might never have.

The servants’ sea change

Young has mentioned the servants throughout the novel, but Chapter 24 gives us our fullest portrait of what Catherine’s household does to ordinary people over time. “After an hour or a year or many years in this employment,” even the most sensible servants undergo what Young calls a sea change. They reach for door knobs that are not door knobs. They open doors that are not doors. They “stagger to and fro chasing illusions like butterflies.”

And yet (and Young gives this its own line, which stops you) after all, “how else should they keep their jobs?”

The servants have adapted. They have entered into Catherine’s spirit because that is the only way to function in this household. The one who polishes imaginary guests’ shoes, the valet who waits on Wellington, the housemaid who speaks only to herself and is several fine ladies simultaneously; these are not mad people. They are people who have found the only workable response to an impossible situation: go along, elaborate, make yourself useful to the dream.

Young is generous about this. She does not mock the servants. She presents their adaptation as logical, even wise. The alternative (refusing the dream, insisting on the real) is Miss MacIntosh’s approach, and we know what that cost her. The servants chose differently. Neither choice is free.

Catherine’s telephone

The image of Catherine as an entire telephone exchange, calling dead numbers and reaching wrong parties, is one of the novel’s great comic inventions and also one of its most moving.

She calls Athens and gets Rome. She calls the Bishop of Hippo and he has just stepped out. She calls the Emperor Hadrian and he has gone into his garden. King Canute is on a long voyage. The Lowells and the Saltonstalls never seem to be home. Cousin Hannah’s number was disconnected long ago. Uncle Ronald is dead. Uncle Bernard died in Moscow carrying a message to the czar.

Her telephone, it turns out, is connected only to the servants’ quarters. She never guesses this. She thinks she is placing transatlantic calls, “calls ship to shore, star to star, these calls from the living to the dead.” She is leaving messages with the second butler who believes he is the Great Emir.

The gap between what Catherine believes she is doing and what she is actually doing is the gap the novel is organized around. She is in her room. She is talking to the servants. She believes she is in communication with the dead, the famous, the cosmic. Young does not decide which of these is more true. The Bishop of Hippo always just stepped out. He may be just around the corner.

Cousin Hannah

This is the first time Cousin Hannah’s name appears in the novel, and Young drops it so quietly that you might miss it. Catherine has been trying to reach her on a telephone number that was disconnected long ago. Why had Cousin Hannah never called?

Cousin Hannah is one of the novel’s major figures: the Boston feminist, the balloonist, the mountain climber, the militant suffragette known through the seraglios of the East as Al Hamad. She will have her own chapters later, and she is one of Young’s most extraordinary characters. But she arrives here first as an absence: a disconnected number, a name Catherine reaches for and cannot find.

Notice it. She will arrive in full later. For now she is a name in a list of unreachable people, and that is where Young wants her to begin: among the dead and the missing and the ones who have sailed away.

To whom should I have turned?

The chapter’s final question is the one that closes the entire Miss MacIntosh sequence. Vera has spent nine chapters living through the revelation and its aftermath, learning something enormous about the one person she trusted to be solid and ordinary and real. And now, at the breakfast table in the morning sunlight, she asks: who is left?

Not Catherine, who places “her faith only in the unreal.” Not the servants, who have adapted to the dream. Not Mr. Spitzer, who is so unsure of himself that he cannot remember his own memories as well as strangers’, whose evasions exceed even his own understanding. And not, anymore, Miss MacIntosh in the way Vera once understood her, though she is right there, “coarse-grained and ruddy, her red hair gleaming like another light.”

Vera’s imagination wanders “like a dark and formless cloud, seeking” a certitude it might never have. Young leaves her there, wandering. The breakfast is over. The novel is about to move on. Vera will keep wandering (across cities, across years, across eight hundred more pages) looking for Miss MacIntosh in What Cheer, Iowa, and finding, instead, the whole of America.

What to watch for as you keep reading

Light spoilers: This section hints at what happens later in the novel. Skip it if you want to meet the story fresh.

The novel is about to open dramatically. Chapter 25 and beyond will introduce new characters and new storylines, and you will sometimes feel as if you have lost the thread entirely. You have not. Young is building what Anaïs Nin described as spokes of a wheel: every digression, every new character, every detour leads back to the same center, which is the question Vera cannot stop asking: what is real, what is illusion, and what do we do when the only person who taught us the difference turns out to have been something other than we thought?

Catherine’s phrase for Mr. Spitzer, “a roundhouse of the trains which run no more,” is one of the novel’s great compressed portraits of a character. Mr. Spitzer as a building designed to house trains that no longer run, a structure whose purpose has been overtaken by time, whose tracks are crossed in eternal darkness, whose signal lights show red where they should show green. It is tender and precise and entirely in Catherine’s voice.

The gardener who believes he is the spouse to Potiphar is a detail worth holding. In the book of Genesis, Potiphar is the Egyptian captain whose wife falsely accuses Joseph of assault: a story about betrayal, false witness, and the person who tells the wrong story about another. Young places one of the servants inside that story without comment. In this household, everyone is inside a story. The question is always which one.

guide-61-the-frog-in-his-throat:
Chapter 61: The Frog in His Throat

← Chapter 60 · Guide Home · Chapter 62 →

Research notes: Chapter 61

Characters: Joachim Spitzer

Themes: Duality and Doubles

Symbols: Mirrors and Reflections · Silence and Deafness

Philosophy: Heraclitus and Flux · Kant and Hegel · Marguerite Young on Her Craft · Plato and Platonism

Allusions: American Writers · Deafness and Sign Language · Music and Composers

There is an old idiom, "a frog in his throat", that means the inability to speak, especially from overwhelming emotion. Young knows this. Chapter 61 is built on it, very deliberately, and by the end of the chapter she has made it into something that will stay with you.

What actually happens

Mr. Spitzer encounters an old mute who has trained a frog to speak for him. The frog lives in the mute's mouth. It has learned to croak human words, including, we are told, the Lord's Prayer. The mute is his voice. The frog is the mute's voice. The chain of substitution goes all the way down.

When Mr. Spitzer meets him, the frog has died.

Together, the two men (a near-deaf composer who makes music no one hears, and a mute who has just lost the only voice he ever had) walk to an upland meadow scattered with wildflowers and bury the frog. Then they walk back. The way back, Mr. Spitzer notices, seems shorter than the way there.

That is all that externally happens. Everything else is what Mr. Spitzer thinks while it is happening.

The mute as mirror

By this point in the novel, you know Mr. Spitzer well: a man whose music is inaudible, who exists at the edges of perception, who cannot always “tell the living from the dead.” The old mute is his perfect double. Here is someone for whom silence is not metaphor but reality: a man who has never been able to hear the world's sounds, who exists in a country whose language he cannot access, a stranger in every room he enters.

Mr. Spitzer watches the mute's hands moving through their complex sign language (crosses, circles, directions, shapes that mean many things at once or nothing that can be pinned down) and tries to interpret them. He cannot, entirely. But he doesn't need to. He understands the essential thing: this man is grieving, and the grief has no outlet, and it is immense.

He wonders, as he walks with the mute toward the meadow, whether the mute is his ideal audience. His music, after all, is inaudible. A deaf man who cannot hear it is no different, in practical terms, from anyone else. And yet the mute is present. He is there, walking beside him. Sometimes presence is the thing.

The meadow

Young gives the frog's burial meadow one of the most extraordinary passages in the novel: a long inventory of wildflowers, grasses, and herbs, each one carrying its own symbolism. Milkwort and moonwort, nightshade and heliotrope, frog lilies and star grass and wild rambler roses and moon vines. The meadow is a threshold, and Young populates it accordingly: plants associated with nurturing and plants associated with poison, plants that turn toward the sun and plants that thrive in shadow, plants named for the creatures of water and plants named for the stars.

You don't need to look up every plant, though the "For the Curious" section at the end touches on a few, but do notice what Young is doing: she is making the act of burial into something cosmic. The frog was small. Its grave is surrounded by nature's symbolic vocabulary. This is not disproportionate. Young believes that everything small contains everything large.

Mr. Spitzer drops a red rose into the grave before the earth covers it. The red rose: immortality, resurrection, love that persists. For a frog.

The idiom made literal

The mute's frog was in his throat (literally, the animal living in his mouth) and also in the older, emotional sense: it was the block between silence and speech, between feeling and expression. Now the frog is dead, and the mute is left with nothing but his hands. His frog in his throat is gone. He cannot even croak the Lord's Prayer.

Young is doing something very quiet and very devastating here. The idiom "a frog in my throat" describes a temporary condition: a moment when feeling overwhelms speech. For the mute, this was his permanent condition, his whole life. And the frog that literalized it, the creature that bridged his silence and the world of sound, is in the ground under the wildflowers.

"No being but becoming"

While walking back from the burial, Mr. Spitzer finds himself meditating on a line that cuts to the heart of everything Young has been saying across the novel: there is no being but becoming. The wheel turns, and that is all. Images flow into images, like water into water, without stopping anywhere, without fixing into a stable self.

This is not nihilism. It is the opposite of nihilism. It is the claim that existence is not a state you can arrive at and possess, but a process you are always inside of. There is no moment when you have finally become yourself. There is only the next moment, and the one after that, and the frog lilies growing over the grave.

The airplane

Through most of this novel, time has been soft and uncertain; you might be in the 1900s, or earlier, or somewhere outside of calendar time altogether. In Chapter 61, Mr. Spitzer looks up at what he thinks is a moving star and realizes it is an airplane light seen through clouds.

Young drops this quietly, almost without emphasis. But it is the novel's first clear glimpse of the modern world. The airplane is there, overhead, moving through the same sky where the wild ducks flew in Chapter 60 and the moose's antlers reached toward the Pleiades. The mystical and the contemporary inhabit the same clouds. They always did.

What to hold onto

Two men in a flower-strewn meadow, burying a frog. One cannot hear. The other makes music no one hears. Between them, they hold a red rose and everything that has been lost. The way back will feel shorter.
