guide-12-the-garden-of-the-blind:
Chapter 12: The Garden of the Blind

← Chapter 11 · Guide Home · Chapter 13 →

Research notes: Chapter 12

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Symbols: Clocks and Watches · Eyes and Blindness · Keys, Doors, and Locks

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology · Hinduism · Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Astronomy · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · The Bible

Chapter 12 is the longest and most important chapter we’ve had in a while, and it ends on a sentence that will change how you read everything that comes after it.

Stay with this one. It earns its length.

What actually happens in Chapter 12

It is past ten o’clock at night. Vera is in her bedroom, kept company by Miss MacIntosh’s alarm clock: the one reliable clock in a house where all the others have been stopped. Restless and lonely, she gets up, picks up Miss MacIntosh’s Coca-Cola fan, and eventually slips out of the house into the night.

She wanders into the garden and finds herself, without having planned it, in a very particular place: a garden her mother’s father planted long ago for his blind wife. A garden designed not to be seen but to be touched and smelled. Vera closes her eyes and moves through it with her fingers, feeling the petals and stamens and whorls of flowers she cannot name in the dark.

In this heightened, strange state (joyful, almost ecstatic, certain of the reality and beauty of the world) her mind opens into a long meditation on Miss MacIntosh. What Miss MacIntosh taught her. What she was like. What it meant to have her. And then, at the very end of the chapter, a sentence arrives that tells you something enormous is about to happen.

Young is preparing you. Chapter 13 will deliver what Chapter 12 has been building toward.

The clocks, and what they mean

Before Vera goes into the garden, Young gives us two kinds of clocks, and the contrast between them is one of the most precise things in the novel.

Miss MacIntosh’s clock is Old Reliable: plain, practical, no carved figures, no weeping ladies, no sporting cupids. It keeps accurate time. It does “not repeat the hours, a day being gone when a day was gone.” It was made for servants, Vera tells us, for people who must actually wake up and do things at a specific hour.

“All the other clocks in the house” have been stopped, each one frozen at a different hour from the long period when Catherine gradually retreated from the world. Sometimes, deep in the night, one of them shudders awake and strikes (three bells here, four bells there, from distant corners) but the darkness does not lift.

This is Young telling you, with great economy, exactly what the house is: a place where time has been refused. Where a woman decided, slowly and not without hesitation, to stop. Miss MacIntosh’s one wound clock is the only thing in the entire house insisting that time is real and moving and will require something of you in the morning.

The garden of the blind

The garden Vera wanders into is one of the most beautiful and strange settings in the novel. Catherine’s father built it for his wife, who was blind. Not a garden to look at, but a garden to move through by touch and smell: odorous blooms, textured petals, flowers chosen for their whorls and stamens and the way they move under a moving finger.

His wife, we are told, was the most immediate of persons. Practical. Unimaginative. She used to walk a circular path in the garden, and it was for her simply a household habit, nothing poetic about it. She argued with her coachman about whether it looked like rain. She chose clothes in muted, inconspicuous colors. She had no interest in art, until she was blind, and then she traced the stone faces in the garden with her fingers, and the lips and nostrils seemed to move.

Vera steps into this garden at the height of her happiness, certain that the world is real and beautiful and made for human senses to inhabit. She closes her own eyes and touches the flowers. And Young quietly notes: this “first vision of the wonders and glories of this planet” would also be the last.

Something is coming.

What Vera remembers about Miss MacIntosh

The center of the chapter is a long, spiraling memory of what Miss MacIntosh was and what she did for Vera.

At seven years old, Vera was, in Miss MacIntosh’s words, a nervous wreck. “She was baying at the moon.” Pretending to be a dog. Digging for bones in the garden. She believed she was the reincarnation of Chopin. She had a wireless attached to her head through which she heard the voices of the dead. She held conversations with a gentleman in a snuff-colored velvet coat who carried a music box full of buzzing bees.

Miss MacIntosh solved most of these problems by ignoring them. Where she could not ignore them, she applied firm, practical remedies: box a sandbag dummy, run a mile on the beach, restore your circulation and your waning common sense. She held Miss MacIntosh’s thimble over Vera’s forehead (the one engraved with the word Juliet, 1899, though who Juliet was or why 1899 we are never told) and tapped it authoritatively.

She taught Vera “to admit, quite simply, that nothing had happened, that not a leaf had fallen,” not a blow had struck, not a wave had broken. That “omniscience had not been given to us, fortunately,” because if we could see everything “we should all most certainly lose our minds.”

And it worked. Miss MacIntosh held Vera’s “attention by yelling louder than the dead.” That is the sentence Young gives us, and it is both funny and heartbreaking: the only thing that could compete with Vera’s hallucinations was a very loud, very matter-of-fact woman from What Cheer, Iowa.

Miss MacIntosh’s philosophy, in her own words

This chapter gives us the most extended portrait of Miss MacIntosh’s worldview we’ve had yet.

She believed that God, having created this world somewhat erroneously and filled with remorse ever since, does “not ask us to understand His traffic.” We should attend to our own knitting. We are plain. “We were intended for no high” office, “no imaginary diadem, no fine feathers.” The wisest man is a fool in God’s eyes. We are here to endure ourselves, not to test God.

On love, she can only guess. Love is “not an inquiry beyond what meets the natural eye.” It is greatest when it sees another’s face in daylight and hears another’s voice. She is, she admits without self-pity, “a plain, old-fashioned, unvarnished spinster, her” shirtwaist bristling with needles and pins “to forbid inquiry and to suggest that hers was not a good shoulder to weep on.”

And on the question of time and its passing: “she would not give a pin for” the suggestion that time passes through us rather than us through it. When something is gone, it is gone. She kept her feet planted on earth, which she acknowledged was not solid, and she let her head drift nowhere.

She had only one face. Not two: one for the world, one for heaven. Only one.

Hold that. It matters enormously in Chapter 13.

The sentence at the end

The chapter closes with Vera’s mind circling back to Mr. Spitzer, and her mother’s old suspicion that he sometimes imagines “himself to be his dead brother.” And then the chapter simply ends, mid-thought, carrying you directly into Chapter 13.

Chapter 13 begins: “Farewell to the last certitude, even that tender night of my fourteenth birthday when I trembled on the margin of sentient life—farewell to Miss MacIntosh.”

Something happened in that garden. Something Vera saw. And Young has spent all of Chapter 12 making sure you understand what Miss MacIntosh meant to Vera before she shows you what Vera found.

Don’t stop here. Chapter 13 is why this chapter exists.

For the Curious

  • The thimble engraved with “Juliet, 1899”
  • Absalom
  • Miss MacIntosh’s line
guide-74-the-chicago-detective:
Chapter 74: The Chicago Detective

← Chapter 73 · Guide Home · Chapter 75 →

Content note: The Esther Longtree chapters (72 to 81) deal with stillbirth and pregnancy loss, rape, infanticide, racist violence including lynching, and cruelty to children. This chapter is one of the hardest in the novel: Esther describes being raped by the Chicago detective, and the chapter deals with racism.

Research notes: Chapter 74

Characters: Esther Longtree · Joachim Spitzer · The Chicago Detective

Themes: Death and Mortality · Grief, Loss, and Mourning · Memory and the Past · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Angels, Devils, and Myth · Clothing, Hats, and Skirts

Allusions: Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · Pregnancy, Abortion, and Midwifery

Chapter 73 told you that a Chicago detective was circling Esther, that she feared arrest, that the undertaker had complained she brought him no business because she hid the evidence of her stillborn children in streams and snow and tree stumps. The detective was a threat at the edges of the previous chapter’s frame.

Chapter 74 brings him fully into focus, and what comes into focus is one of the novel’s most disturbing configurations: the detective is also the rapist. The man investigating Esther is the man who assaulted her. The figure of authority pursuing her for the deaths of children is the same figure whose violence set the terrible cycle in motion. He comes “three times in three different years,” in three different disguises. He has not solved the mystery. He has not found a murderer. But he always finds Esther. This is a chapter about the machinery of judgment brought to bear on a woman who has done nothing wrong, operated by the very man who wronged her. Young does not make this easy to read. She is not trying to.

Esther also, in this chapter, reveals something she has not told anyone: she was adopted. And she hints at a real stillborn from when she was very young: a death that may have been the first, the one that started everything. Her childhood reproaches her. She doesn’t fully understand why.

What Actually Happens

Esther continues her account, her voice marked now by the triple repetitions that entered in Chapter 73: the epizeuxis that gives her speech its quality of grief pressing against language. She describes the detective’s repeated appearances: three times, three different years, three different disguises. He comes looking for evidence of murder. He catalogues his clues with the precision of the Golden Age detective novel: eyeglasses, footprints, a calling card, a bone button, a thread, “a single spot of brown blood.” He solves “all mysteries but his own, and” his own is the one that matters: that he is what he is hunting.

He raped her, she says, when he thought she was dead, or perhaps sleeping, or perhaps simply because she was there and he could. She describes it with the detachment of someone describing weather: a whirl, an aching, a dullness. It was over too soon. It left behind evidence: the symptoms, the signs of his presence in her body. Another pregnancy. Another absence.

He is, she notes, the kind of detective who only deals “with the deaths of little white children.” The deaths of little Black children are “not his business, there being so many and so unimportant,” in his accounting. Young states this without additional commentary. The accounting speaks for itself.

He gets confessions from murderers “by confessing his own imaginary crimes.” He is trapped in the system he enforces, both agent and victim of the machinery, unable to solve the mystery at the center of his own life.

Esther fears the trial she imagines waiting for her: the jury of women who will look at her enormous pregnant body and her history of hidden stillborn and reach conclusions she cannot counter. She is innocent. She has also hidden everything. These two facts coexist and cannot be reconciled by a jury that only sees the second one.

She is adopted, she says. She was not told this for a long time. She hints at something that happened when she was very young: a real death, a real hiding, a first stillborn or something worse that her memory approaches and then retreats from. Her childhood reproaches her. “Who was innocent? Who was guilty?” She is not sure. She does not explain further.

Despite all of this, Esther ends the chapter radiant. She has “done much lying but no laying,” she says; she has been misjudged, misread, accused of immorality she did not commit in the way they imagine. She is self-sufficient. She is luminous. “No one from the outside world” can annoy her or frighten her. She is more hopeful now than she has ever been. Time’s passage has helped her, not hindered her. The little shadow boxer is still there.

The Detective as Both Perpetrator and Pursuer

The Chicago detective is this chapter’s central paradox, and Young constructs it without flinching. He is the man who assaulted Esther, who came to her when she appeared dead or sleeping, who left his evidence in her body, who produced at least one of the stillborn children she has been hiding. He is also the man sent to investigate the disappearance of those children. He is the crime and the investigation of the crime simultaneously. This is not a mystery novel’s twist. It is a structural observation about power. The person with authority to investigate, to accuse, to bring to trial is also the person who committed the original violation. His investigation of Esther is therefore not a search for truth but a performance of authority over a woman he has already violated: a continuation of the original act by institutional means. He catalogues clues. He solves mysteries. He does not solve his own.

Young gives him the full toolkit of Golden Age detective fiction: eyeglasses, footprints, a calling card, a bone button, a single thread, a spot of blood. The clues are meticulous and they lead nowhere, or rather, they lead him back to Esther every time, which is where he was going anyway. The investigation is circular. The mystery is not designed to be solved. It is designed to maintain his presence in her life.

The Racial Accounting

One of the chapter’s most precise and most chilling moments is the description of the detective’s professional scope: he only deals “with the deaths of little white children.” The deaths of little Black children are not his business. There are too many of them. They are not important enough.

Young states this in Esther’s voice, flatly, without irony, because Esther has no irony to spare for it. It is simply true. It is the accounting of a system that has decided, by the allocation of investigative resources, which children’s lives matter and which do not. The detective is not a corrupt aberration from this system. He is the system operating correctly, according to its own values. This passage sits alongside the woman in curlers from Chapter 71, her insistence that there are no Black people in the county and no one wants any, as Young’s documentation of the specific texture of American racism in the mid-twentieth century Midwest. It is not ideological in the abstract. It is institutional, practical, embedded in the professional scope of the man sent to protect children. Some children. The ones whose deaths count.

Esther’s Adoption and the First Death

The revelation that Esther is adopted arrives without ceremony in the middle of the chapter and without full explanation. She was not told for a long time. She hints at something that happened when she was very young: a first stillborn, or perhaps something else, a death in the circumstances of her earliest girlhood that her memory circles without landing. Her own childhood reproaches her. She asks: “Who was innocent? Who was guilty?”

Young does not answer. The ambiguity is deliberate. What Esther may be carrying (in addition to everything else, in addition to the little shadow boxer) is guilt about something that happened before she was fully old enough to understand it. A death that may not have been her fault, that she may have been too young to prevent, that is now entangled in her mind with all the subsequent losses. She cannot separate them. Her childhood is reproaching her for something she cannot fully name.

Her adoption is also relevant to her situation in another way: she does not know her biological history, her ancestry, the medical inheritance of her body. The “everlasting pregnancy” may have roots she cannot trace because she does not know where she came from. The mystery of her condition is also the mystery of her origin.

The Shroud with Many Pockets

One of the chapter’s central images is a shroud, the garment of the dead, with many pockets. A shroud with pockets has nowhere to go. The dead do not need pockets; they have no belongings to carry, no errands to run. A shroud with many pockets is a garment of death that has been prepared for living: the carrying of things forward, the retention of evidence, the keeping of secrets. Esther wears this shroud figuratively. She is a woman whose body keeps carrying things that have died. The pockets hold the fragments: an eye, an ear, a fingernail, the evidence of the detective’s presence, the first death of her girlhood. She cannot empty the pockets. The shroud does not come off.

Esther’s Radiance

After everything in this chapter (the detective, the assault, the adoption, the first death, the fear of trial, the accusation of murder for children she did not kill) Esther ends radiant. Suffused with radiance, the chapter says. Self-sufficient. “No one from the outside world” can annoy her or frighten her.

This is not denial. Esther knows everything that has happened. Her clarity is one of the chapter’s recurring emphases: she is luminous inside, whatever her body and the world have done to her. She has been misread as mulish, as crazy, as immoral, as a murderer. She has “done much lying but no laying.” She is more hopeful now than she has ever been.

Time has helped her. This is one of the stranger things Esther says, because time has brought her assault, her hidden stillborn, the detective’s repeated visits, the undertaker’s complaint, the imagined jury of women. But time has also brought her further from the first death, further from the girlhood that reproaches her, closer to the conviction that the little shadow boxer will make it. The passage of time has, for Esther, accumulated more hope than despair. This is not logical. It is true.

What to Hold Onto

The detective who is both the crime and the investigation. The man with the eyeglasses and the calling card and the bone button, who solves all mysteries but his own, who comes back “three times in three different years” and always finds Esther.

The racial accounting: only “the deaths of little white children.” Stated flatly. The system, operating correctly.

Esther adopted, her childhood reproaching her for something she cannot name. A first death before all the others. “Who was innocent? Who was guilty?” She does not know.

The shroud with many pockets. A garment of death prepared for living, for carrying things forward. And Esther radiant, at the end. Suffused with light. More hopeful now than ever. Time’s passage has helped her. The little shadow boxer is still there, still fighting, still two hearts.

Chapter 68: The Tavern

← Chapter 67 · Guide Home · Chapter 69 →

Research notes: Chapter 68

Characters: Homer Capehorn · Madge Capehorn · Marie Weed · Miss MacIntosh · Moses Hunnecker · Mr. Weed · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Death and Mortality

Symbols: Cards, Games, and Chance · The Bus and the Journey · The Sea and Water

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Angels and Archangels · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Gambling and Playing Cards · Lynching and Racial Violence · Romantic Poets · Suicide in History and Literature

Chapter 68 is the chapter where the bus stops.

After all those miles of grey midwestern mist, the endless circling of Vera’s mind, the somnambulant passengers and Moses Hunnecker’s whiskey-fueled navigation through fog, the bus finally arrives. Vera, Madge, and Homer disembark. And then, quietly, without ceremony, Madge and Homer walk away and disappear from the novel entirely. You may have spent sixty-seven chapters with these people. They are simply gone now.

What Vera walks into instead is the Tavern: a decaying, mildewed hotel built in 1827 by what its sign calls “God’s servants,” now given over to shadows and thin walls that seem to hear everything. And at the bar, she finds Mr. Weed.

Mr. Weed is a professional hangman. A Christian one. And he would very much like to tell you about his work.

What Actually Happens

Moses parks the bus badly. Vera watches Madge and Homer leave the novel without looking back. She waits to check in at the Tavern while, at the bar, the Tavern’s landlord and Mr. Weed, a large man in a wide-brimmed Western hat, are deep in conversation.

Mr. Weed is a hangman by profession and a family man by inclination. He has two wives: a first one, Marie, who hanged herself from a peach tree in their orchard because she feared another pregnancy, and a second one, Julia, who has the mind of a child and sometimes wears Marie’s old clothes. He has children who play at hanging themselves. He carries a Parker fountain pen given to him by a condemned man, a Jew’s harp he plays on the shortcut home through the orchard, and a black poker chip he found in his coat pocket one day, in the suit he wears to hangings and to church, and has no idea how it got there.

He sees himself as a humanitarian. He makes death painless. He is, in his own estimation, more merciful than the alternatives.

The landlord is skeptical. He has a “Remember the Marne” tattoo and a hotel that, he says, sinks every night. He would rather talk about knots, not hangman’s knots, but lovers’ knots, the marital kind that hold until Gabriel blows his horn. He thinks Mr. Weed doesn’t even know how to tie his own bow-tie properly.

Vera listens to all of this. That is what she does in this chapter. She listens.

The People You’re Meeting

Mr. Weed, the Christian Hangman

He is one of Young’s great grotesque figures: a man whose profession is death and whose self-image is one of mercy. He is a good father, he says. He attends church. He is a vegetarian who dreams of cooking live pigs. He is haunted by the memory of cutting Marie down from the peach tree “a split second too late.” He tried to hang a man in Kentucky “for sleeping with a white woman,” and the rope was cut too soon, and the man survived and was seen months later pushing a baby buggy through town, which frightened everyone. This is the kind of efficiency problem that troubles Mr. Weed. Not the injustice of the hanging. The incompleteness of it.

He is not a monster. That is what makes him so disturbing. He is ordinary. He is integrated into American society, into its churches and its courtrooms and its sense of civic duty. He is the man who makes it all painless, and the rest of the people are, as the novel puts it, “silent accepters of death.”

His three symbolic objects tell you everything you need to know about him: the pen that was a dead man’s last gift, the harp that can’t quite drown out the darkness, and the poker chip that appeared from nowhere and connects to nothing. Clues that lead nowhere. Evidence that explains nothing.

Marie Weed, the First Wife

She is only present through her absence, through the hangman’s fractured memories, through the peach tree in the orchard, through Julia wearing her old clothes. She hanged herself because she could not bear another pregnancy. She was afraid of her own body, of what it might produce against her will. Young is quietly, devastatingly precise about this: the Comstock Laws were still in effect, women had essentially no legal right to contraception, and a woman’s body under those conditions was not entirely her own. Marie’s suicide is individual and it is also historical.

Her maiden name was Oliver, and Mr. Weed notes that “the Olivers were known for hanging” themselves. Young has chosen this carefully: Oliver Cromwell was posthumously hanged; Andrew Oliver was hanged in effigy; Oliver Moore was lynched in North Carolina in 1930. The name carries the history of bodies suspended from ropes, official and unofficial, sanctioned and not.

Moses, the Bus Driver

Moses reappears briefly here, struggling to park the bus, anxious about getting home to his old mother. His mother, he says, thinks he is her bridegroom. He keeps traffic rules, metaphorically, even in her bridal chamber; he maintains distance, refuses to enter her delusion fully, remains tethered to her by guilt and obligation rather than love. He won’t cut his hair until the Democrats stop running things. He made that promise to her. He dreams of escape. He goes home instead.

Moses has led his passengers through the grey wilderness. He never reaches the promised land himself. That’s always been his job.

The Landlord

A WWI veteran, a man who has heard everything and trusts none of it, who runs a hotel that sinks every night and somehow surfaces every morning. He grounds the scene. He is the voice of the mundane world pushing back against Mr. Weed’s philosophical self-justifications. His counter-argument is the marital knot: love, he implies, is the only knot that matters, and Mr. Weed, for all his expertise with rope, doesn’t understand it at all.

The Farewell to Madge and Homer

Don’t let this pass you by. For sixty-seven chapters, Madge Capehorn has been sleeping her resistant, unhappy sleep on the bus: pregnant, possibly with someone else’s child, returning to a life she didn’t choose. Homer has been sleeping his innocent, placid sleep beside her. They have been one of the novel’s first quiet jokes: the woman who knows too much, awake and suffering; the man who knows nothing, peacefully asleep.

And now they simply walk away. No resolution. No reckoning. They disappear into their lives the way people in novels almost never do but people in reality always do: mid-story, without explanation, while you’re still watching. This is Young telling you something about the structure of attention. Vera’s attention, and yours, has been so focused on the question of Miss MacIntosh that the rest of the world continues, and ends, at the edges of that focus. We never find out what happens to Madge. That is the point.

The Tavern

Built in 1827 by God’s servants, now given over to mildewed brick and claw-like vines and walls so thin they seem to hear everything. The sign out front reads “GENtLE INCLINe—BRIDE AHEAD.” It is supposed to say “Bridge Ahead.” This is the first thing Vera notices.

A gentle incline. A bride. Ahead. The Tavern is a crossroads between life and death: the kind of place you stay when you are between one thing and another, when you have left what you had and haven’t yet arrived at what comes next. It is filled with human-faced wasps and shadows that don’t lift. Its interior, Vera notes, surpasses her imagination. The place exceeds expectation in the wrong direction. It is, in short, America: built with faith, decayed into commerce, full of secrets, haunted by history, and somehow still operating.

The Black Poker Chip

This is one of Young’s great images of futile evidence. A black poker chip found near the head of a murdered woman wearing rose-colored sunglasses. A clue. Except it leads “nowhere, nowhere at all, like a” businessman’s address book “found in the hollow of a nearby oak tree.” It is simply confusing.

And then Mr. Weed reaches into his coat pocket and finds a black poker chip there. He has no idea how it got in. He doesn’t gamble. It is the suit he wears to hangings and to church. This is what the novel does with truth and evidence: accumulates them without resolving them. The chip is real. The chip is meaningless. Both things are true at once. Reality, as Vera reflects in this chapter, is whatever is experienced: “even the unreal things were real.” The chip is in his pocket. That is all we know. That is enough.

The Central Paradox: Mercy and the Rope

Mr. Weed sees himself as a missionary of painless death. He is there to make the terrible thing as humane as possible. He is, in his estimation, the most merciful man in the room.

Young does not let this go unchallenged, but she also doesn’t refute it cheaply. Mr. Weed is not wrong that the alternative: a botched hanging, a man cut down too soon, surviving his own execution to push a baby buggy through a town that cannot look at him: is worse. He is not wrong that the people who hire him are comfortable outsourcing their discomfort. He is not wrong that he is the only one who has to live with what happens in that room.

He is entirely wrong that this makes him good. The chapter holds both things. It is the novel’s way with American mythology: the story we tell ourselves about mercy, about justice, about painless efficiency, about the man who does the difficult work so the rest of us don’t have to. We make him respectable. We put him in a church pew. We let him carry a Parker pen and a Jew’s harp, and we don’t look too hard at the suit he wears to both.

What to Hold Onto

The misread sign: “GENtLE INCLINe—BRIDE AHEAD.” You are on a gentle incline now, moving toward something. Whether it is a bride or a bridge is not yet clear.

The black poker chip in the pocket of the suit worn to hangings and to church. Evidence that goes nowhere. Keep it.

Marie Weed “hanging from the peach tree in the” orchard, her husband arriving a split second too late. He plays the Jew’s harp on the shortcut home through that same orchard. He still takes the shortcut.

And Vera, at the edge of all this, watching. Listening. Adding these people to the great interior catalogue of her mind. She cannot save any of them. She can only bear witness.

Miss MacIntosh believed in facts. In the cold honest surface of things. Vera has been traveling toward that belief for sixty-eight chapters now, and what she keeps finding instead is this: Mr. Weed’s poker chip. A clue that leads nowhere. The truth that keeps arriving in the wrong suit.

Chapter 53: The Pale Replica

← Chapter 52 · Guide Home · Chapter 54 →

Research notes: Chapter 53

Characters: Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer

Themes: Death and Mortality · Isolation and Connection · The Search for Meaning

Symbols: Cards, Games, and Chance

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft · Phenomenology · Plato and Platonism

Allusions: Gambling and Playing Cards · Suicide in History and Literature

Chapter 52 gave us the secret in its physical form: the trunks, the gowns, the no slippers. Chapter 53 gives us the other secret: the one that has been the novel's deepest structural question since Chapters 45 and 47 first began to surface it.

Peron apparently died by suicide.

And since Peron's death, Mr. Spitzer, Joachim, has been mistaken for him. Has been addressed as Peron. Has been seen as Peron by people who knew them both. Has been walking through the world in the afterimage of his dead twin, unable to assert his own identity against the force of the resemblance, perhaps no longer entirely certain which of them he is.

He describes himself as a pale replica. A mask or dream rather than flesh and blood. And this chapter gives us the most explicit statement yet of what the novel has been implying: Joachim “divided himself between himself and his dead brother.” Since Peron's death he has access to knowledge he should not have: the underworld of gambling, speakeasies, boxing, billiards, the shady and illegal and flamboyant life that was Peron's domain, not his. He has become, somehow, both.

What actually happens in Chapter 53

Mr. Spitzer meditates on “the difference between himself and his” brother, and on the dissolution of that difference since Peron's death. Peron was volatile, colorful, many-sided: a chameleon changing colors, a crazy patchwork of identities and experiences. Joachim was opaque, timorous, marked by a search for equilibrium and an inability to make the irreversible move. He was the timid chess player afraid to take the final action that would mean his definitive defeat.

He has “missed his brother by only a minute.” Trains keep passing the wrong station. Connections are not made. He wanders through empty landscapes seeking a place of reunion that does not arrive.

But something has changed since the death. Mr. Spitzer knows things he should not know. He knows the boxing records with the precision of someone who was at the fights: the 110-round bout of 1893, the fighters who continued with broken hands, the featherweight champions and their exact reigns. He knows the gambling underworld, the speakeasies, the shady corners of the city where Peron moved and Joachim never went. He has absorbed his brother through mourning, or through the dissolution of the border between them, or through the possibility that he was always Peron and only thought he was Joachim.

Peron's apparent suicide

Young gives us this information almost in passing, the way she gives all the most important information: in subordinate syntax, surrounded by other matter, requiring you to slow down and re-read. Peron's apparent suicide. Apparent: the word is doing work. Either the death was made to look like a suicide and was not, or the suicide itself was somehow ambiguous, uncertain, not definitively established. Young uses apparent and does not explain it.

What it adds to the Peron/Joachim question: if Peron died by suicide, then the identity substitution becomes even more unstable. Suicide is an act of will: a decisive, irreversible choice of the kind Joachim is described as incapable of making. A timid chess player who cannot take the final action. And yet if Peron, the reckless one, the one who burned brightly, made that choice, and if Joachim has been living as Peron since, then who made the choice? The impulsive twin or the cautious one? The one who lived by chance or the one who calculated every move?

Young does not answer. She gives you apparent and lets the word sit there, doing its work.

The chameleon and the black velvet pall

Young gives the two brothers contrasting textures: Peron is a chameleon, shifting colors to match every environment, a crazy patchwork of many-sidedness. Joachim is a black velvet pall: the cloth draped over a coffin, fixed, dark, the thing that marks the boundary between the living and the dead and does not change its nature regardless of what is placed beneath it.

The chameleon is Peron's gift and his instability. He could be anything. He was many things. His identity was performed and re-performed in the gambling halls and boxing clubs and speakeasies: a different suit for every occasion, a different face for every game. What was true of him was that he was always changing, which means it is very difficult to say what the truth of him was.

The black velvet pall is Joachim's identity: the mourner, the keeper, the one who marks the death and stands at its boundary. He is the thing that does not change while everything beneath him changes. And yet: since Peron's death, Joachim has absorbed Peron's knowledge, Peron's world, Peron's shady acquaintances and gambling records. The pall is beginning to take on color. The fixed is beginning to shift. The two identities are becoming what they always were in some deeper sense: not two but one, expressed through alternating facets.

Knowledge from the other side

Mr. Spitzer's knowledge of the boxing world deserves attention because it is so specific. He does not know boxing in the abstract. He knows the 1893 fight between Andy Bowen and Jack Burke: 110 rounds, seven hours and nineteen minutes, ending as a no-contest when neither fighter could come out of his corner, Burke having broken all the bones in both hands. He knows Henry Armstrong, who held world championships in three different weight classes simultaneously. He knows the fighters who continued after their hands broke, who went the distance when the spectators had fallen asleep.

This is not research. This is memory. And if it is memory, it is not Joachim's memory. Joachim, the cautious musician and lawyer, the man who valued his dignity more than his life, does not attend 110-round prize fights in New Orleans or follow featherweight title reigns. Peron did. Peron moved in those circles, knew those people, had that knowledge. And now Joachim has it.

Young is giving us the phenomenology of becoming someone else through grief: the way the mourner absorbs the dead, takes on their knowledge and their habits and their way of being in the world, until the boundary between mourner and mourned becomes unreliable. Mr. Spitzer, the pale replica, is not just wearing his brother's identity. He is, in some increasingly real sense, becoming it.

The missed connection, over and over

He “missed his brother by only a minute.”

Young's image of the perpetually missed connection (trains passing the wrong station, encounters that nearly happen and don't, the minute that keeps coming between Mr. Spitzer and the reunion he needs) is one of the chapter's most persistent and precise metaphors. He is always a minute late. He has always been a minute late. This is his existential condition rendered in schedule form: the train that was supposed to connect him to his brother, to the life he was supposed to have, to the moment of recognition he needed; it keeps passing without stopping. And he keeps arriving at the platform exactly one minute after it leaves.

To All My Darlings notes that recent research suggests humans perceive the world on approximately a fifteen-second delay: the brain processing and organizing experience slightly behind the moment it occurs, to prevent sensory overload. Mr. Spitzer's minute-late condition is this delay at its extreme: a man perpetually out of sync with the present moment, always processing what has just passed rather than what is happening. He could not have caught the train even if he had tried. He was built to arrive after it left.

The timid chess player

Mr. Spitzer is “a timid chess-player, afraid to” make the move that would mean his final defeat.

This is one of Young's most compressed portraits of a certain kind of consciousness: the person who will not make the decisive move because the decisive move would resolve the game. As long as the move is not made, the game continues. As long as the game continues, neither winning nor losing has been confirmed. The timid chess player's strategy is not to win. It is to defer the moment of determination indefinitely.

This is also Mr. Spitzer's strategy with his own life. He will not vote because “the dead cast no vote—and” he is not certain which side of that line he stands on. He will not declare himself Peron or Joachim because to declare would be to resolve the question and live with the resolution. He will not turn to Cousin Hannah at the moment when he almost could, because turning would mean the move that changes the board. He defers. He defers. He arrives a minute late to everything, and the game continues, and he is still in it, technically, having not yet made the move that ends it.

Death danced with the lady

Near the chapter's close, the novel returns to Cousin Hannah: death danced with the lady. Young reaches back to the danse macabre tradition: death as the intimate partner, leading everyone regardless of rank or accomplishment in the inevitable procession. But for Cousin Hannah, the dance was not simply imposed. She went toward it. She climbed mountains. She flew. She crossed every border. She lived in such intimate proximity to risk and extremity that death was less a surprise arrival than a companion she had been dancing with for years before it finally led her off the floor.

Mr. Spitzer, watching from the sidelines as he always has, knows this dance. He collected the alpenhorn. He kept the secret. He opened the trunks. He is still here, a minute late, having missed every connection, having never been certain whether he was the dancer or the audience. The pale replica. The one who stands at the edge of the floor holding the other's coat.

What to hold onto

Chapter 53 is the chapter where the novel's great structural secret comes as close to the surface as it will come: Peron died, apparently by suicide, and since then Joachim has been living in the space the death left, absorbing his brother's knowledge and world and possibly his identity. The pale replica. The mask or dream.

What Young is doing with this is more than a mystery plot. She is asking whether a person's identity is theirs in any absolute sense, or whether it is always partly composed of those they have lost, whether the mourner, by mourning completely enough, becomes in some real way a continuation of the mourned. Mr. Spitzer is the answer she proposes: not definitively either twin, but the space between them, the echo that forms when two things that were almost the same finally become one.

The train keeps passing. He keeps arriving a minute late. The game continues. He has not yet made the final move.

guide-10-the-wedding-that-became-a-funer:
Chapter 10: The Wedding That Became a Funeral

← Chapter 9 · Guide Home · Chapter 11 →

Research notes: Chapter 10

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Solomon the Turtle · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Dreams and Imagination · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Weddings and Funerals

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology · Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Astronomy · Genesis · Milton · The Bible · The Book of Job

In Chapter 9, Vera danced alone at her birthday party and declared she was dancing with Death. In Chapter 10, she falls asleep thinking about marriage and has one of the strangest, funniest, and most quietly heartbreaking dreams in the novel. Young does not always announce when the narrative shifts from waking to dreaming. You may not realize at first that the wedding ceremony Vera is witnessing is a dream. That is entirely intentional. The dream and the waking world use the same prose, the same density of attention, the same quality of presence. Learning to move between them without a handrail is part of reading this book.

What actually happens in Chapter 10

Vera, still awake after the birthday, is thinking about what Miss MacIntosh said: that you don’t truly know the person you marry until after the ceremony, when it is too late. She is thinking about marriage in general, what it is, what it requires, who she might someday know.

And then she is in a dream.

The dream is a wedding. Mr. Spitzer is there, and Miss MacIntosh is there, and a preacher is presiding. But the roles have been inverted: Mr. Spitzer is the bride, in a veil, and Miss MacIntosh is the bridegroom. The preacher’s words begin as wedding vows from the old Sarum rite an ancient medieval English ceremony and then slide, almost without notice, into a funeral oration. The wedding is becoming a funeral. The vows are becoming last rites. The guests are few and vague and the preacher seems to be dissolving as he speaks.

Biblical figures appear in the preacher’s litany: Gorgons and Hydras and Chimeras, Lucifer who was brightest and fell farthest, Beelzebub, the Day of Judgment. The cosmic and the domestic are sitting in the same room, which is what Young’s dreams always do.

Vera wakes or surfaces from the dream feeling not amused but troubled. She has been thinking unkindly of Miss MacIntosh in the dream, seeing her as colorless, as someone “none would have.” And now, awake, she feels the pity of it: this woman who has given her whole life to practicality and discipline and has never been loved the way she deserved, who has aged into a kind of invisibility that the world imposes on women who do not marry and do not perform the expected ceremonies.

Vera is hungry. She wants to go to Miss MacIntosh. She has been warned not to wander at night. She does not go.

She stays in her room, hungry in more ways than one, and the chapter ends.

The dream wedding, and why it matters

This dream is doing several things at once, and they are all worth naming.

First, it is doing something with gender. Mr. Spitzer as bride, Miss MacIntosh as bridegroom, the expected roles reversed. Young is not simply playing with visual incongruity. She is asking what it means for a ceremony to require a bride and a groom at all, for those roles to be fixed and assigned rather than chosen or earned. The inversion makes visible something that the normal ceremony hides: that the roles are arbitrary, that they could be otherwise, that we have agreed to pretend they are natural when they are not.

Second, it is doing something with ceremony itself. The wedding vows that slide into funeral liturgy are not an accident of Vera’s dreaming mind: they are a truth the dream is telling. In the era Young is writing about, marriage for women was frequently described as a kind of death: the woman’s legal identity was absorbed into her husband’s, her name changed, her previous self declared over. The Sarum rite, which is the source of many of the phrases in the preacher’s speech, was the medieval English marriage ceremony: old, authoritative, carrying the weight of centuries. Young puts it in a dream and lets it dissolve. She is not respectful of the ceremony’s authority. She is watching it come apart.

Third, and most quietly, the dream is about loneliness. Mr. Spitzer, who has spent his whole life mourning his dead twin brother, is here as a bride with no real groom. Miss MacIntosh, who has spent her whole life resisting the softness the world tried to take from her, is here as a bridegroom with no real bride. Two lonely people, dressed in each other’s costumes, presided over by a preacher who is dissolving. This is not comedy. This is sorrow wearing a costume.

Miss MacIntosh, seen from the outside

One of the most important things Chapter 10 does is show us Miss MacIntosh through Vera’s eyes at a moment when Vera is being uncharitable and then show us Vera catching herself.

In the dream and in the waking thoughts that follow it, Vera notices Miss MacIntosh’s ordinariness. Her colorlessness. The fact that she is aging, that “none would have her,” that she has resigned herself to a life without the love and partnership that the world holds up as the measure of a woman’s worth.

And then Vera stops herself. Because Miss MacIntosh did not fail to marry. She chose or was shaped by her life into choosing a different kind of existence. She gave Vera discipline and geography and the facts of the world. She swam in cold surf. She kept time with a silver dollar watch. She was the truest thing in the house. The world’s judgment of her, that she is a spinster, colorless, someone who never achieved the central ceremony, is not the same as the truth of her. Vera knows this. The guilt of having thought unkindly, even in a dream, is real.

This moment is a small lesson in how the novel works. Young will keep showing you characters who appear, from a certain angle, to have failed and then she will rotate the angle. She is always rotating the angle.

The preacher’s words

The preacher’s speech in this chapter is one of Young’s great set pieces of Biblical ventriloquism, she draws from Job, from Corinthians, from the Book of Common Prayer, from the Sarum rite, weaving them together into a ceremony that is simultaneously a wedding, a funeral, and a cosmic reckoning.

Some of the phrases worth holding:

“This life is very short and full of mortal sorrow” is from Job, the book of undeserved suffering, the book of questions that God does not answer.

“He cometh up, and he is cut down” is also from Job, about the brevity of human life, the flower that blooms and withers.

“Oh, death, where is thy sting? Oh, grave, where is thy victory?” is from Corinthians, the famous challenge to death, which in this context sounds less like triumph and more like a question asked into the dark.

“Ashes to ashes, dust to dust” is the burial rite, the reminder of what we are made of and what we will return to.

Young is not quoting these to comfort you. She is using them to show you how thoroughly the language of endings has been woven into the language of beginnings. The wedding ceremony and the funeral oration are made of the same words. They always have been. We just don’t usually notice.

Vera’s hunger

The chapter ends with Vera hungry. Literally, she has not eaten, it is late, she wants to go to Miss MacIntosh’s room. But the hunger is also something else: the want of connection, the wish to undo the unkind thoughts of the dream, the desire to say something true to this woman who has been trying to teach her truth all along. She does not go. She has been warned not to wander at night. She obeys, and she stays hungry.

This is a small, precisely calibrated moment of regret. The not-going. The obedience that costs something. In a novel where missed connections and delayed understandings accumulate like unpaid debts, this one of Vera lying in her room, wanting to knock on Miss MacIntosh’s door, choosing not to is worth noticing.

What to watch for as you keep reading

Light spoilers: This section hints at what happens later in the novel. Skip it if you want to meet the story fresh.

Mr. Spitzer as bride. The image of Spitzer in a veil is strange and funny and also heartbreaking when you understand him as a man who has spent his whole life in grief for his dead twin, who has never fully inhabited his own identity because so much of it died with his brother. Young dresses him as a bride in Vera’s dream, and the costume fits in its own terrible way. He is always waiting for a ceremony that already happened without him.

The Sarum rite. This was the medieval English marriage service used before the Reformation, the source of many of the phrases we still recognize in wedding ceremonies today as including “to have and to hold,” “till death do us part,” and the question of whether anyone knows of an impediment. Young reaches back to the oldest layer of the ceremony because she is interested in what marriage has always been, beneath the layers of custom and sentiment.

“Familiarity breeds contempt.” This proverb, attributed to Chaucer and Augustine and others, appears in this chapter in the context of Miss MacIntosh’s observation that you don’t know your spouse until it’s too late. Young is building a sustained meditation on intimacy and knowledge, the paradox that the closer you get to someone, the more clearly you see what you didn’t know, and the less romantic the seeing becomes.

Solomon the turtle, still there. He is present in the dream too, slow and ancient, witnessing everything. He does not judge. He does not hurry. He will be there when the ceremony is over.

What to hold onto

Chapter 10 is a dream chapter which means it operates by association rather than by logic, and it is asking you to feel your way through it rather than parse it.

Here is what to hold: Vera is fourteen, she has just danced alone at her own birthday party, she is lying awake thinking about marriage and what it means and whether she will ever truly know the person she marries. She dreams a wedding that turns into a funeral. She wakes feeling she has been unkind to someone she loves. She is hungry and does not go to ask for food or comfort.

And outside, in the darkness, Miss MacIntosh is alone in her room, not knowing she was dreamed.

For the Curious

  • The Book of Job
  • “Ashes to ashes, dust to dust”
  • Lucifer
  • “One who could know us and yet love us”
guide-32-weddings-are-funerals-and-funer:
Chapter 32: Weddings Are Funerals, and Funerals Are Weddings

← Chapter 31 · Guide Home · Chapter 33 →

Research notes: Chapter 32

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh

Themes: Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Weddings and Funerals

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Exploration and the Poles · Fairy Tales and Folklore · The History of Opium · Women's Suffrage

Chapter 32 is the completion of the Cousin Hannah portrait and, simultaneously, the fullest account we will receive of Catherine’s marriage, or what passed for one. Young weaves the two together because they are the same story: Hannah’s lifelong battle to rescue Catherine, and Catherine’s marriage to the absent bridegroom who was always already gone.

This is a long, rich chapter and it asks a lot of you. Take your time. Young is doing something philosophically ambitious at the end, her final statement about death and travel and partial knowledge, that rewards the full weight of everything that came before it.

What actually happens in Chapter 32

The chapter deepens the Cousin Hannah portrait through Catherine’s eyes. Hannah was explosive and instantaneous, always hurried, “the greatest courier of every storm.” She flourished upon renewed discouragement, almost with a terrible zest. “She had lived through so many dangers” that her face was ravaged, her eyes burning, “a saber wound upon her cheek, a grizzled chin.”

We learn that Hannah had tried to break up Catherine’s marriage, had beaten at the bridegroom with her white umbrella, screaming like ten thousand demons, attempting to carry Catherine away in the manner of a robber. And we learn, finally, what Catherine’s marriage actually was: something spectral, a ceremony with a faceless bridegroom, a wedding “to all the fading images of this world.” “She had been married to a sail-boat which suddenly lifted its wings and sailed away. She had been married to a porpoise and a star,” an iceberg, a church bell.

The chapter closes with Catherine’s final statement: she “had always wanted to die while travelling—as then she would never completely die.” “Death is that which is caused by our partial knowledge.”

Hannah’s philosophy of woman

Chapter 32 gives us Hannah’s feminist argument in its most developed form. She had been “the high-souled lover of woman,” she said, come to rescue her “from slavery to man worse than enchantment by an Eastern drug.” She “had urged woman to use her parasol as her sword,” to fly her skirts as banners on tallest mountain peaks, “to show her little bird feet” and arise and make war.

But Hannah had also been opposed to what she saw as women’s frivolities: the great garden hats with billowing plumes, the silks, the secretive veils, the narcotic flowers, the parasols used as flirtation weapons. This is where her feminism develops its own tension. She loved woman and was opposed to femininity as she found it. She wanted to rescue women from men and also from the performance of womanhood that men had imposed.

Young presents this honestly and without resolution. Hannah is right about the oppression. She is also something of a tyrant in her prescriptions. She had urged Catherine to arise and take horse and make war, but Catherine’s nature required the opium bed, the dark tower, the dreamed bridegroom. You cannot save someone by demanding they become you.

Catherine’s marriage

The account of Catherine’s marriage is the most important revelation in the chapter, and Young delivers it sideways, through Catherine’s own uncertain and shifting memory.

“She had been married on the tennis court,” in flying veils, passing a “great ball which was the winged moon.” “She had been married on the clouded archery range,” shooting “a golden arrow through a cloud. She had been married to a sail-boat,” a porpoise, a star, an iceberg, a church bell. She had never seen her bridegroom’s face. In the midst of the wedding ceremony, she had felt herself “hypnotized, drawn by a magnetic force which came from no known place or star,” not knowing “what she was doing or who the bridegroom was.”

This is not madness. It is the most honest account available of a marriage to someone who was constitutionally, essentially absent. Catherine’s husband left her, she is vague about when and how and who he was, and went into the mountains and never returned. Young has given us glimpses of him across the novel: the man who walked a frozen cable between snow-capped peaks and fell. What Catherine married was the “great traveller who never would return.” She married, in other words, the void that all the others in her life have been orbiting: the man who was already gone at the moment of the wedding.

Hannah had tried to interrupt this wedding, beating at the phantom bridegroom with her umbrella. She could not break it up. Catherine had married the absent one. That is the only marriage available to a woman whose capacity for love requires absence as its condition.

Weddings are funerals, and funerals are weddings

Near the chapter’s end Young gives Catherine one of the novel’s most compressed philosophical statements: weddings are funerals, and funerals are weddings. “When one marries, a part of one must die. When one dies, one is forever married, married through separation unto eternity. The great lover is always the absent one. He is one whom no one has ever known or loved.”

This is Catherine’s philosophy of love in its final form, and it is not evasion. It is observation. The love that persists is always the love that was never consummated, never fixed in the ordinary daylight of a shared life. Miss MacIntosh loved someone she could not name. Cousin Hannah loved someone she could not reach. Catherine loves someone who was never there. Mr. Spitzer loves Catherine who will never choose him. The novel’s great lovers are all loving across an absence that cannot be closed.

The wedding to the absent bridegroom is not, in Catherine’s understanding, a tragedy. It is the condition of love itself. “The great lover is always the absent one.” The moment you catch him, he becomes something smaller. The marriage to the iceberg, the church bell, the sail-boat that “lifted its wings and sailed away”; these are not failures of love. They are its most accurate forms.

Hannah’s end

The chapter gives us something heartbreaking near its close: Hannah’s deathbed confession. She had told Catherine, in some final visit, “that these great battles had been as nothing to her, had been as mere incidents in a busy life.” She realized now “that the greatest heroes were not those who perished in the loud clash of arms.” “The greatest battles were fought in the domestic wars by those who had never left home. They were fought by man and woman. It was always an unequal battle, for woman reigned supreme. The man who had left home was a coward who should never be forgiven.”

This is Hannah’s final reversal. The woman who had been to Persia and Arabia and the Alps and Hudson Bay and fought against Spanish cavalcades and Turkish lords, who had believed her entire life that action was the answer, at the end acknowledged that she had been fighting the wrong battles in the wrong places. The domestic war was the real one. She had gone far away to avoid it.

Young delivers this through the uncertainty of how the confession could have occurred: Catherine had not seen Hannah, and both were bedridden, and it may have been a dream. But Mr. Spitzer acknowledges it was possible. He had been the go-between. He had seen Hannah in her last days, wrapped “in his dark cape, the snow like ermine” on his collar, and she had known when she saw him that her time was close.

The final sentence

The chapter ends: “my mother had always wanted to die while travelling—as then she would never completely die—for every traveller dies merely by passing through a city, and none will know that landscape which he passes through in the long night. Death is that which is caused by our partial knowledge.”

This is the novel’s most direct statement of its central philosophical proposition. We die because we know only part of the world we pass through. If we could know it completely, if we could see the full landscape of the long night, we might not die, or at least we would not die completely. Partial knowledge is the condition of mortal life. The traveller who passes through a city and does not stay, who does not learn its streets and faces, never fully dies there because he never fully lived.

Catherine wants to die while travelling because she has spent her whole life in one bed, and the one death she fears is the complete one: the death of the person who stayed. The traveller’s death is a partial death. A partial death is a kind of life.

What to watch for as you keep reading

Light spoilers: This section hints at what happens later in the novel. Skip it if you want to meet the story fresh.

The Cousin Hannah chapters are complete. She will continue to surface in the novel’s memory, she is too large a presence to disappear entirely, but Young has now given us everything we need to understand her. The great captain who died in her bed, of her life, having lost the domestic war she fought on every other front.

Catherine’s final sentence, “death is that which is caused by our partial knowledge,” is the novel’s thesis statement in its most compressed form, and everything that follows will be an elaboration of it. Every character in Miss MacIntosh, My Darling is dying of partial knowledge: of themselves, of the people they love, of the world they move through. The novel is Young’s attempt to supply the full knowledge, or at least to map the partiality.

The suitor who “had subscribed heavily to the suffrage movement” after Hannah “left him at the church door with a white bouquet in his hands” is one of Young’s best peripheral figures. He appears in one clause and is never mentioned again. He has spent his entire life supporting the cause of the woman who refused him. Young does not decide whether this is noble or absurd. It is both.

Chapter 55: Carpe Diem / Hoc Opus, Hic Labor Est

← Chapter 54 · Guide Home · Chapter 56 →

Research notes: Chapter 55

Characters: Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer · Mr. Mouse · Peron Spitzer

Themes: Duality and Doubles · Music, Sound, and Silence

Symbols: Horses and Carriages · Music and Instruments · The House · Twins and Doubles · Weddings and Funerals

Allusions: Ancient Egypt · Gambling and Playing Cards · Music and Composers · Suicide in History and Literature · Women's Suffrage

Peron's motto was carpe diem: seize the day. Appropriate for a gambler, a chameleon, a man whose entire philosophy was the embrace of the present moment and the absolute indifference to consequence.

Joachim's motto was hoc opus, hic labor est: this is the work, this is the labor. It comes from Virgil's Aeneid: spoken by the Sibyl when she tells Aeneas that descending to the underworld is easy, but returning to the upper air, that is the task, that is the work. The return. The difficult part is not the going down but the coming back.

Young gives the brothers these two mottoes and lets them stand without commentary. They are not just personality types; they are philosophical positions on what a life is for. Peron: the moment seized and released, over and over, no accumulation, no residue, pure now. Joachim: the work sustained, the labor endured, the descent made and the attempt to return. One died by apparent suicide. The other is still in the underworld, still trying to find the way back up.

What actually happens in Chapter 55

Chapter 55 gives us the most complete biographical account of the Spitzer brothers that the novel offers: their life together in the twin house, the financial disaster of Peron's death, and the specific shape of the resentment and grief that has organized Joachim's existence ever since.

The house was extraordinary: symmetrical, mirrored, every room doubled. Twin portraits, twin gardens, twin arrangements of objects: a house built to contain two lives simultaneously, to give each brother his half without requiring them to overlap. Joachim planned it meticulously. He envisioned the life it would support: the music, the philately, the careful conservative investments that would preserve enough stability to allow the work to continue. He designed the music as a tomb: an immortal structure in sound that would outlast his physical existence.

Peron disrupted all of this. He borrowed money he did not repay. He forged checks in Joachim's name. He accumulated debts that he did not acknowledge as debts, because for Peron debt was simply another form of tomorrow's problem, and tomorrow was not real to a person who lived entirely in the present tense. When Peron died, Joachim paid for the funeral. He paid the debts. He went bankrupt. He lost the twin house. He moved into a beachcomber's house.

And then he wondered, as he has been wondering through every chapter since, which brother had really died.

The twin house

Young's image of the twin house (each room mirrored, every arrangement doubled, the structure built to make two lives symmetrical) is the architectural rendering of what the brothers were supposed to be: complementary halves of a single whole, each one complete, each one matching the other without requiring either to dissolve.

Joachim designed it. He is, remember, the orderly one: the man who draws maps, makes plans, tries to exclude chance. The twin house is the map he made for the life he intended to live. It has his music and his stamps and his careful china shepherdesses and his butterfly collection and his conservative investments in gilts and estates. It is a house designed to support the work.

Peron lived in the other half and did not treat it as a mirror. He borrowed Joachim's half. He forged documents with Joachim's name. He introduced chance into every room. The house that was designed to make the two lives symmetrical became, under Peron's occupancy, a house where one half constantly threatened the structural integrity of the other.

The house is gone now. Joachim lost it paying the debts his brother left. He lives in a beachcomber's house: the opposite of the twin house in every way: improvised, coastal, exposed, belonging to whoever washes up. He is the beachcomber, picking through what remains after the tide.

Peron's forgeries

That Peron forged checks in Joachim's name is not simply a betrayal. It is the specific shape of the identity confusion that has haunted every chapter since.

A forged check in Joachim's name is Peron signing as Joachim. It is Peron making himself Joachim, at least on paper, at least for long enough to extract the money. This is the literal version of everything the novel has been asking about their relationship: which one is the real Spitzer? Which signature is authentic? When Peron signs Joachim's name, is the check more or less counterfeit than any other document? All money was counterfeit, Mr. Spitzer thinks: “turned out at the great Mint,” valuable only because an institution said so. Perhaps all signatures are the same: assigned value, not inherent truth.

Joachim was furious. He was invisible to Peron, never acknowledged, never appreciated, his order and sacrifice treated as infrastructure to be used and ignored. The resentment in this chapter is real and carefully rendered by Young. She does not let Joachim be simply noble. He is also wounded. He is also the person who planned everything carefully and watched it be dismantled by someone who did not understand that plans had value.

The music as tomb

Joachim's great project (the opus, the dirge, the elegy) was designed from the beginning as a tomb. Not a tomb in the sense of a mausoleum, cold and sealed, but a tomb in the sense of the ancient Egyptian model: a structure built to sustain life beyond death, equipped with everything the person would need to continue existing in another form. His music was to be the architecture of his survival.

Young gives this serious and exact weight. The composition was not a vanity project. It was Joachim's version of what Cousin Hannah's suffrage campaigns were: a structure built to outlast the body that created it, a form of being-in-the-world that could continue after the physical self had ended. The music as tomb is the musician's version of the legacy problem. It is, among other things, the thing Mr. Mouse is eating.

The curse of the ninth hovers over it: the superstition, rooted in the deaths of Beethoven, Schubert, and others after completing a ninth symphony, that the ninth will be the composer's last. Joachim knows the curse. He has organized his life around surviving long enough to finish the work. The bankruptcy, the loss of the house, the move to the beachcomber's cottage: all of these have set back the schedule. He is still in the middle. He has not finished. The tomb is incomplete.

Which brother really died

This is the question the chapter turns over at its close, and it is the question the novel has been building toward since the first hints about the Spitzer twins in the early chapters.

Peron died by apparent suicide. Since Peron's death, Joachim has been living at a second remove, absorbing Peron's knowledge and world, being mistaken for Peron by people who knew them both. He has been using Peron's existence as the scaffolding for what remains of his own. He has been, in the language of philosophy, becoming his brother.

Which means: who is the person living in the beachcomber's house? Is it the man who planned the twin house and designed the music as a tomb and lived by hoc opus, hic labor est? Or is it the man whose motto was carpe diem, who forged the checks and accumulated the debts and moved through every environment like a chameleon, and who now inhabits the cautious twin's body because the cautious twin's body is what survived?

Young does not decide. The novel has never decided. The question which brother really died is the question whose answer would change everything about how you read all the preceding chapters, and Young preserves the ambiguity because both answers are true in their way. The reckless twin died. The cautious twin survived by becoming, in some sense, the reckless one. Or: the cautious twin died in the bankruptcy and the loss and the long years of the second remove, and what is left is the ghost of the reckless one, still gambling, still trying to seize a day that keeps arriving a minute late.

The skeletal coachman

The chapter gives us an image of Joachim unknowingly traveling in the wrong carriage, driven by a skeletal coachman through unfamiliar landscapes. He is the wrong passenger. He does not know where he is going. The coachman does not explain.

The skeletal coachman is the novel's most direct invocation of Death as driver: the Etruscan Charun, who ferries souls across the boundary, or the danse macabre's Death who leads everyone in procession. But Joachim is not being driven to death exactly. He is being driven through a landscape that no longer corresponds to any map he made. He is the wrong passenger because the right passenger, the Joachim who designed the twin house and planned the music and drew the precise financial arrangements, is not the person who ended up in the carriage. The person in the carriage is whatever survived the bankruptcy and the forgeries and the grief. The coachman drives on regardless. The landscape is unfamiliar. The destination is unknown.

What to hold onto

Chapter 55 is where we finally understand, in practical terms, what happened to Mr. Spitzer. The twin house, the debts, the forgeries, the bankruptcy, the move to the beachcomber's cottage; these are the specific material events that produced the liminal figure wandering the fog-bound city a minute late, carrying an alpenhorn and composing an elegy in scraps. He did not begin this way. He was methodical. He had a plan. The plan was sabotaged from inside the house, by the other half of himself, who did not believe in plans.

What to carry forward: the two mottoes, which are the chapter's philosophical spine. Carpe diem versus hoc opus, hic labor est. The seized moment versus the sustained work. The man who lived entirely in the present versus the man who organized his life around a future he would never fully reach. One is gone. The other is still in the underworld, still trying to find the way back up, still doing the labor that the Sibyl named as the difficult part: not the descent, but the return.

guide-02-the-beautiful-corpse:
Chapter 2: The Beautiful Corpse

← Chapter 1 · Guide Home · Chapter 3 →

Research notes: Chapter 2

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Jock Cartwheel · Mr. Chandelier · Peron Spitzer · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Love

Symbols: Birds

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Ancient Egypt · Gambling and Playing Cards · The History of Opium

If Chapter 1 dropped you into a grey bus moving through uncertain mist, Chapter 2 drops you into a bed.

Specifically, into the bed of Catherine Helena Cartwheel, Vera’s mother, where she has been lying, largely motionless, for years. She is not asleep. She is not awake. She is somewhere in between, sustained by opium, visited by hallucinations, and more alive in her dreams than most people are in their waking lives.

New readers sometimes find Catherine’s chapter the most disorienting in the entire novel. It helps to know, going in, that this disorientation is the point. You are inside a mind where the dream is more real than reality. Young is not asking you to follow a plot here. She is asking you to inhabit a consciousness.

What actually happens in Chapter 2

Mr. Spitzer, the family lawyer, a semi-retired, absent-minded man broken by grief visits Catherine every evening, as he has for years. Catherine lies in her enormous bed, surrounded by jewels and phantoms and the light of her chandelier, and receives him. An Egyptian sailor arrives at the house, lost and looking for Mr. Spitzer’s twin brother, Peron, who is dead. Catherine insists the sailor is real and gives him elaborate directions through the labyrinthine house. Mr. Spitzer tries to explain to the sailor that his brother is gone. The sailor dances with joy at seeing Mr. Spitzer, convinced he has found who he is looking for. Nobody fully agrees on what is happening.

Meanwhile, Catherine’s little yellow canary sings in its gilded cage. When the canary dies which it has, many times Mr. Spitzer secretly replaces it, so that Catherine will never know. She believes it is the same bird. It isn’t. It never is.

Who Catherine is, and how she got here

Catherine’s full name is Catherine Helena Cartwheel, née Snowden. Catherine means “innocent.” Helena means “the bright one.” Snowden means “snow hill.” She is, in Young’s naming logic, an innocent brightness buried under snow which is exactly what she is.

She grew up under a domineering father of fierce orthodox faith, whose rituals governed every hour of the household. She married Jock Cartwheel, a reckless sportsman who disappeared in the Alps, and was abandoned. She was socially humiliated. She carries an invisible birthmark on her left cheek that no one else can see, but which she is convinced marks her as flawed, set apart, not quite belonging to the world.

So she left it. The bed is her kingdom now. And in her kingdom, dead kings visit. Angels appear. Movie stars from silent films drift through. An Egyptian sailor arrives bearing a papyrus that turns out to be a horse-racing tip sheet.

The world inside Catherine’s head is not chaos. It is extraordinarily populated, extraordinarily detailed, and governed by its own logic. Young gives us access to it not to show us a mad woman, but to show us a mind that has decided, quite rationally, that the dream world is more honest than the real one.

The love triangle at the center of everything

Much of Chapter 2 establishes a triangular relationship that will echo through the entire novel. Catherine loved Peron Spitzer, the vivid, unreachable twin, who did not love her back. Joachim Spitzer, the devoted, steady, lawyerly twin, loved Catherine and was not loved in return. Peron died young, by his own hand. Joachim stayed.

Their very names encode this: Joachim means “raised by God.” Peron means “rock.” The man raised by God stayed earthbound, faithful, forgotten. The rock fell into the sea. This is why the Egyptian sailor’s arrival matters so much. He comes looking for Peron, the dead one, the beloved one, and sees him in Joachim’s face. Catherine understands this instantly. Mr. Spitzer does not want to.

The canary

The little yellow canary in its gilded cage is one of the novel’s most quietly devastating images. Catherine believes her life is tied to the bird’s: that if it dies, she dies. So Mr. Spitzer, faithfully and without ever telling her, replaces each dead canary with a living one. The illusion of continuity is maintained. The same bird has died a hundred times and is always singing.

Notice that this is also what Young is doing with time in this chapter and in the novel as a whole. The same moments return, slightly altered. The same losses repeat. The same questions are asked again and the answers are never quite the same, and yet the singing continues.

Mr. Chandelier

Among Catherine’s phantoms is one she calls Mr. Chandelier, the actual chandelier of her room, personified, a companion “not always faithful,” holding seven lighted candles in seven crystal hands. He is not decoration. He is what happens when a mind so thoroughly animated by imagination turns even its furniture into characters. The seven candles evoke ritual, illumination, the sacred number that recurs throughout the novel’s mythology. But the light they cast is chandelier light: prismatic, beautiful, not quite revealing anything clearly.

What to hold onto

Catherine is not a cautionary tale about addiction. She is a philosopher who has chosen her medium. Her argument, spoken in this chapter with full lucidity, is that the real world is inevitably a disappointment, a series of promises that fail to materialize, while the dream world is “expansive and protective,” alive with what life actually should have been.

You do not have to agree with her. But you have to take her seriously. Young does.

When you feel lost in this chapter, return to the canary. A woman who believes the same bird has been singing to her for years, and a man who makes sure it always is. That is Chapter 2, held in a single image.
