guide-54-the-elegy-scattered-in-the-wind:
Chapter 54: The Elegy Scattered in the Wind

← Chapter 53 · Guide Home · Chapter 55 →

Research notes: Chapter 54

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Music, Sound, and Silence

Symbols: Pearls and Jewels

Philosophy: Freud and Jung · Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · Milton · Romantic Poets · The History of Opium · Women's Suffrage

Mr. Spitzer writes music on scraps of paper.

He carries the fragments in his pockets and on the lining of his coat and on whatever surface is available when the notes come to him. He is composing an elegy, for his brother, for Cousin Hannah, for the lost, for the downtrodden, for the passenger pigeon, for everything that has been extinguished or forgotten or left at a threshold it could not cross. The elegy is the project of his life. It has been the project of his life since Peron died, and before that, in the long anticipation of the loss it now mourns.

At the end of Chapter 54, the elegy is scattered in the wind. The scraps of paper, the musical notation, the fragments of the composition that might one day have cohered into something; they flutter away from him in a city that keeps moving and shifting and placing the wrong buildings on the wrong streets. He watches them go. He does not chase them.

Young does not present this as a tragedy. It is simply what happens to the music written in fragments, carried in pockets, composed in a world that will not hold still long enough to be notated accurately. The elegy was real. The wind is also real. Both things are true simultaneously.

What actually happens in Chapter 54

Mr. Spitzer moves through a Boston that is simultaneously the city he knows and a city that is rearranging itself around him: streets shifting, the Flatiron Building appearing where it should not be, the Fishback Building misplaced, the Steinway Building in the wrong location. The city of his memory and the city of the present keep failing to correspond. He moves through them both at once, navigating by a map that is perpetually becoming inaccurate.

He encounters the figures who populate the underside of the city: derelicts, forgotten heirs, persons who have lost their bank accounts and their identities and sometimes their names. He helps them when he can: buying clothes and necessities for those in need, trying to restore what has been lost. He is the unofficial representative of the hidden majority, still, the man who carries the causes that were never popular and never formally entrusted to him.

He is agitated about a missing jewel from a rajah's crown: an incident he is somehow implicated in but cannot clearly remember. The great rajah's jewel, foreshadowed chapters earlier, surfaces here as a source of anxiety rather than a resolved narrative. He was accused of being a jewel thief. He does not know if he did it. He prefers glass jewels to real ones, which tells you everything you need to know about where Mr. Spitzer stands on the question of illusion versus reality: the glass jewel is honest about what it is, which makes it more trustworthy than the real one.

The chapter ends with his elegy fluttering away, and Mr. Spitzer standing alone in the city, present and absent simultaneously, a figure the chapter describes as caught in a liminal space beyond human knowledge.

The sound effects man

Among the chapter's figures is the sound effects man: a mysterious character associated with Peron, capable of producing the entire sonic world: trains, roosters, barking dogs, wind, ice creaking. He fills the environment with chaotic noise, a performance of everything the world sounds like when compressed into a single voice.

Mr. Spitzer, who has always sought silence, who is the musician of “silence flowing under the sound of” incidental music, regards this man with an unwilling envy. The sound effects man can produce the world. He can make any sound on demand. He is chaos made vocal, the opposite of the silence Mr. Spitzer values and cannot quite achieve.

Young associates the sound effects man with Peron, with the flamboyant, volatile, many-sided brother who could become anything. Peron was the sound effects man of the family: able to produce any register, any tone, any identity required by the occasion. Joachim was the silence under the sound, the music that was never played because it could not compete with the noise.

But the envy is real. Young records it without judgment. To be the silence is honest, and perhaps even necessary, but it is also lonely. The sound effects man fills every room he enters. Mr. Spitzer empties rooms by arriving in them a minute late, finding only the echoes of what was there before.

The shifting city

The Boston of Chapter 54 is one of Young's great composite cities: part geographical Boston (Beacon Hill, the Common, the State House, Paul Revere's North End, Faneuil Hall with its grasshopper weathervane), part psychological projection of Mr. Spitzer's unstable inner landscape, part memory of a city as it was and a present that keeps displacing it.

The buildings are wrong. The Flatiron Building belongs in New York. The Fishback Building belongs in Indianapolis. The Steinway Building belongs in Midtown Manhattan. Mr. Spitzer moves through a city that has imported the architecture of everywhere he has been or thought about or absorbed from his brother's wandering life, and placed it all on Boston's streets without regard for what was there before.

This is what Catherine's mind looks like from the outside. Vera, narrating this chapter, notes that her mother has influenced Mr. Spitzer so profoundly that he can no longer distinguish reality. He has absorbed Catherine's mode of perception along with Peron's underworld knowledge. He is, by this point, a composite of everyone he has spent time with in this household: the cautious lawyer, the absent twin, the opium invalid's atmospheric logic, the suffragette's legendary life. He is multiple, and the city he walks through reflects the multiplicity.

Glass jewels and real ones

Mr. Spitzer's preference for glass jewels over real ones is one of the chapter's smallest and most precise details.

The real jewel is valuable because it is what it is: its beauty is inseparable from its genuineness. The glass jewel is only beautiful in the sense that it performs beauty, that it catches the light in the way beauty is supposed to catch the light, without the underlying substance that makes that catching matter. Mr. Spitzer prefers the glass one. This is not simply an inversion of values. It is the consistent position of a man who has spent his life trusting the false because the true has already failed him. The glass jewel is honest about being a substitute. The real jewel makes claims about permanence and value that the world keeps failing to honor. Mr. Spitzer, who has watched the most permanent-seeming things dissolve (the suffrage captain, his twin, the music on paper, the cities of his memory) has arrived at the rational conclusion that the thing which admits its substitution is more trustworthy than the thing that does not.

The great rajah's jewel that has gone missing (that he may or may not have taken, that he cannot remember clearly) is a real jewel. Of course it is missing. Of course he cannot account for it. Real jewels in this novel are always already on their way to being lost.

Lost heirs and forgotten legacies

Mr. Spitzer's wandering through the underside of Boston (seeking the lost heirs, the persons who have forgotten their bank accounts, the derelicts and the forgotten) is the chapter's most direct portrait of the man as he actually functions in the world.

He is the unofficial executor of everything unexecuted. The people with legitimate claims who cannot assert them. The people with legacies who have lost track of the fact that they have them. The people whose identities have become so attenuated by poverty or grief or the simple passage of time that they are no longer sure what they are entitled to. Mr. Spitzer finds them and helps them remember.

This is the practical expression of what the novel has been saying philosophically: he could love only by indirection, he was the representative of causes “never popular in any public sense.” In the streets of the shifting city, this means buying a coat for a man who has forgotten he deserves one. Finding the heir who does not know they are an heir. It is unglamorous. It produces no public recognition. It is the love available to a person who cannot love directly, and it is real love, and Young insists on this.

The elegy

The elegy Mr. Spitzer has been composing on scraps of paper, an elegy for everything he has lost and everything that was lost before he arrived to witness it, is the musical form that names his purpose. An elegy is a mournful poem or musical composition for the dead. It is the form that converts loss into artifact, that makes the fact of the gone-thing into something that can be heard or read by those who remain.

Mr. Spitzer's elegy is fragmented because his experience is fragmented. It is composed on scraps because scraps are what are available in a life organized around secondhand experience and belated arrival. The motifs of mistake and truth intertwine in it, as they do in everything he produces: he has been stamping the wrong seals on the wrong documents for decades, and his music is similarly marked by the grace note of error, the way things turned out rather than the way they were intended.

The elegy scattering in the wind at the chapter's close is not a defeat. Young is too honest to present it as one. The elegy was always going to be impermanent; that is the condition of anything composed on scraps, in transit, by a person who was always a minute late. The wind takes it. This is what happens to the music of the dead. It disperses into the atmosphere it was always already part of. It was never going to stay on paper. Paper doesn't hold this kind of music. The air does. The air has it now.

What to hold onto

Chapter 54 is the chapter where Mr. Spitzer is most fully present in the world and most fully lost in it simultaneously: moving through a city that corresponds to his mind rather than to geography, helping the people who are as lost as he is, composing music that will not survive the wind.

What to carry forward: the sound effects man as the form of love Mr. Spitzer cannot perform, the capacity to fill the room, to produce the world on demand, to be all noise where he is all silence. The glass jewel as the honest substitute preferred over the genuine that keeps disappearing. And the elegy, scattered but not gone, now part of the atmosphere of a city that was already half-invented anyway. It is in the air. You are breathing it. This is as close as it was ever going to get to being heard.

Chapter 49: He Wept for Others Who Wept Not for Him

← Chapter 48 · Guide Home · Chapter 50 →

Research notes: Chapter 49

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer

Themes: Light and Darkness · Love · Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos

Symbols: Birds · Lamps, Candles, and Light · The House

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: American Writers · The Bible · Women's Suffrage

Martha died on September 14, 1918, “at one o’clock in the afternoon,” at the Cincinnati Zoo. She was the last passenger pigeon on earth. The clock was tolling one as she died. Young records this with the precision of a monument inscription, which is what it is: the novel borrowing the language of memorial for a death that was also the end of a species, the closing of a door that had once darkened skies across the continent.

Mr. Spitzer weeps for Martha.

He is, by this point in the novel, a man who can weep for a pigeon dead before he was born (or at least, dead at the far edge of his life's possible span) while not weeping for himself, because weeping “for himself would seem an excess since he was already dead or dying to this world, this world” itself dying. He directs his sorrow outward, toward the extinct, toward all those the world has not wept for. “He wept for others who wept not for him.” This is his form of love. It is the only form available to him. It is also, Young makes clear, a form of profound loneliness.

What actually happens in Chapter 49

Chapter 49 is the deepest we have gone into Mr. Spitzer's interior: the chapter where Young gives us the full inventory of his condition: the shipwreck whose hull is broken, “paying out more water than the seas contained”; the living lighthouse seeing his own light only at the moment of dying; the man who knows not whether he is “himself or an image contained within an image.”

He moves through a frozen cosmos, ice formed into shapes of domes and eggs and “spires and minarets and bell towers,” a universe in suspension, waiting for something that does not come. He contemplates the paradox of his own existence: “he died at his zenith because he was at his nadir, died at his nadir because he was at his zenith.” He “died through sickness, died through health.” “Died through happiness which should have saved him, died through sorrow, sorrow by which he lived, died by not dying, died by living, lived by dying.”

He is, To All My Darlings notes, something like Schrödinger's cat: simultaneously alive and dead, the state unresolved until observed, the observation itself changing the state. He does not know which he is. He has stopped being certain anyone outside him knows either.

He mourns Martha. He mourns his brother. He mourns Cousin Hannah. He mourns everyone who has been extinct or forgotten or lost to the indifference of time. He is, as he has always been, the unofficial unelected representative of causes that were “never popular in any public sense”: a minority representing “a hidden majority like those sleeping in the churchyard.”

Martha and the weight of extinction

The passenger pigeon was once the most numerous bird in North America. Accounts from the nineteenth century describe flocks so vast they darkened the sky for hours, the sound of their wings like approaching weather, the weight of their roosting breaking tree branches. By 1914, Martha was the last. By the time her date appears in Chapter 49 (September 14, 1918, one o'clock) the species had been gone for four years, and the world had not particularly noticed.

Aldo Leopold, who would later write A Sand County Almanac, erected a monument to the passenger pigeon in 1947. Young would have known this monument and its inscription, which mourns not just the bird but the human capacity for annihilation: the ability to reduce something that once filled the sky to a single bird dying in a zoo cage, the clock tolling one.

Mr. Spitzer mourns Martha with the same intensity he mourns Cousin Hannah. Young is making something precise here: the extinction of a species and the death of a person are not the same scale of loss, but they are the same kind of loss. Both are irreversible. Both leave a silence that cannot be filled by substitution. Both represent the closing of a world that will not reopen. Martha is every Martha: every last thing, every final instance, every door that shuts for the last time as the clock is tolling one.

The shipwreck lighthouse

Young gives Mr. Spitzer two contradictory images in rapid succession: he is like a shipwreck, his hull broken, “paying out more water than the seas contained and” he is the living lighthouse, seeing his own light at the one moment when he is dying, his own light shining from him.

The shipwreck is disintegration: the structure that was built to float, now taking on more water than the ocean, overwhelmed from the inside by the thing that was supposed to be kept outside. Mr. Spitzer is flooding. His memories, his griefs, his panpsychist suffering, his attribution of consciousness to everything: the interior is now exceeding the container.

But the lighthouse, at the moment of his dying, sees its own light. This is extraordinary. A lighthouse does not normally see its own beam; it projects outward, for others, and is itself in the dark at the source. But Young gives Mr. Spitzer, in the moment of extinction, the simultaneous experience of being the light and seeing the light. He is both the source and the witness. For one moment, the sporadic, intermittent, second-remove consciousness achieves the simultaneous presence it has never been able to sustain in ordinary life.

This is what dying gives him. Not resolution, not peace, but for once, the complete experience of himself.

Trusting only the false

So he had come to trust only the false.

Why “should he trust the truth which had already failed him if the false would never fail” (if inconstancy was the only constancy, if the stone crumbled like a cloud) then trusting the false is not delusion but accurate accounting. It is the epistemological position of someone who has been paying attention.

Young makes this formulation with complete seriousness. Mr. Spitzer is not endorsing dishonesty. He is noting that the things that present themselves as stable (truth, constancy, the solid foundation) have repeatedly proved less reliable than the things that admit their instability from the start. The false is honest about being false. The uncertain is honest about being uncertain. The inconstant never pretends to be permanent. In a world where the stable crumbles and the permanent passes, trusting the false may be the most rational available option.

This is the epistemology of a man who has watched the suffrage captain die sobbing, who has seen his brother go before him into the dark, who has observed the most formidable person he knew reduced by death to a woman crying for her skirt. The stable things failed. The constant things changed. The stone crumbled. What remains is the honest admission of fragility, and the paradoxical reliability of things that never claimed to be solid.

An image within an image

“He knew not whether he was himself or an image contained within an image.”

This formulation has been building since the first chapter: the doubles, the twins, the possible identity substitution, the faces that are not quite what they seem. Now it arrives at its fullest expression: not just the uncertainty about which twin survived, but the more radical uncertainty about whether the self is an original or a copy of a copy of something that may itself have been a copy.

To All My Darlings compares this to Schrödinger's cat: the thought experiment in which a cat in a sealed box is simultaneously alive and dead until the box is opened and the state is observed. Mr. Spitzer is the cat. The box is his own consciousness. He cannot observe himself from outside himself, which means the state remains unresolved. He is both the man he thinks he is and the image of that man, and possibly also the image of his brother, and the image of the man his brother thought he was. Images within images, with no original that anyone can locate.

Young offers this not as a crisis exactly, Mr. Spitzer has been living inside this uncertainty for so long that it has become his habitual atmosphere, but as a description of the furthest reach of his condition. He is as fragmented as the novel itself, as multiple as Catherine, as displaced as Cousin Hannah's spirit wandering through posthumous geographies. He is, in his own modest and cautious way, as vast as any of them.

He could love only by indirection

One of the chapter's most important and least emphasized lines: he could love only by indirection.

Mr. Spitzer is drawn to those who have lost everything: the dispossessed, the wanderers through the storm of years, the hidden majority sleeping in the churchyard. He trusts them. He is nearest them in the city. They are all his loves. And the reason is that he cannot love directly: cannot look a person in the face and say I love you and have that be sufficient to the scale of what he feels, or sufficient to the distance between himself and everyone he has ever wanted to reach.

Loving by indirection is loving Martha the passenger pigeon. Loving by indirection is weeping for the extinct when you cannot weep for yourself. It is carrying the alpenhorn. It is keeping the secret. It is being the lamplighter of stars that no one asked you to tend. All of it is love, Young insists: the oblique form, the sideways approach, the love that does not announce itself because announcement is a mode of presence Mr. Spitzer cannot manage. It counts. She means for it to count.

The pigeon-colored dawn

“If there were no pigeons, could there be people or pigeon people or the pigeon-colored dawn, rose and blue and silver and gold mottled like the pigeon’s wing”?

Young's description of a dawn that is pigeon-colored (“rose and blue and silver and gold mottled,” variegated, the complex light of a sky that once held millions of them) is one of the novel's most beautiful ecological elegies. The passenger pigeon, in its extinction, has become the color of loss itself: the dawn that was once the backdrop for their flight, the light that fell on their wings, now a shade that has outlasted them. The dawn remembers the pigeons even though the pigeons are gone.

Mr. Spitzer has “lost all sense of the hour.” He cannot tell the dawn from the dusk, cannot locate himself in the day's progression. The pigeon-colored light (the light of before-dawn, before-loss, before-the-extinction) is the only time he recognizes, and it does not correspond to any hour on the clock.

What to hold onto

Chapter 49 is one of the novel's most spacious and most sorrowful chapters: the chapter where Mr. Spitzer is given, perhaps for the first time, the full scale of his own consciousness. He is simultaneously the shipwreck and the lighthouse. He is the cat in the box, both states unresolved. He is the mourner for everyone who has not been mourned, the unofficial representative of the causes the churchyard sleepers never got to argue for.

What to carry forward: Martha dying as the clock tolled one, the precision of that record, the finality of it, the way Young turns an ecological catastrophe into a philosophical emblem without diminishing either. The lighthouse seeing its own light at the moment of dying. And the love that can only be expressed by indirection, which is still love, which Young insists is still love, even when the lover is a shipwreck and the beloved is extinct and the dawn is the color of what has been lost.

Chapter 31: Here Lies the Dead Love of the World

← Chapter 30 · Guide Home · Chapter 32 →

Research notes: Chapter 31

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer

Themes: Grief, Loss, and Mourning

Symbols: Keys, Doors, and Locks

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Deafness and Sign Language · The History of Opium

Chapter 31 deepens Cousin Hannah’s portrait in two directions at once: it gives us the great captain’s inner life (her secret grief, her failed mission to rescue Catherine, the love she never spoke of) and it gives us Mr. Spitzer’s relationship to her: the faithful caller at her perpetually empty house, the one who buried her, the one still composing her epitaph.

This chapter contains some of the most beautiful writing in the novel. Read slowly.

What actually happens in Chapter 31

The chapter moves through three connected strands. First: the enduring relationship between Catherine and Mr. Spitzer in Cousin Hannah’s absence, their mutual admiration of the captain who made “their own adventures seem forever unfulfilled.” Second: the full portrait of Hannah’s secret, her grief, never named directly, her failed battle to rescue Catherine from her opium dreams, her verdict on both Spitzer brothers. Third: Mr. Spitzer’s long faithfulness to Hannah’s empty house, his calling cards pushed through the slot, his knocking on the door he was sure would not open, his grief at her death, and his inability to settle on an epitaph.

The chapter’s great set piece is Mr. Spitzer’s cascade of draft epitaphs for Cousin Hannah, each one more expansive and more grieving than the last, all of them crossed out, ending in a simple headstone with only her name and no dates.

Hannah’s secret grief

Chapter 30 told us that Hannah’s “entire life had been perhaps an act of sorrow and redemption,” caused by the loss of a skirt. Chapter 31 tells us a little more, but only a little. “She had never married, for her life had been shadowed with grief which was mentioned whisperingly with hesitation even now by my mother and Mr. Spitzer, both of whom seemed to wish to bury the great secret of Cousin Hannah’s life.”

Young will not name the secret directly. She gives us its shape instead: Hannah searched all her life for a “dead love, a body covered by” snow. She had taken what amounts to a vow against the external man, “giving her gentleman’s word of honor,” as if serving “as a barrier between herself and any other love which wore a human face.” “Her furies had not diminished but had increased as she had furiously tried to climb the walls of forbidden cities of brides, those who were held in thralldom by a cruel bridegroom.”

What Young is tracing, in the most oblique language available to her in 1965, is the shape of a love that could not be named or lived. Hannah’s great adventure, all those decades of disguise and action and desert crossings, was built over a grief she could never speak. She had given her gentleman’s word of honor, which is itself the tell: not a lady’s vow, but a gentleman’s. She lived in the register she was given. The skirt that was lost is the world she could not inhabit.

Hannah’s mission to rescue Catherine

Young reveals something in this chapter that reshapes how we understand Cousin Hannah’s relationship to the household: she had wanted to carry Catherine “away from this dark tower, to rescue her from” the opium dreams of dead love. It had been her losing battle. “She had won greater battles than this” one. She had lost this one.

Hannah’s verdict on Catherine was direct, as everything about her was direct: Catherine “was in love with no man on earth but with a fleeting shadow, the mere shadow of a man.” And her verdict on both brothers was equally unsparing: Joachim “was weak as water, deceitful and wavering,” blown about like foam; Peron was equally deceitful without even pretending otherwise. Hobson’s choice. “A choice between death and death.”

Hannah was right about many things. She was wrong about one: “she did not seem to know that death was necessary to my mother’s love.” Catherine requires the dead man. The shadow is the point. Hannah, who was always in motion, who pitched her tent in far deserts and never stayed, could not understand a love that required stillness and darkness and the opium-maintained preservation of loss. Her directness, which served her in every other battle, failed her here.

Mr. Spitzer at Hannah’s door

Young gives us one of the novel’s great comic-elegiac passages in Mr. Spitzer’s visits to Hannah’s perpetually empty house. He came always “when he knew she was absent”: absent in the Alps, absent in Arabia, absent at sea in an open boat without captain or compass. He timed his visits as an elegant strategy, “a countermove to her ignoring him.”

The signs of her absence catalogued at her door are extraordinary: the closed shutters, the broken lanterns, “the summer furniture left out all winter” under white trees with “long white hair blowing in the wind, the tattered” awnings like Arab tents, the frozen fountains, the old newspapers blowing on the porches. He reads the newspapers for news of her journeys: knowing they are not always accurate, that she had taken many journeys they had not known.

And yet, through the great keyhole large enough for a butterfly to fly through, he sometimes sees a great rounded eye staring back “at him with equal astonishment, its iris streaked like a sunken rainbow.” He calls out, hallo, hallo. He bangs on the door. He concludes “it was a star passing in a cloud.” He pushes “his calling card through the slot” (embossed with the butterfly, “his sign of resurrection and eternal life”) and goes away.

He continued these visits, Young tells us with perfect deadpan, even for a brief period after she was already dead and the house was torn down. He was this empty cocoon, he thought, standing before an address that no longer existed.

The epitaphs

The cascade of draft epitaphs Mr. Spitzer composes and crosses out is one of the novel’s greatest passages, and it deserves to be read aloud. Young gives us eight or nine of them, each one reaching for something truer, each one abandoned:

“Here lies the great captain unhorsed.” “Here lies that great Crusader who rode against the Saracens and the Greeks” and “the Romans and the English and the French. She raided the Etruscan towns. She invaded the cities of night.” “Here lies the greatest captain who fought against all nations and rescued many ladies from their dark towers and cruel lords but could not rescue herself. Here lies one who searched all her life for her dead love, a body covered by the snow. Here lies one who was pitiful. Here lies one who shared our common lot of mortal frailty and died of her life.”

Each epitaph is true. None is complete. The one he settles on is the simplest: her name only, and no dates, because he cannot remember the date of her death and she had never told him the date of her birth. So he gives her, in his own inaccuracy, this extension of time.

The final phrase, “here lies the dead love of the world,” is the one Young uses as the chapter’s emotional summit, and it is Mr. Spitzer’s most honest statement about what Cousin Hannah was. Not the dead love of one person. “The dead love of the world”: the capacity for love itself, as it exists in the world, lying “in a grey New England churchyard” with a jeweled sword and a St. Bernard.

What to watch for as you keep reading

Light spoilers: This section hints at what happens later in the novel. Skip it if you want to meet the story fresh.

Cousin Hannah will return in later chapters with her own narrative space. What this chapter establishes is the emotional register she inhabits in the novel: she is the figure of action whose inner life is entirely secret, the woman who fought every battle except the one closest to her, the captain whose ship, in the end, came home to a domestic war.

“She died at home. She perished in a domestic war.” Young places this quietly, near the end of Mr. Spitzer’s draft epitaphs, without elaboration. After all those Alps and deserts and Moroccan pirates and Spanish cavalcades, Cousin Hannah “died in her own old tent bed set in a windy place with no aide-de-camp.” The greatest captain “was taken by a greater captain” wearing a winding shroud.

Mr. Spitzer’s inability to settle on an epitaph for Hannah mirrors his inability to settle on one for Peron. He has two graves he cannot adequately mark: his brother’s and the great captain’s. Both headstones are incomplete. Both people exceeded his capacity to find the right words. This is, quietly, the novel’s statement about Mr. Spitzer’s music: the silence is not failure. It is the only honest response to what exceeds language.

Chapter 33: The Late Mrs. Catherine Cartwheel

← Chapter 32 · Guide Home · Chapter 34 →

Research notes: Chapter 33

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Peron Spitzer · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Music, Sound, and Silence

Symbols: Music and Instruments

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: The History of Opium

Chapter 33 is a quieter chapter after the great set pieces of the Cousin Hannah sequence, but it does important work. It gathers together threads from across the novel (the newspaper that declared Catherine dead, Mr. Spitzer’s faithfulness, the wedding that may or may not have happened, the music he is still writing) and settles into something that functions almost as a pause, a breathing space before the novel expands again.

It also contains one of the most tender portraits of their relationship we have had: Mr. Spitzer’s decision that her inaccuracy is a kind of freedom, and his determination, for all his impatience, to keep opening the door.

What actually happens in Chapter 33

A Boston newspaper has referred to Catherine as the late Mrs. Catherine Cartwheel, reporting her dead. Mr. Spitzer has not told her. He has allowed the error to stand, reasoning that she is “an opium taker in love with her starry illusions—and” the illusion “should not be corrected, at least not by him.”

He also notes that the same newspaper reported Peron Spitzer “seen recently walking along Benevolent Street, peering into old doorways.” Mr. Spitzer walked down the same street the very next evening “when the lamp-lighters were lighting the lamps,” “his black cape whirling around him like the sobbing of the rain upon the river Styx.” He saw a carriage where for years there had been no carriages.

Catherine’s memory of her wedding is revisited: the bridegroom was a white camel veiled in lace, a church steeple, the wind. “She had been married to Death while” sleeping. She cannot remember the details clearly. Sometimes she thinks she has never been married at all. She is sure she never married Mr. Spitzer.

Mr. Spitzer meditates on Catherine’s inaccuracy, her distended memory, and arrives at his most generous understanding of her: her conscious states are “like the unconscious states of other people,” and she is “probably no more distant from reality than were the lamp-lighters going their lonely rounds,” those who punch time-clocks, “those who must turn great wheels.” They, too, can live only while they dream.

The chapter ends with Mr. Spitzer getting up to open a door Catherine is asking a human-sized blackbird to open.

The newspaper error

The Boston newspaper that declared Catherine dead, and then reported Peron seen peering into doorways on Benevolent Street, is doing what newspapers do in Young’s world: reporting from a position of partial knowledge, getting the essential things wrong and the incidental things right, being corrected by time in ways no one can anticipate.

Mr. Spitzer’s response to the first error is characteristic: he allows it to stand. He is not in the position to correct it. The newspaper will eventually be right, he reasons, having merely mistaken the time. This is Mr. Spitzer’s philosophy of error applied to journalism: inaccuracies are often premature truths. The mistake is not that Catherine is dead but that the timing is off.

The second error, Peron seen on Benevolent Street, is something Mr. Spitzer investigates in person. He walks the same street the next evening. He sees a carriage. For years there had been “no carriages on the streets of Boston.” Young gives us this detail and moves on, but its weight is exact: on the street named for kindness, on the evening after his dead brother was reportedly seen peering into old doorways, Mr. Spitzer sees a carriage that should not exist. He makes no comment. He continues.

The dead letter

Near the chapter’s center, Young gives us one of her most perfect images of Mr. Spitzer: he has been going “to the post office day after day to inquire for a dead letter,” asking that they trace a letter he “mailed to himself many years ago” that was never “delivered though it was marked clearly with his return address.” The envelope contained a piece of blank paper.

A letter to himself, containing nothing, sent years ago, never arrived, still being traced. This is Mr. Spitzer’s entire situation in three sentences. He has been trying to communicate with himself across the gap of his brother’s death, across the years of inaccuracy and grief, and the letter (blank, addressed to himself, never delivered) is the silent music he has been composing all his life. The message is empty because there is nothing to say. The return address is there because he needs to know where he lives. He keeps going to the post office because the alternative is to stop expecting the letter to arrive.

Mr. Spitzer’s defense of Catherine’s inaccuracy

The chapter’s most important passage is Mr. Spitzer’s extended meditation on Catherine’s distended memory, and it represents his greatest act of generosity toward her.

He has come gradually to believe, he says, that her conscious states are “probably like the unconscious states of other people.” She is “enslaved by her drug habit which had robbed her of her sense of time,” but she is “probably no more enslaved than others” are by their predisposition toward illusion, “no more distant from reality than were the lamp-lighters going their lonely rounds or those who must punch time-clocks in great factories.” They, too, can live only while they dream. They, too, are never quite awake.

This is Mr. Spitzer dissolving the distinction between Catherine and the rest of humanity. He is not excusing her. He is insisting that her position is not exceptional: that the opium dreams are a more visible version of what everyone does, and that her inaccuracy is a greater freedom than accuracy would have been. She lives in a wider space. She has not “closed a door or written finis to a deathless dream as” his brother surely did.

And so he gets up and opens the door when she asks the blackbird to open it. Not because he believes the blackbird can hear her. Because the door needs opening, and he is there.

The harp music of bridges

One further detail deserves attention. Mr. Spitzer is writing harp music that “should be the exact imitation of the wind playing through the strings and cables of a bridge”: the bridge reflected upon water, his music to “be finished only with the dying wind, wind dying over the water.” He is “studying the velocity of wind over bridges, the tonnage of wind pressure against cables, ascertaining that sometimes twenty thousand tons of wind” break against a single string.

This is the silent music finally given a specific form. Not silence exactly, but the sound of a bridge: the structure designed to connect two shores, to bear the weight of crossing, trembling under the force of what passes through it. Mr. Spitzer has spent his life as a bridge between the living and the dead, between his brother and the world, between Catherine and reality. Of course his music sounds like the wind through bridge cables. Of course it can only be finished when the wind dies.

What to watch for as you keep reading

Light spoilers: This section hints at what happens later in the novel. Skip it if you want to meet the story fresh.

The novel is approaching the end of Volume One. We have spent thirty-three chapters in and around Catherine’s coastal house, inside the minds of Vera, Miss MacIntosh, Mr. Spitzer, and Cousin Hannah. The world is about to expand dramatically when Volume Two begins. Hold what you have. Every new character, every new geography, will be understood against this foundation.

Mr. Spitzer’s reasoning that the newspaper will eventually be right about Catherine, having merely mistaken the time, is Young’s statement about the novel’s relationship to truth. The novel is not interested in what is factually accurate at any given moment. It is interested in the longer truth, the one the inaccurate clock will eventually strike. Patience with inaccuracy is not moral failure. It is, in this novel’s world, the condition of understanding.

The human-sized blackbird Catherine is talking to when Mr. Spitzer gets up to open the door is one of those small perfect images Young places without comment. Catherine holds a perfectly rational conversation with a blackbird. The blackbird’s response, apparently, is quite rational. Mr. Spitzer looks around, cannot hear the answer she hears, gets up and opens the door. He has learned to make himself useful in the space between what she perceives and what is there.

Chapter 52: So Many Wedding Gowns and No Bride's Slippers

← Chapter 51 · Guide Home · Chapter 53 →

Research notes: Chapter 52

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer

Themes: Dreams and Imagination · Illusion and Reality · Memory and the Past · Music, Sound, and Silence · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · Keys, Doors, and Locks · Weddings and Funerals

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology

Allusions: Women's Suffrage

Mr. Spitzer opens the trunks.

Trunk lid after trunk lid. He has been working through Cousin Hannah's estate for chapters now: the papers, the alpenhorn, the keys that fit no locks, the documents sealed by rust and flame. And now the trunks. And what he finds, in trunk after trunk after trunk, is wedding gowns. Sheets of silk. Veils of lace. “Porous silks so thin that the least touch might cause them to fall into nothingness.” “Many bridal gowns and no bride’s slippers.”

To All My Darlings pauses here and asks all the right questions: had Cousin Hannah secretly wanted to marry even though she had publicly opposed the institution? Had there been forty suitors she backed away from at the last moment? Had there been forty weddings where she was the one who did not appear? Or, the guide ventures this quietly, had there been one, only one, the bridegroom left at the church door, the love killed by false modesty, and all these gowns were the accumulated evidence of the life she had prepared for and could not bring herself to live?

Young does not answer. The trunks are the answer, or as close as you will get. The gowns are the secret. The no slippers are the secret. The secret is not a fact but a shape: the shape of a life organized around a door it never walked through.

What actually happens in Chapter 52

Mr. Spitzer goes through Cousin Hannah's estate and finds what is there to find. He finds the wedding gowns. He finds letters in languages he cannot read. He finds the “skirt embroidered with forget-me-nots”: her lost skirt, the one she called for in the delirium, the one she had sent someone to retrieve from a mountain peak and that person had not returned. He finds evidence of a woman who was both bride and bridegroom, who crossed every gender boundary the culture had placed in her path, who lived simultaneously as Hannah in Boston and Hamid in the East.

He finds her book open to page seven: Tristram and Yseult, the chivalric romance of illicit love, the story of the love that was magnificent and impossible and survived its own prohibition only to end in death. Matthew Arnold's poem about it has seven sections. Page seven of any text is where the story has just begun and you do not yet know what will be lost.

He reflects that “all might have been imaginary in this life as in this death.” He wonders: “surely her entire life could not have been a game of hide-and-seek, for although she was hiding—who was seeking for her?”

He almost turns to her, at this moment. Almost reaches for her even though she is dead, as one who might be rescued by the person you thought you were rescuing. He does not turn. He does not reach. He keeps the secret. Young does not tell us exactly what the secret is. She tells us its shape, and its weight, and the fact that Mr. Spitzer has decided it will remain a secret, and that this decision is the one meaningful thing he has been able to do for her in a life organized around failing to reach her.

The wedding gowns

Think carefully about what it means to find this many wedding gowns in a dead woman's trunks.

The obvious reading: she wanted to marry and couldn't, or didn't, and kept the evidence of that wanting in locked trunks because there was nowhere else to put it. The suffrage captain who publicly had no time for love, no time for feminine wiles, no time for the domestic arrangements of conventional womanhood; she had, in private, accumulated the material evidence of exactly the domestic arrangements she publicly refused.

But Young complicates even this. The gowns are numerous. They suggest not one failed marriage but many approaches to the threshold, each one turned away from, each one packed into a trunk and locked away. The silk so thin it would fall into nothingness at a touch: the same fragility that characterizes the love itself: real, present, accumulated, but unable to survive contact with the world.

And no bride's slippers. The gown without the slippers is the ceremony without the completion. The bride dressed but not shod for the walk down the aisle. The preparations were made and then arrested at the last item. The slippers are what take you forward, what move you from the vestibule into the ceremony. Cousin Hannah never put on the slippers. She put on everything else. She could not take the final step.

The skirt and the forget-me-nots

The lost skirt surfaces again here with its full detail: it was white lace, embroidered with forget-me-nots, the “little flowers which were like the memories of little loves.” It had blown away on a mountain peak or been left there, and someone had gone to retrieve it and not come back. The skirt was retrievable. The person sent for it was not.

Forget-me-nots are the flowers of remembrance: their name comes from a German legend of a knight who drowned while picking them for his beloved, crying Vergiss mich nicht as he went under. The flowers Cousin Hannah embroidered on her skirt are the flowers of the love that went under while trying to bring her something she wanted. This is the story of false modesty killing the love: she wanted the skirt, someone went to get it, the getting killed them, and she came back without either the skirt or the lover.

Young gives you this detail without insisting on it. The forget-me-nots on the lost skirt. The name of the flowers as the injunction of the dead. Don't forget. She didn't forget. She put the injunction in the embroidery and wore it until she lost it, and then called for it at the end of her life, and now Mr. Spitzer holds it in his hands, the lace so thin it might fall into nothingness at a touch, the flowers still there, still saying: don't forget.

Tristram and Yseult, page seven

She had left her book open at page seven, which is where Matthew Arnold's poem about Tristram and Iseult begins the section where Tristram is dying, tended by his wife Iseult of Brittany, while the other Iseult (Iseult of Ireland, the one he truly loved, the one he was not allowed to love) has been summoned but has not yet arrived.

The Tristram legend is the great medieval story of a love that violated every social contract and could not be renounced. Tristram and Iseult of Ireland loved each other through marriage and separation and years of prohibition, until they were dying, and even then the love did not release them. Young places Cousin Hannah at this precise page: the moment of the deathbed wait, the summoned lover who has not yet arrived, the wife who is present but who knows she is not the one who was truly loved.

Whose page is this? Is Cousin Hannah Tristram, dying and waiting for the forbidden love to arrive? Is she Iseult of Ireland, the true love who was kept away? Is she Iseult of Brittany, the legitimate wife who was always the second choice? Young leaves the book open on page seven without assigning Cousin Hannah a role in the story. She may be all three. She may have read the same page so many times that the book opened there of its own accord, the spine broken at the place her grief lived.

Perhaps she should be the husband and not the bride

Young gives Mr. Spitzer this thought: “perhaps she should be the husband and not the bride, for should not death multiply life’s uncertainties and propose no firm foundation stone or unchanging lintel”?

This is the novel's most direct engagement with Cousin Hannah's gender, not just the masculine virtues she claimed, not just the Hannah/Hamid/Great Moor multiple identities, but the question of which role she occupied in the love she could not live. Bride or bridegroom. Both roles are present in the trunks: the wedding gowns are for a bride; the alpenhorn, the iron keys, the campaigns, the decisive way she lived are for someone who functions as a husband. She may have been both, or neither, or she may have spent her life moving between them without being able to settle in either.

Death, Young writes, multiplies life's uncertainties. It does not resolve them. The great social fictions (husband, bride, the firm foundation stone and unchanging lintel of the marriage ceremony) are revealed by death to have never been as stable as they pretended. The lintel shifts. The stone erodes. The certainties that organized a life turn out to have been provisional all along.

The locksmith in a street of dreams

Mr. Spitzer describes himself in Chapter 52 as the “locksmith in a street of dreams where there was neither key nor lock.”

He is the executor. He has the keys to Cousin Hannah's estate. He has spent chapters fumbling with keys that fit no locks, opening trunks that answer no questions, certifying documents that reveal no definitive truth. He is the person whose professional function is to unlock, and he is operating in a space where the very categories of key and lock have dissolved into dream.

The locksmith without a lock is the legal professional without the rule of law, the musician without the instrument, the lamplighter without the stars. He has all the equipment of a person with a purpose. The purpose has been revoked by the environment it was meant to operate in. He is perfectly equipped for a world that does not correspond to his equipment.

And yet he continues. He opens trunk after trunk. He finds wedding gowns. He keeps the secret. The locksmith in the street of dreams does not stop being a locksmith simply because there are no locks. He goes on trying the keys, one after another, in the doors of the place where Cousin Hannah's life was kept.

No language contained truth

The chapter closes on this: “no language contained truth, for the truth was that which could not be expressed.”

Young has been working up to this formulation for the entire novel, but it lands with particular weight in Chapter 52 because the chapter has just shown you what the truth looks like when it cannot be expressed: it looks like trunk after trunk of wedding gowns and no bride's slippers. It looks like a book open to page seven. It looks like a “skirt embroidered with forget-me-nots” that fell into nothingness when Mr. Spitzer touched it. The truth is there. It has a shape. It has a weight. It has a texture: the porous silk, the lace that might collapse. It simply cannot be said in words, because words would make it something that can be argued with, qualified, revised, denied. In the trunks, it cannot be denied.

Mr. Spitzer's decision to keep the secret is, among other things, a decision about language: there are no words that would do what these trunks do. He cannot tell Catherine what he found, not because the information is too painful but because the translation would falsify it. Some truths are only true as objects. The wedding gowns are the truth. The words for them are not.

What to hold onto

Chapter 52 is where the novel's great secret settles into its final form, not revealed as a fact but disclosed as a shape. Cousin Hannah kept wedding gowns. She left her book open to the deathbed page. She called for a skirt embroidered with the flowers of remembrance. She was both bride and bridegroom, both the love and its prohibition, both the suffrage captain who had no time for domestic life and the woman who had packed the evidence of domestic longing into trunk after trunk, sealed with rust and flame.

What Mr. Spitzer keeps is not just her secret. He keeps the space of her contradiction: the space where a person's public commitments and private desires never resolved into a single coherent life, and yet the life was genuinely and magnificently lived. The locksmith in the street of dreams keeps the keys that open no locks, because the keeping is the only form of love still available to him, and love (even by indirection, even without a lock to fit) is what he has always been.

guide-77-who-killed-the-heavens:
Chapter 77: Who Killed the Heavens

← Chapter 76 · Guide Home · Chapter 78 →

Content note: The Esther Longtree chapters (72 to 81) deal with stillbirth and pregnancy loss, rape, infanticide, racist violence including lynching, and cruelty to children. This chapter describes the murder of mothers and newborns and deals with racism.

Research notes: Chapter 77

Characters: Esther Longtree · Justice O’Leary · Miss MacIntosh · Mrs. Hogden

Themes: Death and Mortality · Dreams and Imagination · Motherhood, Pregnancy, and Birth · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Birds · Pregnancy, Birth, and Children · Shadows

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Fairy Tales and Folklore · Judaism · Pregnancy, Abortion, and Midwifery · The Bible

For some, this may be a very dark chapter.

This chapter deepens everything that has come before in Esther’s sequence: the racial dimension of the detective’s work, the history of violence against unmarried mothers and their children, the cosmic scale of Esther’s grief, the parents who never consummated their marriage, the little boy who grew a shadow and mistrusts her, and the exhibits A through U, an abecedary of accusation that Young assembles from the materials of Esther’s life and the world’s indifference to it.

Young wrote this novel over eighteen years, and through all of it abortion and contraception were illegal in the United States. The newspaper clipping the detective sends Esther is not entirely fictional. The quiet murders are not metaphor alone. The chapter holds the literal and the symbolic together without separating them, because for Esther, and for the women whose histories the novel draws on, they were never separate to begin with.

What Actually Happens

The chapter opens with Esther asking who killed the heavens, the earth, love itself. She is pregnant with death, her body watery and vast, “her spinal column curved by the weight” of memory. She works at the Greasy Spoon. She tries to forget the moths and the stillborn who come to her at night. She cannot.

The detective sends her a yellowed newspaper clipping: “Mass Murderess Apprehended, Accused by Dead Mothers and Dead Children.” It describes an old woman abortionist (large, nearly three hundred pounds) who ran a hospital for poor, unmarried mothers. She and her timid little assistant treated the mothers well, right up until delivery. The fathers sent bouquets. Then, at the moment of birth, mother and baby were killed. The babies were buried with lime. The abortionist was caught because she made a fatal error: she killed a woman who was pregnant only in her dreams, who could not have been a mother, whose body showed the impossibility of what she claimed. She had murdered a phantom pregnancy. The impossible evidence exposed her.

Esther reads this clipping and understands what the detective is sending her: a mirror. A warning. A comparison. She is the woman always pregnant. She is always carrying what the world cannot see. He is the man who investigates quiet murders. He only solves the white mysteries. The deaths of little Black children are not his business. He fears what he calls “black mysteries.”

Esther learns something new in this chapter: her first child was born of a Black man. This appears without elaboration, as a fact she is thinking about while the clipping is in her hands. Her first child, of all the fathers, came from a Black man. The detective’s racial accounting (his selective attention to white deaths, his indifference to Black ones) is therefore personal: her first child falls in the category he has written off.

Esther recalls her parents: a large, passive policeman of a father and a small, fragile, child-like mother. They never consummated their marriage. Between them passed a silver spoon, carried by a third woman as go-between, enabling a conception that was strange and artificial from the start. This is how Esther came into the world: through a marriage that was not a marriage, a union that produced her without conventional intimacy. She was adopted, she has already told us. This is the prehistory behind the adoption: the parents who could not reach each other and needed an intermediary even for conception. There is also a little boy, an exception among the stillborn, who grew and cast a shadow, who cried like the night wind and falling leaves, who mistrusts Esther, who obstructs her path and causes her to stumble. He is not the little shadow boxer still living under her heart. He is something else: a child who came further than the others, who exists in a liminal space between living and not-living, who will not answer her questions and will not forgive her. She wants to “reach him once with her hands” and still him. She cannot.

The exhibits: A for agony, M for murder, N for Negro, S for shadow, and onward through the alphabet to U, a catalogue of everything that accuses Esther and everything the world has done. Young assembles the letters of accusation into an abecedary, the most elementary form of learning, as if to say: this is the alphabet of Esther’s life. These are the first things. Learn them before you learn anything else.

Esther asserts, in the end, her preference for silence, for mystery, for the void over explanation or judgment. She is always right, the chapter notes, like Miss MacIntosh, like Mrs. Hogden, she has arranged her world so she is never wrong, or never appears to be. She wants to remain outside old human laws and inquisitions, in the great serenity of her strange condition. She wonders why she should “be punished for a few mistakes” when she has already suffered so much. Why should she be bothered, when there is going to be another war anyway.

The Newspaper Clipping

The old woman abortionist is one of the most chilling figures Young introduces, and she is introduced at one remove, through a yellowed clipping, through the detective’s chosen mirror for Esther. She ran a hospital. She took in poor, unmarried mothers. She treated them well. The fathers sent bouquets. She killed the mothers and the babies at delivery. The babies were buried with lime so the bodies would dissolve into the earth and leave no trace.

She was caught because she applied her method to the wrong woman. The woman was pregnant only in her dreams: a false pregnancy, a pseudocyesis, a body that had produced all the symptoms of pregnancy with no child present. When the abortionist attempted to kill what she believed was there, the absence of a child made the murder impossible to conceal in the usual way. The phantom pregnancy exposed the real murders.

Young has been building toward this figure for several chapters. Esther’s condition (always pregnant, children that come as fragments or not at all) is, To All My Darlings notes, consistent with pseudocyesis: a real medical condition in which the body produces pregnancy symptoms, including abdominal enlargement, breast changes, and felt fetal movement, in the absence of a fetus. Young does not resolve whether Esther’s condition is this, or something supernatural, or something else entirely. What the clipping introduces is the shadow-Esther: the woman who is pregnant only in her dreams, who would have been killed by the abortionist for being exactly what Esther may be.

To All My Darlings notes that this story may have its roots in real events, particularly the practice of baby farming: the Victorian-era and early-twentieth-century practice of accepting custody of infants for payment, which in some cases became cover for systematic murder. The most documented case is Amelia Dyer, who murdered infants over thirty years, disposing of bodies in rivers, and whose “timid assistant” was her own daughter. The detail that the fathers sent bouquets is one of Young’s most precise indictments: the men who produced the children had the leisure for flowers. The women who carried them were killed.

Esther’s First Child

The disclosure arrives without ceremony: Esther’s first child was born of a Black man. Young places this beside the detective’s racial accounting: his exclusive attention to white deaths, his explicit statement that the deaths of Black children are not his business, there being too many and too unimportant, without commenting on the connection. The comment is the placement.

Esther’s first child, her first loss, falls in the category the detective has written off. If there is an investigation to be done into that first death, the detective will not do it. His pursuit of Esther is selective in a way that has nothing to do with justice and everything to do with the racial calculus he has already performed. He is interested in what she might have done to children he considers worth investigating. The first one (the one she carries longest, perhaps, in memory) is not among them.

Esther’s Parents and Her Artificial Origin

Esther’s parents never consummated their marriage. Her father is large and passive, a policeman whose authority is imposing and whose life is lonely. Her mother is small and fragile and child-like, proud of her delicacy, emotionally cold. Between them, conception required an intermediary: a third woman carrying a silver spoon between them, enabling what their bodies and relationship could not produce directly.

This is the strangest detail of Esther’s origin: she came into the world through a kind of assisted reproduction so oblique and archaic that it has the quality of a fairy tale. The silver spoon as an instrument of conception: the spoon born with the privileged child, the utensil of sufficiency and inheritance, here used to bridge an unbridgeable gap. Esther is the child of a union that could not quite happen, produced by a mechanism that no one would have designed if anyone had been thinking clearly.

And then she was adopted out from these parents, or adopted into them. The chapter is not entirely clear on which direction the adoption moved. What is clear is that her origin is strange, artificial, and mediated by others, which is the precise condition of her own reproductive life, where the children come through a process that no one can quite explain or control, and where the fathers are transient and the mother is the only constant.

The Little Boy Who Grew a Shadow

Among all the stillborn (the fragments, the snowflakes, the cobwebs) there is one exception: a “little boy who grew and cast his shadow.” He survived long enough to have a shadow, which is the minimum evidence of a body in the world. He cries like the night wind, like falling leaves. He mistrusts Esther. He walks in her way and causes her to stumble. He will not answer any question. He is not the little shadow boxer, who is still alive and fighting under her heart. He is something older, something from before the shadow boxer, something that came and did not quite die but did not quite live either. He is Esther’s accusation: the child who is just real enough to blame her, who has enough presence in the world to obstruct her, who will not let her pass without consequence. She wants to “reach him once with her hands” and still him. This is Esther’s most maternal impulse and her most tragic impossibility simultaneously: the child she wants to comfort is the one she cannot reach, the one who mistrusts her, the one whose crying she cannot stop. The stillborn who hover around her and applaud at least do not accuse. This one does.

The Exhibits: A Through U

Young assembles an abecedary of accusation: A for agony, M for murder, N for Negro, S for shadow, and onward. The alphabet is the first thing a child learns: the building block of all literacy, all language, all the tools by which the world makes sense of itself. Young gives Esther’s situation an alphabet. These are the first letters of what has happened to her. Before you can read anything else, you must read this.

The letter N for Negro in Esther’s alphabet of accusation is not incidental. It is placed precisely. The racial dimension of Esther’s story (the detective’s selective attention, her first child’s father, the quiet black mysteries that no one investigates) belongs in the first letters of what the world has done. The abecedary runs through twenty-one letters. Twenty-one exhibits. Agony through: whatever U stands for. Young does not give us all the words, only some. The gaps are part of the accusation too.

Pregnant with Death

The chapter’s central image of Esther pregnant with death (her womb watery and vast, her body the site of creation and sterility simultaneously) is Young’s most cosmic rendering of Esther’s condition. She is the “Song of Songs of the sterility which is the creation.” The Song of Songs is the Hebrew Bible’s erotic poem: the text where two bodies reach toward each other in equal desire, where creation is celebrated as sensual and mutual. Young inverts it: the song of the sterility that is also a creation, the pregnancy that is also a death, the body that generates and loses simultaneously. Who killed the heavens, the earth, love itself? Esther asks this at the chapter’s opening and does not answer it, because the answer is everywhere and nowhere, distributed through every institution and every indifference and every detective who only deals with white mysteries. The question is the same question she has been asking since Chapter 72: who killed Cock Robin? Nobody. And everybody. And the forces are too large for individual blame.

The answer in this chapter is broader: it is not just the stillborn children who have been killed. It is the heavens. It is love. The cosmic scale of loss that Young has been building toward this sequence arrives here in its fullest form: Esther’s personal grief is not metaphor for the world’s grief. It is continuous with it. The same forces. The same accounting.

Esther’s Serenity

Despite everything in this chapter, the darkest material yet, Esther ends in something like serenity. Not peace, she is not at peace, but the serenity of someone who has decided to prefer mystery over exposure, silence over the judgment of old human laws. She is stubborn. She is proud. She insists on her innocence. She wonders why she should “be punished for a few mistakes” when she has already suffered enough.

Young notes that she laughs in her sleep. That she finds beauty in the natural world. That she is wilder than people think. These glimpses of Esther’s inner freedom (her laughter, her wildness, her refusal to be entirely defined by what has been done to her) are the novel’s quiet argument against its own darkness. The darkness is real. So is the laughter. Both are Esther.

She is always right, the chapter says, in the way that Miss MacIntosh was always right, in the way that Mrs. Hogden was always right. She has arranged her world so the accusation cannot land. Whether this is wisdom or self-protection or delusion, Young will not say. It is the last thing we will learn about Esther in her own voice: she prefers the void. She reaches toward love, toward “death which is another form of love. She was always right.”

What to Hold Onto

The “newspaper clipping—Mass Murderess Apprehended Accused by Dead Mothers and Dead Children.” Nothing about the fathers. The fathers sent bouquets. Esther’s first child, born of a Black man: falling in the category the detective has written off as too many and unimportant.

The silver spoon carried between her parents by a third woman, bridging what could not be bridged. The artificial origin of the woman who cannot produce a living child.

The little boy who grew a shadow, who mistrusts her, who obstructs her path and will not be stilled.

A for agony. M for murder. N for Negro. S for shadow. The abecedary of accusation, assembled from the first letters of what has happened.

And Esther, in the end, laughing in her sleep. Wilder than people think. Preferring the void. Always right.
