guide-40-the-figurehead-knew-more:
Chapter 40: The Figurehead Knew More

← Chapter 39 · Guide Home · Chapter 41 →

Research notes: Chapter 40

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Time

Symbols: Clocks and Watches

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology · Freud and Jung · Marguerite Young on Her Craft · Phenomenology · Time, Physics, and Chaos Theory

Allusions: Ancient Egypt · Genesis · Greek Mythology · Milton · The History of Opium

Think of Chapter 40 as a great noise arriving from a great distance.

Cousin Hannah's voice opens it: “a husky baritone, ranging between bass and tenor,” as loud “as iron bells ringing in a leaden” northern sky, carrying what Young calls a Gothic cathedral weight. This is not a voice describing events. This is a voice that is itself an event. Before you understand a word it says, you understand its register: something immense and old and uncontainable is speaking.

And what it speaks is everything. Every language. The languages of the living and the dead, of the drowned Egyptian sailor, of the Saracen cavalier, of Sanskrit printed on a snowflake, of Tibetan monks and whirling dervishes and Finnish herons and Greek shepherds. Cousin Hannah has crossed so many borders in her life (geographic, political, metaphysical) that she has acquired the tongues of everyone she passed, including people who have been dead for centuries and languages that were never quite spoken at all.

Chapter 40 asks a question it will not answer directly: what would it sound like if someone had been everywhere and knew everything? It then tries to render that sound.

What actually happens in Chapter 40

Vera continues to narrate Catherine's interior: how she receives Cousin Hannah's voice, how she orders it (she cannot), how she experiences time (she does not experience it as linear), how her many selves move through the infinite house like beautiful volatile Psyches while her body lies propped on satin pillows.

Mr. Spitzer observes from his usual position, the perimeter. He notices, with his particular brand of resigned precision, that Catherine has a serene unconcern for facts. She introduces the living among the dead and the dead among the living as though the categories were purely administrative: a matter of which list you put someone on, easily revised. Mr. Spitzer finds this maddening and also, somewhere beneath the maddening, true.

Time runs strangely in Chapter 40: stranger than usual, which is saying something. The afterglow comes before the sunset. The echo arrives before the song. A step forward is a step backward. Young is not playing games with chronology here. She is describing what Catherine actually experiences: a consciousness in which cause and effect have loosened their grip on each other, in which the usual sequence of events has become a medley, an imbroglio, a Pandemonium, a Saturnalia.

The chapter closes at the water, the novel's recurring shoreline, with a vision of all places dreaming together, flowing into each other like water over mooned sand. And then its final, quietly astonishing image: the figurehead of a ship knows more than the captain. The figurehead always goes first.

The polyglot voice, and what it means

Cousin Hannah's linguistic range is one of the chapter's most deliberately excessive flourishes, and Young means every word of it.

The Tower of Babel, in Genesis, is where God scatters the human family into a confusion of mutually incomprehensible languages: the origin myth of why we cannot understand each other. Cousin Hannah reverses this. She has gathered back those scattered tongues. She speaks fourteenth-century Saracen and Provencal troubadour verse and “Sanskrit from a holy text printed on a snowflake” and “the hieroglyphic language of the drowned Egyptian sailor.” The dead languages and the languages of the dead: not just Latin or Ancient Greek, but the actual idioms of people whose words went under with them.

What does it mean that Catherine (who had no formal education, who spent her adult life horizontal) understands all of this? Young suggests it is not comprehension in any rational sense but a deeper kind of knowing, the kind that bypasses the educated mind and arrives directly in the dreaming one. Catherine understands Cousin Hannah's voice the way you understand music you've never heard: the meaning precedes the translation.

There is also something Young is saying about the reach of a certain kind of life. Cousin Hannah traveled. She fought. She crossed borders that were supposed to be closed to her. She accumulated experience the way a coastal cliff accumulates weather. By the time she died, she had absorbed so much of the world that the world's languages had become, in some sense, hers. This is not magic. It is biography carried to its extreme.

Time backward, time sideways

The afterglow came before the sunset. “The echo came before the song.”

Hold these phrases. Young is not being willfully obscure; she is giving you the phenomenology of Catherine's consciousness as precisely as she can. In a mind organized by association rather than sequence, by emotional resonance rather than clock time, the effect often arrives before the cause. You feel the grief before you know what you've lost. You hear the silence before you know the music has ended. The afterglow illuminates the moment before the sun has set, because in Catherine's interior, time has the structure of feeling rather than the structure of physics.

Einstein, as we've noted in earlier chapters, said the distinction between past, present, and future is a stubbornly persistent illusion. Young renders what it feels like to live without that illusion as a stabilizing frame. It is not peaceful. It is a medley, an imbroglio: the Miltonic word Pandemonium, which Young deploys with full awareness that Milton invented it for the capital of Hell; Saturnalia, the Roman festival when social order was deliberately inverted and all rules suspended. Catherine's experience of time is festive and infernal simultaneously. The sequence has been freed and the freedom is terrifying and beautiful.

Mr. Spitzer's serene unconcern

The phrase is almost affectionate: Catherine's serene unconcern for facts. Not frantic unconcern, not anxious unconcern. Serene. She has made her peace with the unreliability of the factual order.

Mr. Spitzer observes this the way a person observes weather they cannot change. He notes that she introduces the living among the dead as a matter of course; she assumes that certain living people have already passed to the other shore, and greets the dead as though they have simply stepped in from a long journey. This is, from one vantage, delusional. From another, it is a form of perception that takes seriously what official reality prefers to ignore: that the dead are still present in memory, still active in the way the past is always active in the present, and that the line between them is a social convention more than a metaphysical one.

Mr. Spitzer, who has been waiting his entire life to prove that he himself died long ago, has no standing to dismiss this. His entire existence is organized around a boundary, between his living self and the dead twin he never stopped mourning, that he too refuses to honor in practice. He is the rational observer who cannot leave the territory he claims to be merely observing.

Many beautiful volatile Psyches

Young's image of Catherine's inner “selves, many beautiful, volatile Psyches wandering about”) is one of the novel's most precise and generous formulations.

Psyche, in Greek mythology, is the soul itself: the mortal woman who becomes divine through love and suffering, who is given impossible tasks and completes them, who descends to the underworld and returns. She is also the human mind: the totality of the self, conscious and unconscious, Jungian and Freudian at once. To say Catherine is many Psyches is to say she is not one soul but a gathering of souls, each of which has its own history of impossible tasks and descents and hard-won returns.

And the Psyche knot, a woman's hair twisted into a coil at the nape, is one of the incidental details Young folds in, the physical memory of the mythological. Catherine's body carries, even in its horizontal stillness, the residue of every self it has housed.

Cousin Hannah's possible conversion, and final skepticism

To All My Darlings notes, almost in passing, something the chapter implies rather than states: that Cousin Hannah may have converted from Christianity to Islam during her travels, and subsequently abandoned religion altogether, possibly arriving at atheism or a radical skepticism that found no shelter in any creed.

This trajectory (from the faith she was born into, to a faith she chose, to no faith at all) is entirely consistent with the Cousin Hannah we know. She was a woman who moved through everything: countries, causes, languages, belief systems. She did not settle. She tested things by living them, and if they failed the test, she left. Her final skepticism, if that is what it was, is not cynicism. It is the earned position of someone who went further into faith's claims than most believers are willing to go, and found the territory did not hold.

Young holds this alongside Catherine's opium religion, and alongside Mr. Spitzer's inherited melancholy, without deciding which of them is right. The novel is not a theology. It is a house with many rooms, and each room has a different answer to the question of whether anyone is listening.

The figurehead knew more

Save the last image for last, because it earns its place.

A ship's figurehead is the carved figure mounted at the prow: the part that goes first, that meets the water before the hull, that faces everything the ship is sailing into. It is not the captain. It has no authority. It cannot steer. But Catherine believes the figurehead knows more than the captain does, because it always goes first.

This is Young's image for intuition, for the part of consciousness that precedes rational navigation, that meets experience before the organized mind has had time to categorize it. The figurehead is the part of us that runs ahead of our explanations, the part that has already felt the thing before the captain has been informed.

In Catherine's case, this is her entire mode of being. She is all figurehead, no captain. She meets everything first, raw, before the organizing intelligence can sort it into the proper categories of real and imagined, living and dead, past and present. The water roars at her mouth. She has been going first for as long as anyone can remember.

Whether this is a gift or a catastrophe, Young declines to say. Both, the novel suggests. Both, always.

What to hold onto

Chapter 40 is the novel moving at full velocity inside Catherine's mind, and you should let it move. Don't try to inventory every allusion or keep track of every historical figure who passes through. Let the medley be a medley. Let the Pandemonium be Pandemonium.

What to hold onto: Cousin Hannah's voice, arriving with Gothic cathedral weight, carrying the languages of everyone who ever lived and crossed a border and left a word behind. Catherine's many selves wandering the infinite house, none of them the captain, all of them the figurehead, all of them going first into the water. And Mr. Spitzer at the edge of it, tapping his “tiny diamond-headed gold walking stick” against his teeth, knowing he is watching something he cannot explain and cannot leave.

The water flows over the mooned sand. The sentinels sleep at the shifting borderlands. There is no place, but there are all places dreaming together.

guide-11-the-alphabet-of-everything:
Chapter 11: The Alphabet of Everything

← Chapter 10 · Guide Home · Chapter 12 →

Research notes: Chapter 11

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology · Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Ancient Egypt · Astronomy · Exploration and the Poles · Greek Mythology · Music and Composers · Sir Walter Raleigh · The History of Opium

Chapter 11 is one of the shortest in the novel. You could read it in five minutes. But don’t let that fool you into thinking it’s minor, because it contains one of the most quietly devastating sentences Vera will speak in the entire book, and it sets up the long comedy of Mr. Spitzer’s structural absence that will run through dozens of chapters to come.

Take a breath. We’re in good shape here.

What actually happens in Chapter 11

Almost nothing, in terms of external event. Vera pauses in her narration to reflect on her own situation. Her mother, Catherine, is somewhere deep in her opium voyage, working through the P’s, Q’s, and R’s of her alphabetical guest list. Phantom visitors from history, geography, mythology, and art are assembling in her velvet bedroom. Mr. Spitzer, as always, has missed the whole thing.

That’s it. But what Young puts inside that frame is extraordinary.

What Vera is thinking about

The chapter opens with Vera asking herself a question she has no answer to: “how should I endure this isolation”?

She cannot be like her mother. She knows that. Catherine has retreated entirely into hallucination, and the opium world she inhabits is complete and self-sustaining. But Vera can’t go there. Miss MacIntosh trained her too well. She will always be able to tell exactly where the dream ends and the reality begins, and that clarity, which sounds like a gift, turns out to be its own kind of sentence. If you can’t dissolve into illusion, and the real world is as bleak as the one Vera is living in, what exactly do you do with yourself?

Young doesn’t answer the question. She pivots, as she so often does, into the gorgeous absurdist theater of Catherine’s guest list. But hold onto that opening. It’s the emotional engine underneath everything that follows.

Catherine’s guests, and why the alphabet matters

Catherine has been working through her visitors alphabetically, and by Chapter 11 she is somewhere in the Q’s and R’s. This detail is funny, but it’s also doing real work.

The alphabet is humanity’s most basic tool for organizing everything. We sort libraries with it. We file documents. We impose order on the chaos of the world by putting it in A-B-C sequence. What Young is showing you is what happens when you apply that system to the entire universe: geography, history, mythology, the living, the dead, the imagined. The system keeps trying to hold, and the universe keeps overflowing it. The Q’s alone are “a naval battle, an island, and a continent.” The R’s sprawl into pharaohs, composers, portrait painters, constellations, and a headless Elizabethan aristocrat running an atheist society.

The alphabet cannot contain what Catherine contains. Nothing can. That’s the joke, and also the tragedy.

The guests worth knowing

Queen Charlotte Islands arrives quietly, exchanging a word or two with Catherine about the climate and a missing courtier. She is a real place, an archipelago off the coast of British Columbia, made into a person, a cold and polite acquaintance from another summer. Young loves this move: collapsing the geographical into the personal, turning landscape into someone you might have known.

Queen Maud Mountains is a different order of visitor entirely. This is an Antarctic mountain range (five hundred miles of frozen, phantasmal peaks) arriving in Catherine’s bedroom as the most imperious houseguest imaginable. She wears glacial white. She exchanges no words. Her skirt is “five hundred miles long and made of pure Brussels lace.” She carries a white parasol that happens to belong to Catherine.

That last detail is the one to hold. The guest has absorbed the hostess’s own possessions. The boundary between Catherine and her visitors is completely porous. What is hers and what has been dreamed into the room can no longer be distinguished.

Rameses I, II, and III arrive as a single bemused pharaoh who is in fact three pharaohs layered inside each other, each unwrapping to find an older king inside. He has been “partitioned into many selves without his knowing it, without his consent.” As Rameses III, he has been dreaming “the dreams of Rameses I who” is already dead. This is one of Young’s most precise images of what fragmented identity actually feels like from the inside: not dramatic, not chosen, just the quiet discovery that you are multiple, and that some of those selves preceded you.

Sir Walter Raleigh arrives last and most spectacularly. He wears white satin embroidered with seed pearls. He removes his hat, and removes his head along with it. He asks to be called “by his intimate name, Ocean or Water.” His detached head then explains that he presides over a secret society devoted to atheistic propositions, including the one that God is dog spelled backward.

Raleigh was actually beheaded in 1618, so his appearing with a removable head is grounded in historical fact, delivered with perfect Young deadpan. He really was known for facing his execution with unusual composure. Young takes that historical detail and runs it to its logical absurdist conclusion: if you can face the removal of your head with equanimity, you might as well carry it around with you.

Mr. Spitzer, who is always missing the party

Mr. Spitzer does not appear in this chapter. He is defined entirely by his absence from it.

Catherine catalogs, with tactless relish, everything he missed: Rimski-Korsakov, Sir Joshua Reynolds, the Great Ram constellation, “Raphael’s tomb, the songs of Ronsard,” and of course Sir Walter Raleigh with his detachable head. She reminds Mr. Spitzer of his absences the way you might remind someone that they missed the best party of the year, with the particular cruelty of someone who knows they will keep missing it.

And Rhadamanthus, one of the mythological judges of the dead, has already tried Mr. Spitzer in absentia and found him guilty of many forgotten crimes.

Poor Mr. Spitzer. He is always out performing dusty legal errands for people who don’t particularly want them performed. He is always arriving just after the extraordinary thing has happened. Young will spend hundreds of pages building this portrait of a man who is structurally, constitutionally, cosmically late to everything that matters. It is one of the novel’s great sustained jokes, and underneath the joke is something genuinely sorrowful.

What to watch for as you keep reading

Light spoilers: This section hints at what happens later in the novel. Skip it if you want to meet the story fresh.

The question Vera asks at the opening of this chapter (how do I endure isolation when I can’t dissolve into illusion?) is the question the entire novel is organized around. Every character in Miss MacIntosh, My Darling is working out some version of it. Some dissolve. Some can’t. Some spend the entire book trying to decide.

The alphabetical guest list will keep going. As Catherine moves through the letters, the guests will keep arriving and multiplying, and Mr. Spitzer will keep missing them. Let the comedy build. It is doing something serious underneath.

Notice how often Catherine’s guests bring their own geography with them. Queen Charlotte Islands brings her climate. Queen Maud Mountains brings five hundred miles of skirt. Raleigh brings the Atlantic Ocean in his name. The outer world keeps collapsing into the bedroom, which is another way of saying: Catherine’s inner world is large enough to contain everything.

guide-50-the-hyphen-was-all:
Chapter 50: The Hyphen Was All

← Chapter 49 · Guide Home · Chapter 51 →

Research notes: Chapter 50

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Death and Mortality · Dreams and Imagination · Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos

Symbols: Fireflies · Keys, Doors, and Locks · The Sea and Water

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Astronomy · Music and Composers · The Bible · The History of Opium · Women's Suffrage

There is a moment near the end of Chapter 50 where Mr. Spitzer recalls Cousin Hannah's hyphenated name, Freemount-Snowden, and reflects that the hyphen was more important to her “than the two names it joined.” The hyphen was all.

Read that slowly. The two names on either side of the hyphen are the public record, the inheritance, the official account. The hyphen is the connection itself: the joining, the and-also, the refusal to be reduced to only one thing. Cousin Hannah was Freemount and Snowden and the passage between them. She was the hyphen. And when she lost her love, she lost what the hyphen had been pointing toward: the person or the life that would have made the joining make sense.

Chapter 50 is the chapter where Mr. Spitzer finally turns away from Cousin Hannah's death and back toward his own existence, and finds that his own existence is the most uncertain thing he has yet tried to describe. He is a dream dreamed by another dreamer. He is a flyleaf between testaments. He is the one who dreamed not, left to live inside other people's dreams because he has no dream of his own. He is alive after his death, or dead during his life, and he cannot reliably distinguish which state he occupies at any given moment.

What actually happens in Chapter 50

The chapter opens with Mr. Spitzer's universe going “off key and out of course”: familiar structures multiplying, two golden chairs where there should be one, the question of which chair is real and which is its dream. He is cautious: he cannot touch “the strings of the constellation Lyre for fear” of touching something imaginary and finding it has more substance than he expected, or less. Everything seems slightly offset from itself, the sensorium failing not in any catastrophic way but in the way of a clock that runs a few minutes slow: the readings are all there, but they no longer correspond reliably to the time.

He reflects on what he learned and did not learn from Catherine: the opium lady, the invalid, the woman who blurred life and death so thoroughly that her experience offers him no reliable map. He did not learn from her the sense of mortality, or the failure of perception. He absorbed something else instead: the atmosphere of a world where the borders are permeable, where the ordinary distinctions have been smoothed away by years of disregarding them.

“All that happened happened only once.” This is the chapter's most quietly devastating formulation: the non-recurrence of events, the impossibility of going back, the knowledge that every moment is singular and cannot be repeated or revisited. A train derailed in grass. A star derailed. The world spinning slightly off its expected axis, and no one coming to correct it.

The chapter closes on the firefly (his key of gold, his soul, the small light he reads by in the vast dark) and on Cousin Hannah's hyphen, and on the pause in a broken melody that her death represents. A pause that may be a rest. A silence that is not the end of the music, only a place where the music held its breath.

A dream dreamed by another dreamer

This phrase, the central formulation of Mr. Spitzer's condition in Chapter 50, reaches back through the novel to Chapter 37's unanswered question: but who was the dreamer? Young has been circling this question for thirteen chapters, and here she gives Mr. Spitzer's version of the answer: he is not the dreamer. He is the dream. He is what happens inside someone else's dreaming, a figure that arose in another consciousness and has been navigating a world he did not generate and cannot fully read.

This is not despair, though it sounds like it. Young is working through a genuine philosophical possibility: what if some people (the cautious, the second-remove, the ones who missed the present moment by arriving a minute late) are simply not the originators of the reality they inhabit? What if they are always living by other people's terms, other people's dreamwork, other people's versions of what the world is? This would explain why Mr. Spitzer's sensorium is always slightly off: he is reading the transcript of someone else's direct experience, and transcripts are always approximate.

The novel's own structure mirrors this. Vera is the narrator, but she is narrating something she partially witnessed and partially imagined and partially inherited from the people who came before her. The novel is itself a dream dreamed by several dreamers simultaneously, each one contributing a fragment of the whole, none of them holding the master copy.

A flyleaf between testaments

He sees himself as a “mere flyleaf stuck between two passages or testaments.”

A flyleaf is the blank page at the beginning or end of a book: the paper between the cover and the first page of text, or between the last page of text and the back cover. It is part of the book. It is also not part of the text. It is the place where someone might write a dedication, or a name, or nothing at all. It exists between what comes before and what comes after, belonging fully to neither.

Mr. Spitzer between the Old Testament and the New. Between his brother's life and his own. Between Catherine's household and the world outside it. Between Cousin Hannah's death and whatever comes next for the novel. He is the transition: the connective tissue, the white space, the pause that allows two very different things to be bound together in the same volume without directly touching.

And yet the flyleaf matters. Remove it and the cover damages the text. The flyleaf protects. The flyleaf receives the inscription that makes the book personal, that makes it this copy rather than any copy. Mr. Spitzer is the novel's flyleaf: not the story, but the thing that holds the story in its hands and keeps it from being damaged by the world. This is not nothing. Young means it not to be nothing.

The sea urchins who knew not

Young gives Chapter 50 one of the novel's most philosophically dizzying sentences: the “sea urchins who knew not whether they lived or were dead or were sleeping—or if they knew, we knew not that they knew, and they knew not that we knew not that they knew not.”

This is a precise rendering of the problem of other minds, taken to its recursive extreme. We cannot know whether sea urchins are conscious. We cannot know whether they know they are conscious. We cannot know whether they know we are uncertain about whether they are conscious. And they cannot know any of this about us. Each layer of ignorance reflects another layer, and the reflection continues past the point where any of the parties involved can track it.

The sea urchin is an apt figure for this meditation: it is one of the longest-living creatures on earth, some individuals surviving two hundred years, yet it is famously difficult to tell a live sea urchin from a dead one. It exists in a state of apparent ambiguity that is entirely real: the animal is either alive or not, the question is only our ability to tell. Young finds in this creature the perfect emblem for Mr. Spitzer's own condition: alive or dead or sleeping, and perhaps no messages have ever arrived to clarify the matter. Perhaps no messages were ever sent.

Gleaming cells that knew not death or life

Mr. Spitzer contemplates “those gleaming cells which knew not death or life or these definitions, knew not whether they lived or were dead, for perhaps no messages had ever arrived.”

Young is pushing panpsychism in a new direction here: not the agonized attribution of consciousness to everything, but its inverse, the possibility that certain things exist in a state prior to the categories of consciousness and death, never having received the information that would allow them to know which side they're on. Not ambiguous. Not uncertain. Simply prior to the question.

To All My Darlings points to Henrietta Lacks and the HeLa cell line: cells taken without consent from a dying woman in 1951 that became the most widely used human cell line in history, still alive in laboratories worldwide while Henrietta Lacks herself died and was buried. Her cells are immortal. She was mortal. The gleaming cells knew not death or life; they simply continued, dividing and dividing, neither the body that generated them nor the woman who was that body, something else entirely. Young was writing in 1965; the HeLa story was not yet widely known. But the image she gives Mr. Spitzer is prescient: life persisting past the point where anyone intended it to, in forms that have escaped the definitions that once organized them.

Nothing twice the same

“All that happened happened only once.” “There was nothing twice the same.”

This is the chapter's most austere formulation, and it hits differently after fifty chapters of a novel that has done everything it can to make time non-linear, to make the past present, to insist that memory and reality and dream are all equally real. You might expect Young, given all that, to offer some consolation through repetition: some sense that what happened happens again, that nothing is finally lost because everything recurs.

She does not. She gives Mr. Spitzer this instead: once, only. Every moment is singular. Every departure is the last time anyone leaves by that particular door in that particular light at that particular age. Every encounter with Cousin Hannah, in memory or dream or the afterimage the dead leave in the consciousness of those who knew them; each one is different from the last. The event happened once. What we have now are the echoes, and echoes are not repetitions; they are the evidence of the original's passage, distorted by every surface they have bounced off since.

This is, Young suggests, both the sorrow and the dignity of existence. The singularity is the sorrow. The singularity is also what makes each moment the thing it is rather than a copy of something else. There was nothing twice the same. Including Mr. Spitzer. Including you.

The hyphen was all

Cousin Hannah's hyphenated name, Freemount-Snowden, carried in it the story of her identity: the two family lines she was born between, the social structures she inhabited, the formal record of who she was supposed to be. But Young's insight is that for Cousin Hannah, none of that was the point. The hyphen was the point. The connection itself. The joining.

The suffrage movement was a hyphen: between the world as it was and the world as it should be, between the legal status of women before the vote and after it, between this life and a life not yet available. Cousin Hannah devoted herself to the hyphen, not to either of the things it connected. She was the passage, the transition, the place where one thing becomes another thing.

And when she lost her love (whatever that love was, whoever the blackamoor, whatever the secret the hyphen was meant to join) she was left with the two names and no connection between them. The hyphen remained in her name. The thing it had been reaching toward was gone. She carried the form of the connection without the content. This is, Young suggests, a particular kind of grief: to be defined by a relationship to something you can no longer reach.

The firefly as key of gold

Among all the vast and complex imagery of Chapter 50 (the frozen cosmos, the Cassiopeia chair, the constellation Lyre, the golden horn of Istanbul, the sidereal clocks) Young gives Mr. Spitzer a single small light as his key of gold: the little firefly. His soul. The light he reads by.

The firefly has appeared throughout the novel as one of its recurring emblems of consciousness: brief, intermittent, visible only in darkness, the light produced not by combustion but by a chemical process that generates no heat. Cool light. Living light. A light that flashes and goes dark and flashes again, following a pattern no individual firefly chooses, each one part of a larger display that only makes sense from a distance.

Mr. Spitzer is a firefly. His consciousness is a firefly. His love, expressed by indirection, mourning the extinct, carrying alpenhorns into the fog: all of it is firefly light: brief, cool, intermittent, beautiful specifically because it is not the sun. You need the dark for it. You need the absence of stronger light. In the great blazing consciousness of Catherine or the blazing trajectory of Cousin Hannah, Mr. Spitzer would be invisible. In the long dark of the aftermath, he is exactly visible enough.

What to hold onto

Chapter 50 is Mr. Spitzer's most fully self-aware chapter: the chapter where he looks at himself with the same steady patience he has given to everything else and reports what he sees without flinching. He is a dream dreamed by another dreamer. He is a flyleaf. He is the one who dreamed not. He reads by firefly light. He is a tide that advances and retreats without ever quite arriving or quite receding.

What Young is doing with this, across these chapters of his long vigil, is building the novel's most unexpected argument: that the cautious, the second-remove, the men who value their dignity more than their lives and arrive a minute late to every experience and cannot maintain sustained attention; these people are not failures of consciousness. They are a different form of it. The firefly is not a failed sun. The flyleaf is not a failed chapter. The hyphen is not a failed word.

The hyphen was all. Keep that with you.

guide-07-the-doctor-between-worlds:
Chapter 7: The Doctor Between Worlds

← Chapter 6 · Guide Home · Chapter 8 →

Research notes: Chapter 7

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Gertrude Hathaway Tidings · Homer Capehorn · Justice O’Leary · Madge Capehorn · Miss MacIntosh · Moses Hunnecker · Musidora Tidings · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Faith, God, and the Supernatural · The Search for Meaning

Symbols: Keys, Doors, and Locks · The House · Weddings and Funerals

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology · Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Fairy Tales and Folklore · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · Shakespeare · The Bible

By now you have your bearings on this bus. You know Moses: his hair, his politics, his whiskey, his raging at the dark. You know Madge: her grief, her fury, her two faces, her clear-eyed understanding of the trap she is in. You know the landscape outside: flooded roads, fallen pillars, a midwestern darkness that goes on and on.

Chapter 7 deepens all of it. We stay on the bus, but the bus now feels less like a vehicle and more like a vessel, like something crossing between states. And Justice O’Leary, the old doctor who has been sitting quietly in the background since Chapter 1, finally takes his place at the center.

What actually happens in Chapter 7

Moses is driving through rain and flood when he spots something on the side of the road: the skeletal chassis of Old Doc’s Model T (no wheels, no engine parts, barely a car at all) faintly illuminated in the dark. Old Doc is out there, tending to his patients. Except his patients, as Moses describes them, are shades. Ghosts. People who may never have been born, or who have been dead for years.

Moses watches, rationalizes, mocks, and underneath all of it is moved. He debates whether to help the old man or leave him to his fate. He does not stop.

Then the chapter shifts to the bus interior, where Madge and Homer are talking or rather, Madge is talking and Homer is resisting. She tells stories about the people back home: the Hathaway and Tidings families, a tangle of death, suspected murder, and generational suffering that reads like a dark fairy tale from the rural Midwest. Josh Hathaway is dead. His brother Rudolph died before him. Their wife or widow, or both, in sequence, Gertrude, is accused by Madge of having killed them both. The evidence is circumstantial, the story murky, the locked door and the fire never quite explained.

And then there is Musidora, Gertrude’s sister, mentally impaired, living in poverty, sold by her mother to an old man who became her husband and the father of too many children. Musidora’s pale, moth-like children play in the graveyard because it is one of the last public spaces where they are allowed to gather.

Homer wants to believe the best. Madge knows better. And Vera witnesses all of it from her place on the bus, adding it to the archive of human suffering she has been quietly assembling since the novel began.

Old Doc and the question of what he is doing

Justice O’Leary is one of the stranger figures in a novel full of strange figures.

He was once a real doctor, a country physician who made house calls, who delivered babies, who was a figure of practical care in his community. Now he is old and his mind has gone. His Model T has no wheels. His instruments are rusted. But he keeps going out. He keeps answering calls. He keeps doing what a doctor does, even when there are no patients left who are truly alive.

Moses thinks this is madness. And in a literal sense, he is right. But Young is doing something more complicated. The old doctor’s delusion, that he is still needed, still helping, still bringing life into the world is in its way a kind of faithfulness. He cannot stop being what he was. He cannot accept that the world he served has gone.

There is a question this chapter asks without answering: Is it worse to be deluded and faithful, or clear-eyed and resigned? Moses has given up on almost everything. The old doctor has given up on nothing. Who is actually more alive?

Madge’s stories, and what they are really about

The Hathaway and Tidings families might seem like a detour, local gossip, small-town tragedy, a locked-room mystery Young drops into the middle of a chapter and never fully resolves. But look more carefully at what Madge is describing.

Gertrude married one brother, then the other. The first died mysteriously. The second died under suspicious circumstances. She is accused of murder but never charged. She drinks and her house falls apart around her.

Musidora was sold, that is the word, sold, by her own mother to an old man who became her husband. She is described as “peculiar,” which in this context is Young’s careful way of suggesting cognitive or developmental disability. She has too many children and not enough of anything else. Her pale children play in the graveyard because it is one of the few spaces that hasn’t been closed to them.

These are not unusual stories for the time and place Young is writing about. They are the stories that didn’t get told: the lives of poor rural women in the American Midwest, ground up by poverty, limited options, and a legal and social system that offered them almost no protection. Marital rape was not considered a crime in the United States until 1978, and not in all states until 1993. Women were frequently passed between men, from fathers to husbands, from one brother to another because their independence was not a category the law recognized.

Madge tells these stories with the flat, unflinching tone of someone who knows they are true because she has been watching from nearby her entire life. Homer resists them because he prefers not to know. This dynamic of the woman who sees clearly, the man who would rather not, runs through the entire chapter.

The graveyard as gathering place

One of the most haunting images in Chapter 7 is Musidora’s pale children playing in the graveyard. Young doesn’t linger on it. She just puts it there, matter-of-factly, and moves on.

But think about what it means. The graveyard is a public space, one of the few that remains. It costs nothing to enter. No one tells you to leave. The children of a poor, marginalized woman are welcome there in a way they are not welcome elsewhere.

Young is not being sentimental about this. She is being precise. The dead are more hospitable to these children than the living have been. The graveyard is where life happens, for people who have been pushed to the margins of everything else.

The locked-room mystery

Young had a minor in criminology and loved murder mysteries, and she planted one here: Josh Hathaway dead behind a locked door, a fire, circumstances that suggest murder but prove nothing. Gertrude is accused. Nothing is resolved.

This is deliberately unsatisfying, and it is meant to be. The locked-room mystery, a staple of detective fiction in which a murder seems to have been committed in circumstances that make it impossible, traditionally promises resolution. The detective figures it out. The truth comes out. Young denies you that comfort.

Life in this novel is full of locked rooms. Miss MacIntosh’s disappearance is a locked-room mystery. Catherine’s inner world is a locked room. The truth about almost every character is locked away behind a door that may never open. The Hathaway murder is Young’s way of telling you, directly: don’t expect clean answers. The evidence is always incomplete. The door stays locked.

What to watch for as you keep reading

Light spoilers: This section hints at what happens later in the novel. Skip it if you want to meet the story fresh.

Old Doc’s violin. He plays it in Chapter 7, a broken or barely functional instrument, a smoky lantern at his side. Music in this novel is never just music. It is a form of reaching toward something that cannot be said directly. Watch what instruments appear and who is playing them, and under what circumstances.

The names Young gives to Madge’s small-town cast. They are thick with Biblical allusion: Solomon, Bathsheba, Reuben, Gad, Manasseh. Young is layering the ordinary horror of these Midwestern lives with the weight of ancient stories: the stories of women desired and disposed of, of brothers in conflict, of families destroyed by the decisions of powerful men. The names tell you that these stories are not new. They have always been happening, everywhere, to women who were never given the chance to tell them themselves.

The jeremiad. Moses’s long, raging monologue in this chapter falls into a specific American literary tradition, the jeremiad, a lament over the moral decay of society, the nation fallen from its promise. Young knew this tradition well. Moses is not just a drunk bus driver railing at Democrats. He is speaking in a voice that goes back to the Puritan preachers, to the founding of the country, to the original American anxiety that things are not as good as they were supposed to be.

Homer’s hope. Notice how consistently Homer chooses not to know. He believes in an afterlife. He resists Madge’s grim accounts. He prefers the version of events that ends better. This is not stupidity, it is a choice, and Young is watching it the way she watches everything: carefully, without judgment, and without quite letting it off the hook.

What to hold onto

Chapter 7 is a chapter about people who keep going when they should, by all reasonable measures, have stopped. The old doctor tends to patients who aren’t there. Moses drives roads that aren’t really roads. Madge tells truths that no one wants to hear. Musidora’s children play among the headstones because it is the only space left to them.

None of these people have what they need. All of them are still moving. That is, quietly, what this chapter is about.

The bus is still going. So are you.

Chapter 79: The Silver Spoon

← Chapter 78 · Guide Home · Chapter 80 →

Content note: The Esther Longtree chapters (72 to 81) deal with stillbirth and pregnancy loss, rape, infanticide, racist violence including lynching, and cruelty to children.

Research notes: Chapter 79

Characters: Esther Longtree · Joachim Spitzer · Rosemary

Themes: Death and Mortality · Duality and Doubles · Faith, God, and the Supernatural · Light and Darkness · Motherhood, Pregnancy, and Birth · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Angels, Devils, and Myth · Lamps, Candles, and Light · Pregnancy, Birth, and Children · Weddings and Funerals

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology · Marguerite Young on Her Craft · Spiritualism and the Occult

Allusions: Judaism · Pregnancy, Abortion, and Midwifery · Suicide in History and Literature · The Bible

Chapter 78 gave us the accusation: Esther killed Rosemary in the womb, and was called Little Jackass, and grew up in the shadow of the perfect child who died. Chapter 79 goes further back still, to before Esther’s conception, and explains the mechanism by which she came to exist at all.

Her parents never consummated their marriage. Seven years passed. And then, over the course of those seven years, a large dark woman came regularly to their house (at night, sometimes knocking, sometimes whistling) and carried a tiny silver spoon between them. This is how Esther was conceived. Across a great arid distance. Through an intermediary. With an instrument.

The chapter also contains the most mythically charged episode of Esther’s childhood: on her seventh birthday, her mother takes her to visit the other woman. They make a difficult journey. They find the go-between dying, blind, nearly unrecognizable. And Esther, looking at this woman who smells of manure and old tulip bulbs, who wears men’s clothes and casts “a man’s shadow on the wall,” who slapped and pinched Esther’s mother to arouse life where there was none: Esther sees her as the father she never had.

What Actually Happens

Esther reconstructs her parents’ marriage as a structure of sustained non-connection: two people who “dreamed of heaven as something far away” and never reached each other. Her father, the large passive policeman, reading old baseball scores. Her mother, the tiny fragile pallid woman, unable to conceive without intervention. Between them: nothing that could produce a child. The other woman arrived. She was large and dark and somewhat grotesque, wearing a man’s hat and coat, her shadow falling “like a man’s shadow on the wall.” She smelled of manure and old tulip bulbs rotted by rain. She had a slow anger and a patience that spanned years. She carried a tiny silver spoon. She came at night, set an alarm clock, performed the rituals of conception across the arid distance between Esther’s parents. She slapped and pinched the mother to wake her body into possibility. She did this again and again, over seven years, until it worked.

Esther was born kicking and afraid, requiring instruments, producing also the dead twin Rosemary. The other woman was there for the birth too, or thereabouts. She is present at Esther’s origin in the way that a force is present, not warmly, not lovingly, but essentially.

The uncle, a pugilist who died of cancer and left his estate to a spiritualist medium, told Esther about all this “laughing until his face turned purple.” He confirmed the nickname: Little Jackass, given by the father himself, because of the unnaturalness of her conception. “The child of the unnatural mating.” Mulish from the start. On her seventh birthday, Esther’s mother takes her on a difficult journey to visit the other woman. The chapter presents this as a pilgrimage of sorts, marked by hardship: clothing lost, the natural and social world harsh against them. When they arrive, the other woman is dying. She is blind. She is monstrous in her decay. And Esther, standing before her, perceives her as the father she never had: the one who made her possible, the one whose will and method produced her life out of nothing. The go-between is cruel and strange and more wonderful and more beautiful, in some inner invisible way, than either of Esther’s actual parents.

The chapter closes with Esther reflecting on her gradual death, not a physical death but the slow fading of someone born without the foundation of natural love, who has spent her life trying to be good in a world that finds her awkward and wrong, who stands at the fence between life and eternity with arms akimbo and legs astraddle, belonging fully to neither side. She is the happy dead. She is cloud-like. She is driven to the edge of existence. She has a big leaking heart full of regrets and expectations.

She also, in this chapter, says she is Jesus Christ. She says this in the context of her endless pregnancy, her suffering, her bearing of what the world will not acknowledge. She does not elaborate. She has made her identification and moved on.

The Other Woman

She is one of the most extraordinary figures Young has created, and she arrives without a name. Large and dark and misshapen, wearing men’s clothes, casting a man’s shadow, smelling of earth and rot and rain. She is foreign: speaks with a strange accent, possibly carries what the narrative hints is an old crime or exile. She has flat dark hands capable of warmth but used mainly for slapping and pinching. She is methodical and patient in a way that has nothing to do with tenderness.

What she does is not insemination in any medical sense; it is stranger than that, mediated by a silver spoon, performed across the emotional and physical distance of a marriage that was never consummated. Young is not describing assisted reproduction as we would understand it. She is describing something that sits in the space between the literal and the mythological: a ritual of conception, performed by an intermediary, for parents who could not reach each other. The silver spoon is the chapter’s central symbol, and Young loads it with multiple meanings. The idiom “born with a silver spoon in one’s mouth” means to be born privileged, to inherit rather than earn. Esther is born with the silver spoon as her instrument of creation, not privilege but the cold mechanism of her existence. She is the child who was wanted enough that someone paid a strange woman to come in the night with a spoon, but not wanted in any way that translated into warmth or love or the ordinary comforts of being a child who is simply loved.

The other woman is more wonderful and more beautiful than Esther’s actual parents. This is Young’s most difficult observation about Esther’s origin: the figure who made her possible, who had the will and patience and physical power to produce life where there was none, is more alive in Esther’s imagination than either of the people who were supposed to love her. She is the dark father. She is the one who did the work.

The Seventh Birthday Visit

The pilgrimage Esther’s mother takes her on for her seventh birthday, to visit the woman who produced her life, is one of the novel’s most unsettling scenes, and one of its most mythologically resonant. Seven is the number of completion, of the sacred week, of fairy-tale transformation: the seventh year, the seventh son of a seventh son, the age at which, in various traditions, a child is held to reach the age of reason. On Esther’s seventh birthday, she is brought to see the origin of her own existence, and what she finds is dying. The other woman is blind and monstrous in her decay, barely recognizable as the powerful figure who came at night with her alarm clock and her slow anger. She is disintegrating. And Esther, at seven, looks at this disintegrating figure and sees her as a father. This is a precise and devastating reversal. The large passive policeman who gave Esther her nickname and read baseball scores and never came close to his wife is not Esther’s father in any sense that matters to her. The dying woman who smells of manure and wears men’s clothes and slapped her mother’s body awake; she is the father. She is the one who insisted on Esther’s existence. She is the will behind the conception. She is already leaving.

After this visit, something changes in Esther: every day will seem like that birthday. She is marked by the encounter in a way she cannot fully articulate: the knowledge that the person most responsible for her being in the world is dying, that she met her origin just as her origin was ending, that the father she recognized is a woman who is almost already gone.

Esther as Jesus Christ

She says it plainly, without elaboration: she is Jesus Christ. The identification is not blasphemy in Young’s framing; it is structural. Esther has been carrying what the world will not acknowledge: children the law has decided did not exist, suffering that has no official record, a pregnancy that has lasted beyond all reasonable duration. She has been accused of crimes she did not commit. She has been misunderstood and rejected by those around her. She is the bearer of suffering for others: the dying fathers’ illusions, the detective’s investigation, her mother’s grief for Rosemary.

Young has also told us that Esther is the mother of us all, and Mr. Spitzer is the father of us all. If Esther is both the mother of us all and Jesus Christ, she occupies simultaneously the role of origin and the role of sacrificial bearer of the world’s accumulated sorrow. She is Everywoman and the Redeemer simultaneously. Young is building a mythological structure around Esther that the novel never quite makes explicit, because to make it explicit would be to reduce it. The immaculate conception enters here too: To All My Darlings connects Esther’s unnatural origin (her parents who never consummated their marriage, the silver spoon as instrument, the third person as go-between) to the tradition of miraculous or unmixed conceptions. Saint Anne and Joachim, the parents of Mary, were similarly infertile and similarly received their child through divine intervention. Mary herself was conceived without the taint of original sin. The tradition of the child born out of the ordinary mechanisms of human reproduction (born through some other means, marked from conception for something the world will not understand) is the tradition Esther enters when she says she is Jesus Christ.

Gradually Dying

The chapter’s closing meditation on Esther’s gradual death is one of the most purely beautiful passages in her sequence. She is the happy dead. She stands at the fence between life and eternity, arms akimbo, legs astraddle, belonging to neither. She is cloud-like, illusive, driven to the edge of existence. Her heart is big and leaking. This is not suicidal ideation or despair in the clinical sense. It is the honest description of someone who was born without the foundation of natural love, who has spent her life in the space between what was supposed to be and what is. She is alive in every physiological sense (enormous, muscular, wind-burned, pregnant with the little shadow boxer) and she is also dying in the sense that every day subtracts from her something she cannot replace, because what was taken from her was taken before she existed and cannot be given back.

She tries to be good despite it. She has a maternal heart. She wants to love and be loved. She has the starlight and the wind and the water that her father’s lineage gave her. She is wilder than people think. She is Little Jackass. She was born kicking and she has not stopped.

What to Hold Onto

The other woman: large, dark, men’s clothes, men’s shadow, slow anger, alarm clock, silver spoon, seven years of night visits, slapping and pinching Esther’s mother awake. More wonderful and more beautiful, in some inner invisible way, than either of Esther’s parents.

The silver spoon: not privilege but mechanism. Cold instrument of a conception that happened across a great arid distance.

The seventh birthday pilgrimage to find the origin dying. The father Esther recognized in the dying woman. After this, every day will seem like that birthday. Esther saying she is Jesus Christ. Not elaborating.

The gradual death: not a dramatic end but a slow subtraction, the happy dead standing arms akimbo at the fence between life and eternity. Big heart, leaking. Still there.

And the little shadow boxer, still under her heart. Still two hearts. The child produced by the unnatural mating is still expecting the child who will be born.

Chapter 36: Where Has She Gone

← Chapter 35 · Guide Home · Chapter 37 →

Research notes: Chapter 36

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh

Themes: Duality and Doubles · Memory and the Past · The Search for Meaning

Symbols: Angels, Devils, and Myth · Mirrors and Reflections

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Judaism · Napoleon and Wellington · Revelation and the Apocalypse · The History of Opium

There is a particular kind of grief that doesn't look like grief from the outside. It looks, instead, like a logical problem. Like a question of coordinates. Like someone who has mislaid an object and is working, methodically, through all the places it might be.

This is Catherine in Chapter 36. Cousin Hannah is dead, and Catherine knows she is dead, and Catherine's response to this fact is to treat it as insufficient information. Dead is not a location. Dead does not tell you where someone has gone. And Catherine (who has spent her life in a household where the borders between waking and dreaming, real and imagined, present and departed have never been firm) sees no particular reason why death should be any more conclusive than anything else.

Chapter 36 is one of the novel's great meditations on what we do with the dead when they refuse to arrive.

What actually happens in Chapter 36

Catherine wants to know where Cousin Hannah is. Not in any mystical or vague sense; she wants this information concretely. Cousin Hannah is dead, yes, but Catherine considers herself to be living among both the living and the dead, and she sees no reason why this shouldn't grant her access to Cousin Hannah's whereabouts.

Mr. Spitzer was the last living person to see Cousin Hannah alive. Catherine blames him, with a frustration that has calcified over years into something close to contempt, for not being able to tell her more. He is obtuse about it. He won't say, or can't say, or the knowledge has slipped through the particular kind of consciousness he has: one that receives everything a beat too late.

In one of the chapter's sharpest moments, Mr. Spitzer briefly rouses himself from his usual lassitude to accuse Catherine of never having “loved any living being—not even” his dead twin brother. This lands. Young doesn't linger on it, but you should.

Meanwhile, Catherine turns over the question of what Cousin Hannah would look like now, having undergone her transformation. Would she be a man or a woman on the other side? Queen of the dead, or invader of heaven? Catherine suspects heaven will not contain her for long. A woman like Cousin Hannah, Catherine thinks, would make heaven into chaos inside of a week.

Mr. Spitzer, and the problem of arriving late

Young gives us, in Chapter 36, one of the novel's most precise and quietly devastating portraits of Mr. Spitzer. His eyes and ears are out of sync. He hears sounds a minute after they happen. Every singer he listens to is slightly off-key. He exists at what Young calls a second remove from life, not absent, exactly, but never quite present either, always receiving the world a half-step behind the moment it occurs.

He is also, Young tells us, a counterfeit of himself. His twin brother is dead, and something in Mr. Spitzer died with him, and what remains is a copy, a man who goes through the motions of being a person without quite filling the shape.

Notice how Young has arranged this. Mr. Spitzer, whose identity is fractured by the loss of his twin, is the person Catherine needs to locate Cousin Hannah. The keeper of the last information is the person least able to reliably hold information. The bridge between the living and the dead is a man who is already, in his way, only partially alive.

This is not cruelty on Young's part. It is the novel's particular understanding of how grief compounds. Loss doesn't distribute itself evenly. It lands on the people least equipped to carry it, and then it asks them to be of service anyway.

Catherine, memory, and the lie of the mirror

The chapter gives us an image of Catherine looking at her own face in an inaccurate mirror. The reflection is there, but it does not quite match. This is not played for surrealism; it is, for Catherine, simply accurate. She has never been able to hold a fixed image of herself. She is made of fragments, partial selves, vague thoughts that don't resolve into a continuous person.

Young draws the contrast explicitly: Catherine's approach to memory is radical, imaginative, porous. She cannot distinguish what she remembers from what she has invented, and she is not entirely sure the distinction matters. Mr. Spitzer, by contrast, is conservative, precise, buttoned against the flood of association. He trusts only what he can verify. He trusts very little.

They are, in this sense, a perfect mismatch for the conversation Catherine needs to have. She wants to swim out into the deep water of what might have happened to Cousin Hannah. Mr. Spitzer will not leave the shore.

Cousin Hannah, and the question of what comes next

Catherine's meditation on Cousin Hannah's afterlife is one of the chapter's great set pieces, and it deserves to be read slowly.

She imagines Cousin Hannah having traveled after death through Moscow, St. Petersburg, Siberia, Babylon: the same vast, border-crossing restlessness she showed in life, now loosed from the constraint of a body. Young gives us Cousin Hannah as a great traveler, a figure whose posthumous geography is as improbable and sweeping as her biography.

But then Catherine gets to the real question: what is Cousin Hannah now? Is she still a woman? The chapter floats the possibility that death might dissolve that category: that Cousin Hannah could have become something neither man nor woman on the other side, something that has escaped the classifications entirely. This is not a question Young resolves. It is a question she wants you to sit with.

And then: Catherine's conviction that Cousin Hannah would not last long in heaven. That she would be too disruptive, too restless, too constitutionally opposed to any hierarchy, including celestial ones, to remain a peaceful resident. Heaven, in Catherine's cosmology, is not equipped for a woman like Cousin Hannah. She would turn it into another campaign.

The bridges, and what they cross

Young threads through this chapter a series of bridges: the “Brooklyn Bridge, Waterloo Bridge, the Bridge of Sighs” in Venice, the Bridge of Lies in Sibiu, Romania. Each one a different kind of crossing, a different relationship between what is on either side.

The Bridge of Sighs, named for the sighs of condemned prisoners who crossed it from the courtroom to the cells, and the Bridge of Lies, which legend says will collapse under anyone who tells a lie upon it, are the ones to hold. Chapter 36 is a chapter about what cannot be crossed, about the gap between the living and the dead that Catherine keeps trying to negotiate and keeps finding uncrossable. The bridges are there. The other side is not accessible.

The accusation, and what it costs

Return, for a moment, to Mr. Spitzer's accusation: that Catherine never loved any living being. Not even his dead twin brother.

It is the kind of thing that is said in exhaustion, in the specific tiredness of someone who has watched another person love the absent more devotedly than they have ever loved the present. And it may be true. Catherine's great loves are Cousin Hannah, who is dead. Miss MacIntosh, who is gone. The opium dreams that are more real to her than the room she sits in. She is a woman whose most passionate relationships are with things that cannot require anything of her in return.

Mr. Spitzer, living and corporeal and difficult and obtuse, does not stand a chance against that kind of devotion. He never did. He knows it. The accusation is not an attack. It is a grief of its own.

What to hold onto

If Chapter 36 feels like it is circling without landing, here is what it is circling: Catherine is trying to grieve, and she cannot find the form for it. The dead are supposed to go somewhere. They are supposed to be locatable, even if unreachable. But Cousin Hannah has not gone anywhere Catherine can name, and Mr. Spitzer, the only witness, cannot tell her, and the mirrors show an inaccurate face, and the bridges are there but the other side is fog.

This is the chapter where the novel asks, as quietly and as relentlessly as it can: what do you do with a loss that won't tell you where it went?

You keep looking. You imagine. You write letters that are illegible. You wait for sounds that arrive a minute late. You hold the question open like a door and let the wind come through.

Chapter 1: The Endless Grayness

← Introduction · Guide Home · Chapter 2 →

Research notes: Chapter 1

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Homer Capehorn · Madge Capehorn · Miss MacIntosh · Moses Hunnecker · Vera Cartwheel

Symbols: The Bus and the Journey

Philosophy: Freud and Jung · Kant and Hegel · Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Don Quixote · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · The History of Opium

If you’ve just opened Miss MacIntosh, My Darling and put it down in bewilderment after the first twenty pages, this is for you.

You are not failing the book. The book is doing something unusual to you on purpose, and once you understand what that is, the bewilderment transforms into something closer to awe.

Here is the first thing to know: Marguerite Young is not hiding the story from you. She is giving it to you in the way memory actually works by circling, doubling back, lush with digression, lit from odd angles. The story is there. Let’s find it together.

What actually happens in Chapter 1

A young woman named Vera Cartwheel is on a bus somewhere in the American Midwest. It is grey out. The bus driver, Moses Hunnecker, is large-headed, bushy-haired, drinking whiskey openly, and calling on God and angels while driving erratically through heavy mist. A young married couple, Madge and Homer Capehorn, are asleep in their seats. Madge is pregnant and visibly unhappy about it. Homer is placidly, blissfully asleep.

That is all that happens, in terms of external events. The bus moves through a grey landscape. Vera watches.

Everything else in the chapter and it is considerable resides in Vera’s mind.

What Vera is thinking about

Vera is on this bus because she is looking for someone: Miss Georgia MacIntosh, her childhood nursemaid, who disappeared years ago and may be dead. The search is both literal (she is actually going to Miss MacIntosh’s hometown of What Cheer, Iowa) and something more: a search for truth, for stability, for a self that isn’t consumed by illusion.

Vera grew up in a household ruled by illusion. Her mother, Catherine, is an opium addict who has taken to her bed and never left it, living entirely inside her own hallucinations. Miss MacIntosh was the opposite: plain, practical, red-haired, broken-nosed, a woman who believed in facts and schedules and the cold, honest surface of things. She was the one solid thing in Vera’s life. And then she was gone.

So when Vera watches Moses Hunnecker drinking and praying at the wheel, and when she watches Madge sleeping her resistant, unhappy sleep while Homer sleeps his innocent one, she isn’t just watching passengers on a bus. She is watching the question her life has been organized around: what is real, what is illusion, and what do we do when the only person who taught us the difference has disappeared?

Why Young writes this way

Young herself described the structure of Miss MacIntosh, My Darling as “spokes of a wheel, with Miss MacIntosh in the middle.” Everything radiates outward from that absent center. And the prose radiates the same way: each sentence proliferates into the next, association breeding association, the way a mind actually moves when it is obsessively circling something it cannot resolve.

This is not accidental difficulty. It is the form enacting the content. Vera cannot think in straight lines because the thing she is thinking about (loss, truth, the gap between reality and dream) does not resolve into straight lines.

Once you accept this, the prose stops feeling like an obstacle and starts feeling like weather you’re moving through. Let it wash over you. The meaning accumulates.

The people on the bus, and what they mean

Young chose her characters’ names with great care. Moses Hunnecker, the bus driver calling on God while driving recklessly, is named for the prophet who led people through the wilderness but never reached the promised land himself. His enormous hair (he never cuts it), his whiskey, his invocations: he is a figure of chaotic faith, which is to say, faith under pressure. Vera imagines he has a wife and children at home. She may be inventing this entirely. The novel will keep doing this to you: offering you something that might be real, might be projection, might be both.

Madge is short for Madeleine, which means “woman from the high tower.” She is pregnant with a child that may not be her husband’s, trapped in a marriage she didn’t choose, returning to a town she doesn’t want to return to. Homer, whose name means “hostage” or “pledge”, sleeps on, peacefully, pledged to a life whose complications he does not register. The contrast between them is one of the book’s first quiet jokes: the woman who knows too much, awake and suffering; the man who knows too little, peacefully asleep.

What to hold onto

Roadside, the bus passes a double-headed man standing in the mist, staring at nothing. Young uses this figure, strange and briefly glimpsed, to open one of the chapter’s great philosophical passages about the illusion of individual selfhood: the idea that every face, every soul, every heart is somehow interconnected, that the borders of the self are not where we think they are.

It sounds abstract, but hold this image. The double-headed man will make sense later in ways you cannot yet anticipate. This is a book that rewards trust.

What to watch for as you keep reading

Light spoilers: This section hints at what happens later in the novel. Skip it if you want to meet the story fresh.

Miss MacIntosh’s whaler’s hat and rubber mackintosh coat and her name itself comes from Charles MacIntosh, who invented waterproofed cloth. She is, literally and symbolically, a woman who keeps the rain out. Keep noticing what she wears, what she refuses to wear, and when.

The mist. Young will use fog and grayness throughout the novel as the atmosphere of uncertainty, the dissolution of clear borders between real and imagined. The “endless grayness” of this first chapter is not just a weather condition.

Vera has a tendency to imagine backstories for the people around her. She does not know that Moses has a family, she supposes it. This habit of supposing is central to who Vera is, and to what the novel is doing.

What to hold onto

If you feel lost, come back to this: a young woman on a bus in the grey American Midwest is looking for the only person who ever told her the truth, and she isn’t sure if that person is alive or dead. Everything else, every digression, every philosophic spiral, every strange figure in the mist is Vera’s mind trying to prepare itself for what she might find.

That search is the spine of the entire novel. You now have it in your hands.
