Chapter 30: Cousin Hannah

← Chapter 29 · Guide Home · Chapter 31 →

Research notes: Chapter 30

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Eustace · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Grief, Loss, and Mourning · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Clothing, Hats, and Skirts

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology · Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Angels and Archangels · Astronomy · Gambling and Playing Cards · Napoleon and Wellington · Suicide in History and Literature · The History of Opium · Women's Suffrage

After thirty chapters of preparation, Cousin Hannah arrives. Not in person, she died years ago and is buried “in a grey New England churchyard where many tombs were marked only with the sign of the codfish,” but in full force, through Catherine’s memory and longing and Vera’s reconstruction of what she knows.

This chapter is the novel’s great opening of doors. Young has been building a closed, interior world: the coastal house, the opium bedroom, the Miss MacIntosh sequence, the Spitzer portrait. Cousin Hannah blows all the doors open. She has been to Persia, Babylonia, Arabia Deserta, the Alps, the Himalayas, the deserts of Moab. She has ridden against Spanish cavalcades disguised as an Arab king. She has heard muezzins and archangels and the whispers of dying sea captains to their wives. She is everything the coastal house is not.

Who is Cousin Hannah?

Cousin Hannah Freemount-Snowden is Catherine’s cousin, or was, before she died. She was a Boston feminist, suffragette, world traveler, balloonist, mountain climber, swordswoman, archer, markswoman, and spy. She traveled disguised as an Arab king, a Tibetan jockey, “a lazar ringing his bell in” holy cities. She rode her white horse El-Burraq, named for the horse Mohammed tethered at the Wailing Wall before ascending to heaven, through howling desert sands. She attacked Spanish soldiers who were assaulting a Riff caravan, routing them single-handedly, and disappeared back into the sandstorm.

She never stayed anywhere long. She left no forwarding address. When Catherine tried to call her by telephone, it rang through empty rooms in a house that had been torn down to make room for an asphalt highway. Cousin Hannah was always already gone.

She is buried “in a grey New England churchyard” with a “jeweled sword at her side and” a great star sapphire on her breast, pinned there by Mr. Spitzer when he laid her out. That detail, Mr. Spitzer as the one who dressed her for burial, is Young’s way of connecting the novel’s poles: the most adventurous spirit in the book was put to rest by its most earthbound one.

What Cousin Hannah represents

The novel has given us two responses to an untenable world. Catherine dissolves into hallucination. Miss MacIntosh insists on the practical surface. Cousin Hannah takes a third path: she acts.

She is the novel’s figure of pure will. She sees hazards before they occur and chooses the lesser danger, but she always chooses. The iceberg moved to allow her passage. She cut “through great cables of iron as if they were silken threads.” Where the road crumbled into a chasm, she went “on, crossing great stone deserts and viewless abysses as if they were city streets.” She found the dangers of the Alps less than the danger of crossing traffic-crowded Boston streets.

Young describes her as a being “dedicated to the overthrow of the dream and of the dreamer in all countries.” This is what makes her the opposite of Catherine and the uncanny double of Miss MacIntosh. Both Hannah and Miss MacIntosh are anti-dreamers, insisting on the real. But where Miss MacIntosh insists through proverbs and schedules and the plain surface of the domestic day, Hannah insists through action, through bodies in motion, through the actual material world of camels and swords and mountain passes.

She is also, Young makes clear through Catherine’s memories, an emancipated extension of Catherine herself: the “Captain Derring-Do who engaged in” the adventures Catherine only dreamed of through the endless years. Catherine’s longing for Hannah is a longing for her own unlived life.

The loss of a skirt

Young drops one detail about Cousin Hannah with characteristic lightness and moves on: “because of the loss of a skirt, it was known now, her entire life had been perhaps an act of sorrow and redemption.”

This is the novel’s most compressed statement of Cousin Hannah’s inner life, and Young never elaborates it. What skirt? Lost how? To what sorrow? We are not told. What we are told is the consequence: her entire life, all those years of adventure and disguise and camels and swords and mountain passes and Arabian nights, was a response to one lost garment. A sorrow to be redeemed through sixty years of action.

Young places this in the same chapter as the Miss MacIntosh sequence’s distant echo: the old nursemaid who never looked in mirrors, who carried needles and pins to forbid inquiry, who slept in the cold and kept the windows open. Both women have built elaborate lives around something that cannot be named directly. Both have turned a private wound into a public performance. Hannah’s is grander and more spectacular. The wound is the same order of magnitude.

Eustace

Before Cousin Hannah takes over the chapter, Young gives us one more of Catherine’s phantoms: Eustace. He is the most volatile of her imaginary visitors, taking many forms: a mocking bird, an old woman, an old bearded man like a cypress tree, Wellington “at the head of his troops,” a blind astronomer, a Venetian murderous valet, the murdered gentleman who walks abroad at midnight. He is limitless, “not confined to any one form by the laws of nature, which” have been suspended in his case.

Catherine calls to him the way she calls to all her visitors: “Eustace, Eustace! Oh, is it you, Eustace dear, and the golden-antlered stags, the large planets, the small planets? Come in, Eustace, and do close the door, for there’s a great draft.” It is the most ordinary hospitality, extended to the most extraordinary being.

Eustace functions as a hinge between the Spitzer chapters and the Hannah chapter: he is the figure of pure mutability, the visitor who cannot be fixed into a form, the one Catherine summons when Mr. Spitzer’s too-solid flesh becomes oppressive. He is the possibility of radical transformation. Cousin Hannah, in her own way, is Eustace made flesh.

Cousin Hannah’s views on the Spitzers

Young gives us one of the novel’s great comic passages through Cousin Hannah’s opinions of the twins. She “had never cared for the Spitzer boys,” had stanchly predicted “they would come to no good end,” and described them in terms that collapse the distinction between them: “the musical gambler with his piano-playing and horn-blowing friends, the horse-playing musician, the gambling lawyer who would take his last chance, the philanthropic dice-rattler,” “and the suicidal butterfly-chaser chasing himself with his butterfly net. Both brothers were profligates.”

She is partly right and wholly wrong simultaneously, which is Young’s method with characters who are powerful but limited. Hannah sees through things with a ruthless sangfroid. She cannot always see what she is looking through them at. “The suicidal butterfly-chaser chasing himself with his butterfly net” is the most precise and most wrong description of Mr. Spitzer ever offered. He is chasing himself. But not with a butterfly net.

What to watch for as you keep reading

Light spoilers: This section hints at what happens later in the novel. Skip it if you want to meet the story fresh.

Cousin Hannah will return in her own chapters later in the novel; she is one of the most important characters in the book, and Young will give her considerably more space. What Chapter 30 does is establish her presence, her history, and her relationship to the household. She is the great absence in Catherine’s life: the cousin who never answered the phone, who never left a forwarding address, who is now dead in a codfish churchyard but still more alive in the imagination than most living people.

The question Catherine keeps asking through Hannah (Have you seen my husband?) is the question that unifies the chapter. Catherine’s husband walked “between two frozen mountain peaks, and” was lost. Vera’s father walked a frozen cable between snow-capped peaks and fell. Young is doing something deliberate with this rhyme. The father who went into the mountains and did not return is the novel’s founding absence, the wound before the wound. Cousin Hannah, who knows the Alpine abysses with intimacy, is the only person in the novel who might have looked.

El-Burraq, Cousin Hannah’s white horse, is named for the horse that carried Mohammed on his night journey from Mecca to Jerusalem and then to heaven. It is the horse of the miraculous journey, the crossing from one world to another. That Cousin Hannah rode this horse through howling desert sands is Young at her most quietly magnificent.

guide-47-the-skirt-over-the-wound:
Chapter 47: The Skirt Over the Wound

← Chapter 46 · Guide Home · Chapter 48 →

Research notes: Chapter 47

Characters: Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Peron Spitzer

Themes: Death and Mortality · Fear and Courage · Love · Music, Sound, and Silence · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · Mountains · Music and Instruments

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft · Plato and Platonism · Schopenhauer · Spinoza · Wittgenstein

Allusions: Women's Suffrage

Mr. Spitzer lays the skirt over her body.

He speculates, in the long meditation that follows, that “perhaps her love was her skirt”: the thing “hiding her great wound, her disappointment, her bleeding heart.” The skirt she called for in the delirium. The thing that kept the rain out in the way the rubber coat kept the rain out, the way Miss MacIntosh kept the rain out, except that the rain got in anyway, as it always does with the things we love most fiercely by covering.

Chapter 47 is a chapter of laying-to-rest and of the thoughts that come in the long hours after a death when there is nothing left to do but think. Mr. Spitzer thinks. He thinks about Cousin Hannah and his brother and the nature of identity and the road not taken and the rejected possibility and the way time fails to tell him the time. He thinks about what it means that he feared change more than he feared death, and about whether a person should be held accountable for their “entire life or for one moment of” transmutation that happened beyond consciousness or memory or desire.

This is one of the novel's great reckoning chapters. It is quiet and immense in equal measure.

What actually happens in Chapter 47

We remain with Mr. Spitzer in the long aftermath of Cousin Hannah's death. The executor's work continues: papers, objects, the alpenhorn already claimed. He lays her skirt over her body as a final gesture, and the gesture opens into the chapter's long meditation.

He reflects on his twin brother, on owing much to him, financially and spiritually, on the possibility of forming “a Welcoming Committee of One on the other side,” waiting for himself to arrive. The relationship between the twins, Peron and Joachim, surfaces here as a philosophical pairing: materialism and immaterialism, the external world and the internal one, the reckless embrace of life and the cautious withdrawal from it.

He is “agonized by attributing consciousness to everything”: clouds, waves, shadows, stars. The world will not stay inanimate for him. Everything is alive in a way that troubles rather than comforts, because if everything is conscious then the dead are conscious too, which means they are somewhere suffering their unfinished business, crying at many gates, forever searching for the image of what they lost.

He meditates on the rejected possibility: “among all things possible, there was the rejected possibility.” The road not taken. The love not said. The life that existed as pure potential and was never actualized, which shapes reality just as powerfully as the life that was.

The skirt as love, love as wound

Young returns one final time to the skirt, and here she gives it its fullest meaning. “Perhaps her love was her skirt hiding her great wound, her disappointment, her bleeding heart.”

The logic is precise and terrible. The skirt was what Cousin Hannah refused: the feminine convention, the domestic enclosure, the mark of the life she chose not to live. And it was also, in the delirium, what she called for most desperately. She wanted the thing she had refused. She was covered, in death, with the thing she spent her life refusing to wear.

Young is saying: the love and the wound were the same thing. The cause that covered her heart (the suffrage movement, the iron keys, the decades of campaigning) was both the means by which she protected the wound and the wound itself. You cannot separate them. The skirt covers the body. The cause covered the grief. Both coverings are real. Both conceal something that was real underneath.

Mr. Spitzer lays the skirt over her because it is the right thing, the only right thing, and because he understands now what it meant that she called for it. He covers her wound with the symbol of her wound, which is also the symbol of her love, which is also the symbol of everything she refused and could not stop wanting.

Peron and Joachim: matter and spirit

Chapter 47 develops the twin pairing more explicitly than any chapter before it, and the philosophical framework To All My Darlings offers is clarifying: Peron represents materialism, the external world, its pleasures and its follies, its impermanent beauty. Joachim represents immaterialism: the internal realm, thought, memory, spiritual seeking.

In the novel's cosmology, neither twin is complete without the other. The material world without the inner life is just appetite, just flux. The inner life without the material world is just abstraction, just ghosts. The twins together made a whole person, which is why the death of one half left the surviving half as a counterfeit, a man at a second remove from life, unable to be fully present in either world.

And the question the chapter presses: which twin survived? To All My Darlings has suggested it was Peron, not Joachim, who continued. If so, what is the materialist doing in Joachim's life? The reckless one playing the cautious one, the one who embraced chance living out the life of the one who feared it? This possibility, that Mr. Spitzer has been performing a borrowed identity for decades, deepens everything. The man who valued his dignity more than his life may have been living his dead brother's dignity all along.

He feared change more than death

This is the chapter's most psychologically precise formulation, and Young sets it down with characteristic quietness: “for more than life or death he feared change, change of any kind.”

Death is at least a stable concept. Death is a destination, however unknown. Death is the end of change, or the beginning of a different kind that you are no longer around to suffer. But change (the ongoing transformation of identity, of circumstance, of what you thought you knew) that never stops. That is what Mr. Spitzer cannot bear.

He is a man already profoundly altered by the loss of his twin, already living between two worlds, already uncertain which of the Spitzer brothers he actually is. Any further change threatens to dissolve what little continuity he has managed to maintain. So he keeps the silk hat. He keeps the routine. He keeps the dignity. He does not vote because “the dead cast no vote—and” he is not sure which side of that line he stands on. He maintains appearances because appearance is all that is holding the shape of him together.

Young is not dismissive of this. She is precise about it. The man who fears change more than death is not simply cowardly; he is a man whose sense of self has been so thoroughly disrupted by loss that any further disruption feels like erasure. His conservatism is a form of survival. It is the only form available to him.

Panpsychism and the agonized attribution

“He was agonized by attributing consciousness to everything.”

This is one of the novel's most exact descriptions of a particular kind of suffering: the suffering of a mind that cannot maintain the boundary between the animate and the inanimate, that perceives consciousness in clouds and stars and shadows and waves, that cannot move through a room without registering the inner life of every object in it.

Panpsychism (the philosophical position that consciousness is a fundamental property of the universe, not confined to biological life) is ancient, running from Thales and Plato through Spinoza and Leibniz to contemporary philosophy of mind. Young would have known it. But she gives Mr. Spitzer not the philosopher's intellectual pleasure in the idea but the experiential cost of living it without choosing it. He did not adopt panpsychism as a theory. He suffers from it as a condition. Every cloud has a mind. Every wave intends something. Every shadow of Cousin Hannah's passing life is still present somewhere, carrying its freight of unfinished consciousness. This is why he cannot fully grieve. The dead are not gone for him; they are mislocated. He keeps looking for them because he cannot stop attributing consciousness to the universe, and the universe keeps offering him shapes that might be them.

The rejected possibility

“Among all things possible, there was the rejected possibility.”

This is Young's formulation for the unlived life: the life that existed as potential and was not taken, which does not simply disappear but shapes reality from its position of non-actualization. The road not taken is as real as the road taken. The love not spoken is as present as the love that was. The skirt not worn for fifty years is what she called for at the end.

Young is not making a case for regret. She is making a case for completeness: a life is not only what happened in it. A life includes its rejections, its suppressions, its great disciplined refusals. The rejected possibility is the shadow that gives the actualized life its shape. Without it, there is no contrast, no definition, no meaning to the choices that were made.

“Should one be held accountable for one’s entire life or for one moment of unforeseen” transmutation “beyond all consciousness or memory or desire?” This question, which Mr. Spitzer turns over in the long hours after the death, is unanswerable, and Young knows it is unanswerable and asks it anyway. That is what the novel does. It asks the unanswerable questions with complete seriousness, gives them the space they deserve, and moves on.

Music never to be played

Mr. Spitzer imagines “music written never to be played”: a composition that encompasses all sounds and all silences, all the notes that were sounded and all the notes that were not, the complete score of a life including everything that went unperformed.

This is the novel's image for what Mr. Spitzer is doing with Cousin Hannah's estate: not just the papers and the alpenhorn and the legal documents, but the incompletable archive of what she was. The music that was never played is the love she never said, the life she never lived, the skirt she never wore. It is real music. It exists, as all unplayed music exists: in potential, in the silence that contains it, in the ear that knows what it would have sounded like if it had been given air.

Whereof one cannot speak

Wittgenstein's closing proposition from the Tractatus surfaces here: whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.

Young invokes this not as capitulation but as the appropriate frame for everything Mr. Spitzer cannot say. There are things that exceed language: the full truth of another person's private life, the experience of the dying, the exact quality of a love that was never expressed. These are not things you can say precisely. You can approach them. You can circle them with prose that circles. You can lay a skirt over a body and know, without being able to say, what the gesture means.

Mr. Spitzer is fluent in this silence. He has practiced it his entire life. He held the secret. He kept the vow. He was silent in the dread presence of death as Susan B. Anthony was silent at her sister Hannah's deathbed. The silence is not emptiness. It is the form that respect takes when language is insufficient. Young knows this. Wittgenstein knew it. Mr. Spitzer, in his limited and faithful and inadequate way, knows it too.

What to hold onto

Chapter 47 is a chapter of vigil and reckoning: the long thoughts that come when the body is laid out and the papers are sorted and there is nothing left to do but sit with what you know and cannot say. Mr. Spitzer is the last person who saw Cousin Hannah alive. He is the keeper of the great secret. He feared change more than death, and now the greatest change of his life, the death of the woman who organized his existence around her absence, has happened, and he is still here, still in the silk hat, still keeping vigil.

What to carry forward: the skirt as love as wound. The twins as matter and spirit, and the question of which one survived. The rejected possibility as the shadow that gives a life its shape. The “music written never to be played.” And the silence that is not emptiness but the only honest response to what exceeds language.

Chapter 65: Mr. Bonebreaker's Umbrella

← Chapter 64 · Guide Home · Chapter 66 →

Research notes: Chapter 65

Characters: John Knox MacIntosh · Miss MacIntosh · Moses Hunnecker · Mr. Titus Bonebreaker · Richard MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Symbols: Eyes and Blindness · Pregnancy, Birth, and Children · Snow, Ice, and Winter · The Sea and Water · The Umbrella

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Ancient Egypt · Don Quixote · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · Revelation and the Apocalypse · The Bible

Miss MacIntosh had a romance once. This is the chapter where she tells Vera about it.

His name was Mr. Titus Bonebreaker, and he was a Gospel salesman from Missouri, and he preached the end of the world on street corners, and he could not, in the end, accept the truth of her body. He left his umbrella behind when he fled. She kept it.

What actually happens

Miss MacIntosh tells Vera the story of Mr. Bonebreaker: how they met, their courtship, their engagement, and the night she showed him who she really was (bald, scarred, missing a breast) and he ran. She tells it plainly, with the dark humor she brings to everything. After he leaves, she works for a time among the blind in Chicago, where her physical differences are less visible. Then she drifts eastward, carrying his umbrella and a luminous watch he gave her, and eventually, she keeps going until she walks into the ocean.

This chapter is the romance of Miss MacIntosh's life, told in the past tense, because it is already over.

Mr. Bonebreaker

He is one of Young's great comic-tragic figures. A Gospel salesman, meaning he sold religious literature door to door, from the Missouri Ozarks, gaunt and stoop-shouldered with a beaked nose and bright eyes, perpetually preaching the Last Day. He ate no meat because cattle inhabited the earth, fowl the heaven, and fish the sea and rivers, and he would not consume any of them. His bones, he was fond of saying, quoting Psalm 22, were out of joint. He carried a long black umbrella. He believed Chicago would be destroyed, Babylon sunk into the sea, the Egyptians spoiled, the sinners called to account.

He is, in other words, a man who has organized his entire existence around the end of everything. And yet he falls in love with Miss MacIntosh.

This is not accidental on Young's part. The man who preaches annihilation falls for the woman who stands for endurance. The man who carries his umbrella as a symbol of prophetic shelter falls for the woman who has carried her own umbrella all her life as practical protection. They are, briefly, a perfect pair: two people with umbrellas, facing the weather together.

And then he sees her without her wig.

"He had put away childish things"

Mr. Bonebreaker is fond of quoting 1 Corinthians 13: the great chapter on love that concludes with the line about seeing through a glass darkly, about knowing as we are known. He often said “he had put away childish things.” He believed this about himself: that he had transcended his past, his sins, his attachments, and become a man of pure spiritual purpose.

Miss MacIntosh observes, with characteristic sharpness, that there was still a child inside him, as there is inside everyone, and that the childlike parts of him were precisely the ones he refused to see. His dream of a heavenly crown. His rage at those who contradicted him. His brushes with the police. His inability to face her physical reality.

He preached that love is not blind, that true love sees clearly. He was wrong about himself.

The night he fled

Miss MacIntosh showed him everything. The bald head. The missing breast. The scars of a body that had wandered, broken its nose, walked into traffic, kept going anyway. She showed him the truth she had been carrying under her wig and her mackintosh.

He ran. He left his umbrella. He left his Bible literature. He did not come back.

Young gives this moment without melodrama. Miss MacIntosh tells it the way she tells everything: flatly, with a dark joke at the edge of it. She had known, perhaps, that this would happen. She had lived long enough with her own body to know how people responded to it. And still she showed him. That is not naivety. That is courage of a particular, unglamorous kind: the courage of giving someone the chance to stay, knowing they will probably go.

He called himself a man who could love truly. He could not. She let him discover this about himself.

Chicago and the blind

After he leaves, Miss MacIntosh works with the blind in Chicago. This is one of the chapter's quietest, most telling details: among people who cannot see, her baldness and her scars disappear. She is only herself, as she sounds and moves and speaks. For a time, she is simply a woman among people who meet her without the visible weight of her difference.

She does not stay. She drifts. She had been chasing Dutch windmills, she tells Vera: a phrase she uses for the illusions she had allowed herself to pursue: connection, romance, being seen clearly and loved anyway. Young is in conversation here with Don Quixote, as she is throughout the novel. Miss MacIntosh, who of all people should know better than to tilt at windmills, tilted at one. She is not ashamed of it. She is just done.

Niagara Falls, alone

She goes to Niagara Falls. She stands there alone, with her umbrella, among the honeymooners: "Shuffle Off to Buffalo," the song of people going to the falls for their first nights together, playing somewhere in the background of Young's imagination. The noise and joy of other people's new beginnings. Miss MacIntosh, with no bridegroom, no escort, only the black umbrella Mr. Bonebreaker left behind.

This image is almost unbearably concentrated. Niagara Falls is where people go to begin. She is there to mark an ending. And the falls keep falling, indifferent to the difference.

"She walked into the roaring ocean on a cold September morning"

Your notes confirm what the text implies: Miss MacIntosh's death, or disappearance, happens in September. She walks into the ocean. We are not told exactly when (in the novel's chronology, it is still coming) but Chapter 65 places it clearly in view. The woman who stood at Niagara Falls alone will eventually walk into the sea. The woman who kept the rain out will go, finally, into the water.

The black umbrella will not help her there.

Mr. Bonebreaker's umbrella

She kept it. This is important. The woman whose own umbrella has been her signature (her shield, her symbol, her practical shelter) kept the umbrella of the man who could not love her truly. She carries both now. It is not clear whether she carries his as an act of mourning, or as a kind of dark joke, or simply because she needed an extra umbrella and there it was.

Young leaves this open. Miss MacIntosh would probably say she kept it because it was a perfectly good umbrella and she saw no reason to waste it.

What to hold onto

Miss MacIntosh standing at Niagara Falls, alone, holding her umbrella, or maybe his, while the water falls and falls, and somewhere behind her the honeymooners are beginning their lives. She is a woman whose heart was broken not by cruelty but by someone's failure of courage. She accepted this. She moved on. She kept the umbrella.

Chapter 16: Falada

← Chapter 15 · Guide Home · Chapter 17 →

Research notes: Chapter 16

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Falada · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Symbols: Horses and Carriages · The House

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Angels and Archangels · Deafness and Sign Language · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Gambling and Playing Cards

We have been building toward this chapter since Chapter 13 told us that something happened on the night of Vera’s fourteenth birthday that changed everything. Chapter 14 gave us Mr. Spitzer’s grief. Chapter 15 gave us Vera at the sea, giddy and briefly rebellious. Chapter 16 takes us inside the house and down the long corridor to Miss MacIntosh’s door.

Young does not give us the revelation in this chapter either. But she brings us to the threshold and stops there, the door swinging open, the moonbeams cutting through the dark, Miss MacIntosh standing by the window, unbelievably not herself.

The revelation is in Chapter 17. But Chapter 16 is the approach, and it is one of the most beautiful sustained passages in the novel. Don’t rush it.

What actually happens in Chapter 16

Vera is riding her black pony, Falada, through the grounds of the estate on the night of her fourteenth birthday. She rides through the dark allees and orchards and abandoned sports courts, past the gargoyles and marble statues and the garden of the blind. She is exhilarated, wild, laughing, whispering her secrets into the pony’s drooping ear.

She decides not to visit her mother: Catherine is either deep in her dreams or rising to the surface, and bringing a real horse into that bedroom could kill her with shock. So Vera and Falada climb the stairs of the great house instead, moving through its extraordinary interior: the mosaic emperors, the funeral gondola in the fountain, the phoenix above the fireplace, the tomb of the unnamed musician, the tapestries of angels restoring “sight to the blind and hearing to the deaf.”

They are heading to Miss MacIntosh. She is the one who will know they are real.

The door to Miss MacIntosh’s bedroom, which is always “locked and barred from the inside,” swings open of itself. Falada snorts. In the moonlight, Miss MacIntosh is standing by the window. And the chapter ends on the moment before Vera can fully take in what she sees.

Falada

The pony’s name carries an enormous amount of freight, and Young makes sure you know it.

Mr. Spitzer traces the name to an old Arabic fairy tale with parallels across many countries and ages. Falada is the horse whose head is “cut off and nailed above the city gates and whose” severed head then speaks “oracles and parables to the people passing through.” A head that speaks after death. A horse that carries truth even when it has been silenced.

The fairy tale Young is drawing on is most familiar in its German version, collected by the Brothers Grimm, called The Goose Girl. In that story, a princess is betrayed by her handmaid, who steals her identity and her prince. The princess’s magical horse Falada is killed to prevent it from revealing the truth. Its head is nailed above a gate. Every morning, as the true princess passes under it, Falada’s severed head speaks to her: Alas, alas, if thy mother could see thee now, her heart would break.

Young chose this name with exquisite care. Falada is the horse that speaks truth from beyond death. Vera rides him directly toward Miss MacIntosh’s door. He seems to know the way, she says. He is “my head, my intelligence. I was the headless rider.”

The headless rider going where the speaking head leads her. Toward the truth she has not yet been able to see.

The interior of the house

The chapter’s long central passage, as Vera and Falada move through the house’s interior on their way to Miss MacIntosh, is one of Young’s great architectural inventions. Read it slowly.

The house contains multitudes. A funeral gondola in an interior fountain. A phoenix above a fireplace of cold ashes. The empty tomb of a musician who has “gone to join the world of music”: its lid a gold grand piano held up by cherubim with folded wings. A “marble boy lying on his tomb with a marble book opened in his hand and marble rose petals upon its pages and his marble dog sleeping at his feet,” with no one knowing if the tomb was ever occupied. “Mosaic emperors like the faces of old playing cards.” Sleeping marble lions from a Venetian doge’s palace.

This is Catherine’s house, and it reflects her: it is a world where art and death are indistinguishable, where music leads to a tomb, where tombs may be empty, where angels on tapestries restore the senses the novel has been mourning, sight to the blind, hearing to the deaf. The house is the inner landscape of a woman who has refused the outer world for decades, accumulated into architecture.

And through all of it, Falada’s hooves clatter. He and Vera make no sound. They move like a pair of moths.

Why Vera goes to Miss MacIntosh

The logic of this moment is quiet but precise. Vera cannot go to her mother because Catherine lives in a world where the boundary between real and phantom is completely dissolved. If Catherine saw a girl on a horse, she might think they were phantoms (which would be fine, she is not afraid of phantoms) or she might recognize them as real, which could kill her with shock. Either way, Vera cannot be known there.

So she goes to Miss MacIntosh. Because Miss MacIntosh, “though she might condemn us, would know that we were real.”

This is everything. After four chapters of approaching and circling and withholding, Young gives us the clearest statement of what Miss MacIntosh means to Vera: she is the person who confirms reality. Not who loves Vera most. Not who knows Vera best. The person whose recognition makes Vera real. In a house full of hallucination, with a mother who lives entirely inside her own mind, Miss MacIntosh is the one solid witness. Her knowing you are there means you are there.

And the door, which is always “locked and barred from the inside,” swings open of itself.

The sentence at the end

Young ends the chapter on one of her most carefully constructed sentences.

“She had greatly changed since last I had seen her, and she was unbelievably not herself, and yet—how was it that I recognized her instantly as if she were something I had always dimly known, and the shock of this knowledge was but the affirmation of some older shock which had been forgotten and laid over by the autumn leaves, the snow falling, the first buds of spring?”

Two things are happening at once here. Vera sees something that shocks her. And in the same moment she recognizes it as something she has always, at some level, already known. The shock is not of discovery but of confirmation. The older shock (the one that was forgotten, buried under the seasons) surfaces.

Young is telling you, without yet telling you, that the revelation about Miss MacIntosh is not a betrayal. It is a recognition. The truth was always there, waiting under the ordinary surface of things, and Vera is about to stop not knowing it.

Chapter 17 delivers it. Go there now.

guide-80-walter:
Chapter 80: Walter

← Chapter 79 · Guide Home · Chapter 81 →

Content note: The Esther Longtree chapters (72 to 81) deal with stillbirth and pregnancy loss, rape, infanticide, racist violence including lynching, and cruelty to children. This chapter describes an infanticide and a man fleeing a lynching.

Research notes: Chapter 80

Characters: Esther Longtree · The Chicago Detective · Walter

Themes: Grief, Loss, and Mourning · Guilt, Innocence, and Justice · Memory and the Past · Society, Class, and Race

Philosophy: Freud and Jung · Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Lynching and Racial Violence · The Civil War

We have been nine chapters with Esther Longtree. We know her stillborn children, her dying fathers, the mud baby in the river, the Chicago detective who is both the crime and its investigation, the twin she was accused of killing before she was born, the silver spoon, the go-between who was more wonderful than either parent. We have come to know her everlasting pregnancy, her luminous stubbornness, her knitting and unraveling in the dark. And now Young gives us the thing Esther has been holding back through all of it: the one child who actually lived. His name is Walter. He is alive somewhere in the world. And Esther pressed her thumb to still his birth cry.

This is the darkest confession in Esther’s sequence, and Young delivers it with the same unhurried obliqueness she has used for everything else. Walter was born. Esther was young and frightened and alone. She pressed her thumb to his mouth to silence his first cry. She believed she had killed him. She hid the body and fled. But Walter did not die. He lived. He is out there, somewhere, growing, and he comes back to her in visions asking: “Mother, why have you killed me? Where is my father?

What Actually Happens

Esther is still at the Greasy Spoon, still pregnant with the little shadow boxer, still performing the rituals of the woman who lives between the living and the dead: making small clothes for no one, setting out breadcrumbs for spirits, building a little house of straw in a “tree for the spirit to come home to,” answering every knocking at the door.

She tells the story of Walter’s father. He came to her in the darkness of a summer night, half sleeping and half waking. His face was white in the moonlight. At dawn she saw that he was Black. “A Negro, a Negro, a Negro”; she says it three times, the epizeuxis of shock and revelation. He was a stranger, a “poor fellow, a tramp, a fugitive,” a prince. The white people in that place “had tried to kill him because he was black and had wanted to sleep with a white woman.” They had “tried to hang him from a white-blossoming tree for revenge, but the rope had broken.” He “fled for fear the white people would see him and kill him.” He had been nearly lynched. He ran.

Esther was pregnant. She was young and frightened and had no one to tell. She delivered Walter alone, or nearly alone, in circumstances the chapter renders fragmented and terrible. She pressed her thumb to still his birth cry. She believed she had killed him. She hid what she believed was a body. She fled. But Walter lived. He has grown up somewhere outside her knowledge. He is “black as my true love, black as my heart”; she loves him and fears him simultaneously, in the particular way of someone who believes she has committed an irreversible act and then discovers the act was not irreversible, only terrible. He comes to her in visions. He asks her why she killed him. He asks where his father is. She has no answers. He haunts her with a cruel, hard heart, not the hovering innocent stillborn who applaud at the edges, but an accuser, a child who has lived long enough to be angry.

He is the “beloved obstacle”: the one who prevents her from moving fully forward, the one whose memory blocks the path between her past and any possible future. Every subsequent pregnancy has been, in some sense, an attempt to atone for or replace or redeem what happened to Walter. Every stillborn is haunted by his presence as the one who should have been the first stillborn and wasn’t.

Walter’s Father

He is described through Esther’s shock and retrospective love simultaneously: a Black man, a stranger, who came to her in the dark of a summer night when his face looked white in the moonlight, and whose race she only saw at dawn. He had been nearly lynched for being Black in proximity to a white woman. He ran because running was the only alternative to death.

Young is writing this in the period between 1945 and 1965, in a country where anti-miscegenation laws remained on the books in most Southern states until the Supreme Court’s 1967 decision in Loving v. Virginia declared them unconstitutional. Interracial marriage was not merely socially stigmatized; it was illegal in most of the South and several other states. A Black man perceived as having had a sexual relationship with a white woman faced not just legal penalty but lynching. This is not metaphor in Walter’s father’s case: the white people “tried to hang him from a white-blossoming tree.” The rope broke. He survived. He ran.

Esther’s description of him carries the ambivalence of someone who loved in fear and lost what she loved before she could fully acknowledge it: a stranger, a “poor fellow, a tramp, a fugitive,” a prince of Africa. Each descriptor carries a different weight. Together they form the portrait of a man who was real and present and then gone, whom Esther has spent years trying to hold in memory across the gap of everything that happened.

His face was white in the moonlight. Only at dawn did she see he was Black. This moment (the revelation of race at dawn, after intimacy) is one of the chapter’s most precisely situated details. It is not that Esther did not know. It is that the dark erased the visible category, and then the light restored it, and by then the category had already been irrelevant for a night.

The Thing Esther Did

Young has been careful, across nine chapters, to distinguish between what happened to Esther and what Esther did. The stillborn children happened to her. The detective’s assault happened to her. The mud baby in the river; she buried it because she loved it, not because she was guilty of anything. She has been accused of murder for the children who came and did not live. She has not murdered them. Walter is different. She pressed her thumb to still his birth cry. She believed she had killed him. This is what Esther actually did, or tried to do, and it is the thing that has organized her guilt ever since. Not the accusation her mother installed before her birth. Not the detective’s manufactured case. This.

She was young. She was alone. She had no one. The father had fled. She had just delivered a child in secret, in fear, in a country where the child’s race would have compounded every other stigma she already carried. The circumstances do not erase the act. They also do not erase the circumstances. Young holds both.

Walter lived. This is the twist that makes the guilt permanent: she tried to end his life and failed, and he has gone on living, somewhere, without her, growing into a child who asks why she killed him. She did not kill him. She tried to. He does not know the distinction. Neither, quite, does she.

The Haunting

Walter is qualitatively different from the other presences in Esther’s inner life. The stillborn hover and applaud and whisper. The mud baby returns swollen and beautiful and ugly in dreams. These are the presences of the lost, who have nowhere to be except in the consciousness of the person who lost them.

Walter accuses. He has a cruel, hard heart. He asks questions she cannot answer. He is not the presence of the lost; he is the presence of the living, of someone who is out there in the world, growing, carrying his own history, asking his own questions, and visiting Esther’s conscience with the specificity of someone who survived. The black hand laid across the womb, one of the chapter’s central images, is Walter’s hand, or its shadow: the presence of what she did blocking the path forward. Every subsequent pregnancy is gestated in the presence of that hand. Every stillborn carries his shadow. The little shadow boxer, the current pregnancy, the one Esther believes will finally live; it too must make it past Walter’s hand.

Race, the Lynch Rope, and the White-Blossoming Tree

The image Young chooses for the attempted lynching of Walter’s father is exact: a white-blossoming tree. Not a bare tree, not a dead tree: a flowering one, beautiful in the way that spring trees are beautiful, and from its branches a rope, and below the rope a Black man who survived because the rope broke. Young was writing this during the era of the Civil Rights Movement: the NAACP’s anti-lynching campaigns, the murder of Emmett Till in 1955 and the published photographs that catalyzed the movement, the ongoing documentation of racial terror. She does not name these events. She gives Esther a Black lover who fled for his life, and she gives him the white-blossoming tree and the broken rope, and she lets these stand in the landscape of Esther’s memory without commentary.

To All My Darlings notes the history of anti-miscegenation law in the United States: the first prohibition on interracial marriage was passed by Maryland in 1691, more than three hundred years before Loving v. Virginia finally ended them all. The prospect of Black men marrying white women was described by many Americans before the Civil War as the greatest threat to society. When William G. Allen, a Black professor, announced his plans to marry a white student in 1853, he narrowly escaped lynching and had to leave the country permanently. In 1958, Sammy Davis Jr. briefly married a Black actress to protect himself from mob violence after his relationship with a white actress became known. Walter’s father is not a named historical figure. He is a Black man in a summer night who survived a lynch rope and ran. He is every Black man who ran. His child (Walter, black as my true love) is the child of that history, born into Esther’s fear and her love simultaneously, born into a country where his existence was illegal in some states and dangerous in many more.

Breadcrumbs for Spirits

Alongside the revelation about Walter, the chapter also gives us Esther’s daily rituals of the liminal: making small clothes for no one, setting out breadcrumbs for spirits, building a little house of straw in a “tree for the spirit to come home to.” These are the practices of someone who lives at the border between the living and the dead, who sets a place at the table for what cannot come to dinner, who leaves the door open for what has no body to walk through it.

They are also, in context, the practices of someone who has had a child she does not know the location of. Walter is out there, alive, growing. Esther does not know where. She cannot reach him through the ordinary channels because she does not know where to look and because the circumstances of his birth mean that looking would be dangerous. So she leaves breadcrumbs for spirits, and perhaps one of those spirits is Walter’s: the child who is alive but lost to her, who is both in the world and in the category of what she cannot touch.

What to Hold Onto

Walter: the first child who actually lived. Born in a summer night, his father Black and nearly lynched, Esther young and alone and frightened. She pressed her thumb to still his birth cry. He survived. He is somewhere in the world, asking why she killed him.

Walter’s father: a stranger, a “poor fellow, a tramp, a fugitive,” a prince. His face white in the moonlight, Black at dawn. He ran because the rope had broken and the white people would finish what they started. He had no other choice.

The white-blossoming tree and the broken rope. The particular beauty Young gives to the instrument of racial terror.

The black hand laid across the womb. Walter’s shadow blocking the path to every subsequent child.

The breadcrumbs set out for spirits. The little house of straw in the tree. The small clothes made for no one. Esther keeping the table set for what cannot come. And the little shadow boxer, still fighting. Still two hearts. Still the one she believes will finally make it through.

  • On the Kentucky Derby and Black Jockeys
  • On Walter’s Name
guide-21-let-bygones-be-bygones:
Chapter 21: Let Bygones Be Bygones

← Chapter 20 · Guide Home · Chapter 22 →

Research notes: Chapter 21

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Symbols: Clothing, Hats, and Skirts

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology · Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Chapter 21 is the last chapter of the birthday night sequence, and it does something no reader quite expects after chapters 17 through 20: it ends with comedy.

Not the dark comedy of the novel’s great surreal passages, but something lighter and more precise: the comedy of two people who have been through something enormous together, silently agreeing to say nothing about it, and returning to ordinary life with the particular relief of survivors.

Young earns this ending. Don’t be fooled into thinking it undoes what came before.

What actually happens in Chapter 21

Vera is still lying in Miss MacIntosh’s bed, still watching the bald head on the pillow, still composing her resolution to pretend. Young gives us one final extended description of Miss MacIntosh as she is in this moment: the gnarled hands and feet, the missing breast and its scar, the absent eyelashes and eyebrows, the woman’s clothes strewn in bundles on the floor, the “green hair ribbon looped over the bust of Martin Luther.” The Irish green ribbon on Luther. Young cannot help herself, and neither can we.

Then Vera falls back to sleep.

When she wakes, Miss MacIntosh is standing at the foot of the bed, fully dressed and wigged, her red hair shining, her silver-dollar watch blotted out by sunlight, in a remarkably good humor. The bedroom is neat. Nothing has changed. The pact is already in effect without a word being spoken.

Miss MacIntosh says Vera has “been very sick and unusually stubborn, but” has recovered. She scolds her mildly for dancing when there was no partner at the birthday party. She holds up the party dress Mr. Spitzer had sent (that filmy, floating creation) and says it cannot be mended and must be thrown away. “Into the ash bin it goes.”

The second inventory

Before Vera falls asleep, Young gives us one last full look at the body as it is in morning light, and it is the most complete description in the sequence. The stalk of a breast “cut away so early, the scar, the tissues like a baby’s fist.” “No eyebrows, no eyelashes, no single hair or feather, the hairless body shining in the” sound of surf. The “gnarled hands with veins knotted by old labors.” The “brassiere with a wad of cloth” concealing what is missing.

And in the middle of this: the pity, pity, pity. Young uses the word three times in close succession, and it is doing the work that nothing else in the sequence could do. Not grief, not outrage, not the rage of a child who has been deceived. Pity. The feeling that arrives when you understand something about another person’s life that they never chose to show you, that they have carried alone for years, that is simply larger than any response you have.

This is what Vera carries forward from this night. Not the shock, not the fight, not even the decision. The pity that is not the end but the beginning, only the beginning, of understanding another person.

Miss MacIntosh returns

The scene of Miss MacIntosh standing at the foot of the bed, restored, is one of the most carefully handled moments in the novel. Young gives us her return in full detail: the green hair ribbon, the pin-striped shirtwaist, the turtleneck “sweater with holes at the elbows,” the “faded woolen scarf pinned with a large black safety pin.” Every piece of the assembly back in its place.

And Vera’s response: she “looked at her without the slightest astonishment, completely forgetful that she had ever been different than now she seemed.” Not pretending to forget. Actually, momentarily, forgetting. The vision of the night slipping under the surface of the ordinary morning like something covered by a wave.

This is what Young has been building toward across five chapters. Not a confrontation, not a confession, not a reckoning. Two people standing in a bedroom in the morning, one of them asking what Mr. Spitzer was thinking when he sent that party dress, and neither of them saying anything about the bald head on the pillow an hour ago. The pact holds. The ordinary day begins.

The party dress

The chapter ends on the party dress, and Young gives it real weight. Mr. Spitzer sent it in a long white box. “It was a filmy, floating creation,” cloudlike. Vera was supposed to wear white roses in her hair. She “should have worn white roses in” her hair.

It cannot be mended. We should only tear it further. Into the ash bin.

The dress is the fourteenth birthday itself: the party that had no guests, the night that went so far from what it was supposed to be. Miss MacIntosh holds it up to the light and finds no hole in it, no seed pearl out of place, all the little ribbons intact, every rosette of yellowed lace exactly as it was when it came out of the box. The dress survived the night intact. The night did not.

Miss MacIntosh’s verdict is cheerful and final: it cannot be mended. Throw it away. There will be no new one. This is Miss MacIntosh at her most characteristic: pragmatic, slightly bleak, refusing to pretend that the unrepairable can be repaired. She has been making this assessment all her life, about things rather more significant than party dresses.

It is also, read against the night, the novel’s most compressed statement about what has happened: the dress is fine, but it cannot be worn again. The occasion is over. “Let bygones be bygones. We shall turn over a new leaf.”

What to watch for as you keep reading

Light spoilers: This section hints at what happens later in the novel. Skip it if you want to meet the story fresh.

The Miss MacIntosh sequence, chapters 13 through 21, is complete. The novel will not return to this night directly, though it will return to Miss MacIntosh constantly, in memory, in Vera’s search, in the questions the novel keeps circling. You now have the full picture. Everything else is aftermath and extension.

Notice, from here forward, how often other characters in the novel are described in terms that echo Miss MacIntosh’s situation: the disguised, the concealed, the person whose outer life is a performance built over a private reality. Young is going to show you this pattern in many different lives. You are now prepared to see it.

The “green hair ribbon looped over the bust of Martin Luther” will stay with you. It should. It is one of those small, exact, irreducible images that Young places in a scene and lets stand without comment. The ornament of the woman’s secret self (the Irish green, the softness of a ribbon) resting on the shoulders of the man who said here I stand, I can do no other. Young does not explain this. She never explains these. You carry them.

guide-59-the-borrowed-skeleton:
Chapter 59: The Borrowed Skeleton

← Chapter 58 · Guide Home · Chapter 60 →

Research notes: Chapter 59

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Duality and Doubles · Fate and Chance · Light and Darkness · Music, Sound, and Silence · Order, Chaos, and Discipline

Symbols: Lamps, Candles, and Light · Music and Instruments · Twins and Doubles

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Music and Composers · Suicide in History and Literature · The Bible · The History of Opium

If Chapter 58 left you with the image of two men making invisible music together on library steps, Chapter 59 takes you somewhere deeper and stranger: inside Mr. Spitzer's growing conviction that the body he inhabits is not his own.

Stay with him. This is one of the novel's most philosophically rich chapters, and it arrives exactly when you're ready for it.

What actually happens

Mr. Spitzer walks the city, tossing coins to street musicians and beggars with indiscriminate generosity. He cannot always tell who is poor and who is wealthy, who is living and who is dead, who is a professional musician and who is destitute. He gives anyway. And as he walks, he thinks: about his dead brother Peron, about chance and randomness and order, about the strange fact that he cannot be certain the skeleton inside his body is his own.

By the chapter's end, he arrives at a provisional, tentative conclusion: perhaps everything would be explained by simply admitting that he is already dead.

The stolen skeleton

This is the image that will stay with you from Chapter 59. Mr. Spitzer becomes convinced that at some point, he cannot say when, there was a "substitution": his original skeleton was replaced by another, and the body he moves through the world in is not quite his. He feels like “a shadow trembling in the air,” a man wearing a borrowed mask.

Young is not playing this for comedy or horror. She means it philosophically. If you cannot be certain that your own body is yours, what exactly is "you"? Mr. Spitzer distinguishes between three things: the body (which he suspects is illusion), the soul (which is all-informing, the deep water of a person), and the spirit (which is temporary as the wind). He suspects that transformations between these can happen without a person noticing. That you could wake up, or not wake up, as someone slightly other than who you were.

And here is the twist: Mr. Spitzer suspects this isn't unique to him. "Every man and every woman might have suffered a substitution like his own," he thinks. He distrusts himself and therefore cannot trust others, not because they are dishonest, but because they may not know what they are either.

This is Young's deepest quarrel with the stable, bounded self. She doesn't think there is one.

The horn-blower's double life

Among the street musicians Mr. Spitzer passes is an old horn-blower: ragged, playing glassy jazz, apparently destitute. Mr. Spitzer gives him coins. Then he discovers that this same man is also a member of a prestigious symphony orchestra.

The man is simultaneously a beggar and a professional. Both are true. Neither cancels out the other. Young offers this not as an ironic twist but as evidence for something she has been building across the entire novel: that appearances are unreliable not because people are deceitful, but because people genuinely contain multitudes that don't resolve into a single identity.

Mr. Spitzer already knew this, of course. He is both a lawyer and a composer. He is both alive and, possibly, already dead.

His brother Peron

Peron Spitzer (Mr. Spitzer's twin brother, now dead) appears throughout this chapter as a kind of shadow twin, a constant companion to every thought. Where Mr. Spitzer fears the length of life, Peron feared its brevity. They are mirror images: one man terrified life would go on too long, the other terrified it would end too soon. Between them, they cover the entire territory of human anxiety about time.

Peron's suicide comes up here as a meditation, not a wound. Mr. Spitzer turns it over carefully: what if suicide were not a negative impulse, but a creative one? What if it were, his words, "the most creative act, even like sexual love begetting another person"? A desire not to escape life, but to transcend its limits, to seek an immortal love beyond what living allows?

This is not a position Young endorses or condemns. It is what Mr. Spitzer genuinely wonders, as he walks and gives away coins and feels the creaking of a skeleton that may not be his.

Darkness as illumination

Peron, we learn, feared darkness. Mr. Spitzer has made a different peace with it. He has come to experience darkness as his "only light," his illumination. In the dark, he can see things the daylight conceals: the glimmering fins of invisible fish, the iridescence of hidden stars, the interior gleamings that ordinary perception misses.

This is one of Young's recurring arguments: that those who dwell closest to darkness, to loss, to dissolution, can perceive things the comfortably solid cannot. Vera, living in her mother's opium-haunted house, learned to navigate hallucination while others had never needed to. Mr. Spitzer, carrying his dead brother and his borrowed skeleton, can hear silent music and see in the dark. The loss is real. So is the seeing.

Chance and the music of billiard balls

Chapter 59 is one of the novel's most explicit meditations on chance, and it's worth slowing down for. Mr. Spitzer composes music based on the patterns of migratory birds in flight, or the trajectories of billiard balls struck at random: patterns that cannot be exactly repeated, that produce something beautiful precisely because they are unrepeatable.

He is asking: is life like this? Are we governed by chance? And if so, does chance produce chaos, or does it produce its own kind of order, like foam patterns on surf that are never twice the same but are always, unmistakably, foam?

He cannot answer this. He is afraid of everything (afraid of loss, of silence, of thresholds, of his own shadow) and he admits that he "would be most afraid if he had no fear," because his fear is the sign that something in him is still paying attention, still alive to what might be lost. Fear, for Mr. Spitzer, is not the opposite of courage. It is the proof of engagement.

No dividing line

The chapter keeps returning to a single, insistent claim: there is "no dividing line, no distinction between life and death." Birth and death are a "wild sea without a shore." The living and the dead are not in separate rooms. They are in the same room, breathing the same air, and the walls between them are thinner than we pretend.

Mr. Spitzer is not certain he is on one side of this line or the other. And by the end of the chapter, he arrives at his tentative conclusion: perhaps the simplest explanation, the one that would make everything else cohere, is that he is already dead. Not dramatically. Not with trumpets. But quietly, in some way he passed over without noticing, and has been walking through the aftermath ever since.

This is not despair. It is, he says, his "only wisdom." The confusion is not failure. It is what he knows.

What to hold onto

“Mr. Spitzer in his black cape,” walking through the city, giving coins to musicians he cannot quite see clearly, carrying a skeleton that may not be his own, hearing bells ringing underwater, unable to find the shore between life and death. He is afraid of everything. He keeps walking. He keeps giving.

That is Chapter 59.

guide-13-farewell-to-the-last-certitude:
Chapter 13: Farewell to the Last Certitude

← Chapter 12 · Guide Home · Chapter 14 →

Research notes: Chapter 13

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Music, Sound, and Silence

Symbols: Horses and Carriages · Silence and Deafness

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Angels and Archangels · Deafness and Sign Language · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · Romantic Poets

We have been building toward this chapter for twelve chapters. Young has been placing the pieces with great care: the plain alarm clock, the stopped clocks, the garden of the blind, the portrait of Miss MacIntosh’s philosophy, the sentence at the end of Chapter 12 that told you something enormous was coming.

Chapter 13 is where it arrives.

Something happens to Vera on the night of her fourteenth birthday that changes how she sees Miss MacIntosh, and therefore how she sees everything. Young tells us this has happened before she shows us what happened. That choice is deliberate and important, and we’ll come back to it.

What actually happens in Chapter 13

Vera wanders through the estate’s gardens on the night of her fourteenth birthday. She moves through what she now calls the garden of the deaf: a different garden from the blind one in Chapter 12, or perhaps the same garden understood differently, a place where sound has died. She sees chessmen moving on a chessboard of light and shadow, life-sized, played by invisible hands. She sees marble statues, mist-flowers that fly away like moths when she reaches for them, gargoyles spouting water, cherubim made of barnacles.

And somewhere in this night, she sees something about Miss MacIntosh that she will never unsee.

Young does not show us the moment directly. Not yet. What she gives us instead is its aftermath: the knowledge that Vera now carries, the understanding that Miss MacIntosh (the one solid, ordinary, unambiguous person in the entire novel) was not what she appeared to be.

The chapter then moves into a long, extraordinary conversation between Catherine and Mr. Spitzer about the garden of the deaf: a garden where, Catherine insists, the ear is dead, where no sound reaches, where Mr. Spitzer’s music can only be silence because no voice carries and no one can hear another speaking farewell.

The rider over Lake Constance

Before anything else, pause at the passage near the chapter’s opening. It is one of the most important in the entire novel, and Young places it here for a reason.

A traveler on horseback crosses Lake Constance in winter, in a blizzard, at night. He cannot see anything, not the landscape, not his reflection, not where land ends and lake begins. He rides the forty-six miles in blinding snow, thinking he is crossing solid ground. When he reaches the other shore and looks back and sees what he has actually crossed (a lake that was never completely frozen, that no one had ever ridden across and survived) he drops dead from “the shock of the after-knowledge.”

He was safe as long as he didn’t know. The knowing killed him.

This is what Vera says her ignorance about Miss MacIntosh was: the thing that kept her alive and sane. And this is what she is about to lose. She has reached the other shore. She is looking back. She is about to see where she has been.

What Vera now knows, without telling us yet

Young builds the chapter around an absence at its center. We know that Vera saw something. We know it changed everything. We know that after this night she will never again see Miss MacIntosh as she knew her. But Young withholds the specific revelation for just a little longer.

This is not coyness. It is the structure enacting the experience. Vera’s knowledge arrived the same way: she saw something she wasn’t prepared for, and then she had to live inside the new reality while the old one dissolved around her. Young makes the reader inhabit that same disorientation. You know something happened. You are not yet sure what. You are on the shore, looking back at the frozen lake, not yet able to name what you crossed.

What we are given instead of the revelation itself is the cascade of farewells that opens the chapter. Farewell to Miss MacIntosh. Farewell to the last certitude. Farewell to the old moralities and the proverbial wisdom and the rote questions and answers. Farewell to What Cheer and its cherry blossoms and peach orchards. Farewell to the “fabric of self-deception we two persons had lived by, and farewell to the past and its illusion, and farewell to the reason, the purpose, the goal, the future.”

All of it. Everything that Miss MacIntosh represented is dismantled in a single page, before Young has told us why.

The garden of the deaf

The chapter’s second half is a sustained, heartbreaking conversation between Catherine and Mr. Spitzer about a garden where, according to Catherine, the ear is dead.

She is not speaking metaphorically, or rather she is, but she means it literally too. In this garden (part of the vast estate, companion to the garden of the blind from Chapter 12) sound has ceased. One can see the bird but not hear the song. One can see a lover’s face but not hear his voice speaking farewell. The ear that is dead, when Mr. Spitzer asks whose ear she means, is his: his dead brother’s ear, buried somewhere without ceremony, silent in the ground.

Mr. Spitzer pushes back, carefully. He points out that his brother was not buried on this estate. He also admits, in his precise, lawyerly way, that in his right ear there is “always a subdued roaring, a noise” his brother’s physician told him does not come from this world, and that he is learning “not to turn his head every time he” hears a traffic horn that isn’t there.

Catherine is not persuaded. She keeps talking, louder and louder, even perhaps after Mr. Spitzer has quietly left, still arguing with the sense of him that remains in the room. The sound is fled from the universe. His music can only be silence. “One should see the bird.” “One should not hear the song.”

For Mr. Spitzer, whose life’s work is music he never plays and never finishes, this is a more devastating verdict than Catherine probably realizes she is delivering.

What to watch for as you keep reading

Light spoilers: This section hints at what happens later in the novel. Skip it if you want to meet the story fresh.

Chapter 14 will give you what Chapter 13 withheld. Young has prepared you as carefully as she can. The revelation about Miss MacIntosh is coming, and when it arrives it will be both shocking and, in retrospect, inevitable: all the signs were there.

Notice, going forward, how the novel’s language around Miss MacIntosh shifts. The plain, practical, unambiguous woman remains present in Vera’s memory, but she is now always seen from the other shore. Everything she said and did carries a different weight. The thimble engraved Juliet, 1899. The needles and pins bristling from her shirtwaist. The one face, not two. All of it will mean something different now.

The garden of the deaf joins the garden of the blind as one of the novel’s organizing spaces. Young is building a landscape of absent senses: a world that can be touched but not seen, heard but not touched, seen but not heard. Pay attention to which sense is missing in each passage. It tells you something about what kind of knowledge is available in that moment.

For the Curious
