  • The chessmen moving on a chessboard
guide-09-i-am-dancing-with-death:
Chapter 9: I Am Dancing with Death

← Chapter 8 · Guide Home · Chapter 10 →

Research notes: Chapter 9

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Solomon the Turtle · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Guilt, Innocence, and Justice · Motherhood, Pregnancy, and Birth · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Pregnancy, Birth, and Children · Weddings and Funerals

Philosophy: Hinduism · Marguerite Young on Her Craft · Pythagoras and the Music of the Spheres

Allusions: Astronomy · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Greek Mythology · Music and Composers · The Bible · The History of Opium

We step back from the bus now. Chapter 9 is one of the novel’s memory chapters, the kind Young writes when she wants to take you deep into the life that preceded the journey, into the texture of the years Vera spent under Miss MacIntosh’s care before everything broke apart.

If the early bus chapters showed you Miss MacIntosh through Vera’s grief and longing, Chapter 9 shows you what their daily life together actually looked like. And it is rich, strange, funny, tender, and shot through with an approaching darkness that Vera can feel but not yet name.

What actually happens in Chapter 9

Vera opens the chapter with a question she has been carrying since Miss MacIntosh disappeared: was she responsible? Did she cause it, in some way she cannot fully articulate? She does not answer this question. She turns it over and over like a stone.

Then she takes us back. She shows us the schoolroom: Miss MacIntosh at the blackboard, drilling Vera on geography, history, facts about the Chicago fire and the glaciers and the grasshoppers. She shows us the embroidery hoop, the straight basting stitches, the hemming of handkerchiefs, Miss MacIntosh’s program for turning Vera into a competent, marriageable woman, delivered with the focused intensity of someone who believes that discipline is protection.

She shows us Solomon the turtle, ancient and slow, hauling a clay flower pot with a geranium across the schoolroom floor while Miss MacIntosh eyes him with undisguised contempt. She shows us the silver dollar watch Miss MacIntosh wore, always producing it to remind Vera that time was passing, that they had work to do, that there was no room for sloth.

And she shows us Vera’s fourteenth birthday. Mr. Spitzer sends a party dress: filmy, sleeveless, embroidered with seed pearls. No guests come. Vera dances alone in the empty room, imagining a partner, and declares to Miss MacIntosh: I am dancing with Death.

Miss MacIntosh’s response is immediate and serious. Death is not a dance partner for a fourteen-year-old. Death is real, universal, coming for everyone, and not to be romanticized. Vera listens. And in the darkness afterward, she begins to think about marriage, about the man she might someday know, and whether she would ever truly know him at all.

Miss MacIntosh as teacher

The schoolroom scenes in this chapter are among the most vivid in the novel, and they deserve your full attention.

Miss MacIntosh’s education program for Vera is not gentle. It is relentless. Geography, history, domestic skills, moral instruction and all of it delivered by a woman who came from nothing, who believes that preparation is the only armor a girl has, and who is determined to give Vera the tools that her mother’s opium dreams never provided.

But notice what is underneath the curriculum. When Vera asks Miss MacIntosh about her ovaries, a reasonable question from a girl navigating adolescence, Miss MacIntosh redirects immediately to an unrelated historical lecture. When Vera asks about Miss MacIntosh’s eyebrows, she gets another lecture. Personal questions are deflected. Bodily questions are redirected. The space between them is full of things Miss MacIntosh will not say.

Young is not suggesting that Miss MacIntosh is a hypocrite. She is showing you a woman with her own private architecture, her own rooms that stay locked, teaching the best she can from the rooms that are open. Miss MacIntosh believes in honesty and reality. But there are aspects of her reality she is not prepared to share with a child. Not yet. Perhaps not ever.

Solomon the turtle, and what he represents

The turtle named Solomon has lived in the schoolroom for so long that his origins are unknown. Vera wonders if he might be the World Turtle or the mythological figure found in cultures across the globe, the great creature whose back holds the world on its shell. He carries a clay flower pot with a geranium that smells of tobacco, moving with the patience of something that has been alive longer than anyone can remember.

Miss MacIntosh despises him. She associates his slowness with sloth, with the absence of discipline, with everything she is trying to train Vera away from. He is the anti-Miss MacIntosh: ancient, unhurried, indifferent to schedules.

But Young gives Solomon a name and not just any name. Solomon was the wisest king in the Bible, famous for his wealth and his discernment. By naming this slow, contemptible-to-Miss-MacIntosh creature after wisdom itself, Young is gently undermining the idea that speed and discipline are the only forms of intelligence. Solomon the turtle does not hurry. Solomon the turtle does not care about Miss MacIntosh’s watch. Solomon the turtle has been here longer than any of them and will likely outlast them all.

The birthday party that wasn’t

Vera’s fourteenth birthday is one of those passages that Young renders with particular precision, every detail chosen to make you feel both the beauty and the sadness at once.

Mr. Spitzer sends the party dress. It is lovely: filmy, sleeveless, embroidered with seed pearls. He is not there to give it to her in person. No guests come. Miss MacIntosh is present but not celebratory. And Vera, in her beautiful dress, alone in the room, dances with an imaginary partner.

This is Vera at fourteen in miniature: imaginative, yearning, already accustomed to the absence of what she was promised. She creates what isn’t there. She dances with the invisible.

And then she says, to herself or to Miss MacIntosh: I am dancing with Death.

It might be adolescent drama. It might be genuine metaphysical awareness. Miss MacIntosh takes it as the latter because she takes everything seriously, because she is not a woman who dismisses what children say. She sits Vera down and tells her about death plainly: it is real, it comes for everyone, it is not romantic, it is not a partner you choose. You do not invite it in as a companion. You acknowledge it and you keep living.

This is the truest and most direct thing Miss MacIntosh says in the chapter. It is also, in retrospect, haunted. Because she will walk into the sea. Because the dance Vera was imagining is not far away.

What Miss MacIntosh says about marriage

In the darkness after the birthday, Vera asks or thinks about asking what marriage is really like. Miss MacIntosh’s answer is not comforting.

You do not truly know a person until after you have married them. And then it is too late.

This is not cynicism from Miss MacIntosh, it is realism. She is not saying marriage is bad. She is saying that the self people present before marriage is not the entire self, and the discovery of the self comes after the contract is already signed. She is preparing Vera for the truth that the person you marry is, in some essential way, a stranger. And that learning to live with a stranger, with their full, complicated, sometimes disappointing reality, is what marriage actually is.

Vera, at fourteen, wants something else. She wants adventure, passion, a union with someone worth knowing. She wants the story. Miss MacIntosh is trying to give her the facts.

Neither of them is wrong. That tension between the story Vera wants and the facts Miss MacIntosh insists on is the tension that runs through everything.

The guilt Vera carries

The chapter opens and returns to a question Vera cannot resolve: did she cause Miss MacIntosh’s death? Was there something she did, something she said, something she failed to do that set the ending in motion?

Young does not answer this. She will not answer it for many chapters yet. What she does instead is show you the weight of the question, the way it sits in Vera, the way she turns it over, the way she can reconstruct every detail of their life together and still not arrive at a clean cause and effect.

This is what guilt without resolution feels like. Not a verdict. Not even a clear accusation. Just the loop of memory, the same moments replayed, the same question asked again at the end that was asked at the beginning.

Notice that Vera’s guilt does not stop her from loving Miss MacIntosh. The two things exist together: grief and guilt, love and the possibility of responsibility. This is one of Young’s most honest emotional observations.

What to watch for as you keep reading

Light spoilers: This section hints at what happens later in the novel. Skip it if you want to meet the story fresh.

The party dress. Mr. Spitzer sends it, but does not attend. He is always doing this, providing for Vera at a distance, present in her life through gestures and objects but absent from the actual moments. The party dress is a generous and useless gift: beautiful, and belonging to a party that doesn’t exist. Watch how Spitzer operates throughout the novel. His presence is always slightly off.

Miss MacIntosh’s watch. She produces it constantly, checking the time, reminding Vera of the time, insisting that time is moving and there is work to do. It is her instrument of discipline. In a novel where time bends, loops, and dissolves, Miss MacIntosh’s silver dollar watch is the attempt to keep it straight. Notice what happens to time in the chapters where she is absent.

The question about ovaries. Vera asks. Miss MacIntosh redirects. This evasion matters more than it seems. Miss MacIntosh is a woman who believes in truth about everything except certain things about herself and her body. Those things are hidden. The novel will eventually show you why.

“I am dancing with Death.” Hold this phrase. It is not the last time the image of dancing appears in the novel, and it is not the last time death is present in a moment that should be celebratory.

What to hold onto

Chapter 9 is a chapter of preparation for what is coming in the novel, and for what has already come. Vera is learning, under Miss MacIntosh’s strict and loving supervision, to face facts. To hem a handkerchief straight. To know her geography. To understand that marriage is not a fairy tale and that death is not a dance partner.

She does not fully learn any of this. She is fourteen and dreaming of adventure and she dances alone in her beautiful dress with an invisible partner and says she is dancing with Death, and some part of her believes it is romantic.

But Miss MacIntosh is watching. And trying. And the watching and the trying are, in their way, as close to love as this household gets.

For the Curious

  • The World Turtle
  • Pythagoras believed in metempsychosis or the
  • Proteus
  • Pandora
  • “There but for the grace of God go I”
  • Marguerite Young’s own sexuality
guide-62-the-will-and-the-water-music:
Chapter 62: The Will and the Water Music

← Chapter 61 · Guide Home · Chapter 63 →

Research notes: Chapter 62

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh

Themes: Faith, God, and the Supernatural · Music, Sound, and Silence

Symbols: Fire · Music and Instruments · Snow, Ice, and Winter · The Sea and Water

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Astronomy · Deafness and Sign Language · Suicide in History and Literature

Chapter 62 is, among other things, the chapter in which Mr. Spitzer writes his last will and testament. It is not a conventional will. It is one of the most beautiful documents in the novel.

What actually happens

Mr. Spitzer, still moving through his interior life with the slow deliberateness we have come to expect, does three things in this chapter: he dreams of a river that transforms from fire to ice; he rewrites his will, leaving his music to the world; and he learns the full story of the old violinist from the library steps, the man from Chapter 58 who played an imaginary violin with an imaginary bow.

He also contemplates a clarinetist he once knew who died by suicide, leaving a note that said he was going to join a greater orchestra.

The river of fire and ice

The chapter opens in a dream, or something like one: Mr. Spitzer rowing down a river that shifts from molten fire to frozen ice, surrounded by walruses and seals wearing diamond necklaces, seagulls transforming into musicians mid-flight, a great water orchestra assembled on the banks. The imagery is extravagant and dreamlike, but its logic is consistent: the river is always the same river, just in different states. Fire and ice are the same element transformed. The orchestra assembles from birds.

Mr. Spitzer wonders, at the opening of this chapter, whether he has ever truly slept. This is not insomnia; it is something more fundamental: the suspicion that perfect rest, like perfect music, is always just beyond reach, always slightly unattained. He has been pursuing sleep the way he has been pursuing the right notes, and neither has fully arrived.

The will

The will is extraordinary. Mr. Spitzer bequeaths his music (all of it, the compositions that exist only in his head and on scraps of paper and on his shirt cuffs) to the world, to be played on water. "Even to indifferent ears," he writes, "and even to deaf ears and even to dead ears and to sea conches." He cancels his subscriptions. He leaves instructions about eggs and milk, small domestic rituals elevated into symbolic gestures.

What is he doing? He is an artist accepting that his work may never be widely heard, and leaving it anyway. He is giving his music to the world even as he acknowledges that the world may not notice. The gift is unconditional. This is what the will says, in its legal and poetic and slightly mad form: I give all of this to everyone, including those who cannot hear it.

A legal term appears here: mortmain, from the French for "dead hand", the legal concept of property held in perpetuity by an institution, a dead hand continuing to shape the living world. Mr. Spitzer's will is an act of mortmain in the best sense: his silent music reaching forward, past his death, into whatever ears might eventually receive it.

The old violinist's story

Here, in Chapter 62, we learn what we didn't know in Chapter 58: the old violinist on the library steps was not simply a street musician. He was a second violinist with the Philadelphia Orchestra. He had played, without ever touching his strings, for years. His silent bowing was not eccentricity; it was his entire technique. He had found a way to perform invisibly within the orchestra, contributing nothing physical to the sound, but present, bowing, part of the whole.

Then, one night, he accidentally produced a false note, a single audible sound, and was dismissed.

Read that again. He was dismissed not for failing to play, but for accidentally succeeding. The moment he made actual music, the illusion was broken, and the orchestra no longer had a place for him. Young is making an argument here about the nature of performance, visibility, and institutional belonging: some artists are tolerated only as long as they remain inaudible. The moment they sound, they are expelled.

Mr. Spitzer recognizes in this man's silent bowing what he had intuited in Chapter 58: this was perhaps the best music, the truest music, the music that exists only in gesture and attention and the imagination of whoever is watching.

The clarinetist who joined a greater orchestra

Mr. Spitzer knew a clarinetist who committed suicide because he felt perpetually out of tune. This was not a technical problem; everyone who heard him assured him he was perfectly in tune. But he could not reconcile what he heard inside himself with what the world reflected back. The dissonance was internal and total and could not be argued away.

He left a note saying he was going to join a greater orchestra.

Mr. Spitzer takes this seriously. He does not dismiss it as metaphor or delusion. He considers it as a genuine possibility: that somewhere beyond this life there is an orchestra that includes all the lost music, all the unplayed compositions, all the clarinetists who were never quite in tune with the world they inhabited. His own music, which no one has ever played or evoked, might find its place there.

"My God! I thought I was in Philadelphia."

Near the end of the chapter, Mr. Spitzer looks up, disoriented, and realizes he is not where he thought he was. The city has shifted on him again. His grasp of place is unstable (he drifts between cities, between states, between realms) and this moment of confusion is both comic and heartbreaking. He has been walking through his interior world so completely that the exterior world has rearranged itself around him without his noticing.

This is not mere absentmindedness. It is the logical consequence of being the kind of person Mr. Spitzer is: someone for whom the music in his head is more real, more present, more insistent than the street he is standing on.

The music that no one has ever played

The chapter keeps circling back to this fact: Mr. Spitzer's music has never been played. Not by anyone. Not even, perhaps, by him, since he is deaf, or nearly so, and his compositions exist as patterns on paper and in memory, as the trajectories of migratory birds and billiard balls, as elegies with names like Music for Polar Bear and Butterfly and Iceberg Music and Music for the Southern Cross.

And yet he keeps writing. He is not discouraged by his failures. The music is real to him, and it will be real in his will, bequeathed to the sea conches who will receive it without judgment. This is, quietly, one of the most radical arguments in the novel: that the unheard work is still work, that the unplayed music is still music, that creating in obscurity is not the same as creating in vain.

What to hold onto

Mr. Spitzer sitting down to write his will, leaving everything (the water music, the bird-flight compositions, the impossibly complex elegies) to deaf ears, dead ears, sea conches, and anyone else who might happen to be listening. The dead hand reaching forward. The music given away before it was ever received.

  • On the aubade
  • On Orion, Taurus, the Pleiades, the Hyades
  • On the clarinetist's greater orchestra

guide-45-the-great-secret:
Chapter 45: The Great Secret

← Chapter 44 · Guide Home · Chapter 46 →

Research notes: Chapter 45

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Esther Longtree · Gertrude Hathaway Tidings · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Peron Spitzer · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Love

Symbols: Roses and Flowers

Philosophy: Kant and Hegel · Marguerite Young on Her Craft · Nietzsche

Allusions: American Religious Movements · Music and Composers · Women's Suffrage

The bus is still moving. Vera is still on it. The novel's wheel keeps turning. But you are in new territory now, and Chapter 45 opens it with one of the volume's central revelations hanging just out of reach, the way all of Young's revelations hang: present, half-stated, trembling on the edge of being said.

Mr. Spitzer has a secret. He has had it since the deathbed, since the papers, the letters, the unintelligible languages, the evidence of the double life. He has vowed not to tell it until long after Cousin Hannah is gone. Chapter 45 keeps that vow while circling the secret so closely that its shape becomes visible even through the silence.

The shape is this: the great public captain of suffrage, the woman who had no time for love and devoted everything to the cause, was haunted her entire life by a love she never fully had. And the question the chapter turns over, slowly and from every angle, is whether the cause and the grief were separate things, or whether they were the same thing, the grief finding the only form available to it, the love becoming the movement because it could not become the person.

What actually happens in Chapter 45

We remain in the long aftermath of Cousin Hannah's death, still in Mr. Spitzer's consciousness, still sorting through the papers and the memories and the last words. The deathbed has ended but it hasn't ended; it echoes forward into this chapter the way all of Cousin Hannah's chapters have echoed, each one unable to contain her completely, each one requiring another.

Mr. Spitzer contemplates what he calls her double life, perhaps even a triple life. The public figure and the private person were so thoroughly separated that he, who was her lawyer and her witness, cannot reconcile them into a single coherent portrait. He knows what she did. He is beginning to understand what she felt. The two do not map onto each other cleanly.

Cousin Hannah's dying words continue to surface: the cry for her lost love, the accusation of betrayal (of herself, by herself, the false modesty), the question (was I always falling?) that sounds like despair but might be the most honest accounting she ever gave of what it felt like to reach as high as she reached. “I aspired to greater heights than most, so I fell a greater distance.”

Mr. Spitzer reflects on fame and oblivion. He considers what will be written on her grave. Twelve miles, he thinks: a distance that is both literal and symbolic, a measure of how far she traveled and how far she still was from where she meant to arrive. He meditates on pigeons as symbols of memory and the soul, on the way public memory reduces even the greatest lives to monuments, losing the secret heart.

If one knew all hearts, one should know none

This is Mr. Spitzer's formulation, and it is one of the chapter's philosophical centers: the person who has heard every confession, who has been the keeper of everyone's secrets, who knows the hidden sorrow and the private love of every person she encountered, that person, paradoxically, knows no one. Because knowledge at that scale becomes abstraction. The individual disappears into the pattern.

Cousin Hannah was the confidante of many. She received whispered loves and private griefs and kept them. She knew more about human feeling than most people accumulate in a lifetime. And she herself, behind all that knowing, remained unknown: to Mr. Spitzer, to Catherine, possibly to herself.

Young is working through a genuine epistemological problem here: what is the relationship between breadth of knowledge and depth of experience? Can you understand love by witnessing it in a thousand people, or does understanding require the particular, the singular, the one? Cousin Hannah had the breadth. What she may have lacked was the particular singular love that would have made everything else legible from the inside.

Love infinitely postponed

“Shall love be infinitely postponed? If infinitely postponed, then it is love.”

This is one of Young's most compressed and exact formulations, and it arrives in Chapter 45 as a kind of philosophical coda to everything that has happened in the deathbed chapters. The idea, drawn from Hegel's logic of negation, is that the very act of deferral defines the thing deferred. A love that is kept waiting, kept just out of reach, kept perpetually on the verge of being claimed: that love acquires a particular intensity from the waiting. It becomes absolute precisely because it was never made conditional on reality.

Catherine's love for Peron, kept alive by his silence and her interpretation of it. Cousin Hannah's love, killed by false modesty, surviving its own death as a wound that never closed. Mr. Spitzer's love, if he has one, conducted entirely in the second remove. The novel is full of loves that were infinitely postponed. And Young asks, through Mr. Spitzer's meditation: what if that is what love actually is? What if the loves that got lived out, that arrived and were received and settled into daily life: what if those became something else, something valuable but no longer love in the absolute sense? What if love requires the infinite postponement to remain itself?

The novel does not endorse this as a prescription for how to live. But it takes it seriously as a description of what happens to certain kinds of people: people like Catherine, like Cousin Hannah, like everyone in this household who loved most fiercely what they could not have.

He was become his brother

To All My Darlings pauses over a line Young drops almost in passing: he was become his brother.

This is potentially the novel's largest bomb, buried in subordinate syntax. Mr. Spitzer (Joachim Spitzer, the surviving twin, the lawyer, the cautious and conservative keeper of dignity) may not be Joachim at all. The line hints that he is Peron. That the twin who survived is not the one we were told survived. That the man Catherine refused to love, the man who spent decades in this household waiting to be seen as a unique individual, was the very man she thought was dead, and she never knew it, and he could not tell her, and so he waited and was not seen and became, over the years, his brother, which is to say became no one.

Young will not confirm this explicitly. She is not that kind of novelist. But the possibility, once planted, reshapes everything that came before. Every time Mr. Spitzer faded into the background of Catherine's dreams, every time she looked past him toward the dead, if he is Peron, she was looking past him toward himself. The grief and the love were in the same room the whole time, wearing each other's clothes.

Susan B. Anthony and the model behind the captain

Chapter 45 surfaces what To All My Darlings makes explicit: Young may have modeled Cousin Hannah in part on Susan B. Anthony and her sister Hannah.

The parallels are striking. Anthony devoted her life to suffrage with the totality Cousin Hannah displays. She never married: journalists asked her repeatedly why, and her answers shifted depending on the day: the men she wanted she could not have; she never found the man necessary to her happiness; she could not give up her freedom to become a man's housekeeper. Anthony's religion followed a trajectory similar to Hannah's: Quaker roots, Unitarian drift, eventual agnosticism, the refusal of a God made happy by submission. Work and worship are one with me, Anthony said. I can not imagine a God of the universe made happy by my getting down on my knees.

When Anthony's sister Hannah was dying, she asked Susan to speak about the great beyond. Anthony later wrote that she could not dash her faith with my doubts, nor could I pretend a faith I had not; so I was silent in the dread presence of death. Mr. Spitzer at Cousin Hannah's deathbed, keeping the great secret, being silent in the dread presence of death: the echo is exact. The silence is the same silence. Young knew her Anthony, and she built her captain from that knowledge.

Anthony predicted, in an 1877 speech, an epoch of single women: that women who would not accept marriage with subjugation, and men who would not proffer it without, would have no alternative but to live without it. Cousin Hannah is one of those women. She lived without it. She died calling for the thing she lived without. The epoch Anthony predicted, and the cost it exacted on the women who inhabited it first, is what Young is elegizing in these chapters.

She knew her Carthage

Young's phrase, she knew her Carthage, is dense with meaning and deserves unpacking.

Carthage was founded, in legend, by Dido: the queen who built a city from nothing, who led her people across the sea, who created something magnificent and enduring. In Virgil's Aeneid, Dido also loved Aeneas, the Trojan hero who stayed in Carthage and then left because the gods required him to found Rome. She died for love of him, by her own hand, after he sailed away. The city she built survived her. Her love did not.

To say Cousin Hannah knew her Carthage is to say she knew what it was to build something great and lose what mattered most. She built the suffrage movement with the same energy Dido built her city: relentlessly, magnificently, against every resistance. And she lost, somewhere along the way, the love that might have sustained her privately. She knew the shape of that loss. She had lived inside it her whole life.

The dwarf with the rose of consciousness

“Who is that dwarf, a turret on his head, a rose at his collar? It is the rose of consciousness.”

Young's image here draws on Nietzsche's Zarathustra, where the dwarf (the spirit of gravity, of self-doubt, of conventional thought) is the obstacle that must be overcome before the highest truths can be faced. Zarathustra confronts the dwarf at the gateway moment of eternal recurrence: the place where all time meets, where past and future coil around the present instant. The dwarf represents everything that makes a person shrink from the full size of their life.

But Young gives the dwarf the rose of consciousness. This is not Nietzsche's dwarf exactly; it is Young's revision of him. In her version, even the spirit of gravity, even the self-doubt and the limitation, carries the rose: carries awareness, carries the capacity to feel and perceive, carries the knowledge of what is being missed. The dwarf knows what the hero knows. He simply cannot act on it. This is Mr. Spitzer. This is the man who has been watching from the second remove, who has all the knowledge and none of the mobility, who carries the rose and cannot place it anywhere it might bloom.

What to hold onto

Chapter 45 is a chapter of aftermath and accumulation: the settling of everything the deathbed chapters stirred up, and the first hints of what Volume 2 will do with it. The secret Mr. Spitzer holds is the chapter's center of gravity, and you do not need to know it to feel its weight. You feel it in every passage where he circles and does not land, every reflection where he approaches and retreats.

What to carry forward: love infinitely postponed as the novel's governing paradox. The possibility that Mr. Spitzer is Peron: that the living man and the dead man have been the same man all along, and Catherine never saw it. The Susan B. Anthony parallel, which roots Cousin Hannah in a specific and real historical tradition of women who gave everything to a cause and died without the private life they secretly wanted. And the rose of consciousness on the dwarf's collar: the awareness that cannot act, that watches and knows and cannot change what it sees.

The bus is still moving. Volume 2 has just begun.

Chapter 25: Mr. Spitzer Had Been Told That Mr. Spitzer Was Dead

← Chapter 24 · Guide Home · Chapter 26 →

Research notes: Chapter 25

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Mr. Chandelier · Peron Spitzer · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Death and Mortality

Symbols: Mirrors and Reflections

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Judaism · Suicide in History and Literature

Chapter 25 is the most sustained portrait of Mr. Spitzer we have had yet, and it arrives with a gift: at last, in full detail, we learn exactly how Peron died. We also learn what Mr. Spitzer did the day he walked through a glass wall and was told, afterward, that he was dead.

This chapter is one of the funniest in the novel, and also one of the saddest. Young achieves both simultaneously, which is her particular genius, and nowhere more clearly than here.

What actually happens in Chapter 25

Still at the breakfast table, still in the morning light, Vera’s mind moves through everything she knows about Mr. Spitzer. Young gives us the full account: his relationship with Catherine, his dead brother Peron, his habits and hesitations, his theory of his own existence.

We learn that Peron fell “through a glass window on the fourteenth floor of an office building.” Mr. Spitzer cannot decide whether it was suicide or accident. Perhaps Peron, rushing impetuously ahead, simply mistook “a window for a door. If the floor level had continued on the other side,” Peron would have lived. It didn’t. He fell through “the first gleamings of the first stars” to the pavement below, screaming as he recognized, too late, the void.

We learn that Mr. Spitzer once walked through a glass wall in another lawyer’s office. He felt nothing, heard nothing, noticed nothing. His valet found glass particles behind his ears that evening, like the prisms of a chandelier. Days later, he received a bill for the wall. He ignored it. More bills came, and threatening letters. Finally, seething with an uncharacteristic fury, he tried to collect for his own discomfort. He was told by a “desk clerk, that Mr. Spitzer was dead, having departed this mortal life several years ago.” His arguments fell upon the empty air.

The hesitant suicide

Young gives Mr. Spitzer one of her most precise self-descriptions in this chapter: he is not “the sudden, untimely suicide as his brother had been but rather the hesitant suicide who takes his luxurious time and considers, weighs and measures all the lost possibilities and disappointments until life ends upon its own account without anyone’s permission or objection or desire.”

This is one of the most exact things Young says about anyone in the novel. Peron was the decisive one: “quick to live, quick to die,” taking the last chance when the odds were all against him. Mr. Spitzer is the other kind: the man who rehearses his ultimate passage so many times, dying so many fugitive deaths, that when the final one comes he hopes it will be imperceptible, that no one will notice when quietly he slips away.

He has been dying slowly since his brother died. Perhaps, he suspects, since before. He cannot remember exactly when he started. He has gained weight as his sorrow has “increased. A fat man, well protected by his dreaming flesh,” treading softly where angels fear to rush ahead, never knowing whether the next step will bring stairway or dissolving stairway or chasm.

And he is proud, ridiculously and tenderly proud, of his little accidents. He has walked through a glass wall and survived. Peron walked through a window and did not. Mr. Spitzer considers this the essential difference between them.

How Peron died

The account of Peron’s death is the most specific thing Mr. Spitzer allows himself to know about it, and even here he cannot hold it steady. It shifts between suicide and accident in the same paragraph, Young giving us Mr. Spitzer’s mind working the question from every angle and arriving at no conclusion.

What is certain: Peron rushed impetuously ahead. The window was on the fourteenth floor. The building “looked out only upon the pavements of the evening clouds, the first gleamings of the first stars.” He screamed as he fell, recognizing too late “the void, the pavement of the city, and his nullification so final, so complete that he had perhaps hardly been able to judge” it.

What is uncertain: whether he knew. Perhaps, Mr. Spitzer reasons carefully, Peron simply mistook the window for a door, as Mr. Spitzer himself once mistook a door for a window. Perhaps he was not suicidal at all but only, in one bright disoriented moment, wrong about where the floor was. “If the floor level had continued,” he would have lived and carried on with his usual pleasures.

Mr. Spitzer cannot settle this. To decide it was an accident would relieve him of something. To decide it was suicide would give Peron’s death a meaning, a choice, a finality that Mr. Spitzer cannot quite claim for his own life. Either way, it was Joachim who has had to think so much about death, beautiful death, all these years since. Peron, smiling in his grave, would probably “not know that he was dead” until someone asked.

The glass wall

Mr. Spitzer walks through a glass wall and leaves a hole in it that he cannot remember making. He feels nothing. He hears nothing. He goes on about his errands. His valet finds the glass behind his ears like chandelier prisms at the end of the day.

Young plays this for comedy and she earns every laugh. The bills arrive. Mr. Spitzer ignores them. More bills. Threatening letters from the other lawyer. Finally, and this is where Young lets us see a flash of Peron in Joachim, he loses his patience. There is still, it seems, a spark of life in Mr. Spitzer. He decides to collect for his discomfort. He presents himself as the aggrieved party.

He is told he is dead.

The desk clerk is not wrong, exactly. Mr. Spitzer has been dying by degrees since his brother died. He has been mistaken for his brother on streets, at race tracks, at parimutuel windows. He has been allowing people to believe he is Peron. He has been living in his brother’s clothes, with his brother’s cufflinks, drinking his brother’s coffee, living in his brother’s house of wreckage. Of course the desk clerk thinks he is dead. The living Mr. Spitzer has made every possible effort to become a ghost. And his arguments fell upon the empty air. Young ends the episode there. The bill is never paid. The glass wall stays broken. Mr. Spitzer, told he is dead, has no further recourse. He was the one who should have died.

What Mr. Spitzer finds in Catherine

Young gives us something unexpected near the chapter’s center: Mr. Spitzer’s account of why he keeps coming to Catherine’s bedside, year after year, evening after evening. It is not entirely about love, or not only.

He has found in Catherine “the bulwark of his own greater delicacy.” She accuses him of falsehood, theft, unsound perceptions, faulty memories. She tells him he is dead, that he has been buried, that he is married to the worm. And through all of this, paradoxically, he gains a “sense of his own precarious being.” Without “her constant, fickle reminder that he” exists (even if only as a ghost, even if only to be accused of things) “he might have forgotten both brothers, the living and the” dead.

She needs him to be real enough to argue with. He needs her to insist that he exists, even wrongly. They sustain each other’s reality through mutual incomprehension. It is one of the novel’s strangest and most honest portraits of what keeps two people together.

What to watch for as you keep reading

Light spoilers: This section hints at what happens later in the novel. Skip it if you want to meet the story fresh.

The glass wall is not the last time Mr. Spitzer will walk through something that should stop him and feel nothing. Watch for the pattern: he moves through barriers that break around him, leaving damage he does not register, continuing on about his errands. It is his way of being in the world. He is always the one who survived the window.

The twin golden cradles beside the twin iron beds in Mr. Spitzer’s bedroom (his and Peron’s, from infancy) are one of the novel’s most precise images of what grief looks like lived in daily. He would sooner have parted from his life than from those cradles. They remind him of infancy and death. Everything in his house is simultaneously the beginning and the end.

Mr. Spitzer’s description of the only music worth hearing as the music he has “never heard, perhaps his own which he had never written, and the only friend” as the friend he has “never met, and the only loves” as the loves he has never loved; these are the novel’s statement of his condition in its most compressed form. He is a man defined entirely by absence. The unwritten score. The unlived life. The brother who should have lived.

guide-04-the-long-sleep-of-empty-years:
Chapter 4: The Long Sleep of Empty Years

← Chapter 3 · Guide Home · Chapter 5 →

Research notes: Chapter 4

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · Suicide in History and Literature · The Bible · The History of Opium

You have just spent Chapter 3 falling a little in love with Miss MacIntosh. Young made sure of that. She gave you the red hair and the black umbrella and the fireflies in a jar, the corset and the sensible shoes and the cold morning swims. She gave you a woman who was the truest thing in the house.

And then she reminded you, as she did in Chapter 1, and now again here, that Miss MacIntosh is gone.

Chapter 4 is about what that loss does to Vera. And it is, in its quiet way, one of the most honest portraits of grief in the novel.

What actually happens in Chapter 4

Miss MacIntosh has disappeared. Her clothes were on the beach. “The two pennies were in her purse.” Vera sits by the shore for what feels like years: crying, barely functioning, her body described as “slothful and immense,” her mind “employed by nothing but the dream.” She tries to write a book. She lights fires on the beach. She talks to fishermen and sailors, asking questions no one can answer.

Her mother, Catherine, watches this and makes her own diagnosis: Vera is losing her sanity. Catherine’s solution is the one she has always had: the opium, the withdrawal, the beautiful obliteration. She offers Vera a vision of eternal youth and dreamless sleep, jewels and supernatural servants, an “opium paradise” where nothing can hurt her anymore. She is, in her way, trying to be a good mother. This is simply the only medicine she knows.

Vera refuses. She leaves by way of Grand Central Station, heading toward What Cheer, Iowa, and whatever she might find there.

On the way, she encounters “a fat, soft-faced lady on” a train who offers her a warning: the place she is going is desolate. Out of this world. “No social life, no communication, no human” warmth. Just cold and silence and decay. The golden bowl, the lady says, is broken there.

Young also gives us, in the middle of all this, a brief and haunting story about a young woman who jumped from the Brooklyn Bridge in her wedding veil, suitcase in hand, on her way to be married. She disappears into the dark water. The novel doesn’t linger on it. It doesn’t need to.

What Vera is thinking about

Grief is the engine of this chapter, but Young is not interested in simple grief. She is interested in what grief does to a person over time, how it can become its own kind of opium, its own withdrawal from the world.

Vera has been lost before. She grew up lost, in a house where reality was optional. Miss MacIntosh was the thing that tethered her. And now the tether is gone, and Vera is discovering something terrifying: that without it, she is capable of floating away just as her mother did. That the boundary between herself and Catherine is thinner than she thought.

This is why Catherine’s offer of opium is so dangerous in this chapter, not because it is obviously wrong, but because it is almost tempting. Vera can see the appeal. She can see how a person ends up in that bed, in those dreams, in that beautiful nowhere. She is close enough to the edge to feel the pull.

What saves her, if anything saves her, is the stubbornness of Miss MacIntosh’s memory. The ivory knitting needles she finds in the sand. The fire she lights on the beach. The specific, physical, irreducible realness of the woman she is looking for. You cannot grieve a dream the way Vera grieves Miss MacIntosh. This grief is proof that something was real.

So she gets on a train. She goes toward Iowa. She carries her grief with her like a suitcase.

The woman on the Brooklyn Bridge

Young drops this story into the chapter without explanation or fanfare, and it is easy to read past it. Don’t.

A young woman a working class, about to be married, carrying her suitcase and wearing her veil jumps from the Brooklyn Bridge into the East River. She is never named. We are told very little about her. And then Young moves on.

But the image stays. A woman in a wedding veil, the symbol of a life about to begin, choosing instead the dark water. Young is placing this alongside Vera’s own crisis point: the moment when the pull of oblivion is strongest. She is not saying Vera will make the same choice. She is saying this is the landscape they all inhabit, these women in this novel: a landscape where the alternative to the life you have been handed is sometimes the river.

The reality of women’s lives in the era Young is writing about is part of what this image carries. Marriage was not simply an option, it was, for most women, the entire structure of a viable life. There was no other architecture. The woman on the bridge was on her way to that architecture. And she chose the water instead. Young does not judge her. She just shows you the bridge.

Catherine, again and why she matters here

It would be easy to read Catherine as simply a cautionary tale: this is what happens when you surrender to illusion. But Chapter 4 asks you to look at her more carefully.

Catherine genuinely loves Vera. The opium paradise she offers her daughter is not cruelty, it is the best gift she has. She has found a way to stop hurting, and she wants to give it to the person she loves most. The jewels, the supernatural servants, the eternal youth: these are not a trap she is setting. They are her idea of heaven.

What Young is doing here is complicated: she is asking you to feel the appeal of what Catherine is offering, even as you understand why Vera must refuse it. Illusion is not always ugly. Sometimes it is gorgeous. Sometimes it is the only mercy a person has found. The novel does not let you dismiss Catherine. It makes you understand her.

Vera understands her. That is part of what makes leaving so hard.

The fat, soft-faced lady on the train

She arrives as a voice of experience, warning Vera about where she is headed. What Cheer or wherever Vera is going is not what she imagines. It is cold and silent and the community has collapsed in on itself. The golden bowl is broken.

She is not wrong, exactly. But notice what she represents: the voice that says don’t go. The voice of reasonable caution, of hard-won disillusionment, of the person who has already made the journey and come back diminished. Vera listens to her. And then goes anyway.

This is who Vera is. This is, arguably, who she has to be.

What to watch for as you keep reading

Light spoilers: This section hints at what happens later in the novel. Skip it if you want to meet the story fresh.

The ivory knitting needles. Vera finds them in the sand, Miss MacIntosh’s, left behind like everything else. She keeps them. They become a kind of relic, a physical proof of a life that was real. Watch what happens to objects in this novel. Young uses them the way a poet uses images: precisely, with accumulated weight.

Vera’s fires on the beach. She lights them to signal to Miss MacIntosh, to call her back, to mark the place of loss. Fire in this novel is almost always about wanting to be seen across a great distance. Notice when it appears and who is trying to reach whom.

Iowa’s cold. When Vera remembers Miss MacIntosh’s descriptions of What Cheer (the frozen ears, the frozen horses, the frozen smoke) she is not just receiving travel information. She is receiving a portrait of a life stripped of illusion all the way down to the bone. Iowa, in this novel, is reality at its most unadorned. That is why she has to go there.

Lazarus. Young references the Biblical story of a man raised from the dead after four days in the tomb. Vera is not thinking about miracles here, she is thinking about the desire for one. About the hope that what has disappeared might come back. About the difference between resurrection and delusion. The novel will keep returning to this question.

What to hold onto

Chapter 4 can feel like a long dark passage: Vera at her lowest, pulled toward oblivion, surrounded by people and images that say give up. If you feel the weight of it, that is intentional. Young wants you in the fog with Vera.

But here is what to hold onto: Vera gets on the train. After all of it, the years of grief, the mother’s beautiful offer of oblivion, the warning from the fat soft-faced lady, she gets on the train and goes toward What Cheer, Iowa. She carries her loss with her and she keeps moving.

That is not nothing. In this novel, that is almost everything.

guide-08-the-village-at-the-end-of-the-r:
Chapter 8: The Village at the End of the Road

← Chapter 7 · Guide Home · Chapter 9 →

Research notes: Chapter 8

Characters: Beatrice Fitzgerald · Homer Capehorn · Jacqueline White · Justice O’Leary · Madge Capehorn · Miss MacIntosh · Moses Hunnecker · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Death and Mortality

Symbols: The Bus and the Journey · Twins and Doubles

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology · Descartes and Dualism · Marguerite Young on Her Craft · Plato and Platonism

Allusions: Dante · Edgar Allan Poe · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest

The bus is almost there.

After seven chapters of driving through an American Midwest that has grown increasingly strange with flooded roads, spectral doctors, the stories of Madge and the Tidings family and all the small-town dead we are nearly at the destination. Chapter 8 is the chapter of arrival, or almost-arrival. And Young, being Young, makes the approach as layered and strange as everything that came before it.

The storm intensifies. The road becomes a river. And the bus stops, briefly, at a crossroads that turns out to be one of the novel’s great symbolic intersections.

What actually happens in Chapter 8

The bus drives through a violent cloudburst: thunder, a broken windshield wiper, rain coming down like a deluge, the road nearly indistinguishable from the flooded fields around it. Vera reflects that it feels like the beginning of creation, or perhaps a farewell to the earth as she has known it.

The bus stops at a fork in the road near a graveyard hill. Old tombstones line the slope, their names worn faint. One branch of the fork leads down toward a small village. Moses describes that village as a kind of dreamland: a place where the children dance, where the young do “not grow old, where the old” never die. A land of promise through eternity.

The other side of the fork is Beatrice Fitzgerald’s house, a decrepit tin structure in a flooded yard full of mud, refuse, and wreckage. Moses stops here to change horses. And Madge and Homer argue about who Beatrice is and what she deserves.

Madge calls her the ugliest old woman for miles. A “common prostitute.” Someone who puts out her lights so no one will see her. Homer offers a different picture: a woman who works harder than anyone, who pulls a little red sled over snow with her face turning blue, who lost an eye when a boy shot her with a bow and arrow as a child, whose son, fathered, it’s rumored, by Old Doc, who never claimed him, joined the Navy and travels the world. Homer calls her “royal,” because names beginning with “Fitz” are said to trace back to royal bastard lines in England.

Moses delivers a long, dark, funny monologue about death and medical science, about how Old Doc couldn’t help Jacqueline White, about how no doctor can, about how there is no hell, no heaven, no cure, just the tide going out when it goes. And then the bus rolls into the village at night.

What Vera sees is spectral: upright houses like coffins, a pale moon like a skull, great spaces yawning between the buildings. She wonders if it is real. If any of it is. Whether she is inside a dream, or a dream within a dream.

The fork in the road

Young does not make you work hard to find the symbolism here, she places it plainly, and trusts you to feel its weight.

On one side: the graveyard, the tombstones with their fading names, the dead who have already arrived at their destination. On the other side: the village described as a land of eternal promise, where no one ages, no one dies, the children dance forever.

And right there at the junction, neither one nor the other: Beatrice Fitzgerald’s ruined house.

Beatrice is not dead, but she is not exactly thriving. She exists at the threshold between the graveyard and the village, between what the community has decided she is and what she actually is, between the two versions of her that Madge and Homer offer. She is the novel’s crossroads figure, and she is treated accordingly: as an embarrassment, a mystery, a rumor, and a person who nonetheless pulls a red sled through the snow to do other people’s laundry.

Beatrice Fitzgerald, and what the two versions of her mean

Madge’s version: an ugly old woman, socially disgraced, a prostitute, someone who hides from the world by putting out her lights.

Homer’s version: a woman of possible royal lineage, a tireless worker, someone who bore a son nobody would claim, who lost an eye to a childhood injury and never made a fuss about it, who has endured quietly in a flooded tin house while the rest of the town talked about her.

Both versions are being offered by people who know her only through gossip. Neither Madge nor Homer is her. Young never gives Beatrice a voice in this chapter and she exists entirely through what other people say about her, which is its own kind of statement.

The name Beatrice comes from the Latin for “she who makes happy” and is most famous from Dante’s Divine Comedy, where Beatrice Portinari is Dante’s guide through Paradise, a figure of divine grace, a woman so pure she was thought worthy to speak for God. Young’s Beatrice is the opposite in every external way: old, poor, scorned, living in a flooded yard. And yet Homer calls her royal. And yet she works harder than anyone. And yet her son, out at sea, still remembers her.

Young is doing what she does throughout this novel: placing the grandest possible resonance inside the smallest, most overlooked life. Beatrice Fitzgerald in her tin house is Dante’s Beatrice, reduced and enduring. The guide through paradise, standing at the crossroads, putting out her lights so nobody will see her.

Moses on death, and why it matters

Moses’s monologue in Chapter 8 is one of his longest and most philosophically direct. He is, essentially, delivering a sermon on mortality as one that strips away every comfort. No heaven. No hell. No doctor who can stop the tide when it turns. Jacqueline White is dying and the best doctor in the world couldn’t help her.

This is bleak, and Young means it to be. But notice what Moses is doing underneath the bleakness: he is grieving. His rant about Old Doc and the futility of medicine is not the speech of a man who doesn’t care. It is the speech of a man who cares enormously and has found no way to act on it. He cannot fix Jacqueline. He cannot fix Old Doc. He cannot fix Beatrice’s flooded yard. The rage is helplessness wearing a different face.

This is Moses’s consistent register throughout the novel: a man who sees everything clearly, grieves everything quietly, and expresses it all as fury.

Arriving at the village

The chapter ends with Vera’s description of the village at night, and it is one of the most carefully composed passages in these early chapters. The houses stand like coffins. The moon is pale and dented like a skull. Great spaces yawn between the buildings.

This is not welcoming. This is not the land of promise Moses described. Or perhaps it is and this is what eternal life looks like when you arrive: spectral, silent, emptied of everything ordinary.

Vera asks whether it is real or a dream. Whether the journey has been a dream within a dream, a phrase Young borrows from Edgar Allan Poe, who borrowed it from the long philosophical tradition going back to Plato and Descartes, asking whether what we perceive is ever the world itself or only our representation of it.

You have been on this bus for eight chapters. You may have started asking yourself the same question.

What to watch for as you keep reading

Light spoilers: This section hints at what happens later in the novel. Skip it if you want to meet the story fresh.

Beatrice’s son. He joined the Navy and travels the world: Singapore, Borneo, “the China Sea, the Rock of Gibraltar.” He is out there somewhere, seeing everything, the child of a woman nobody respects and a man who never claimed him. Young will not forget him. Watch for the places he travels through, they become a kind of atlas of the world beyond this narrow midwestern road.

The name Longtree appears among the tombstones on the graveyard hill. Hold onto it. It is the last name of a character who will appear much later in the novel. Young plants names in passing throughout these early chapters, not to confuse you, but because she is building a world that is already fully inhabited before the novel begins. The graveyard names are not decorative. They are a record.

“A dream within a dream.” This phrase, lifted from Poe, will echo through the rest of the novel. Young is building a question here that has no clean answer: at what point does the story we tell ourselves about reality become the only reality we have? When does the dream replace the thing it dreamed of? Vera has been asking this question about Miss MacIntosh since Chapter 1. The village ahead is going to press it further.

Light and darkness. Beatrice puts out her lights so people won’t see her. The village arrives at night, described as spectral and empty. Moses drives through a cloudburst with a broken windshield wiper. Light in this chapter is failing, intermittent, unreliable and characters’ relationships to it tell you something about their relationship to being seen.

What to hold onto

Chapter 8 can feel like a chapter of arrivals and thresholds, the fork in the road, the graveyard on one side, the dreamland village on the other, Beatrice at the crossroads, the bus rolling finally into a place that looks like death dressed up as a town.

If you feel the strangeness of it pressing in, that is exactly right. This is the edge of something. The bus has arrived, or almost arrived. But arrival in this novel does not mean resolution. It means the next question.

What Vera is searching for, Miss MacIntosh, or the truth about Miss MacIntosh, or the truth about herself, is still ahead. The village is spectral and silent. But she is still on the bus. She has not stopped looking.

Neither should you.

Chapter 28: Impalpable Butterflies

← Chapter 27 · Guide Home · Chapter 29 →

Research notes: Chapter 28

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Esther Longtree · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Mr. Weed · Peron Spitzer

Symbols: Butterflies and Moths

Philosophy: Aristotle · Marguerite Young on Her Craft · Stoicism

Allusions: Deafness and Sign Language · Exploration and the Poles · Greek Mythology · The History of Opium

Chapter 28 is the last chapter of the extended Spitzer sequence and one of the most beautiful in the novel. It does something Young has been saving: it gives Mr. Spitzer a passion. Not the silent music, not the legal errands, not the faithful evening visits. Something more intimate and more surprising: butterflies.

This is a short chapter, and the butterflies matter.

What actually happens in Chapter 28

The chapter opens with Mr. Spitzer acknowledging that he may be, even in his own awareness, nothing more than one of Catherine’s hallucinations: a bearded Russian bishop, an Antarctic mountain range in a lace cape, “the headless horseman fording a brook.” His life, except for these enchanted evenings, has “been a dark and empty plain.” It is only here, still denied and turned away, that he is renewed.

Young then gives us the thing Mr. Spitzer has given up: his butterfly collection. For years before Peron’s death, he had collected “beautiful butterflies of every coloration and kind.” Brimstone-colored ones burning like torpid flames. Bejeweled ones precious to him beyond jewels or mosaic emperors. He had maintained “a large correspondence with other meditative butterfly hunters.” He had watched the “birth of a butterfly, the first tremblings of the feeble, dew-lit wings as they unfolded”) and its death. He had observed that if one were called away at the crucial moment, one might never know whether one had seen a beginning or an end.

He has not added to his collection in many years. Many things came “to an end on the day of Peron’s devastating funeral, including, of course, his own capacious heart, the living heart, his way of life or most of it.” But sometimes, “when his memory of his brother” grows dim, he still remembers “the phenomenal world of the butterfly.” Seas of twinkling yellow flowers. “Clouds of yellow butterflies like flowers floating in the pale morning air.” The butterfly on the flower, identical to the flower, twin to twin, until the flower flew away and the winged petals remained.

Mr. Spitzer and his butterflies

The butterfly collection is not incidental. In European literary and philosophical tradition, the butterfly, the psyche in Greek, has been the symbol of the soul since antiquity. Mr. Spitzer, who collects souls for a living in the legal sense (the lost heirs, the disputed estates, the dead people’s properties) collected actual butterfly souls in glass cases with the same meditative scrupulousness. It was his version of his silent music: an attempt to pin down something ephemeral, to hold the beautiful and fleeting still long enough to study it.

The key observation is what the butterflies showed him: that if you “watched at only a certain moment, if one were suddenly called away in the midst of these proceedings, one should never know whether it was death or birth, beginning or end.” “The manifestations of birth and death were the same in this realm.” This is what first caused him to “embark upon his studies of impalpable butterflies.”

Mr. Spitzer began collecting butterflies because he could not tell whether they were dying or being born. He has spent his entire life unable to tell whether Peron’s fall was an ending or a kind of beginning. Whether his own continued existence is a life or a prolonged dying. Whether the moment he is living is the first trembling of the wings or the last. The butterfly collection was his attempt to learn to distinguish these things. He never quite learned. He gave it up when Peron died.

The contrast with Peron

Young uses this chapter to draw the sharpest contrast yet between the two brothers, and she does it through their relationship to time.

Peron cared for the actual, the present, the immediate. “The wastrel wheels of chance, the games of loaded dice, the” swift horses, the present hour that sufficed. He had “no patience to wait for the caterpillar to become the butterfly.” “He had given no thought to a future life.” The present moment was enough, or so it had seemed. Young’s qualification is quiet but exact: or so it had seemed. We know now that Peron removed his watch before jumping. Whatever he thought about the future, he thought about it enough to care for the timepiece.

“Mr. Spitzer had thought only of the impossible future.” He watched the caterpillar. He timed the butterfly’s birth. He composed music for voiceless choirs and deaf listeners. He carried “an out-dated passport for a journey he had not taken.” He is the man who waits, who watches, who outlives the moment he was prepared for.

And yet, Young plants this with precision, it is Mr. Spitzer who still occasionally remembers “the phenomenal world of the butterfly.” The living heart may have stopped on the day of Peron’s funeral. But the memory “of yellow butterflies like flowers floating in the pale morning air” is still there, when he allows himself to find it.

Why Catherine needs him

The chapter opens with a passage about why Mr. Spitzer keeps coming, and Young gives it more weight here than she has before. He finds in Catherine’s house “his only sense of his unbroken continuity in life.” No chair has changed its place for years. There are “these ethereal gleamings of gold and silver,” these intricately woven bellropes, “these candle flames reflected in dark Venetian mirrors.” The constancy of her unchanging world is, paradoxically, what makes him feel continuous.

Everything outside her room shifts and disorients him: glass walls, wrong cities, revolving doors, the dead man’s watch ticking on his wrist. In here, the same candles, the same mirrors, the same denial and the same welcome. He is renewed by her obtuse faith that he will always return. She denies his reality and she counts on it simultaneously. Both are necessary to him.

And he still remembers her as she was in his youth. He comes each evening to see a woman who has not moved in decades, a woman who is preserved by opium and darkness and the unchanged arrangement of her furniture. For a man whose own life stopped when his brother died, she is the only continuity he has.

What to watch for as you keep reading

Light spoilers: This section hints at what happens later in the novel. Skip it if you want to meet the story fresh.

After Chapter 28, the novel leaves the breakfast table and the coastal house and begins its great expansion into the wider world. You will meet Esther Longtree, Cousin Hannah, Titus Bonebreaker, the hangman Mr. Weed, the featherweight champion, many others. Young has spent twenty-eight chapters building you a set of lenses: Miss MacIntosh’s insistence on the real, Catherine’s faith in the unreal, Mr. Spitzer’s inability to tell the difference. Every new character will be refracted through these lenses.

The butterfly as a symbol of the soul, the psyche, will keep reappearing throughout the novel. Young uses it the way she uses most of her symbols: repeatedly, lightly, from different angles. When you see a butterfly in the chapters ahead, it carries the weight of what Mr. Spitzer learned watching them: that at a certain moment, you cannot tell birth from death, beginning from ending, the first trembling from the last.

Young uses the phrase the living heart to mark exactly what Peron’s death took from Mr. Spitzer: not his life, which continues, but the living part of his heart, its capacity for passion and pursuit. The butterfly collection was the living heart’s expression. The silent music, the legal errands, the faithful evening visits; these are what the surviving heart can still manage. It is not nothing. But it is not the living heart.

guide-41-let-me-out-of-my-ear:
Chapter 41: Let Me Out of My Ear

← Chapter 40 · Guide Home · Chapter 42 →

Research notes: Chapter 41

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Peron Spitzer · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Identity and the Self · Music, Sound, and Silence

Symbols: Silence and Deafness

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft · Phenomenology

Allusions: American Writers · Fairy Tales and Folklore · The History of Opium · Women's Suffrage

Catherine Cartwheel is everywhere and nowhere. She controls the tides. She is a great engineer, a mathematical genius, a builder of cities and bridges across impossible distances. She walks naked through warm opalescent blizzards. She rides night trains through the Gobi Desert. She raises the spectral dead. She counts pearls that are worlds.

She cannot walk.

Chapter 41 is the chapter where Young holds these two facts side by side without resolving them, the boundless interior empire and the body that has not left the bed, and asks you to feel the full weight of both simultaneously. Catherine is the most powerful person in the novel and the most confined. Her omnipotence is entirely imaginary and entirely real. It is the only kind she has, and she has made it vast.

What actually happens in Chapter 41

Vera describes her mother's condition with a precision that has accumulated over forty chapters into something close to grief. Catherine believes there is only an infinitesimal difference, a hair's breadth, between life and death. Her spirit moves outside her body regularly; multiple selves depart and may not return, and one of them, she suspects, may be immortal and lost somewhere she cannot retrieve it.

The house shifts around her. Furniture migrates. Mirrors hang lopsided. Windows look out on different seas depending on the hour. Objects appear without explanation: riding gloves, feather fans, footprints in rooms where no one has walked. Invisible guests come and go. The house is not a building; it is Catherine's mind given architecture, and it follows the same laws her mind follows, which are not the laws of physics.

Mr. Spitzer (his full name given here as Joachim, after his dead twin Peron) makes his complaint explicit in this chapter: Catherine has never seen him as a unique individual. If she had, he says, he would have known his own identity. This is one of the saddest lines in the novel. He has been waiting, all his life in this house, for her to see him clearly enough that he could see himself. She never has. She has been too busy being everywhere else.

And Catherine, when she considers Cousin Hannah, the suffrage captain who lived with a clear goal and died having stuck to it, does not envy her. This, too, lands. After everything: the admiration, the guilt, the long meditation on Hannah's life across a dozen chapters, Catherine does not want what Hannah had. The single coherent purpose, the life organized toward one legible end. She does not want to be that clear.

Lost inside the ear

The chapter's strangest and most resonant image is one Catherine offers of herself: she is lost inside her own ear.

Young treats the ear as a labyrinth: a vast continent of passages and echoes, a doorway to the soul through which she entered and cannot find her way back out. She pleads to be let out of her ear. She has been wandering its corridors, hearing the accumulated sounds of her life reverberating in the chambers, unable to locate the exit.

The ear as a labyrinth is anatomically suggestive: the inner ear is literally labyrinthine, a coiled structure of canals and chambers whose malfunction produces vertigo, the sense that the world is spinning without cause. But Young is reaching for something beyond anatomy. The ear is where sound becomes experience, where the external world crosses into the interior. To be lost inside your own ear is to be trapped in the act of receiving: to be unable to stop hearing everything, to be made entirely of the world's noise with no way to stand outside it.

Catherine has been in this condition for the entire novel. Chapter 41 finally gives it a name.

The omnipotent invalid

Young is doing something very deliberate with Catherine's claimed powers. She controls winds, tides, stars. She is a great engineer, a mathematical genius. She constructs bridges and cities. She raises the dead.

These claims, offered within a chapter that also establishes that she cannot walk and that others perceive her life as one long absence, are not simply the grandiosity of a disordered mind. Young takes them seriously as a description of what imagination actually is: a power genuinely exercised, genuinely creative, genuinely world-making, but exercised in a space that does not intersect with the space where other people live.

The novel has been asking, since its first chapter, about the relationship between what is real and what is imagined. Chapter 41 gives you the extreme version of that question in the person of Catherine: a woman whose inner life is so vast and so detailed and so genuinely felt that it constitutes a complete world, and whose outer life has contracted to a bed and a room and the sound of invisible servants moving through an infinite house. Which is more real? Young will not choose. But she will not let you dismiss either.

Mr. Spitzer and the looking-glass self

The complaint Mr. Spitzer makes in Chapter 41 (that Catherine has never seen him as a unique individual, and that this failure has cost him his identity) draws on what the sociologist Charles Horton Cooley called the looking-glass self: the theory that we develop our sense of who we are by observing how others perceive us, by reading ourselves in the mirror of other people's responses.

If the mirror is Catherine, Mr. Spitzer has been looking into a glass that shows him everything except himself. She looks through him toward the dead, toward Cousin Hannah, toward her own innumerable interior selves. He is present in the room and invisible in her perception, and after years of this (decades, perhaps) he has begun to wonder whether he exists at all.

This is one of Young's quietest and most devastating insights in the novel: that the loneliness of being unseen by the person you love is not simply emotional pain. It is an ontological problem. You need to be seen to know that you are there. Mr. Spitzer, who has been a second remove from life since his twin died, has been trying to use Catherine's gaze to confirm his own existence. She has never given him that. She has been too busy looking at the dead.

Catherine and Cousin Hannah: the final accounting

Here, forty-one chapters in, is where we get it plainly: Catherine does not envy Cousin Hannah.

Think about what this means in the context of everything that has come before. The novel has spent enormous space on Cousin Hannah: her strength, her campaigns, her magnificent refusals, her secret wish for the domestic life she publicly rejected, her death into permanence. Catherine has held her as a measure, a plumb line, a rebuke. And now, given the chance to say whether she would trade, she declines.

She does not envy a life organized around suffrage and then ended. She does not envy the clarity. She does not envy the coherence. And the title Young gives Hannah here, the patriarchal suffrage captain, is itself a small, sharp irony: a suffragette who operated within the structure of authority she was fighting, who had to make herself legible to the systems she wanted to change. Catherine has never tried to be legible to anything. She has slipped all the way out of legibility into pure interior, and she would not go back.

This is not an endorsement of Catherine's choice. But it is Young's refusal, one more time, to make the novel's verdict simple.

If she woke up, she would rapidly age

The note tucked into To All My Darlings about this passage is one of the novel's stranger keys: the suggestion that if Catherine really woke up, she would rapidly age and die.

Young is drawing on a deep vein of folk and fairy tale logic here: the enchanted sleeper whose suspension in dream is also a suspension of time, whose waking would mean catching up with all the years the dream held at bay. Sleeping Beauty reversed: not waiting to be woken into life but held in the dream to avoid the life that would kill her. Catherine's horizontal state is not only illness and addiction. It is, in the logic of the novel's symbolic world, a spell. The opium and the dreams are keeping her alive by keeping her out of time.

Miss MacIntosh tried to wake her. Miss MacIntosh is gone. The spell continues.

Sunt lacrimae rerum

Young drops a line of Virgil into Chapter 41: sunt lacrimae rerum, which translates as there are tears in things, or life is tragic. It comes from the Aeneid, where Aeneas, exiled from Troy and newly arrived in Carthage, sees paintings depicting the fall of his city and weeps, and then reflects that even in this foreign place, suffering is known, tears are known, the world mourns what is lost.

This is the emotional key to the chapter. Behind the omnipotence and the labyrinthine ear and the invisible guests and the shifting windows, behind all the magnificent excess of Catherine's interior life, there are tears in things. The absence of sorrow, Catherine reflects, is itself a sorrow. The inability to feel what should be felt is another kind of loss, added to all the others.

She counts her pearls, which are worlds. She loses count. She begins again.

What to hold onto

Chapter 41 is the fullest portrait the novel has given us of Catherine as she actually is, stripped of the mythology Young has been carefully building and reduced, or elevated, to a woman in a bed who is also, simultaneously, everywhere.

What to carry out of this chapter: the ear as labyrinth, and the plea to be let out of it. Mr. Spitzer's need to be seen, and Catherine's inability to see him. The fact that Catherine, given the choice, would not trade her boundless and ungovernable interior life for Cousin Hannah's focused and purposeful one. And underneath all of it, sounding like a bell struck once and still resonating: there are tears in things. The most spectacular consciousness in the novel knows this. It does not make her well. But it makes her true.
