guide-17-she-was-bald:
Chapter 17: She Was Bald

← Chapter 16 · Guide Home · Chapter 18 →

Research notes: Chapter 17

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Falada · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: The Search for Meaning

Symbols: Hair, Wig, and Baldness

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Genesis · The Bible · The History of Opium

Here it is. The moment the novel has been building toward since Chapter 13.

Take your time with this chapter. It is not long, but it is dense with feeling, and Young is doing several things at once. She is delivering the revelation. She is showing you Vera’s wild, fourteen-year-old response to it. She is asking one of the novel’s deepest questions. And she is being very careful, in a way that first-time readers sometimes miss, not to tell you what the revelation means. That is your work. She is only showing you what Vera saw.

What actually happens in Chapter 17

Miss MacIntosh is standing by the window in the moonlight. The curtain that had concealed her head blows aside. And Vera sees that Miss MacIntosh is bald. Completely, coldly, stonily bald, her skull gleaming like an ivory ball, not one hair on her head.

Vera recognizes her instantly (by the broken nose, by something definite in her manner) and in the same moment refuses to accept what she sees. She cycles through shock, resistance, a wild kind of triumph, and then screams: “Miss MacIntosh, you are a man!”

Miss MacIntosh moves toward her. What follows is a fight, or what feels like a fight, or what Vera experiences as a fight, or what may be partly hallucination and partly real. Blows are exchanged. Vera is knocked down, lifted up, laid on the bed. She passes in and out of consciousness. She wonders if her assailant might be a sandbag dummy come to life, or a Roman gladiator, or the angel with whom Jacob wrestled at Peniel. The chapter ends the morning after. Vera’s braids are neatly plaited down her back. There are no scratches on her cheeks except perhaps those made by leafless branches.

The baldness

Young has seeded this moment across many chapters. The mirrors Miss MacIntosh avoids. The umbrella carried indoors. The windows thrown open in winter. The bundling up in hot weather. The bedroom bare of almost everything except a broken-down brass bed and a dressing table with three mirrors she never looks into. The one face, not two, she told Vera: one for the world, one for heaven. Only one.

All of it resolves here. Miss MacIntosh wore a wig. The practical, plain, red-haired woman who denied the existence of everything unreal was herself, at the most literal level, constructed. Her most visible feature (the red hair that gleams throughout the novel, that Vera describes as tawny as an August sunset) was not hers. The anchor of reality was wearing a disguise.

Young does not editorialize. She gives you the bald skull in the moonlight and lets you sit with it.

What Vera screams, and what it means

“Miss MacIntosh, you are a man!”

This is a fourteen-year-old's conclusion, delivered in shock and triumph and cruelty, and Young is careful to frame it that way. Vera herself immediately notes that had she stopped to think, she might have been silent. The laugh that follows is the laugh of someone who has been proved right about something she didn’t know she suspected.

What has Vera actually seen? A bald woman. A woman who is physically powerful (the amazing biceps, the muscular expansion, the skillful boxing) in ways that Vera associates with men. A woman who never looked in mirrors, never discussed her own body, kept herself covered even in summer, whose bedroom was bare of all the feminine furnishings of the house. A woman who Vera had privately imagined with a red, curled mustache, whom she had assigned the role of the bridegroom in her secret dream.

Young is writing in 1965, and she is writing about something the culture of 1965 had almost no language for. She does not give it language here either. She gives you Vera’s scream, and Vera’s scream is wrong in the way that a fourteen-year-old’s first understanding of something vast is always wrong: partially true, coarsely framed, certain in the way only the newly shocked can be certain.

What Young seems to be showing us is a person who built an entire identity (the practical nursemaid, the anchor of reality, the one who denied the existence of dreams) over something hidden so deep and so carefully that even the wig was part of the architecture. Miss MacIntosh’s insistence on the real, on the ordinary, on the surface of things: perhaps it was the most necessary insistence of her life. Perhaps the denial of illusion was her only way of surviving in a world that had no place for what she was.

The fight

The physical struggle between Vera and Miss MacIntosh is one of the strangest and most extraordinary passages in the novel, and Young is very careful about what she does and doesn’t tell us.

Did it really happen? Young gives you both possibilities simultaneously. Vera’s consciousness divides: “one who fought, one who lay still and watched it all.” The blows are described in the precise vocabulary of boxing (the left jab, the straight right, the rabbit punch, the Sunday punch) which is also Miss MacIntosh’s own vocabulary, the language of the sandbag dummy she had Vera box as a cure for daydreaming. Vera wonders if her assailant might actually be that sandbag dummy come to life. The next morning there are no scratches except possibly from branches.

Young is not being evasive. She is being accurate. This is what it feels like to have the foundation of your reality knocked out from under you: you experience it as a physical assault, as something that hits you, lifts you, lays you out. The body registers what the mind cannot yet process. Whether Vera’s knuckles actually connected with Miss MacIntosh’s face or whether the encounter happened partly in the space between shock and unconsciousness is a question Young leaves open on purpose.

What is not in question: Vera is changed. The sandbag dummy: the one Miss MacIntosh told her to box when she was being foolish, when she was daydreaming, when she needed to restore her circulation and her waning common sense: has fought back.

The question at the chapter’s center

In the middle of the fight, falling, Vera asks the question that is the novel’s central question, delivered here in its most compressed form:

“What shall we do when, fleeing from illusion, we are confronted by illusion? When falling from illusion, we fall into illusion?”

This is the question Young quoted in the novel’s front matter as the book’s guiding proposition, and here it arrives not as a philosophical abstraction but as something Vera is screaming into the dark while a bald woman in a moonlit bedroom deals her the rabbit punch.

Vera fled Catherine’s world of opium and hallucination by holding onto Miss MacIntosh. Miss MacIntosh was the real. And Miss MacIntosh, it turns out, was also a construction. The escape from illusion led into illusion. The anchor was wearing a wig. Where, then, is the real world?

Young does not answer. She gives you Vera’s braids neatly plaited down her back the next morning, and leafless branches that might account for the marks on her cheeks, and she moves on.

What to watch for as you keep reading

Light spoilers: This section hints at what happens later in the novel. Skip it if you want to meet the story fresh.

Miss MacIntosh does not disappear from the novel after this. She will be present throughout, in memory, in the search that drives Vera’s journey, in every question the novel asks about what is real and who gets to decide. But she will never again be what she was before this night. Vera will spend the rest of the novel understanding what she saw.

The morning after detail matters enormously. Vera’s braids are exactly as they should be. There are no marks. Life continues on its surface exactly as before. This is Young’s version of the morning after the impossible crossing of Lake Constance: you survived, you are here, everything looks the same. And nothing will ever be the same.

The sandbag dummy has been fighting back since Chapter 1. Notice, from here forward, every time Miss MacIntosh’s boxing lessons appear in Vera’s memory. The dummy was always a stand-in for something. Now you know what.

guide-37-the-land-of-infinite-greyness:
Chapter 37: The Land of Infinite Greyness

← Chapter 36 · Guide Home · Chapter 38 →

Research notes: Chapter 37

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Order, Chaos, and Discipline · The Search for Meaning

Philosophy: Aristotle · Descartes and Dualism · Epicureanism · Marguerite Young on Her Craft · Time, Physics, and Chaos Theory · Wittgenstein

Allusions: Suicide in History and Literature · The History of Opium

You are in the deep water now.

Chapter 37 is the chapter where Young asks her hardest question, and asks it without flinching: what if nothing holds? What if the self is not a fixed point but a series of dissolving reflections? What if the boundary between dreaming and waking, living and dying, is not a line at all but a fog that has no far edge?

If you find this chapter disorienting, that is the correct response. You are not supposed to find your footing here. The chapter's architecture is designed to make the ground shift beneath you, to show you what it feels like to live inside Catherine Cartwheel's consciousness: a place where the ceiling is the floor, trees grow with their roots in the sky, and the dreamer cannot be identified because everyone in the dream might be the dreamer.

Stay with it. Young is not being difficult for the sake of difficulty. She is being precise.

What actually happens in Chapter 37

We are still in Catherine's household. Vera narrates her mother's state of mind, and that state of mind is the chapter's entire landscape. Catherine is lying horizontal, sedated with opium, caught in the half-country between waking and sleep. She is not fully in the world. She is not fully out of it. She is, as she has been for most of the novel, in between.

The chapter opens with a vision (mirrors drifting, clocks striking hours that make no sense, dolphins behaving unexpectedly) and then poses its governing question: but who was the dreamer? Not which character is dreaming. Who, among all of them, is the one whose dream contains the others?

Young never answers this. The question is the point.

Catherine and Mr. Spitzer circle the question of death and order. Catherine declares, in one of the chapter's sharpest lines, that order is a mad man's dream, a suicidal plan that leaves out the irrational elements. Mr. Spitzer, ever the pessimist, contributes his own anguished uncertainty. And beneath all of it, Catherine's refusal (persistent, desperate, and entirely human) to surrender to what the chapter calls the land of infinite greyness.

Cousin Hannah enters the chapter as she always enters: in memory, in force, in the contrast she makes with everyone still breathing. Her death is final. Young is clear about this. She will not return. She has been throttled by death, and what follows that throttling is, the novel admits for the first time without evasion, silence.

The land of infinite greyness

This phrase is the chapter's center of gravity, and you should know what Young means by it.

The land of infinite greyness is not heaven or hell. It is not a destination at all. It is the oblivion Catherine fears above everything else: the place where there is no memory, no ego, no voice, no image. Not darkness: darkness has a quality, a texture, a presence. Greyness is the absence of contrast itself. It is the condition in which nothing can be distinguished from anything else, in which selfhood simply stops having meaning.

Catherine's entire life (the opium, the bed, the household ruled by dream and illusion) can be read as a strategy for avoiding this. She stays horizontal because to stand up would be to move toward a world that might eventually require her to arrive at the grey. She drowns herself in hallucination because hallucination, however unreliable, is still vivid. It still has color. It still has her in it.

This is not weakness, though it might look like it. It is a woman clinging to the fact of her own experience with both hands, refusing to let go even when everything around her has dissolved. Young has considerable sympathy for this refusal. So should you.

The philosophy of reversals

Young fills Chapter 37 with images of inversion: the ceiling as the mirroring floor, trees “growing with their roots in the clouded sky” and their branches underground, night as day, dawn as twilight, beginning as end. His end was his beginning. His sun was his moon.

This is not surrealism for its own sake. Young is working through a genuine philosophical position: that the opposites we rely on to organize reality (life and death, real and dream, self and other) are not opposites at all. They are the same thing seen from different angles. The boundary between them is a convention, a useful fiction, and in Chapter 37, that fiction is wearing very thin.

The image that captures this best is the one Young gives Vera: “love might wear the face of death, the grinning skull, as death might wear the face of love.” This is not a gothic decoration. It is an observation about the structure of deep attachment: that to love something completely is already to have anticipated its loss, and that loss, when it comes, carries the ghost of everything the love was. The two faces belong to the same person. They always did.

Catherine, order, and the irrational

Pay attention to Catherine's declaration that order is a mad man's dream.

She means this seriously, and so does Young. The desire for order (for things to proceed logically, to have causes that explain their effects, to have selves that remain continuous from moment to moment) is, in this novel's cosmology, a form of willful delusion. The universe does not operate this way. People do not operate this way. A plan that omits the irrational elements is not a plan; it is a wish wearing the clothes of a plan.

Mr. Spitzer, who is conservative and precise and trusts only what he can verify, is the character who most wants order. And Mr. Spitzer is the character most obviously undone by his inability to achieve it: hearing sounds a minute late, existing at a second remove from life, never arriving in the present moment that order requires.

Catherine, who has given herself over entirely to the irrational, is paradoxically more honest about reality's actual texture. She is not sane, in any conventional sense. But she is not lying to herself about what the world is like. There is something Young wants you to notice here, about which of these two failures is the more truthful one.

Cousin Hannah, and the finality that Catherine refuses

Young does something in Chapter 37 that she has been careful not to do before: she allows the word finality.

Cousin Hannah is gone. Not transformed, not traveling through posthumous geographies, not available to be found if Catherine looks in the right direction. Gone. Throttled by death. The echoes of her voice, her boots, her campaigns for the vote, her defiance of every seraglio and hierarchy that tried to contain her; they fade in this chapter into something that Young's prose rarely permits: silence.

Mr. Spitzer contributes the chapter's closing image. After the last requiem, he says, there is nothing left but the hearing of silence. Not the silence itself: the hearing of it. The consciousness that remains after the music stops, registering the absence of what was there before.

This is as close as the novel comes to a conventional statement about grief. It doesn't stay there long. But it is there, and it is real, and you should let it land before the next chapter carries you somewhere else.

The question the chapter leaves open

Who was the dreamer?

Young raises this at the chapter's opening and does not close it. Here are the possibilities the novel has been building toward: Catherine is the dreamer and everyone else is her dream. Vera is the dreamer and Catherine is her dream. The novel itself is the dreamer and both of them are its dream. Or, and this is the version that keeps the question alive longest, there is no individual dreamer, only the dream, and what we call selfhood is the dream's way of pretending it has a source.

You don't need to resolve this. Young didn't resolve it. But hold the question as you read forward. It will keep mattering.

What to hold onto

If Chapter 37 feels like it is asking too much of you, come back to this: Catherine is afraid of disappearing. Not dying, exactly; she is already half-dead, and she has made her peace with the border region. What she is afraid of is the grey. The absolute colorless erasure of everything that makes her her.

That fear is entirely recognizable. You don't need opium dreams or a household ruled by hallucination to understand it. It is the fear that runs under all the novel's philosophical circling, all its reversals and cosmic imagery and blurred borders between waking and sleep. Strip everything else away and what remains is a woman who does not want to stop being.

Young treats this with complete seriousness. It is not a small thing to want to exist. It is not a small thing to refuse the grey. Even when the refusal looks like madness, even when it keeps you horizontal in a bed for decades, even when it means you cannot go out to meet the people who love you because going out would mean acknowledging a world that will eventually take you under, even then, the refusal is human, and it counts for something.

guide-22-all-in-all-there-is-no-news-tod:
Chapter 22: All in All, There Is No News Today That Was Not Yesterday

← Chapter 21 · Guide Home · Chapter 23 →

Research notes: Chapter 22

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Peron Spitzer · Vera Cartwheel

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology · Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Exploration and the Poles · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest

Chapter 22 is the first full ordinary day after the revelation, and Young gives it to us in full. It is long and dense and wanders and doubles back on itself, and it does this deliberately: this is what it feels like to sit at a breakfast table with someone and try to act as if nothing has changed.

If you find yourself lulled by the rhythm of Miss MacIntosh’s newspaper recitations, her geography questions, her complaints about dust and housekeeping, that’s fine. That lulling is the point. And then the chapter breaks the lull, twice, with sentences so precise they stop you cold. Stay alert for those. The chapter earns them.

What actually happens in Chapter 22

It is the morning after. Vera sits at an unexpectedly festive breakfast table (the good Haviland china, a silver service, white roses in a hammered silver bowl) while Miss MacIntosh reads the morning newspaper aloud. Her wig is in place. The pact is holding.

Miss MacIntosh reads about Brazilian rebellions, Wall Street, Norwegian storms, horse races, cock fights, needle-workers’ strikes, the price of eggs, divorces, the deposition of Balkan kings. She asks Vera geography questions, creation questions, sports questions. She complains about the housekeeping, the dust, the unmatched socks, the angels in the hallways who need dusting. She talks about the shipwrecks off their coast, the things the sea keeps bringing in. She considers buying shirts from a flooded Boston basement.

Vera, watching the brick-red top of Miss MacIntosh’s wig above the newspaper, seething with a nameless irritation, asks twice about the party dress. Miss MacIntosh deflects both times with more questions.

Near the end, almost in passing, Miss MacIntosh says: “baldness is no cure for sorrow, my dear.” And later: sometimes “the inner man was all that counted—not the outer man, this poor visage and mockery of himself.”

The chapter ends with Vera wondering: was she all others?

The festive table

Young opens the chapter with something small and strange: the breakfast table is decorated as if for a special occasion. The Haviland china, the silver service, the hammered silver bowl of white cabbage roses. They never use these things. They are usually down to the broken crockery bought cheap at a fire sale.

Miss MacIntosh apparently does not notice. She sees only the old oilcloth of What Cheer, Iowa. She has “no eye for artificial beauty or anything” man has made, and she says so, as she always has.

But someone set that table. Someone brought out the good china and the silver bowl and the roses. Young does not say who. The chapter simply begins with Vera sitting before this festive spread, and Miss MacIntosh behind her newspaper, and the morning light on the red wig, and the pact quietly in effect. The table is the only acknowledgment either of them will make of what the night was.

Miss MacIntosh in full voice

Chapter 22 gives us the longest and most expansive portrait of Miss MacIntosh’s newspaper monologue in the novel. It goes on for most of the chapter, weaving between world affairs and geography lessons and housekeeping complaints and sports scores and creation theology, and it is worth reading as a performance, because it is one.

Miss MacIntosh is talking to keep the silence away. The questions come faster than usual, the complaints more insistent, the newspaper’s contents more varied. She reads about cock fights and dog races and steeplechases and shipwrecks and divorces and the price of tallow. She moves from God’s creation of the firmament on Monday to the greatest pearl ever grown to whether Siberian wheat can grow in the Dakotas to the rules of bowling, all without pausing.

Vera notices that their schedule seems “somewhat off course, perhaps by a point or two.” She notices that Miss MacIntosh has eaten before her, which has never happened before. She notices the rasping of Miss MacIntosh’s breathing, the difficulty of it, like a drowning man who sees a wall of water approaching.

Underneath the performance, Vera is listening for something else. And then, late in the chapter, Miss MacIntosh gives it to her: “baldness is no cure for sorrow, my dear.” “Spinach is the best bone-builder. We all require a little salt in our blood—but not much. Death has a salty taste—the same as tears. We came from the sea.”

It is the only direct acknowledgment either of them makes. It is delivered in the voice of a proverb, almost sleepily, “like the continuation of a dream.” And then the newspaper goes back up.

The inner man

Near the chapter’s end, Miss MacIntosh says something she has perhaps been building toward all morning: sometimes “the inner man was all that counted—not the outer man, this poor visage and mockery of himself, so every image should fade.” “The inner man might be an altogether different being from the poor outer man. Only the poorest fool would judge by the appearances, by the outer visage and these poor clothes a man must wear, these mortal garments so ill-fitting and not his choice at all.”

She applies this to herself immediately: “sometimes she thought the inner man was battered, too, impaired by much hard usage. Her soul itself must have, she laughed, this broken crown, these weak and watering eyes,” “this poor, broken nose, these false teeth, these knotted veins, the large hands, the large, long feet.”

This is Miss MacIntosh doing what she does in the night chapters, but in daylight, in her normal voice, filtered through the grammar of proverb and common sense. She is telling Vera, and telling herself, that the mortal garments are not the person. That the outer visage is not the choice. That the inner man and the outer man may be different beings.

It is as close as she will come, in daylight, to speaking directly about what Vera saw.

Was she all others?

The chapter’s final question (was she all others?) is one of the novel’s most compressed. Vera asks it without elaboration and Young does not answer it.

What does it mean? Vera has been watching Miss MacIntosh perform normalcy all morning, and she has been watching the performance crack at the edges: the festive table no one acknowledges, the schedule off course, the breathing like a drowning man, the line about baldness and sorrow. And she wonders: is Miss MacIntosh’s ordinariness not just a performance but a kind of universality? Is she, in her stripping bare, not one particular strange person but somehow everyone, every person carrying a secret the outer self works all day to conceal?

Young has been building to this question since Chapter 18, when Vera thought about the secret man hidden in the woman, and the secret woman hidden in the man. Now, at the breakfast table, in the ordinary morning light, the question arrives in its simplest form: was she all others? It opens outward into the rest of the novel, which will keep asking it, of character after character, in different rooms and different weathers.

What to watch for as you keep reading

Light spoilers: This section hints at what happens later in the novel. Skip it if you want to meet the story fresh.

The novel is about to expand. We are ten chapters away from the end of Volume One, and Young is going to begin widening the frame: bringing in other characters, other histories, other geographies. The Miss MacIntosh sequence has been the novel’s anchor. Everything that comes next will be understood against it.

Miss MacIntosh’s mention of her dead love, the silver-dollar watch “given to her by her dead love,” arrives so quietly in this chapter that you might miss it. It is the only time in the novel that this love is named directly. Young does not elaborate. She does not need to. She has already told you everything about Miss MacIntosh’s inner life. This is just one more detail of the inventory, placed without emphasis, in a sentence about how Miss MacIntosh is protected by her lack of pretence.

The shipwrecks off the coast accumulate in this chapter into a significant catalogue: “the captain’s table set for two” or three, the stringless harp washed up, the cardinal’s hat, the twelve rosaries strewn from here to the lighthouse. These are the things the sea keeps returning. Young is building the novel’s coastal mythology: a world where what has been lost keeps coming back, changed, barnacled, still recognizable.

guide-26-the-department-of-the-dead:
Chapter 26: The Department of the Dead

← Chapter 25 · Guide Home · Chapter 27 →

Research notes: Chapter 26

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Peron Spitzer · Vera Cartwheel

Symbols: Moon and Stars · Twins and Doubles

Philosophy: Hinduism · Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Music and Composers

Chapter 26 continues where Chapter 25 left off (still inside Mr. Spitzer’s world, still at the breakfast table in Vera’s mind) but it shifts the angle. Where Chapter 25 gave us the key events of Mr. Spitzer’s life, Chapter 26 gives us his philosophy. His professional world. His theory of heaven. His understanding of what separated him from his brother, and what that separation cost.

It is a long, ruminative chapter, and it rewards slow reading. Young is building Mr. Spitzer into one of literature’s great portraits of a certain kind of man: the faithful one, the patient one, the one who stayed.

What actually happens in Chapter 26

Vera continues her meditation on Mr. Spitzer. Young takes us into his professional life first: he is a lawyer of the dead, his department “the hidden past, the wills and deeds” and dusty archives, the secret drawers of old houses haunted by those who are gone. He has spent his career locating lost heirs, heirs who turned out to be heiresses, heiresses who turned out to be heirs, wandering derelicts shipwrecked on other coasts, people who could not be found or would not be.

We get the story of the two Boston spinsters, each the reincarnation of Cleopatra, each with a Sphinx in her garden, both clients of Mr. Spitzer, one dying and leaving everything to her “Siamese cats, with the provision that” Mr. Spitzer supervise the arrangement. The cats, having nine lives each, appear to be flourishing indefinitely.

Then the chapter turns to the question at its center: if Peron had lived and Joachim had died, what would Peron have done? Would he have come faithfully to Catherine’s bedside, year after year, bringing winter violets plucked from secret places? Would he have finished Mr. Spitzer’s unwritten music, even adding a hesitant note? Young’s answer, delivered through Mr. Spitzer’s own understanding, is no. Peron would have swept Catherine into the living sunlight, that “magnificent moment of defeat, even though the living sunlight might be” her death.

The chapter ends with Mr. Spitzer contemplating the lower world, the one that lies just under the surface of life, acknowledging “that in order to reach the upper world, one must first travel through the lower world, visiting all streets, lanes, alleys, and the journey might be endless.”

The department of the dead

Mr. Spitzer’s professional world is a perfect mirror of his personal one. He works in the hidden past: the wills departments, the dusty archives, the pigeon-holes and secret drawers of dead people’s houses. He is always entering old houses, “searching through old secretaries in dim, ghost-haunted rooms where he had felt that at any minute the living might appear.”

He has come to doubt that there should be any real heirs whatsoever, any real property handed down in golden perpetuity. There have been so many lost heirs, secret sons and daughters, heirs who turned out to be heiresses. He has come to feel that even “our features, our hair, our eyes, our” hands; these properties too have been confused in metamorphic storms, and are “very, very makeshift, very uncertain, the properties” of a dream.

This is Mr. Spitzer’s professional conclusion applied to the question of identity itself. We do not even inherit our own faces reliably. The self we believe we own is as disputed as any estate, as likely to have a secret claimant, as likely to turn out to belong to someone else.

The two Cleopatras

The story of the two Boston spinsters (rival beauties in youth, rival reincarnations of Cleopatra in old age, rival Sphinxes in adjacent gardens, both clients of Mr. Spitzer) is one of the novel’s great small comic passages, and Young gives it more space than you might expect.

The one who dies leaves everything “to her innumerable Siamese cats, with the provision that” Mr. Spitzer supervise the arrangement for as long as the cats live. The cats, he notes with a sighing remark, each having nine lives, appear to have suffered no deaths whatsoever. He last visited several years ago. The old caretaker had since died and been replaced. The cats were flourishing. A cat walked up and down the piano keys playing a tune from “one of the more obscure eighteenth-century musical composers.” This is Young doing what she does so well: a miniature of the novel’s larger concerns (contested identity, immortal pretensions, the faithful guardian of someone else’s estate, the music that continues without human hand) compressed into a cat story told to amuse a dying woman. Mr. Spitzer is not sure he is not teasing Catherine. He is probably not sure he is not teasing himself.

What Peron would not have done

The chapter’s most important passage is Mr. Spitzer’s extended meditation on what Peron would have done if their positions had been reversed: if Joachim had died and Peron had lived.

He “would not have sat up all night with any corpse.” He would not have brought winter violets from secret places in the whirling snow. He would not have endured Catherine’s pleasure in ignoring him. He would not have finished Mr. Spitzer’s music or attempted to add a hesitant note. He would have swept Catherine out into the living sunlight: one magnificent moment, even if it killed her beauty, even if it killed her.

Peron cared only, it seemed, for old hags, Mr. Spitzer says with painful candor. Catherine holds it against Mr. Spitzer that he did not rescue her. She yearns “for her escape from this illness.” She would rather have been swept away and died in the sunlight than preserved indefinitely in the dark.

And Mr. Spitzer knows this. He has always known it. He is the wrong brother. His faithfulness, his patience, his undying love; these are exactly what she does not want. She wanted Peron’s impetuous, careless, finite love. She got Joachim’s infinite, cautious, immortal devotion instead.

This is the novel’s most heartbreaking statement of the Spitzer situation: the faithful one is faithful precisely because he cannot give her what she wants, and the one who could give it to her is dead.

Mr. Spitzer’s heaven

Near the chapter’s center, Mr. Spitzer offers his vision of what heaven should be, and it is completely in character: perfect oblivion. All souls equal when all are dead. “No rivalry between person and person, none between the divisions of self. There should be no immortal derangement as of this present world with all its stains and cracks and flaws.” Complete forgetting, not Catherine’s complete memory, but the opposite: the silence that “requires neither instruments nor voices, the heavenly harmonies forever fixed above the floods of” dark time.

Mr. Spitzer wants, above all things, to stop being himself. Or rather, to stop being both of them. He believes in “no hell more than this present individual life already” affords. He is not sure that heaven is a place so much as the state when we “have completely forgotten who we were, when we” have been united “as equal brothers, one and the same.”

One and the same. The twin who was always divided wanting, at the last, to be undivided. Not Joachim, not Peron, not the one who survived and not the one who fell. Just the silence where neither needs to be remembered.

What to watch for as you keep reading

Light spoilers: This section hints at what happens later in the novel. Skip it if you want to meet the story fresh.

Mr. Spitzer’s meditation on the lower world at the chapter’s end (the one that lies under this world, “close to the surface of life,” full of thieves and painted street women and dark lanes) points forward to chapters that will take us into exactly those places. The novel is about to widen its geography considerably. Remember that Mr. Spitzer believes you must travel the lower world to reach the upper one, and that the journey might be endless.

Catherine’s desire to be swept into the living sunlight, even at the cost of her life, is one of the novel’s great withheld actions. Mr. Spitzer cannot do it. He knows only the darkness and the night. This is what he means when he says his love is immortal: it is precisely because it cannot be enacted in mortal life. The love that can be acted on belongs to Peron. The love that survives Peron belongs to Joachim. Neither is what Catherine wants.

The lost heirs Mr. Spitzer spends his professional life locating (heirs who turned out to be heiresses, heiresses who turned out to be heirs, people who inherited features that were not quite theirs) are a professional echo of the Miss MacIntosh sequence. Everyone in this novel is the uncertain heir of a self they did not fully choose. Mr. Spitzer, whose profession is to locate such people and establish their claims, cannot quite locate himself.

  • The phrase heirs
guide-57-the-tailors-bill:
Chapter 57: The Tailor's Bill

← Chapter 56 · Guide Home · Chapter 58 →

Research notes: Chapter 57

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer · The Great Tailor

Themes: Dreams and Imagination

Symbols: Cards, Games, and Chance · Roses and Flowers

Philosophy: Freud and Jung

Allusions: Gambling and Playing Cards · Suicide in History and Literature · The Civil War

The bill keeps arriving.

Mr. Spitzer has paid for Peron's funeral: paid for everything, the suit, the ceremony, the violinist with the empty sleeve, the track bugler. He went bankrupt paying. And yet the tailor's bill keeps coming in the mail, addressed to him, demanding payment for the black funeral suit he had made for his brother. He does not know who the tailor is. He does not know where the shop is. The address on the bill does not correspond to any street in any city directory he can find.

He begins to look for the tailor. He follows directions in his dreams. He follows directions in waking life. The directions contradict each other. The shop is not there. The street is not there. The bill keeps arriving.

Chapter 57 is a chapter about the debt that cannot be settled: the grief that sends bills long after you believe you have finished paying. It is also, in its dreamlike wandering through Boston's libraries and streets, one of the most quietly comic chapters in the novel: Mr. Spitzer seeking an address that does not exist, consulting city directories, encountering a Confederate soldier who insists the South won the Civil War, trying to find the soul's permanent address in a library reading room full of people who are equally lost.

What actually happens in Chapter 57

Mr. Spitzer receives the tailor's bill and attempts to pay it. The tailor is the Great Tailor (possibly the mad tailor from Chapter 56, the one who stitched him with basting threads) and the bill is for the black funeral suit worn by Peron at his burial. Joachim is the executor. He arranged the funeral. He paid for it. The bill should not be arriving. And yet it arrives, persistently, from an address that cannot be found in any directory.

He searches. He tries following the dream logic of the directions, knowing that dreams operate by opposites (dark is fair, life is death, man is woman) and allowing for reversals and contradictions in his navigation. He visits the library reading room, that last open space where anyone can stay as long as they cause no distraction, and consults city directories and old newspapers looking for the tailor's address. He finds nothing. The shop does not exist in the records. It may never have existed.

In the library he encounters the characters who populate the margins of sanity: a Confederate soldier who is certain the South won the Civil War and is living accordingly; others engaged in debates about the soul's existence and the nature of immortality. Mr. Spitzer wants to join the debate about immortality (he has opinions, he has longing for certainty) but holds back, afraid of rejection, afraid of being seen as the kind of person who takes these questions seriously in a reading room.

He leaves without finding the address. He watches the twilight sky, sees clouds shaped like skulls and hands and birds. He imagines a rose named after both brothers (red and white together, the two colors of the two men) and in his mind the rose changes from red to white. The bill will come again tomorrow.

The debt that cannot be settled

Young's choice of a tailor's bill as the emblem of Joachim's unpayable debt is characteristically precise. A tailor's bill is a mundane, legible, legal thing: it specifies what was made, for whom, at what price. It is a record. It is a claim. It demands response. And it keeps arriving, the same bill, addressed correctly, from an address that does not exist.

The debt the bill represents is not financial. Joachim paid the financial debt; he paid everything, until there was nothing left, until the twin house was gone. The debt the bill represents is the debt of grief, which is not a financial category and does not respond to payment. You cannot settle grief by paying the bill. The bill comes back. The executor who arranged the perfect funeral, who placed the poker chips in the grave and gave away the wardrobe and kept only his own threadbare suit; he cannot close the estate because the estate is not a legal matter. The estate is the relationship. The estate is what remains when a person is gone and the person who loved them is still here.

The tailor is the mad creator from Chapter 56: the one who stitched existence from the wrong materials with the wrong stitches. Now the creator is sending bills for his work. Mr. Spitzer, who was made by this creator, is being asked to pay for his own construction. The bill is for the suit that dressed the dead man. The dead man was his brother. He was his brother. The bill is for himself.

Dreams operating by opposites

Mr. Spitzer knows that dreams operate by opposites. Dark is fair. Life is death. Man is woman. North is south. The place you are looking for is never where the dream says it is; it is where the dream says the opposite thing is.

This is an old understanding, present in folk traditions and in Freudian dream interpretation: the manifest content of a dream (what it seems to be about) is the reversed or disguised form of its latent content (what it is actually about). Young gives Mr. Spitzer this knowledge and lets him apply it practically: he consciously allows for reversals when following the dream directions to the tailor's shop, accounting for the logic of the opposite, navigating by a map that he knows to be a mirror image of the territory.

And still he cannot find it. Because the tailor's shop is not in the dream's logic or in its reversal. It is in neither city and neither street. It is the shop that should exist but does not: the place where the unpayable debt was contracted, which has no address because its address is wherever Mr. Spitzer is. The debt travels with him. The bill arrives wherever he lives. The shop cannot be found because it is not a place.

The library and its inhabitants

Young's library reading room is one of the novel's most humanely observed spaces: the last open place where anyone can stay as long as they cause no distraction, where the homeless and the lost and the obsessively researching all share the same long tables and the same institutional light. Mr. Spitzer fits here. He is all three: homeless in the sense of having lost the twin house, lost in the sense of having lost his sense of which world he inhabits, obsessively researching the tailor's address.

The Confederate soldier who insists the South won the Civil War is the chapter's clearest figure of the alternative history that becomes necessary when the actual history is unbearable. He is living in a world where the outcome was different. His flags, his certainty, his reconstruction of events; these are not madness exactly. They are the logical endpoint of refusing to accept a historical fact. If you refuse the fact long enough and thoroughly enough, you need to build a replacement. The replacement is internally consistent. It just does not correspond to what happened.

Mr. Spitzer, listening, recognizes the man. Not because he agrees with him about the Civil War but because he understands the impulse: the construction of an alternative to the unbearable fact. The unbearable fact for Mr. Spitzer is Peron's death. He has not built an alternative history (he is too rigorous for that, too committed to the truth even when the truth fails him) but he understands the need that generates one. The Confederate soldier and the executor of Peron's estate are the same species of mourner. One built a new history. The other keeps paying a bill that cannot be paid.

The rose named after both brothers

Near the chapter's close, Mr. Spitzer imagines a rose: red and white together, named after himself and Peron, the two brothers unified in a single flower. The rose, in his imagining, changes from red to white. Peron's color bleeding into Joachim's. The reckless twin becoming the cautious one, or the cautious one absorbing the reckless one, or the two finally becoming inseparable in the form that horticulture occasionally achieves and that grief sometimes produces in the living who remain.

A rose named after both brothers would be a memorial. It would be the thing that persists when the persons have not: the named variety that growers catalog, that appears in gardens, that is neither fully red nor fully white but something that contains both. Young gives Mr. Spitzer this vision at twilight, in the sky full of skull-shaped clouds, as the practical search for the tailor's address has definitively failed. He cannot find the shop. He can imagine the rose. Both things are true, and the rose is the more useful of the two.

The penny with heads on both sides

Mr. Spitzer carries a penny with heads on both sides: a gambler's coin, a cheat's coin, a coin that cannot lose because it has no tails. He carries this talisman of certainty in an uncertain world: a coin that always comes up heads, that refuses the possibility of loss built into every genuine coin.

This is Joachim carrying Peron's logic. The two-headed penny is the gambler's tool, not the cautious lawyer's. It belongs to the world of the speakeasies and the racetracks and the 110-round boxing matches that Joachim has absorbed from his dead brother. He carries it as a charm against the chance that keeps arriving anyway: the chance that the tailor's bill brings in the mail, that the twin house's loss brought, that Peron's apparent suicide brought. The two-headed penny cannot prevent these things. It simply refuses, in its small stubborn way, to have a losing side.

What to hold onto

Chapter 57 is a chapter of futile searching and unexpected company. The tailor's shop does not exist. The Confederate soldier has built a better country in his mind. The debate about the soul's existence continues in the reading room without Mr. Spitzer's contribution, because he is afraid they will not want it.

What to carry forward: the bill that keeps arriving as grief's specific texture, the way it comes back with the same address, the same claim, the same demand for settlement that cannot be met. The dream logic that operates by opposites, which Mr. Spitzer knows and accounts for and which still does not lead him to the shop. The rose named after both brothers, changing from red to white in the twilight sky. And the two-headed penny: the inherited gambler's charm in the cautious lawyer's pocket, heads on both sides, refusing to lose.

For the Curious

  • On the Boston Public Library as sanctuary
  • On the Confederate soldier and alternative history
  • On the Automat
  • On dream logic and the logic of the opposite
guide-00-introduction:
A Guide to Reading Miss MacIntosh, My Darling

Guide Home · Chapter 1 →

There is a novel that most American readers have never heard of. It was published in 1965, took eighteen years to write, and runs to 1,198 pages. Anaïs Nin called it the American Ulysses. The New York Times compared it to Joyce and Melville. It has been out of print more often than in it, praised extravagantly and then quietly set aside, the culture moving on the way cultures do when something is too large and too strange to metabolize quickly.

The novel is Miss MacIntosh, My Darling by Marguerite Young.

If you have never heard of it, that is not a failure of your attention. It is a fact about what American literary culture decided to remember and what it decided to let go quiet. This guide is, among other things, an argument that the letting-go was a mistake.

Here is what I want you to know before you begin: this novel is not difficult the way difficult books are difficult. It does not punish you for arriving without a degree or a reading list. What it asks for is a different kind of attention than most novels ask for, one that is slower and more patient, willing to let a sentence return and find it changed, willing to stay with an image longer than feels strictly necessary, willing to trust that the not-resolving is the point rather than a problem.

This guide is here to help you do exactly that.

Each chapter entry covers the characters, what happens, the themes and symbols worth tracking, the passages worth pausing on, and a section called "For the Curious" that opens outward into context and connection. You can read it alongside the novel, chapter by chapter, or come to it after a section when you need someone to say: yes, that happened, here is what I think it means.

You do not need to have read anything else first. You do not need to have any prior knowledge of Young or her world. You need only the willingness to give a very large and very alive book the kind of attention it was made for.

Young spent eighteen years writing this novel because the novel took that long. It is worth the time it takes. I have read it five times and it keeps changing on me, which is the mark of the thing that knows more than you do and is patient enough to wait for you to catch up.

Come in. The door is open.
guide-81-the-little-toy-salesman:
Chapter 81: The Little Toy Salesman

← Chapter 80 · Guide Home · Chapter 82 →

Content note: The Esther Longtree chapters (72 to 81) deal with stillbirth and pregnancy loss, rape, infanticide, racist violence including lynching, and cruelty to children.

Research notes: Chapter 81

Characters: Esther Longtree · Vera Cartwheel · Walter

Themes: Guilt, Innocence, and Justice · Love · Motherhood, Pregnancy, and Birth · Time

Symbols: Clouds and Storms · Pregnancy, Birth, and Children · Snow, Ice, and Winter · The Sea and Water

Philosophy: Freud and Jung · Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Gambling and Playing Cards · Judaism · Revelation and the Apocalypse · Suicide in History and Literature

Chapter 81 is the penultimate chapter of Esther’s sequence, and it turns outward. After ten chapters deep inside Esther’s interior life (her stillborn, her dying fathers, her mud baby, her detective, her twin, her silver spoon, her Walter) Young now introduces a figure from outside: a man who comes into the Greasy Spoon and tells Esther the story of the end of the world.

He is the little toy salesman. He is small and childlike, bandy-legged, tearless, with only three teeth and pale blue eyes and patchy hair. He drinks milk from a baby bottle. He carries rubber ducks and teddy bears and a baby bottle as his samples. His mother was a world-famous beauty and spy. His father was a windowpeeper. He was a bottle baby, never held at the breast, never given the ordinary comforts of being someone’s child.

He is the lone survivor of a great storm at sea that drowned everyone else: “the captain, the crew, the women, the children,” and in Young’s cosmic rendering, even the moon and the stars. He sat in a rubber life boat while the world ended. And now he sits at Esther’s counter, and he whispers to her that there will be a great war, and the bad men will “blow up the world some day of calm just for fun.”

Esther is considering marrying him. Not for love. For legality. She wants a legal father for the little shadow boxer. He is the best available option.

What Actually Happens

The little toy salesman comes into the Greasy Spoon. He drinks milk from his baby bottle. He flirts with Esther in a childlike way. He cannot see that she is enormously pregnant. He cannot see much of anything clearly anymore.

He tells her his story, or she reconstructs it: the chapter blurs the line between what he says and what she knows about him. His mother was a spy, beautiful and famous, the Mata Hari type. His father was a windowpeeper. He was a bottle baby from the start, a child who had no one to hold him. He sold toys: rubber ducks, teddy bears, baby bottles. He was at sea when the storm came.

The storm is described with apocalyptic imagery: “a wild, raging storm between the cracking Poles,” “the sea rising in billows to the dark heavens,” the moon and stars falling like sparks and rain of blood. The captain, old and German, goes down with the ship conducting, bright with rage and love. The passengers (conceited, snobbish, oblivious to their doom) drown. The women take the lifeboats. The men jump into the sea. Everyone drowns except the little toy salesman, who survives by accident in a rubber life boat, upheld by swollen bladders and heaving breasts of ocean, not because he wanted to live but because the sea didn’t take him.

The calm after the storm is worse than the storm. He drifts. Around him: floating debris, bloated bodies, the detritus of a world that has ended. A great white shark circles him, which he initially mistakes for a woman. And there is a dead child’s ivory-colored hand, “always uplifted from the slow, swelling waters,” wearing a gold ring like his own. The hand tugs at him. The hand clings to him. He cannot make it let go.

He loses his memory. His taste buds. His tear ducts. His reason. He washes ashore in America: the shore littered with purple oyster sponges, crab shells, jellyfish like glass, bones of dead fish, “little carcasses of other little children,” “playing cards, old junk, rubber tires, birth control devices.” America as the shore where everything washes up and nothing resolves.

He is pursued by a great white shark on the return journey. He survives. He is smaller now than he was before; he tells Esther he is getting smaller all the time. Until the world blows up, things will be this way, so he doesn’t mind too much if the world blows up. When there is a new creation, he can begin again. He whispers into her ear: there will be a great war. The bad men will “blow up the world some day of calm just for fun.” Everything will be poisoned and disappear forever. Music, stars, fireflies, everything.

Esther listens. She remains forever pregnant with her dreams. She wonders who fathered the little shadow boxer. The dead loved the dead, she thinks, and perhaps that is how the world goes on.

The Little Toy Salesman

He is a figure of compressed ironies. He sells toys (the objects of childhood, of innocence, of the uncorrupted) but he was himself never given childhood. He was a bottle baby, never held, never nursed. His mother was a spy; his father a peeping tom. He carries rubber ducks as his samples. He drinks from a baby bottle. He is, in some sense, still the baby he was never allowed to be.

He is also, in his survival, a figure of survivor’s guilt taken to its extreme. He did not want to live, or so it seems: the sea simply didn’t take him when it took everyone else. And Esther, who has presided over so much death, who has carried so many dead children, calls him a murderer for not drowning with the rest. This is the logic of guilt applied in reverse: to survive when others die is to have killed them by surviving. The little toy salesman did not drown “the captain, the crew, the women, the children.” He simply continued to exist when they did not. This is what Esther cannot forgive.

And yet she is considering marrying him. For legality. For the little shadow boxer. She will teach him how to behave, she thinks: how to have normal emotional responses, how to live a normal life. She is maternal toward him in the way she is maternal toward everyone: she sees someone who never had what they needed and wants to provide it. He is her most peculiar candidate. He is also her most available one.

The Storm as Apocalypse

Young does not write the shipwreck realistically. She writes it cosmically. The moon and stars fall. The Poles crack. The sea rises to the dark heavens hammering. The captain conducts as he goes down: “a golden flood of music more beautiful than Bach, Beethoven, or Brahms.” A black mourning band spans the sky from horizon to horizon.

This is not merely a ship sinking. It is the end of the world, rendered in miniature aboard a single vessel. And the little toy salesman sits in his rubber life boat and watches it happen and survives. He is the one person who witnesses the world ending and then washes ashore in America to report it. Young is writing during the nuclear age: the Cold War, Mutually Assured Destruction, the knowledge that the bad men could “blow up the world some day of calm just for fun.” The little toy salesman’s prophecy, whispered into Esther’s ear at the counter of the Greasy Spoon, is the period’s ambient terror made personal: everything will be poisoned and disappear forever. Music, stars, fireflies. To All My Darlings connects his description of the burning sunlight blackening his skin to a nuclear blast, and his account of the world turning into salt or smoke to the specific imagery of Hiroshima. He has already seen the end. He came back to report it.

The German captain who goes down with the ship, bright with rage and love, conducting music as the ship sinks: To All My Darlings connects this to Hans Langsdorff, the German captain who scuttled the Admiral Graf Spee in 1939 to save his crew and then died by suicide to prove he had acted with honor. And to Gustav Schroeder, the German captain who tried to bring 937 Jewish refugees from Germany to Cuba in 1939, was turned away by Cuba, Canada, and the United States, and was forced to return his passengers to Europe. Both men (captains who prioritized their passengers over orders, who faced impossible situations with what honor was available to them) are present in the captain who goes down with the ship conducting.

The Dead Child’s Hand

Throughout the long calm after the storm, one image persists: a dead child’s ivory-colored hand, “always uplifted from the slow, swelling waters,” wearing a gold ring like his own. The hand tugs at him. The hand clings to him. He cannot make it let go and he cannot look away from it. This is the chapter’s most quietly devastating image, and its resonance with Esther’s own history makes it exact. She has buried children in rivers and streams and tree stumps. She has carried children who were never born. She has pressed her thumb to still a birth cry. The dead child’s hand reaching up from the water is what she has been reaching toward and what has been reaching toward her for ten chapters. The ring the dead child wears is like his own. This is the detail that locks the image in place: the hand is recognizable, is kin, wears what he wears. The dead child could be him: the child he never was, the childhood he was never given, the self that the storm should have taken. He survived but his self did not, or not entirely. What clings to him from the water is the part of himself that was supposed to be innocent and was not protected.

America’s Shore

The shore where the little toy salesman washes up is littered: purple oyster sponges, crab shells, jellyfish like glass, bones of dead fish, “little carcasses of other little children,” “playing cards, old junk, rubber tires, birth control devices.” Young’s inventory of what America receives when the world ends and washes ashore is not flattering. It is the accumulated detritus of a civilization: the natural and the manufactured, the chance and the controlled, the bones and the prophylactics.

The birth control devices on the shore are not accidental. Young has spent ten chapters in the world before birth control was legal: Esther’s everlasting pregnancy, her stillborn, her Walter, all of it occurring in a legal and social landscape where women had no effective recourse. The devices washing up on the shore with the dead fish and the old junk and the little carcasses of children: this is where reproductive control ends up in the American accounting, thrown away, found on shores, mixed with everything else that did not get used or was used wrong or was too late.

The End of the World as Prologue

The little toy salesman’s prophecy is that there will be a great war and the bad men will blow up the world. This comes one chapter before Chapter 82, which is the last chapter of Esther’s sequence and the final chapter before the novel returns to Vera’s story. Young is positioning the apocalyptic vision here deliberately: the end of the world is not the end of Esther. She remains forever pregnant with her dreams. The little shadow boxer is still there, still fighting. The dead loved the dead, she thinks, and perhaps that is how the world goes on.

This is not optimism exactly; it is something stranger and more durable. Esther has witnessed so much death and generated so much life and lost most of what she generated. She is still here. The world may blow up on a “day of calm just for fun,” and Esther will still be at the counter of the Greasy Spoon, still swelling with the little shadow boxer, still setting out breadcrumbs for spirits, still knitting the invisible, still more hopeful now than she has ever been.

She is the survivor. Not the accidental survivor of the little toy salesman, who lived because the sea didn’t take him. Esther survives because she refuses not to.

What to Hold Onto

The little toy salesman: bottle baby, spy’s son, peeper’s boy, seller of rubber ducks, survivor of the end of the world, three teeth, tearless, getting smaller all the time.

The German captain conducting as he goes down. “A golden flood of music more beautiful than Bach, Beethoven, or Brahms.” “Bright with rage and love as if he had realized his strength, at last, his weakness.”

The dead child’s ivory-colored hand, “always uplifted from the slow, swelling waters,” wearing a gold ring like his own. The hand that clings and will not let go.

America’s shore: purple oyster sponges, rubber tires, playing cards, birth control devices, “little carcasses of other little children.” The whisper into Esther’s ear: there will be a great war. The bad men will “blow up the world some day of calm just for fun.” Everything will be poisoned and disappear forever.

And Esther, forever pregnant with her dreams. “The dead loved the dead, and” perhaps that is how the world goes on.

guide-43-the-dance-of-death:
Chapter 43: The Dance of Death

← Chapter 42 · Guide Home · Chapter 44 →

Research notes: Chapter 43

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer

Themes: Death and Mortality · Decay and Ruin · Love · The Search for Meaning

Symbols: Clothing, Hats, and Skirts

Philosophy: Freud and Jung · Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Greek Mythology · Women's Suffrage

If Chapter 42 brought you to the room where Cousin Hannah is dying, Chapter 43 keeps you there. It does not let you leave. And what it shows you, hour by hour in the long unraveling of a great life, is that dying is not peaceful and it is not dignified and it does not sort itself into the clean stages of acceptance that we would prefer it to have. Cousin Hannah is screaming. She is delirious. She is asking, in the chaos of her final consciousness, the most fundamental question available to anyone: “am I the anvil which is struck or the hammer which strikes?”

Young gives her this question at the end of everything. It is the question of agency itself, of whether a life is something that happens to you or something you do. And the answer, as Cousin Hannah has always known and the delirium now makes impossible to avoid, is that it is both. It was always both. The hammer and the anvil are the same person. The blow falls and is received simultaneously. This is what a life is.

What actually happens in Chapter 43

We remain at Cousin Hannah's deathbed. Mr. Spitzer maintains his vigil, wearing “his high silk hat and black” cape: the full formal costume of mourning, as if sartorial correctness can hold something steady in a room where everything else is dissolving. He is not sure, he tells us, whether he himself is living or dead. The boundary he has been approaching all his life has become, at this bedside, genuinely unclear.

Cousin Hannah's dying is not a drift toward peace. It is a storm. It is a dance: Young uses the medieval term danse macabre, the dance of death, where Death comes for everyone regardless of rank or accomplishment and leads them in an inescapable procession. But Cousin Hannah does not go quietly. She screams through dreamlike, surreal landscapes: deserts, mountains, clouds, ice. She speaks to Caesar, to a blacksmith, to a golden archer, to the blackamoor she calls her love.

She asks for a mirror and cannot find one. She clings to the vanity of silken skirts and great parasols fringed with gold: beauty, adornment, the things she spent her public life refusing to care about, surfacing now in the delirium as desires she had apparently always had. She is fragile as all mortal things, weeping because “a wandering snowflake touched her hand.”

The chapter closes without closing. Mr. Spitzer keeps watch. The lid (is it lowering or raising?) remains ambiguous. Death is not peace. Death is the great crucible where opposites meet. Death is “that which blew us all along.”

The hammer and the anvil

Cousin Hannah's question (“am I the anvil which is struck or the hammer which strikes?”) is Chapter 43's philosophical center, and it arrives exactly when it should: at the moment when every certainty she built her life around is dissolving.

In Isaiah 41, the craftsmen are encouraged when the hammer and the anvil work together to make an object. In ancient Greece, Hephaestus (the disabled god, the one thrown from Olympus) was the divine blacksmith, the maker of things, the one who transformed raw material into form by striking it repeatedly. The hammer creates. The anvil receives. Both are necessary. Neither the hammer alone nor the anvil alone makes anything.

Cousin Hannah spent her life as a hammer. She struck. She forged. She beat the soft metal of convention into new shapes through sheer relentless force. And now, in the delirium, she discovers that she was also always the anvil: the thing being shaped by forces larger than herself, by the history she was born into and the body she inhabited and the losses she sustained and the love she never quite allowed herself to have. She struck and was struck. She made and was made.

Young does not offer this as a diminishment. The hammer and the anvil together make the thing. Both matter. The question is not which one you are (you are both, always) but whether you can hold that knowledge at the end, when the forge is cooling and the work is done and the hands are finally still.

The blackamoor and the love she called her own

In her delirium, Cousin Hannah calls repeatedly for a blackamoor: a figure she addresses as her love. This is one of the chapter's most charged and carefully handled passages.

The term blackamoor, as Young uses it, carries the weight of the novel's long engagement with Cousin Hannah's identity as Hannah in Boston, Hamid in the East, Al Hamid. The figure she loves in the delirium is associated with the same crossing of cultural and religious borders that has defined her life: the Moors, the Islamic world she moved through, the identities she acquired in her travels and may have briefly inhabited. The blackamoor is both a specific person she loved (perhaps the secret lover, perhaps the caliph who supported her cause) and something larger: the part of the world she went toward when she went away from New England, the self she became when she left the self she was supposed to be.

To All My Darlings notes that the black moor becomes a black rooster in the chapter's imagery. The rooster crows at dawn, at the threshold between darkness and light, between death and whatever comes after. Cousin Hannah's love, in her dying hours, is also the thing that might guide her through.

Mr. Spitzer's hat, and the question of being alive

Mr. Spitzer arrives at this deathbed in “his high silk hat and black” cape, and the image is so precisely chosen that it deserves a moment.

The high silk hat was a clear symbol of authority, wealth, and prestige: the hat of capitalism, of enterprise, of Victorian and Edwardian gravitas. It represents everything Mr. Spitzer has always valued: appearance, dignity, the surface held intact. He wears it to a deathbed where the dying woman is screaming. The hat cannot help him. It cannot help her. But he puts it on anyway because it is the only armor he knows how to wear.

He is not sure, in this chapter, whether he himself is living or dead. He reflects “that the dead cast no vote—and” uses this, along with his general policy of non-competitive withdrawal from life, as a reason for his habitual abstention. He is a man so thoroughly at a second remove from experience that the question of whether he is technically alive has become genuinely open to him.

What he does, in this ambiguous state, is watch. He keeps vigil. He is present for Cousin Hannah's dying in a way he has not been present for much else in his life, and Young seems to regard this (the faithful keeping of watch, even when you cannot help, even when you are not sure you exist) as a form of love available even to the most constrained and self-evacuated people.

The dance of death

The danse macabre, the dance of death, was a medieval and Renaissance artistic tradition depicting Death as a skeletal figure leading a procession of people from all walks of life: pope and peasant, king and merchant, young and old, the great and the forgotten. Death does not care about rank. Everyone dances.

Young's invocation of this tradition for Cousin Hannah's dying is pointed. Here is a great captain, a warrior, a woman who faced greater dangers than most men knew, and Death comes for her the same way it comes for everyone: uninvited, insistent, indifferent to her accomplishments. The dance is compulsory. The music does not stop for negotiations.

And yet the dance, in Cousin Hannah's case, is her own. She does not go gently. Her dying has the quality of her living: excessive, stormy, full of voices and visions and the unfinished business of a life that was never quite finished with anything. She dances with Caesar. She dances with the blacksmith and the golden archer. She dances with the love she never quite named. She takes the hand of Death in the costume of the blackamoor and goes, not quietly, but going.

The lid: lowering or raising

Young gives Mr. Spitzer a question he cannot answer: is the lid lowering or raising?

He is watching something close, and he does not know whether it is closing a life or opening something else. The coffin lid lowering is the most legible image of finality available to the culture Young is writing in. But the chapter has been insisting, since its first pages, that death is not finality; it is transformation, it is storm, it is a great crucible where opposites meet. Death is “that which blew us all along.”

The eternalism note in To All My Darlings is relevant here: some philosophers of time argue that all moments exist equally, that the past is not gone but simply located elsewhere in the block universe, that the dead are not absent but present at a different coordinate. Cousin Hannah's dying is, in this framework, not a disappearance but a permanent fixture of what exists. The moment of her death exists as surely as the moment of her first campaign speech, her first border crossing, the first time she “played a mean game of cards” and won.

The lid. Is it lowering or raising? Mr. Spitzer does not know. Young does not tell him. The question stays open like a door that swings both ways.

Vanity at the end

One of Chapter 43's most humanizing and unexpected details is the vanity that surfaces in Cousin Hannah's delirium: the silken skirts, the great parasols fringed with gold, the desire for a mirror. She has spent decades refusing these things: refusing the feminine decorations of her era, refusing self-pity, refusing the courtly graces and intimate revelations. And here they all are, returning in the delirium like furniture she thought she'd given away and finds packed in a box at the back of the attic.

Young is not making a point about the shallowness of her convictions. She is making a point about the depth of what we suppress. The things we refuse do not disappear. They wait. The suffrage captain who had no time for silken skirts had, apparently, wanted them all along, or wanted something they represent: beauty, attention, the pleasure of being seen as a woman rather than only as a warrior. The delirium gives her back what life refused.

She “wept if a wandering snowflake touched her hand.” She was fragile as all mortal things. She always was. She simply did not allow the evidence to be entered into the record.

What to hold onto

Chapter 43 is the deathbed chapter, and it is long in the way that deaths are long, and difficult in the way that watching is difficult. What Young asks of you here is patience and presence: the same things Mr. Spitzer is managing, with his silk hat and his uncertain existence, at the side of the bed.

The hammer and the anvil. The snowflake and the wept-for hand. The blackamoor and the love she called her own. The lid that might be lowering or raising. These are what Cousin Hannah takes with her into whatever comes next, if anything comes next, if the lid is raising, if the storm she is dancing through leads somewhere rather than ending.

Young does not promise it leads somewhere. But she does not promise it doesn't. The question is the chapter. The question is the novel. The question is what we have been asking together since page one.
