guide-70-mrs-hogden:
Chapter 70: Mrs. Hogden

← Chapter 69 · Guide Home · Chapter 71 →

Research notes: Chapter 70

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer · Lisa Lunde · Miss MacIntosh · Mrs. Hogden · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Duality and Doubles

Symbols: The House · Twins and Doubles

Philosophy: Aristotle · Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Exploration and the Poles · The History of Opium

Things have quieted down at the Tavern. Vera is in her room at last, in the dark, in something approaching stillness. And so she tells you about Mrs. Hogden.

Mrs. Hogden is one of the strangest and most indelible figures in a novel full of them. She arrives in this chapter as a memory: Vera’s memory of a woman who appeared at her mother Catherine’s house years ago, burdened with packages and birdcages and Javanese temple bells and at least four coats of graduated sizes, smelling of over-ripe apples, her hair plastered and bleached into curls, her face blandly expressionless except for an aggressive chin and abnormally large, unfocused eyes. She had sold her Dutch windmill home to take up a position as Catherine’s arithmetic teacher, based on a letter of employment that Catherine denied ever writing.

Catherine did not want her. The household did not want her. Mrs. Hogden, with the serenity of a woman who has never once in her life accepted evidence that contradicted her expectations, stayed for months. Here is what you need to know before we begin: Vera tells you explicitly, partway through, that she never actually saw Mrs. Hogden. That Mrs. Hogden is “a trick of my imagination”: a substitute for the dream life she wanted, a figure her mind invented or elaborated or projected. “My mind’s betrayal of my mind,” she calls her.

So: everything that follows may be true. Everything that follows may be Vera’s dreaming. Young will not choose between these options for you. Neither should you choose for yourself. Hold both.

What Actually Happens

Mrs. Hogden (or Logden, or Fogden, or Dogden, or Bogden; the name slips) arrives at Catherine’s house in a two-door Ford, piled to the ceiling with her worldly goods. She has sold her home. She has come to be Catherine’s companion and arithmetic teacher. She has a letter of employment. Catherine has never heard of her.

Lisa Lunde, who replaced Vera as Catherine’s companion when Vera escaped, sizes Mrs. Hogden up immediately as a very dubious character, possibly a shoplifter. Catherine calls her “an impostor, a liar, a day-dreamer, a thief.” But Mrs. Hogden knows intimate details of Catherine’s inner life: details only Catherine could have shared, about whales swimming into her bedroom and the head of Alcibiades in the drainpipe. Catherine denies having shared them. She claims she has “gone to Boston to see a podiatrist,” or to the North Pole. She refuses to come out. Mrs. Hogden is installed in the deserted playroom: closed for years, filled with forgotten objects, umbrellas and old trunks and the detritus of a household that has been dreaming too long to keep things clean. She is given a hospital cot too short and too narrow. She does not complain. She has her chess set, her radio, her birdcage, her Javanese temple bells. She talks to herself and answers her own questions. She plays chess alone, crying over victories and defeats with equal feeling. She argues with radio announcers. She teaches arithmetic to no one, using wormy apples and later buttons as counters, because “two and two always making four” is, she believes, a triumph of reason.

Catherine’s revulsion grows. She cannot tolerate a rival invalid. She orders Mr. Spitzer, her lawyer, to remove Mrs. Hogden by any means necessary. He arranges a generous financial settlement. Mrs. Hogden leaves.

She leaves behind, on a small three-legged blackboard in red chalk: “All a’s are b’s,” it read, “all b’s are c’s—and therefore, dear heart, all a’s are c’s. You know me.”

The playroom is closed again. No one knows where she went. No one knows where she came from. She had no relatives, no friends anyone knew of. She vanished without trace, as she had arrived: out of nowhere, into nowhere, with the serenity of someone who has always known that the universe had no particular obligation to explain itself.

Mrs. Hogden

She is both comic and tragic, which is to say she is one of Young’s most fully achieved characters. Comic: her four graduated coats, her aggressive chin bow, her empty birdcage, her argument with the radio announcer about the stock market, her chess set with an atomizer substituting for a bishop, her claim to be descended from Daniel Boone, William the Conqueror, and Alexander Graham Bell, as well as “three signers of the Declaration of Independence.” Tragic: her Dutch windmill home sold and gone, her worldly goods in a two-door Ford, her hospital cot too short and too narrow, her chess played alone with tears, her unshakeable faith that she had been invited somewhere she was not wanted.

She is described as the “least critical human being”, not as a compliment, exactly, but as a kind of stunned acknowledgment. She does not judge. She does not resist. She adjusts, permanently, to whatever temporary situation she finds herself in, and finds within it the materials for contentment. She pulls an imaginary bellrope to summon servants who do not come. She imagines social seasons in an empty playroom. She is the mistress of the house in a house that has forgotten her name.

She is also, Young suggests through the accumulation of detail, a figure for something larger: the American self-myth, the national character at its most buoyant and most deluded. She claims the founding fathers. She insists on arithmetic (two and two making four, the simplest truth, the foundation of all others) while inhabiting a world that has made no sense for decades. She collects things from everywhere (Dutch windmill, Javanese bells, ivory back-scratcher) without integrating any of them. She is “permanently adjusted to her temporary situation.” She does not hear arguments to their close, and therefore wins them all.

She is, in her way, the Anti-Miss-MacIntosh: where Miss MacIntosh was Miss Reality, Miss Plain-and-Average and Clear-Eyed, Mrs. Hogden is Miss Optimism, Miss The-Evidence-Will-Not-Discourage-Me, Miss The-Universe-Will-Accommodate-My-Expectations. They are the novel’s two poles of response to a world that does not cooperate. Miss MacIntosh’s solution was to hold to the surface of things, the facts, the cold and clear. Her solution ultimately failed her, as we will learn. Mrs. Hogden’s solution is to simply not see the contradiction. It works, in its way. She leaves, eventually, with a generous settlement and an intact worldview.

Catherine, Confronted with Her Double

This is what makes the chapter so rich and so strange: Catherine, who lives entirely inside her own hallucinations, who has taken to her bed and left it only in imagination, who has lost her mind “several times” and considers herself not responsible for her actions, Catherine finds Mrs. Hogden intolerable. She calls her “a gross, stinking parody” of her own “distended world of shimmering, loosely woven textures.”

She is right. Mrs. Hogden is a parody of Catherine: the same disconnection from reality, the same confidence in a world that doesn’t exist, but made common, made corporeal, made loud and smelling of over-ripe apples. Catherine’s madness is refined, beautiful in its way, private, the madness of a woman with expensive sheets and an opium habit and the memory of better days. Mrs. Hogden’s madness is cheerful, baggy, layered in four coats, eating wormy apples in a playroom.

What Catherine cannot forgive is the recognition. Mrs. Hogden knows things about her (the whale in the bedroom, the head of Alcibiades in the drainpipe) that only Catherine could have shared. Which means Catherine, in some moment she does not remember or refuses to admit, reached out to Mrs. Hogden. Called to her. Invited her. The letter exists. Catherine denies it. The denial is her madness and also her dignity and also her cruelty: she invited someone in and then refused to know her. She also mistakes Mrs. Hogden, at moments, for her dead Cousin Hannah. Identity is fluid in this house. Everyone substitutes for someone else.

Lisa Lunde

Lisa Lunde is Vera’s replacement: the young companion who came to take care of Catherine when Vera escaped. She is a would-be physicist working to support her own poor and mentally ill mother; she has entered one dreamhouse in order to fund her life outside it. She is sharp, skeptical, and not taken in: she sizes Mrs. Hogden up as a dubious character within minutes and never entirely revises this assessment.

But she is also, quietly, vengeful. When Catherine blames her for Mrs. Hogden’s presence and demands she get rid of her, Lisa Lunde runs back and forth between them with meaningless messages, deliberately not interpreting either one to the other, watching the situation escalate with something that functions as satisfaction. She is the trapped rationalist, the person who sees clearly and is therefore left to manage the chaos that the dreamers create, and finds her small pleasures where she can.

She will reappear later in the novel. Remember her: the woman who wanted to be a physicist and ended up carrying messages between two invalids who refused to communicate.

The Playroom

The room Mrs. Hogden is given, and Young spends time on this, is the deserted playroom: closed for years, filled with things the household no longer uses and can’t bring itself to throw away. Old trunks, umbrellas, boxes, broken objects, the accumulated sediment of a family that has been dreaming instead of living. It is a room for things that have no place and no owner, which makes it exactly right for Mrs. Hogden.

Moonlight comes in and silvers the walls. Mrs. Hogden sits under a frieze of gargoyles. The novel notes, without elaborating, that if she sat there “long enough, she would become a gargoyle herself”: stone, permanent, grotesque, part of the architecture. It is both a joke and a precise description of what happens to people who stay too long in houses that are dreaming.

The evidence she leaves behind when she finally goes: “derelict whiskey bottles, empty coat hangers, withered apple cores, broken” eggshells, dead flies, and, Vera notes specifically, an artificial eyelash. The precise inventory of a life that was here and isn’t.

The Blackboard

She leaves behind a small three-legged blackboard, the kind a child’s teacher might use. On it, in red chalk: “All a’s are b’s,” it read, “all b’s are c’s—and therefore, dear heart, all a’s are c’s. You know me.”

The logic is valid. If all a’s are b’s, and all b’s are c’s, then yes: all a’s are c’s. This is how syllogisms work. This is the foundation of reason. Two and two make four.

But “dear heart” is not logic. “You know me” is not logic. The equation ends with a personal claim (a claim of recognition, of intimacy, of being known across the gap of unreality) that the syllogism cannot support. She is saying: I am the conclusion of a chain of reasoning you have already accepted. You know me. You have always known me.

Vera cannot refute this. Neither can we. The woman who was never there has left proof of her own logic on a three-legged blackboard in a closed room. The proof is sound. The proof is absurd. Both things are true.

Vera’s Confession

Partway through this chapter, Vera tells you that she never saw Mrs. Hogden. That the whole thing (or some of it, or most of it) is a trick of her imagination. A substitute for what she actually wanted, which was a lost companion, the other half of a self that has only ever loved its own right hand.

This is one of the novel’s most important moments of self-disclosure. Vera is not a reliable narrator, not in the sense of lying, but in the sense that her consciousness is the medium through which everything is filtered, and that medium is not neutral. It is imaginative, it is obsessive, it is organized around absence. The people in this novel are sometimes real and sometimes Vera’s projections and sometimes both. Miss MacIntosh is both. Mrs. Hogden is both.

What Vera is telling you is not that Mrs. Hogden didn’t exist. She is telling you that the distinction between “real” and “imagined” has never been, for her, the distinction that matters. “There was only one definition of reality: that it was real.” “Even the unreal things were real.” Even the imagined companion is a companion. Even Mrs. Hogden, if she waddled in and out of Vera’s dreams, was there.

What to Hold Onto

Mrs. Hogden’s four graduated coats, her birdcage, her Javanese temple bells. The physical accumulation of a person who carries everything with her because she has nowhere left to put it down.

Catherine and Mrs. Hogden as mirror images: the private dreamer and the public one, the refined madness and the corpulent one, both refusing reality, neither able to bear the sight of the other.

Lisa Lunde, running between them with meaningless messages, not translating, watching the situation with quiet satisfaction. She wanted to be a physicist. She is here instead.

The blackboard: “All a’s are b’s,” it read, “all b’s are c’s—and therefore, dear heart, all a’s are c’s. You know me.”

And Vera’s confession, which is not a confession of lying but of imagination: that Mrs. Hogden is her mind’s betrayal of her mind, a substitute for what she always wanted and never found, the companion that the self invents when no real companion appears. She is looking for Miss MacIntosh. She has been, this whole novel, looking for Miss MacIntosh. What she finds instead, sometimes, is Mrs. Hogden. The next best thing. The wrong answer that has the shape of the right one.

Chapter 15: The Night of My Fourteenth Birthday

← Chapter 14 · Guide Home · Chapter 16 →

Research notes: Chapter 15

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Dreams and Imagination · Motherhood, Pregnancy, and Birth · Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos

Symbols: Pregnancy, Birth, and Children · The Sea and Water

Allusions: Deafness and Sign Language · Ecclesiastes · Gambling and Playing Cards · Revelation and the Apocalypse · The Bible

After the long, enclosed darkness of Chapter 14 (that claustrophobic bedroom, Catherine and Mr. Spitzer circling each other in the lamplight) Chapter 15 throws open a door and sends you outside.

We are back with Vera. It is still the night of her fourteenth birthday. She is standing at the sea.

This chapter is the last breath before the revelation. Something extraordinary happens at its close, and Young earns it by spending the chapter inside the particular texture of being fourteen and alive and standing at the edge of the Atlantic in the dark, feeling like the universe has just become available to you.

What actually happens in Chapter 15

Vera has wandered from the garden to the shore. The night is wild: fog, a skull-white moon, black roaring water, phosphorescent surf. She runs into the waves. She is soaked, her hair streaked with salt. She doesn’t care. She laughs aloud.

In this state of exhilaration, her mind turns to Miss MacIntosh, but differently than before. For the first time in the novel, Vera turns a critical eye on her. She thinks about what Miss MacIntosh doesn’t know: the undertow, the waywardness of water, the deeper things of life. She thinks about Miss MacIntosh’s strange habits: the umbrella carried indoors, the windows flung open in winter, the bare cold bedroom with its broken-down brass bed. She replays the long lecture Miss MacIntosh delivered all day on her birthday: proverbs about death, about marriage, about disorder and men and the proper life of an industrious ant.

And then the sea performs something extraordinary. Young gives us a passage of apocalyptic beauty: the water turning to glass, the clouds pregnant with impossible colors, the harpers harping on the sea at the end of time. It lasts only a moment. Then the waters go black again.

The chapter ends with a blind sheep dog barking at the waves.

Vera’s revolt

This is the first time we’ve heard Vera think critically about Miss MacIntosh rather than yearningly. It is important, and it feels true to being fourteen.

What Vera notices, standing in the surf on her birthday night, is that Miss MacIntosh’s practical wisdom has limits. She couldn’t swim a stroke. She avoided the greatest waves. “She would have been dragged down at the first blow by her rainproof” and her sea boots and all her needles and pins. All that famous common sense, and she couldn’t breast the roaring tide.

There is something fond in this critique, even as it sharpens into something harder: “Miss MacIntosh knew less than I did, hers being” “a deadness, a dullness, a coldness of heart.” That is a fourteen-year-old's verdict, delivered with a fourteen-year-old's certainty, standing wet in the ocean at midnight feeling immortal. Young knows exactly what she’s doing. This is not the novel’s judgment. It is Vera’s judgment on this particular night, in this particular mood, before she knows what she is about to find out.

The revolt is the preparation for the grief.

Miss MacIntosh’s birthday lecture

The chapter gives us, in Vera’s memory, the full length of Miss MacIntosh’s speech on the day of her fourteenth birthday. It is extraordinary. It goes on all day, through breakfast and dinner and in between, and it is almost entirely about death and marriage in that order, as if they were the same subject.

“Death, like our mother and our father,” “is an old harpoonist who will capture the swimmer in narrow streams.” “Our cradle stands in the grave.” Death “loves a young maid and an old man. Death loves a shining mark.”

On marriage: all women should certainly marry, but no man. “Perhaps no man should marry woman.” Before marriage, keep your eyes open; after marriage, “keep them half shut for fear of what” you might see. True marriages are “few and far between due to the sins of our first parents and the high cost of living.”

And woven through: wheat markets, bowling scores, black hens laying white eggs, the sinking of the Titanic, Ecclesiastes, the Farmer’s Almanac, Benjamin Franklin, John Bunyan. Miss MacIntosh does not separate the sacred and the practical. They are the same shelf.

What makes this extraordinary is that Young has given us, in this extended monologue, Miss MacIntosh in full voice, not filtered through Vera’s admiration or grief, but rendered directly, on a grey rainy birthday morning, in all her sour and loving and slightly unhinged glory. She is funny. She is bleak. She is preparing Vera, in her own completely idiosyncratic way, for a world she knows is hard. And underneath every word, if you listen, is the sound of a woman who has made her peace with having been loved by no one.

The vision at the sea

Young saves the chapter’s most extraordinary writing for the end, and it arrives like weather: suddenly, fully, and then it passes.

The sea turns to oily green and gold. The sky lights up with colors outside the mortal spectrum. The waves slow, almost stop. Vera hears what she describes as “harpers harping on those seas of glass which man shall behold at the end of time when the heavens are parted, when the sky rolls back like a scroll.”

Then it’s over. The waters go black again. The clouds fade. A dead seagull lies cold on a rock. The marble statue of Saul, we learn in passing, was once swept out to sea by a musical tide and never returned. A strange marble head came in and took his place.

This is Young at her most formally ambitious: a moment of genuine apocalyptic vision, framed on either side by the mundane, the barking sheep dog, the dead seagull, the empty playing cards the sea leaves behind. The heavens part and the harpers play, and then the sheep dog barks at the waves. Young will not let the transcendent stand alone. She always puts it back in the world.

The secret dream

Briefly, almost in passing, Vera mentions a secret dream she has been carrying: a false wedding, one that begets no other wedding, where Mr. Spitzer is married to the bridegroom. The only guests are “the northern light beams, the stars, and droves of seals on a solitary shore.”

Young plants this without explanation. We are not told whose wedding it is, what the bridegroom represents, why Mr. Spitzer appears in it. It feels significant, and it is, but the novel will take its time with it. For now, file it away. Vera carries a dream about a wedding that cannot produce another wedding, and it makes her laugh in the dark.

What to watch for as you keep reading

Light spoilers: This section hints at what happens later in the novel. Skip it if you want to meet the story fresh.

The sea has now been established as the novel’s site of revelation and dissolution. It sweeps statues away. It brings unknown heads in their place. It briefly parts to show you something outside the mortal spectrum and then closes again. Every time you encounter the sea in the chapters ahead, remember what it did on the night of Vera’s fourteenth birthday.

Miss MacIntosh’s bedroom (bare, cold, the windows open in winter, the three-mirror dressing table she never looks into) has been described here for the first time with some strangeness. Why does she carry her umbrella indoors? Why does she refuse to look in mirrors? Why does she sleep in the cold? These are the details that will matter when Chapter 16 finally delivers what has been withheld since Chapter 13.

The blind sheep dog barking at the waves is the last image of the chapter, and it echoes Chapter 13’s garden of the deaf. An animal whose sight is gone, barking at something it cannot see, that cannot hear it. Young places this image carefully at the close of the chapter. It is not decorative.

Chapter 82: The End Is the Beginning

← Chapter 81 · Guide Home

Research notes: Chapter 82

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Esther Longtree · Joachim Spitzer · Jock Cartwheel · Justice O’Leary · Lucie Bell · Madge Capehorn · Miss MacIntosh · Moses Hunnecker · Mr. Weed · Mrs. Hogden · Peron Spitzer · Rosemary · The Stone Deaf Man · Vera Cartwheel · Walter

Themes: Death and Mortality · Illusion and Reality · Music, Sound, and Silence

Symbols: Clouds and Storms · Music and Instruments · Silence and Deafness · The Bus and the Journey · The House

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Angels and Archangels · Deafness and Sign Language · Homer's Epics · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · The Bible · The History of Opium

This chapter carries Young’s use of Alpha and Omega, which To All My Darlings traces through the novel, to its simplest form: the end is the beginning, and the beginning is the end. After eighty-one chapters, the grey bus in the Midwest mist, Moses Hunnecker drinking and praying at the wheel, Madge sleeping her resistant sleep, Vera looking out at the grey American landscape wondering what she will find at What Cheer, Iowa; after Catherine and her opium and her pearls and her Italian thief; after Mr. Spitzer and his twin; after the Tavern and Dr. O’Leary and the hangman and Mrs. Hogden; after ten chapters with Esther Longtree and her stillborn and her Walter and her shadow boxer, the novel returns to where it began. The bus has arrived. The journey is over, or a version of it is over. Vera is home, or somewhere that used to be home. And everything she went looking for has changed into something she did not expect.

Catherine is dead. The sea-blackened house with its gold towers and cornices is gone: destroyed by a storm, scattered along the shore, its chandeliers lying broken in the sand. The only thing Vera has left from her inheritance is the string of pearls around her neck: the impossible arithmetic of her mother’s lost estate, the thing that multiplies when it is lost.

And she has fallen in love with a stone deaf man.

What Actually Happens

Vera mourns three deaths: Catherine’s, the old clam-digger’s, and one that may be harder to name, perhaps the death of the self she was looking for, the clarity she hoped Miss MacIntosh would restore. She is in love with “an older love than memory provided.” Catherine died while Mr. Spitzer carried her in his arms “into the garden by the sea.” He had waited years to tell her he loved her. He told her. She died as he spoke. The timing is the novel’s most bitter joke and most tender observation simultaneously: love arrives, is declared, and the beloved is already leaving. It was too late and it was the only moment available and it was enough and it was not enough. Mr. Spitzer then reveals what has been hidden since the beginning: he is not Joachim. He is Peron: the twin who survived by taking his dead brother’s place, who has been living Joachim’s life all this time, who has been Mr. Spitzer when he was always really Jock. His life, he says, has been a celestial joke. His grief over the old clam-digger, the loyal valet who drowned in the storm that destroyed Catherine’s house, is greater than his grief over Catherine. The man he loses most is not the woman he loved but the companion who was simply there, every day, without drama, until suddenly he was not.

Vera’s understanding of Miss MacIntosh deepens here, at the end. She loved Miss MacIntosh late, only when she could see past the surface of her character, past the rubber mackintosh and the whaler’s hat and the two and two making four. Underneath the practicality, the clearness, the plain average steadiness: a phantasmagoric dream. Miss MacIntosh dismissed religious belief as mockery and yet sang hymns. She believed in the cold surface of things and yet was drawn to the ocean’s depths and drowned in them. She was real, and she was not real in the way Vera thought, and Vera loved her most when she understood that the two things were simultaneously true. And then: the stone deaf man. He comes into Vera’s life in this final chapter, or she finds him, or hears his voice calling out for Lucie Bell, the silent girl who was not his love because she could not answer him. He hears with his eyes and his fingers. He lives in a world of silence that is not empty but full: full of the sounds the mind makes when the ears stop, of music remembered and music imagined. He says life is imaginary. This is an imaginary world. He cannot hear the silent horn that Gabriel will blow.

Vera loves him. They will marry. They will invite everyone. Their children, he believes, will transcend his limits: will hear what he cannot, carry forward what he has preserved in silence.

Vera says: “Esther Longtree would be me.”

Catherine’s Death and the House in the Storm

Catherine, who has been alive in the novel only in the mode of someone who has been dying for decades, who took to her bed and never left it, who lived entirely inside her opium hallucinations and her accumulated dreamwork: finally dies. The sea-blackened house goes with her. Storm, tide, dissolution: the material form of Catherine’s world is scattered along the shore.

What remains: the pearls. Young has been preparing this since Chapter 71, when Vera put on the pearls for the Tavern. Catherine believed they “could not be lost or stolen.” She believed that losing them made them multiply. The pearls are the only inheritance that survived. They are impossible and they are real. Catherine’s death, when it comes, is described as a change of state rather than a cessation. She had not walked for many years. She had not been entirely in the world for longer. Vera had been seeing her mother as a “beautiful lady sleeping in her swan boat”; by the end, she sees her as poor, as if “evicted from her house long before she died and wandered like a beggar through the streets.” The transformation is not in Catherine but in Vera’s seeing: she has learned, through eighty-two chapters of circling, to look at what is actually there rather than what she needs to see.

Mr. Spitzer Is Peron

This revelation has been structurally prepared throughout the novel: the twin brothers, one dead, one surviving by taking the dead one’s name and place; the question of which twin did the killing and which was killed; the guilt of the survivor who has been living as his brother, but it still lands with weight when it arrives. Mr. Spitzer has been Peron all along. He is Jock. He has been the wrong twin in the right place, or the right twin in the wrong name, for the entire novel.

The parallels to Esther Longtree’s situation are precise: she too has been the twin who survived, accused of killing Rosemary before birth. She too has carried that guilt as the organizing principle of her identity. Mr. Spitzer’s celestial joke (living as Joachim, who he is not) is Esther’s joke inverted: she lived as Esther, who she was told she had no right to be.

His grief for the old clam-digger exceeds his grief for Catherine. This is one of Young’s most precisely observed truths about loss: the death that destroys you is not always the dramatic one, the romantic one, the one with a name. Sometimes it is the companion who was simply present (the valet who buried himself in the sand, who developed nervous tics, who became over time barely distinguishable from the landscape) and who drowned quietly in the storm while Mr. Spitzer was declaring his love for someone else.

Miss MacIntosh, Finally Seen

Vera’s retrospective understanding of Miss MacIntosh in this final chapter is the novel’s most important statement about its own central figure. She loved Miss MacIntosh late. She could not love her fully while Miss MacIntosh was being Miss MacIntosh: plain, practical, real, dismissing illusions, insisting on two and two making four. It was only when Vera could see past that surface, when she understood that the woman who dismissed faith still sang hymns, that the woman who believed in the cold honest surface of things was drawn to the ocean’s depths: that she could love her fully.

Miss MacIntosh’s hymns in this chapter are the novel’s final gift from her. She sang them while performing mundane tasks, dismissing the religious belief they embodied, and singing them anyway. They are hymns of being lost, of needing guidance, of the waters drowning the soul: “Lo, she would lift her eyes to the hills from whence cometh help.” “Thou didst turn Thy face from me, and I was troubled.” “The waters have drowned us. The stream has gone over our soul.” These are not the hymns of someone who has certainty. They are the hymns of someone who has been through the water and survived and is still not sure if survival was the right outcome. Miss MacIntosh drowned in the ocean. She was drawn to the depths. She had hidden beneath her wig and her rubber mackintosh and her plain-average-clear-eyed practicality an entire phantasmagoric inner life, and the ocean claimed it. Vera could not have known this while she was looking for her. She knows it now that she has stopped looking and started mourning. The search ends not in What Cheer, Iowa but here, in the understanding that arrives too late and is therefore the only understanding available.

The Stone Deaf Man

He arrives at the novel’s end as its strangest and most necessary figure. He is stone deaf: deaf since he was fourteen, when all the waters of creation smashed against his ears. He hears with his eyes and his fingers. He lives in the silence that is not empty but full of the sounds the mind generates in the absence of the actual: music imagined, voices remembered, the world rebuilt from what was known before it went quiet. He cannot hear Lucie Bell: the silent girl he loved, who loved a jukebox or a tired marathon skater instead of him, who did not stay. He calls for her in his voice, this man who cannot hear his own voice. Vera hears him. Vera falls in love with him. She loves him not despite the deafness but through it, through the paradox of a man who speaks in a world of silence, who communicates in a language that is not language, who is closer to death than the hearing because he cannot hear the horn Gabriel will blow at the end of the world.

Their love is the novel’s final image of connection: not the connection Vera was looking for, not Miss MacIntosh’s plain-and-clear-eyed steadiness, not the cold honest surface of things. Something quieter and stranger. Something that requires a different kind of listening than the kind she arrived on the bus with.

They will marry. They will invite everyone. His deafness will not be passed to their children; he believes this, anyway, and Young lets him believe it. The next generation will hear what he cannot. Life goes on through the accumulation of what the living and the dead pass forward, imperfectly, into futures they cannot quite hear.

“Esther Longtree Would Be Me”

This is the novel’s most important sentence in the final chapter, and Young places it without fanfare. After all of Vera’s searching for Miss MacIntosh, for the plain average woman who believed in facts and schedules and the cold honest surface of things, Vera arrives at the end of the novel and says: Esther Longtree would be me. Not Miss MacIntosh. Not Catherine. Esther.

This is the full pivot of eighty-two chapters. Vera began her journey looking for the woman who represented clarity, practicality, the opposite of her mother’s opium dreaming. She ends by identifying herself with the woman who is always pregnant with the impossible, who loves “all things hurt or silent or broken or dead or living,” who buried her children in rivers and tree stumps and kept setting out breadcrumbs for spirits, who was called Little Jackass and was a murderer before she was born and survived everything that came after with a stubbornness that was neither wisdom nor delusion but simply life insisting on itself.

Esther is the average: the plain, the hidden, the one the world overlooks. And she is also the phantasmagoric dream beneath the surface. She is both, simultaneously, in the way that Miss MacIntosh was both: the cold surface and the depths that claimed her. What Vera has learned, across the entire novel, is that the surface and the depths are not opposites. They are the same thing seen from different angles, and to love the surface is to love the depths, and to look for the plain honest truth of things is to find that it contains a dream, and the dream contains a truth, and Esther Longtree is all of it.

The End Is the Beginning

The novel does not resolve. Miss MacIntosh does not walk back out of the ocean. Walter does not come home to Esther. Catherine’s house does not un-scatter from the shore. Mr. Spitzer does not stop being Peron-pretending-to-be-Joachim. The questions that opened the novel (what is real, what is illusion, what do we do when the only person who told us the truth has disappeared) are not answered. They are, by the end, better questions. Vera has learned to hold them without expecting resolution.

The stone deaf man says life is imaginary. This is an imaginary world. Miss MacIntosh would have disagreed: two and two make four, and don’t let anyone tell you otherwise. And yet she sang hymns. And yet she drowned. The facts and the imagination are not opposites. The cold surface and the depths that claim you are the same water.

The bus is still moving, in some sense, or has arrived at a place that is not the destination Vera expected but is nevertheless where she is. The grey American mist is still there. The world may blow up on a “day of calm just for fun.” The bad men may finish what they started. The little shadow boxer is still fighting. The stone deaf man is listening with his eyes and his fingers. “The dead loved the dead, and” perhaps that is how the world goes on.

Vera came looking for Miss MacIntosh. She found Esther Longtree.

She found herself.

What to Hold Onto

Catherine dying as Mr. Spitzer finally speaks his love. Too late and the only moment. It was not enough and it was what there was.

Mr. Spitzer revealing he is Peron. His life a celestial joke. His greatest grief: the old clam-digger who drowned in the storm, not the woman he loved.

Miss MacIntosh’s hymns: “Lo, she would lift her eyes to the hills.” The waters have drowned us. She dismissed faith and sang it anyway.

The stone deaf man who calls for Lucie Bell in the silence. Who hears with his eyes and his fingers. Who cannot hear the horn Gabriel will blow.

The pearls, scattered along the shore with the chandeliers. Only the pearls remain. Lost and multiplied, as Catherine promised. And Vera’s final sentence: Esther Longtree would be me. The woman who came looking for plainness and clarity and found the woman who is always pregnant with dreams. The woman who learned to love the depths the surface is made of.

A Note on the Journey

You have read Miss MacIntosh, My Darling. Or you have read alongside it, chapter by chapter, with this guide as your companion through the grey American mist.

What you have been inside is one of the longest and most singular novels in the American tradition: 1,198 pages, eighteen years in the writing, published in 1965 to stunned reviews and a readership that did not quite know what to do with it. It is not a novel that offers easy gratification or clear resolution. It asks you to surrender to its rhythms, to accept that meaning accumulates rather than arrives, to trust that the circling and digressing and doubling-back are the form enacting the content.

You have met Vera on her grey bus, and you have stayed with her through the Tavern and Esther Longtree and Mr. Weed and Dr. O’Leary and Mrs. Hogden and all the rest, and you have arrived here at the end, which is the beginning. Miss MacIntosh drowned in the ocean. Esther Longtree is always pregnant with the little shadow boxer. The stone deaf man cannot hear the horn Gabriel will blow. The pearls have multiplied.

Marguerite Young spent eighteen years building this wheel. You have traveled its spokes. That is not a small thing.

Thank you for reading. If you are interested in learning more about Young’s work, please see coralrussell.substack.com.

guide-27-the-two-watches:
Chapter 27: The Two Watches

← Chapter 26 · Guide Home · Chapter 28 →

Research notes: Chapter 27

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Peron Spitzer · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: The Search for Meaning

Symbols: Clocks and Watches · Twins and Doubles

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Astronomy · Deafness and Sign Language · Suicide in History and Literature

Chapter 27 completes the three-chapter portrait of Mr. Spitzer that began in Chapter 25. We are still at the breakfast table, still inside Vera’s meditation, and Young is still deepening our understanding of Mr. Spitzer before the novel moves outward to other characters and other lives.

This chapter is quieter than the previous two. It circles around a single image: the two watches, one ticking and one broken. And it gives us the most precise account yet of what Mr. Spitzer is actually like as a presence in the world: ponderously dignified, perpetually late, always caught in revolving doors and between traffic streams, walking through glass walls and barely noticing, asked by a stranger on a crowded street if he wants to die.

What actually happens in Chapter 27

Vera continues her meditation on Mr. Spitzer. Young builds him outward from the inside: his preference for isolation and neutrality, his knowledge of his own deficiencies, his habit of carrying calling cards and an out-dated passport and scrolls of silent music so that, if found among the drowned women and fallen men of a city morgue, he might be identified as himself and distinguished from his brother.

The chapter’s center is the two watches. Mr. Spitzer wears his dead brother’s wristwatch, which is accurate and fine, used by Peron for timing horses at the races. His own identical watch is broken: its crystal shattered, its wheels rusted, its mechanism clogged with dust, stopped long ago, perhaps “several days after his brother’s death,” perhaps several days before. He has recently found it again behind bottles and scrolls on his dressing table and begun wearing it on his left wrist, under his cuff, as a reminder that his brother’s life was brief.

The chapter ends with Mr. Spitzer being escorted through traffic by a stranger who asks if he wants to die. He replies in the negative while “shaking his head in the affirmative.” The stranger leads him safely across.

The two watches

The image of the two watches is one of the novel’s most precise and most economical symbols, and Young gives it the space it deserves.

Peron’s watch, now on Mr. Spitzer’s right wrist, is intact, accurate, excellent for timing horses. Peron removed it thoughtfully before jumping; this detail, Young notes carefully, destroys “in some people’s minds, the hypothesis of an impulsive, thoughtless suicide.” A man who removes his watch before jumping has planned something. Or at least has cared about the watch. Mr. Spitzer, who has been equivocating about whether Peron’s death was an accident or choice, finds himself forced to acknowledge: the watch was removed. Deliberately. It ticks on now on Joachim’s trembling wrist, marking “the course of the inaccurate planets, the recurring years, the unknown flow of time.”

Mr. Spitzer’s own watch, now on his left wrist under his cuff, is broken. Crystal shattered. Wheels rusted. Mechanism clogged with dust. It stopped around the time of Peron’s death; he cannot remember if it was before or after, having been in a state of shock that negated personal memory. He may have fainted while walking under a light snowfall “at about the time of his brother’s death, perhaps through sympathy, for they had always suffered” “the same accidents, one not falling unless the other fell.”

So: the living brother wears the dead one’s running watch and the dead one’s broken watch simultaneously. The time that moves is Peron’s. The time that stopped is Joachim’s. He tells time by his brother’s clock and carries the evidence of his own stopped life against his skin.

His paraphernalia

Young gives us, in this chapter, the full inventory of what Mr. Spitzer carries on his person at all times. It is a list worth holding:

His flowing cape of darkness. His high silk hat. His black necktie. A rosebud with maidenhair. Numerous calling cards. “An out-dated passport for a journey he” has not taken and has not thought of taking. Scrolls of silent music, “perhaps several abandoned beginnings, mere preludes, perhaps several tentative endings, mere epilogues to the great body of his uncreated work, unfinished epithalamiums and dirges and vast recessionals.” Notes for voiceless choirs, tongueless nightingales, deaf listeners.

He carries this paraphernalia so that if he is ever found “in a city morgue among the drowned women and the fallen men,” he can be identified. He can be distinguished from his brother. The calling cards, the passport, the scrolls of music; these are his proof of existing as himself and not as Peron. They are the documents of a man who is not sure he will be recognizable without them.

The epithalamiums are wedding songs. The dirges are for the dead. The recessionals are for departures. Mr. Spitzer carries, in his pockets, music for occasions he has never attended and will never attend: the wedding that did not happen, the funeral that is always pending, the departure that is always coming. He writes the music for the life he did not live.

The dignity question

Near the chapter’s end, Young gives us one of the most endearing observations about Mr. Spitzer in the novel: there is probably nothing he fears “so much as the loss of his dignity, that he might seem ridiculous in other people’s eyes.”

And then, immediately: he is always caught in revolving doors. He is always caught between traffic streams, always crossing the street just when the red light turns green. He is afraid of icy pavements and polished floors and the crystalline glare of a half-dark sky. He is always being held over from one chord into the next, always experiencing the blurring of effects that produces a terrible discord where he expected a concord.

Young lets these two things stand side by side without resolution: his profound concern for dignity, and his complete inability to move through the world without incident. He is ponderously proud of having walked through a glass wall and survived. He chuckles softly about the desk clerk who told him he was dead. He considers it a joke he played. And then he crosses the street at the wrong moment and a stranger has to ask him if he wants to die and lead him safely through the traffic.

He replies in the negative while “shaking his head in the affirmative.” Young does not comment. She does not need to.

What to watch for as you keep reading

Light spoilers: This section hints at what happens later in the novel. Skip it if you want to meet the story fresh.

After Chapter 27, the novel begins its great expansion. We are about to leave the breakfast table, leave the coastal house, and enter the wider landscape of American life that Young has been preparing us for since Chapter 1. New characters, new geographies, new obsessions. The Miss MacIntosh sequence and the Spitzer portrait are your foundation. Every new character you meet will rhyme, in some way, with what you have learned here.

The “out-dated passport for a journey” not taken is one of the novel’s small perfect images of Mr. Spitzer’s suspended life. He is prepared for a departure that never comes. He carries the credential for a crossing that he has not thought of making. And yet he renews it, presumably, keeps it on his person, because one day the moment might arrive. Mr. Spitzer is always almost ready to leave.

The detail that “one not falling unless the other fell,” the twins sharing their accidents through sympathy, is the chapter’s most concentrated statement of what it means to be a twin who survives. Mr. Spitzer may have fainted at the moment of Peron’s death. His watch may have stopped then. He fell without dying; Peron fell and did not survive the fall. They shared the accident. One got up and one did not.

guide-63-the-wig-comes-off:
Chapter 63: The Wig Comes Off

← Chapter 62 · Guide Home · Chapter 64 →

Research notes: Chapter 63

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Decay and Ruin

Symbols: Hair, Wig, and Baldness · Shadows

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Milton · Revelation and the Apocalypse · Shakespeare · The History of Opium

She is back.

After the long passage through Mr. Spitzer's interior world (the street musicians, the silent violinist, the frog's burial, the water music will) we return to Vera, and to Miss MacIntosh. And in this chapter, something happens that the novel has been building toward since its opening pages: Miss MacIntosh takes off her wig.

This is not a small moment. Hold on to it.

What actually happens

Vera confronts Miss MacIntosh. The confrontation is charged with everything that has accumulated between them across Vera's lifetime: the dependence, the gratitude, the resentment, the love, the fear of loss. Vera demands honesty. She calls their relationship a "hollow pretense" and pushes for something real, something true, beneath the surface of their arrangement.

Miss MacIntosh, in response, removes her wig. She is completely bald: alopecia universalis, a condition in which the body grows no hair anywhere. The red hair that Vera has always associated with her, the hair like "the sunset burning with bees," was never hers. It was a wig. And now it is off, and Miss MacIntosh is speaking more openly than she ever has: about her past, her loneliness, her body, her approaching death.

She also, toward the end of the chapter, foreshadows that she will disappear.

The wig and what it means

Miss MacIntosh has been, from the novel's first pages, Vera's figure of absolute reality. She was the anti-hallucination: the plain, practical, broken-nosed, red-haired woman who believed in facts, schedules, and the cold honest surface of things, in a household drowning in her mother's opium dreams.

And now it turns out that the red hair (the most vivid, most distinctive feature of her plainness) was itself a fiction.

Young is not undoing Miss MacIntosh. She is completing her. The woman who stood for reality against illusion, it turns out, has been wearing an illusion on her head every day of Vera's life. This doesn't make her a hypocrite. It makes her human. She needed protection too. She built her own small shelter of pretense against a world that laughed at bald women, that had no place for someone who didn't fit the expected shape of femininity. Her wig was her mackintosh; it kept the rain out.

When she removes it in front of Vera, she is doing what she has always done: insisting on truth, even when the truth is humiliating. The wig comes off because Vera demanded honesty. Miss MacIntosh gives it.

What Miss MacIntosh reveals

She speaks of sleeping in doorways. Of being broke: financially and otherwise. Of saving on electric lights because she couldn't afford them and because she hated what they stood for: Benjamin Franklin, who had "tampered with God’s nest egg and most private creation," flooding the world with artificial brightness that disturbed natural darkness, natural privacy, natural sleep.

She speaks of her missing breast (a mastectomy, a loss she has carried under her clothes through every chapter she has appeared in) and of her baldness, and of the crooked way her wig sat, and of the laughter she endured.

She says: "I could have slipped unnoticed through the crowds" if she had been a man. "No one would have laughed."

She calls love "a system of mutual deception." She says “people are never quite what they seem.” She says nobody knows anybody.

And then, at the end, she tells Vera to be of good cheer. She says they are pilgrims, and there is a long day ahead, and one must “live each day as if it were the last,” and knit body and soul together even as they unravel faster than you can knit.

Her argument with Franklin, Edison, and Constantine

Miss MacIntosh's hatred of electric lights is not mere crankiness; it is a coherent worldview. She objects to Benjamin Franklin and Thomas Edison for the same reason she objects to Emperor Constantine: all three men imposed an artificial order on the natural world, disrupting the rhythms of darkness and light, sleep and waking, that she believes are fundamental to honest living. Constantine changed the calendar. Franklin discovered electricity. Edison commercialized it. The result, in Miss MacIntosh's view, is a world perpetually overlit, overexposed, stripped of the natural darkness that "dreamless sleep" requires.

She is not simply nostalgic. She is making a philosophical argument: that authenticity requires darkness, that privacy requires shadow, that the soul needs to be allowed to go dark sometimes, and that those who fill every hour with artificial light are doing something spiritually as well as practically disruptive.

You may or may not agree. But for Miss MacIntosh, her preference for candles over electric lights is as principled as anything else she believes.

Vera's world within

Against Miss MacIntosh's catalogue of practical knowledge (monsoons and mackerel skies, the Bering Strait, nautical navigation, Australian shipping, household management, the Stock Exchange) Vera offers only her "world within." She cannot care about the Brooklyn Bridge or harbor buoys or cup racing. Her ears roar with distant reverberations. She is trembling at the threshold of life, not yet through the door.

This has been Vera's condition since page one of the novel. Miss MacIntosh has been trying, all her life, to drag her across that threshold. Into the practical. Into the immediate. Into what is "near and present." And Vera keeps falling back into the interior, into the dream, into her mother's opium-lit world where everything is beautiful and nothing is required.

The confrontation in Chapter 63 is, in part, about this: Vera wanting something from Miss MacIntosh that Miss MacIntosh cannot give, a bridge between the world within and the world without, and Miss MacIntosh insisting that the only bridge is the one Vera builds herself, day by day, by paying attention to monsoons and tides and the names of clouds.

"Bare and ruined choirs"

Miss MacIntosh's prophetic speech in this chapter reaches toward apocalypse: the sun and moon in the same sky, the earth still wrapped in darkness, birds gone silent, flowers perishing in the seed, tides that will not return what they take. She is quoting, consciously or not, from Milton's tradition of Christian elegy, evoking desolation and the loss of divine order.

And then she says: "There will be only, my dear, the dream."

In Miss MacIntosh's mouth, this is not consolation. It is a warning. If you retreat entirely into the dream (if you abandon the work of paying attention to the real, immediate, practical world) you will be left with nothing but illusion when everything else is stripped away.

She is warning Vera about her mother's fate. She is warning Vera about herself.

The foreshadowing

She will disappear. She says so. "I shall surely disappear as surely as the sun sets." This is the chapter that places her death within reach, not yet, but coming. You can feel it in the way she speaks: more openly than she ever has, as if she knows she has little time left for pretense, even the pretense of her wig.

The umbrella is still in her hand. She will keep the rain out until she cannot.

What to hold onto

Miss MacIntosh, her wig off, her bald head bare in the fog, telling Vera to be of good cheer. She who never dreamed, surrounded by a world that dreams. She who stood for reality, revealed to have worn a fiction on her head. She who told Vera to knit body and soul together, unraveling faster than she can knit.

She is not diminished by this. She is, finally, entirely herself.

guide-03-the-truest-thing-in-the-house:
Chapter 3: The Truest Thing in the House

← Chapter 2 · Guide Home · Chapter 4 →

Research notes: Chapter 3

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Madge Capehorn · Miss MacIntosh · Moses Hunnecker · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Illusion and Reality · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Twins and Doubles

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology · Heraclitus and Flux · Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Angels and Archangels · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · The History of Opium

By now you have spent two chapters in the fog traveling on that grey bus, inside Vera’s circling mind, watching Moses Hunnecker drink and pray, watching Madge sleep her resistant, unhappy sleep. You have had glimpses of Miss MacIntosh, heard her name, understood that she is the reason for this journey. But you haven’t met her yet. Not really.

Chapter 3 is where you meet her.

And she is worth the wait.

What actually happens in Chapter 3

Catherine Cartwheel, Vera’s mother and the opium addict who never leaves her bed, has been confined to her room and her hallucinations for some time now. Someone needs to look after Vera. The family lawyer, Mr. Joachim Spitzer, hires a nursemaid: Miss Georgia MacIntosh, from What Cheer, Iowa.

That is the external event. The chapter is Vera’s portrait of her.

Vera describes Miss MacIntosh’s appearance: her marcelled red hair, her greyish-green eyes, her sensible shoes (size eight, like a man’s), her black umbrella, her serge dress, her corset laced tight. She describes her habits: the early morning swims in the surf regardless of weather, the insistence on schedules and physical exercise, the mending of clothes, the building of fires. She describes her philosophy: hard work, self-forgetfulness, the acceptance of necessary deprivations, and a bone-deep suspicion of illusion in any form. She describes an encounter with an Australian bushman who has wandered into Catherine’s household and become obsessed with Miss MacIntosh’s head (he wants to sculpt it) and whom Miss MacIntosh dispatches with contempt.

And then, at the end of the chapter, Vera tells us what she already told us in Chapter 1: Miss MacIntosh is gone. Her clothes were found on the beach. Her purse contained two pennies. Her body was never recovered. Vera blames herself.

The chapter is both introduction and elegy. Young gives us Miss MacIntosh whole, luminous, and entirely herself and then reminds us she is already lost.

What Vera is thinking about

Everything in this chapter is filtered through Vera’s love for this woman and her grief at losing her.

Think about what Vera’s life looked like before Miss MacIntosh arrived. Her mother lived inside hallucinations, receiving imaginary visitors, lost in opium visions of poets and grandeur. The household was full of dreamers, illusionists, and people who had decided that reality was optional. Vera had no one to tell her what was real.

And then: Miss Georgia MacIntosh. A woman who swam in cold water. Who mended things when they tore. Who said that life was made up of necessary deprivations and that you should not waste your time chasing golden apples that weren’t there. Who did not believe in six-winged seraphim or furnished heavens or any of the other elaborate fantasies that the people around Vera used to avoid the fact of being alive.

For Vera, this was not austerity. It was rescue.

So when she describes Miss MacIntosh’s red hair catching the light like sparks, or her umbrella raised against the wind like a challenge, or the way she used a jar of fireflies as a lamp in the dark, these are not just memories. They are acts of preservation. If she can make Miss MacIntosh vivid enough in language, she hasn’t entirely lost her.

This is, quietly, what the novel is doing. Young wrote Miss MacIntosh, My Darling over eighteen years. It is 1,198 pages long. A large part of what drives it is exactly this: the refusal to let someone disappear.

The two women at the center of the book

Chapter 3 is the first place where Young lays out the novel’s central opposition in full, and everything that follows depends on it.

Catherine Cartwheel lives entirely inside illusion. Her opium visions are not mere escapism, they are her whole world. She receives guests who are not there. She inhabits a reality she has constructed and furnished to her own specifications. She is, in a certain light, the novel’s portrait of what happens when the imagination is given everything and the real world nothing.

Miss MacIntosh is her perfect opposite. She believes in what can be touched, worn out, scheduled, and endured. She does not dream, or if she does, she does not trust her dreams. She is the novel’s embodiment of the real, of the position that life requires us to see it clearly, accept its hardships, and do the work.

Young holds these two women in the same story for a reason. She is not asking you to choose between them. She is asking you to hold both: to feel the pull of Miss MacIntosh’s hard, clear-eyed practicality and the pull of Catherine’s bottomless inner world and to sit with the question of what it costs to live at either extreme.

Vera grew up between them. She loves them both. The novel is her attempt to make sense of what that did to her.

The Australian bushman, and what he’s doing here

He seems to come from nowhere this figure who has wandered into Catherine’s household, who has some connection to the wider world of the book’s strange cast, and who fixates on Miss MacIntosh with an intensity she finds contemptible.

He wants to sculpt her head. He corners her. He speaks to her with what Young calls a “calculated, incalculable eloquence” a beautiful phrase and she is completely unimpressed.

Miss MacIntosh sees through pretense immediately. She does not care about his eloquence or his obsession. She dispatches him.

But notice what Young is doing here: the bushman is interested in Miss MacIntosh’s head specifically. Not her practicality, not her values, not the whole woman, just the head. He wants to possess a piece of her, reduced to an aesthetic object. And she refuses. This refusal is entirely in character, and it is also, given what the novel will eventually reveal about Miss MacIntosh’s body and her secrets, quietly significant. Young plants these seeds without calling attention to them. Trust that they will matter.

There is also a feminist dimension worth naming: the bushman feels entitled to her attention regardless of her feelings. He interrupts, corners, and pursues. Miss MacIntosh is having none of it. In 1965, when this novel was published, that was a more radical stance than it might appear now.

The disappearance

Young does not save this for later. We already know, from the novel’s opening pages, that Miss MacIntosh is gone. Chapter 3 confirms it: the clothes on the beach, the two pennies, the unrecovered body. Mr. Spitzer thinks she may have simply returned to the working poor she came from. Vera knows she did not.

What actually happened to Miss MacIntosh? The novel will give you more information as you go, information that will change the shape of what you already know. But it will not give you a clean answer. This is Young’s way: she is more interested in the weight of an unanswered question than in the relief of resolution.

For now, hold what you have: a woman who was the truest thing in the house, and an absence shaped exactly like her.

What to watch for as you keep reading

Light spoilers: This section hints at what happens later in the novel. Skip it if you want to meet the story fresh.

Miss MacIntosh’s corset. She laces herself into it every morning as a philosophical act, the body held to its proper shape by an act of will. Young will return to this garment in ways you don’t yet expect. Notice it each time it appears.

The two pennies. In ancient Greek burial practice, a coin was placed in the mouth of the dead as payment for Charon, the ferryman who carried souls across the river Styx to the underworld. Two pennies in a purse on a beach. Young knew exactly what she was doing.

The sea. Miss MacIntosh swam in it every morning, whatever the weather. She was strengthened by it. And then it took her or she walked into it. The sea in this novel is the border between what we know and what we cannot know. Watch where it appears.

Vera’s habit of description. Notice how much of her grief comes out as physical detail: the red hair, the greyish-green eyes, the size-eight shoes. When we lose someone, we often try to hold them through the inventory of their particulars. Young understands this. So does Vera.

What to hold onto

If Chapter 3 overwhelms you with its length and its layering, come back to this: a child grew up in a house full of illusions, and the one person who taught her that reality was real has disappeared. Everything Vera says about Miss MacIntosh, every detail, every memory, every piece of her philosophy is Vera trying to keep her alive in language.

That is what this chapter is. That is what this novel is, in one of its many dimensions.

You are not lost. You are watching someone grieve in the only way she knows how.

guide-06-the-wedding-that-was-a-funeral:
Chapter 6: The Wedding That Was a Funeral

← Chapter 5 · Guide Home · Chapter 7 →

Research notes: Chapter 6

Characters: Homer Capehorn · Jacqueline White · Madge Capehorn · Miss MacIntosh · Moses Hunnecker · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Death and Mortality · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Twins and Doubles · Weddings and Funerals

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Fairy Tales and Folklore · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · Music and Composers · Pregnancy, Abortion, and Midwifery · The History of Opium

We have been watching Madge Capehorn since Chapter 1, asleep in her seat, pregnant, visibly unhappy, the stuffed bird on her hat bobbing in the dim light. She has been a figure in the background, part of the landscape of the bus. In Chapter 6, Young brings her forward. We step inside her.

What we find there is not comfortable. But it is one of the most honest portraits of a woman trapped by the circumstances of her time that you will encounter in this novel. Settle in. Madge has things to say.

What actually happens in Chapter 6

The bus moves through a desolate night landscape: broken gates, fallen pillars, a derelict windmill spinning in the wind, withered leaves. Moses is half-asleep at the wheel. And Madge Capehorn is crying in her sleep.

When she surfaces into a kind of wakefulness, we learn her story. She is five months pregnant. She left her hometown years ago, went to work in a pottery town, grew older than the girls around her, and ended up marrying Homer Capehorn, not because she loves him, but because she needed a father for her child. The real father is a man named Adam. Homer doesn’t know this.

Homer is not a bad man, exactly. He is young, placid, oblivious, physically strong, and emotionally absent. He is asleep for most of the chapter or half-asleep, dreaming of a girl named Jacqueline White, his high school sweetheart, who is dying of tuberculosis. Madge knows he loves Jacqueline. She has always known. She accuses him of it. He denies it, barely awake, insisting he hasn’t thought of Jacqueline in years. They both know this is not true.

In the middle of all this, Young gives us the tragedies stacked beneath the present one: Madge’s mother died in childbirth. Her father, years later, in a moment of grief-addled confusion, mistook Madge for her dead mother and ran out into a winter storm and drowned in the river. Homer’s father, on hearing that Homer’s mother was pregnant, went out with his hunting dogs and killed himself. Death and birth are not separate events in this chapter. They arrive together, the way they have always arrived in this family.

Madge believes she will die in childbirth, the way her mother did. She believes Homer will die young, the way his father did. She can see the shape of it all. She is driving toward her own end with her eyes open, and there is nothing she can do about it.

What Vera is thinking about

Vera observes all of this while listening to Madge’s half-dreaming monologue, watching the exchange between Madge and Homer, understanding things about both of them that they may not fully understand about themselves.

Remember that Vera is on this bus because she is searching for Miss MacIntosh, the woman who embodied reality, practicality, the plain truth of things. And here, in Madge, she is encountering reality of a very different kind: a woman for whom reality is a trap with no exits, a marriage that feels more like a funeral, a body being remade against her will.

Vera does not intervene. She never does. But she witnesses. And in a novel where so much is illusion and dream, witnessing, truly seeing another person’s suffering, is its own act of moral seriousness.

Madge and what her story is really about

To understand Madge, you need to understand what the world looked like for women in the era Young is writing about. This is not ancient history, it is the America of the 1930s and ‘40s, the America Young herself grew up in and observed.

Marriage was not one option among many for a woman then. It was the only option. It was the entire architecture of a viable life. Without it, a woman had no economic security, no social standing, almost no respectable path forward. Madge left her town, went to work in a pottery factory, which was already an act of independence, grew older, and found herself pregnant and unmarried. In that world, in that moment, her choices had already been made for her.

She married Homer not for love but for survival. She is not a fool. She knows exactly what she has done and why. And she knows that the life she has bought herself is not a life she would have chosen.

Young is not writing a tragedy about a weak woman who made bad choices. She is writing about what happens to a person when all of the choices available to them lead to the same place. Madge’s intelligence, her self-awareness, her fierce and furious understanding of her own situation, none of it is enough to change what is happening to her. That is the point.

Jacqueline White, and the ghost in the marriage

Homer loves Jacqueline White. She is dying of tuberculosis or “consumption,” they called it, the disease that turned people pale and thin and beautiful as it killed them. She is becoming an ideal precisely because she is disappearing: untouched by time, preserved in Homer’s memory as the girl she was, the love he didn’t pursue.

Madge cannot compete with this. No living woman can compete with a dying one in a man’s imagination. Jacqueline will always be young, always be the one he didn’t get to keep. She is becoming the kind of love that only works because it was never tested.

This is one of the more quietly devastating observations in the chapter: that the dead and the dying have an advantage over the living, because they never have to become ordinary. Miss MacIntosh understood something like this. So does Vera. And now Madge is living it from the inside.

The two faces

Madge believes she must maintain at least two faces: the one she was born with, and the painted one she puts on for the world. This is not vanity. It is a survival strategy.

Young knew, and stated in interviews, that everyone wears masks: an inner self and an outer self presented to the public. But for Madge, this doubling is not philosophical, it is compulsory. She cannot afford to show the world what she actually feels. She cannot afford to be the woman who is terrified and grieving and furious and exhausted. So she paints a face over that one, pins the stuffed bird to her hat, and gets on the bus.

The stuffed bird is a perfect image. It is decoration that was once alive. It was killed to become ornamental. It sits on Madge’s hat going nowhere.

The deaths on both sides of this marriage

Young piles up the deaths in this chapter with a kind of brutal patience. Madge’s mother: died in childbirth. Madge’s father: drowned after mistaking his daughter for his dead wife. Homer’s father: killed himself when he learned his wife was pregnant.

Notice what Young is doing here. The news of a new life coming into the world (pregnancy, the thing that is supposed to represent hope and continuation) is the event that triggers the deaths on Homer’s side of the family. His father could not face it. Madge’s family was destroyed by it from a different angle.

This is a chapter in which birth and death are not opposites. They are the same gesture, made in different directions. Madge carrying a child is also Madge moving toward the grave her mother already reached. She knows this. She feels it in her body.

What to watch for as you keep reading

Light spoilers: This section hints at what happens later in the novel. Skip it if you want to meet the story fresh.

The pottery town. Madge worked in a pottery factory before all of this, one of the Midwestern towns, possibly in Ohio, where the clay soil produced the ceramics industry. Young makes something of this: Madge came from a world of clay and making, of things shaped by hand into useful forms. And now she is the clay, being shaped by forces she didn’t choose.

Tuberculosis. Jacqueline White is dying of it, and in the mid-twentieth century it was still the leading cause of death in the United States. It was called consumption because it seemed to consume a person from within and also the “Great White Plague” for the pallor it gave its victims. It had a terrible romantic reputation, for exactly the reason Young is using it here: it made beautiful young people die beautifully. Madge is right to resent it.

Masking. The idea that people show a different face to the world than the one they actually have runs through this entire novel. Madge states it plainly here that she keeps at least two faces. Watch for this idea as the book continues. Almost every character in this novel is wearing something over their real face.

The animals. Chapter 6 is full of them: moths, stags, dragonflies, blackbirds, rabbits, pheasants. Young uses each one as a layer of meaning: transformation, death, fragility, change. You don’t need to decode all of them. Just notice that the natural world in this chapter is saturated with significance, that nothing is merely decorative.

What to hold onto

Chapter 6 can feel overwhelming, so many nested tragedies, so much grief packed into one woman’s half-dreaming monologue on a midnight bus. If you feel the weight of it pressing down, that is exactly right. That is Madge’s weight. You are supposed to feel it.

But here is what to hold onto: Madge is awake when everyone else is asleep. She is the one who sees clearly, who knows exactly what her life is and what it cost her. In a novel full of people fleeing into dreams and illusions, that clarity, however painful, is its own kind of power.

She cannot change her circumstances. But she knows what they are. And in Young’s world, that is not nothing.

For the Curious

  • Tuberculosis
  • Maternal mortality
  • Depersonalization-derealization
  • The Ship of Theseus
  • “The Red Shoes”
guide-60-the-wild-sonata:
Chapter 60: The Wild Sonata

← Chapter 59 · Guide Home · Chapter 61 →

Research notes: Chapter 60

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer

Themes: Fate and Chance · Music, Sound, and Silence

Symbols: Birds · Music and Instruments · Silence and Deafness

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Gambling and Playing Cards · Greek Mythology · Music and Composers

After two chapters of Mr. Spitzer walking the city in philosophical anguish (questioning his skeleton, giving coins to musicians he can't quite see, trying to determine whether he is alive or dead) Chapter 60 offers something unexpected: a moment of grace. Not resolution. Not answers. But something that cuts through all the questions like a flock of wild ducks cutting through fog.

Hold on to that image. We'll get there.

What actually happens

Mr. Spitzer is still walking the city, still thinking. He wonders, with genuine uncertainty, whether he is actually a musician at all, or whether he has been a gambler all along, someone who mistook the music in his head for a vocation rather than a symptom. He reads only the sporting pages. He has never attended a concert. He cannot say “the value of a sand dollar or a Boston dollar or an English pound sterling.”

Then, at dusk, he practices moose calls in the middle of the city. A moose answers. Its antlers loom through the purple fog like tree boughs, merging with traffic lights and the Pleiades.

And then the wild ducks come.

Musician or gambler?

This is the chapter's opening question, and it's worth taking seriously. Mr. Spitzer has been described to us, and has described himself, as a composer. But Chapter 60 introduces genuine doubt: what if the music existed only in his head, as germinal, unwritten, unrealized? What if the gambling, the sporting pages, the horse races, the cards falling: what if that was the real Mr. Spitzer, and the composer was a story he told himself?

Young doesn't answer this. She is not interested in debunking Mr. Spitzer. She is interested in what it means to carry a vocation you cannot verify. Many people live their entire lives with music in their heads they never find a way to express. Does that make them musicians? Does it matter?

Mr. Spitzer suspects he might be what he calls a "cubistic dream player": a self fractured into multiple, simultaneous viewpoints that don't resolve into a coherent whole, like a Cubist painting seen from every angle at once. He is the gambler and the composer, and possibly neither, and the two versions of himself don't reconcile.

The moose in the city

When Mr. Spitzer practices moose calls in the urban dusk and a moose actually answers (antlers rising through the fog, indistinguishable from tree boughs, traffic lights, and the scatter of the Pleiades overhead) you are reading one of the novel's purest expressions of what Young means by the dissolution of borders.

The moose should not be there. The city should exclude it. And yet: it answers. Young is not asking you to decide whether this is hallucination or vision or literal event. She is showing you that Mr. Spitzer inhabits a world where these categories have become permeable, where if you call into the wilderness with enough longing, something wild calls back, regardless of where you are standing.

This is also, quietly, a scene about his dead brother. Mr. Spitzer wonders throughout this chapter how he knows what Peron knew, if he is himself and not Peron. The moose call is a kind of answer to that question: some communication travels across distances that should make it impossible.

The wild ducks

This is the moment the chapter has been building toward, and Young gives it everything she has.

The wild ducks appear overhead: exotic, "beautiful Asiatics" with crested heads and gold-veiled eyes, their wings gold-tipped, drifting through great clouds. Their honking fills the air as a "wild sonata," drowning out the traffic, the city, the noise of ordinary existence. Mr. Spitzer, standing in the street, feels himself dissolving into the sound: imagines himself metamorphosed into wings, suspended between earth and sky, a silent observer caught inside the music.

And here is what he realizes: he doesn't need to write his elegy anymore. He has been trying, across many chapters, to compose an elegy for his brother, for himself, for everything that has been lost. But the wild ducks are the elegy. Their honking calls, unrepeatable and wild and entirely indifferent to human grief, are the music he could never have written. They will accompany him, he thinks, "through the long reaches of the silence."

This is one of Young's most tender moments. The elegy you cannot compose will still be given to you. Not in the form you expected (not as a composed piece, not from a harpsichord with all black keys or a viola da gamba) but as something wild and passing overhead, not made for you, not about you, and somehow exactly right.

Sound moving through imagined silence

Young describes sound in this chapter as something that moves "like the human spirit through heavens of imagined silence." This is her persistent argument about music, and by extension about art: it is not the sound itself but its movement through silence that constitutes the real thing. The wild sonata of the ducks matters because it passes through a world that is, underneath everything, silent.

Mr. Spitzer's dead brother could not imagine silence, we're told. It was unimaginable to him. But Mr. Spitzer has made his peace with it. And maybe that is why the ducks come to him, because he is not afraid of the silence they will leave behind.

What to hold onto

Mr. Spitzer standing in a city street, looking up. The fog. The traffic lights. The Pleiades. And through all of it, a flock of wild ducks with gold-tipped wings and crested heads, honking their way across the sky in a wild sonata he could never have composed, which is his elegy, which is enough.

He doesn't need to write the music anymore. It was always going to come to him from outside.
