guide-23-we-be-creatures-of-the-darkness:
Chapter 23: We Be Creatures of the Darkness

← Chapter 22 · Guide Home · Chapter 24 →

Research notes: Chapter 23

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Light and Darkness

Symbols: Lamps, Candles, and Light · Snow, Ice, and Winter

Philosophy: Aristotle · Augustine and Christian Theology · Descartes and Dualism · Empiricism (Locke, Berkeley, Hume)

Allusions: Gambling and Playing Cards · Judaism · The Bible · The Book of Job

Chapter 23 is the electric lights chapter, and if you read it only as a comic tirade against modern convenience you will miss what it is doing.

Miss MacIntosh spends most of this chapter behind her newspaper, blaming Benjamin Franklin for the ruin of private life. She objects to floodlights, headlights, footlights, tail lights, traffic lights, searchlights, fluorescent lamps, and the two-way lighting systems she sees advertised as available in Boston. It is funny. Young means it to be funny.

It is also a woman who was seen three nights ago, looked at without her wig by a child holding a candle, arguing at enormous length that no one should have to be looked at.

Hold both of those at once and the chapter opens.

What actually happens in Chapter 23

Nothing, in the sense that nothing happened in Chapter 22. It is the same breakfast table, the same August morning, the same newspaper held up between two people who have agreed without discussion to say nothing.

Miss MacIntosh begins on vain man: the Emperor Constantine, the Slough of Despond, the heart that was locked from the inside. She moves to Caesar crossing the Rubicon and asks who alive ever saw him. History lies, she says, and geography is uncertain. She declares her faith in common sense, “the middle brow, the middle way, the average life.”

Then she arrives at Benjamin Franklin and stays there for most of the chapter. Franklin flew a kite, harnessed lightning he was never asked to harness, paved the way for electric lights, and now there is “nowhere a man can hide his” face. She works through the consequences: no dark corner on Skid Row, no privacy in a man's own bedroom, midnight baseball, the poor paying the light bills. She argues that darkness once protected marriage, that Helen of Troy would not have been Helen of Troy if someone had switched on a lamp, that Ulysses would never have come home if “he had seen Penelope under electric” light. She would give Thomas Edison a piece of her mind if it were ever her doubtful pleasure to meet him.

She asks where Baffin Bay is. She gives Vera advice about igloos.

Vera, meanwhile, does something she has never done before. She works out what the talk is for.

The chapter ends with Miss MacIntosh quoting the Book of Job and crying out that “the stars have lighted the heavens from pole to pole.”

Vain man

Vain man giving himself “immortal airs, imagining what is not.” And then, immediately: “when the door of the heart slams shut, it will not be opened by man again. The heart, my dear, was locked from the inside, and that is that.”

She says this at breakfast, to a fourteen year old, apropos of Constantine.

Notice also the shape of the skepticism. “History lies, and geography is uncertain,” says the woman who quizzes Vera on geography every single morning and has done so for years. She is a teacher calling her own curriculum unreliable, and she does it without any apparent sense of contradiction. “Ignorance of the law is no excuse,’ she” adds, and Young tells us she says it without conviction.

This is the chapter's first quiet signal. Miss MacIntosh's certainties have started saying things she does not entirely believe.

Why the electric lights matter

The tirade runs for pages and Young lets it run. Taken as argument it is crank material, the grumbling of a woman who has decided that a century went wrong. Taken as autobiography it is one of the most exposed passages in the novel.

Every complaint is the same complaint. There is no dark corner left. There is “nowhere a man can hide his ugly face.” God's starlight “left us the privacy in which a poor man may die.” Before all this tampering there was always a lightless alley, a street without lamps, a “bedroom where a man could hide” his face from everyone but God.

Three nights ago a child stood over her bed with a candle and saw what she had spent a lifetime covering. Miss MacIntosh has not mentioned it and she will not mention it. She is talking about Benjamin Franklin instead. But everything she says about light is about being seen, and everything she says about darkness is about the mercy of not being seen, and she says it for most of a chapter without once saying I.

Young does not underline this. She simply puts the tirade three days after the candle and trusts you.

The ugly woman safe in her husband's arms

The marriage passage is where the defense stops being general.

In the old days, she says, when darkness fell and it certainly did fall, “an ugly woman was safe in her husband’s arms,” since he could not see what he could not touch. He might even think her handsome. Couples undressed in the dark, each being modest. “Many a wife never saw her husband except when he was clothed. Many a husband never saw his wife.” Then the electric lights come on, and a blushing bride is shown up for what she is, sometimes on the wedding night, sometimes the night before, and look at the divorce rate.

Read this as a joke and it is a good one. Read it as a woman with a mastectomy scar and a bald head explaining why she never married and it is something else entirely. “The wisest men are never married,” she says a few lines later, and moves on.

“Beauty is as beauty does, my dear.” She offers it as folk wisdom. It is the only comfort she has ever been able to give herself, and she is handing it across the breakfast table to a girl who has just learned what it cost.

The igloos

Then, with no transition at all, she tells Vera how to keep house at the top of the world.

Always have two igloos. Keep the permanent one “closed against wind and drifting snow.” Keep “a good supply of frozen seals and” kitchen matches. A new broom sweeps clean. Never build the second igloo on an old ice floe, because it may “move away in a long night’s darkness.” Wait until the ice has stopped moving. “Listen for the crackle of distant ice,’ she said, ‘like the screaming of wild geese.”

And then the sentence the chapter has been circling: “the ice might seem quite firm where we are,” and be in motion “miles behind us or miles ahead.” These appearances are often deceptive. Old “floes have a way of splitting into two. We might lose ourselves. We might lose our sleds and our dogs.”

That is not housekeeping advice. That is a woman describing her own life in the only vocabulary she permits herself, and it is as close to a confession as she comes. Always keep a second shelter. Never trust ground that is not moving yet.

Notice too the small physical detail Young drops in the middle of it. “She coughed into her napkin, and then she seemed to scream.” It is one clause, easily missed, and it belongs with the rasping breath Vera heard in Chapter 22. The performance holds. The body does not.

Covering her hand

Vera's recognition arrives in the sunlight, at the table, in the middle of the geography.

These cosmic subjects, she thinks, the phantasmagoric glaciers and submerged continents and the latitude and longitude of the Austral Islands, are dreams, impersonal and vast, and they cover her hand, “as is said in gambling circles.” They conceal her limitations, the thing missing from the essential human, the thing she does not want Vera to see.

Then comes the harder line. “Of herself, of herself alone, what had she ever said that was personal and sad and revelatory?”

Fourteen years. The woman who raised her, who tested her every morning on rivers and capitals and the first day of creation, has never once told her anything about her own life. Vera notices this for the first time at this breakfast, and it is the notice that makes Chapter 23 a turning point rather than a second helping of Chapter 22. In Chapter 22 Vera watched a performance and wondered whether Miss MacIntosh was all others. Here she works out what the performance is for.

She is always evading something, Vera thinks, something too subtle to evade.

Winter in August

The chapter's last movement belongs to Vera, and it is one of the loveliest things in Volume One.

Miss MacIntosh announces that they “must get ready for winter’s blast,” mend the old woolen drawers, keep a nip of brandy for warmth. It is “the cold hand of death for those who are not ready.”

And Vera asks the obvious question. Why are we talking about winter in “August sunlight, heavy with the perfume of rain-washed flowers, and was there to be no season of transition, no gradual change, no autumn, no Indian summer like the Indian summer of the human soul, no time” for farewell before the world goes colorless?

Then she answers herself with a list. Winter wears “its coat of many colors, too,” dimmed though they are: “the bronze of beach grass, the whiteness of snow upon the heads of the blackened spruce and hemlock, the pale iridescence of the seagull’s eye, the purple and mauve and grey and gold of the winged seed heads. There would be the luminous colors of the winter sea like a great opal seen through” fog.

That is the lesson of the birthday night arriving in Vera's own voice, without anyone teaching it to her. A stripped world is not a world without color. It is a world whose colors have gone quiet. She has just watched a woman be stripped down to the bare fact of herself, and this is what she has made of it.

What to watch for as you keep reading

Light spoilers: This section hints at what happens later in the novel. Skip it if you want to meet the story fresh.

The blind man in the final lines looks like a throwaway joke. “A blind man saw me, certainly, and without electric lights.” It is not a joke. Miss MacIntosh worked in a house for the blind, and Young has been building that history since the garden chapters. It is also the chapter's actual argument, delivered in one sentence after several thousand words of complaint about light bulbs: being truly seen has nothing whatever to do with illumination. The one person who ever saw her could not see.

Watch the doubling. Two igloos. Two lighting systems in the Boston advertisement. Dwarves who dream they are giants and giants who dream they are dwarves. The novel is full of twins, doubles, and second selves, and Miss MacIntosh keeps producing them in pairs without ever noticing she does it.

Watch who she talks to. She would say this to Benjamin Franklin if she met him in the darkness. She would give Thomas Edison a piece of her mind. She would have a word with Caesar, were it her doubtful pleasure. Every argument she wins is with someone who cannot answer. Then turn the page to Chapter 24 and watch Catherine place telephone calls to Augustine and King Canute and Cousin Hannah. Two women in one house, both talking at length to the unreachable, one of them certain she is the sensible one. Young put those chapters side by side deliberately.

guide-38-the-loony-bin:
Chapter 38: The Loony Bin

← Chapter 37 · Guide Home · Chapter 39 →

Research notes: Chapter 38

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Peron Spitzer · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Love · Music, Sound, and Silence · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Angels, Devils, and Myth · Moon and Stars · Music and Instruments

Philosophy: Heraclitus and Flux · Marguerite Young on Her Craft · Plato and Platonism · Pythagoras and the Music of the Spheres

Allusions: Revelation and the Apocalypse · The History of Opium · Women's Suffrage

There is a moment in Chapter 38 when Vera (not abstractly, not philosophically, but with the matter-of-fact clarity of someone who has been living inside a situation long enough to name it) refers to her mother's household as a loony bin.

It lands.

Young has been building this house for thirty-seven chapters: the opium, the bed Catherine never leaves, Mr. Spitzer arriving a minute behind each moment he inhabits, Cousin Hannah present only as memory and legend and the fading echo of iron keys. You have been inside these walls long enough to have forgotten, perhaps, that from the outside, this is what it looks like. A loony bin. A place where the usual rules of consciousness don't apply.

Chapter 38 is the chapter where the novel steps back, just briefly, and lets you see the house from that vantage. And then it steps back inside, because the inside is where the real work of the novel lives.

What actually happens in Chapter 38

Catherine talks about Cousin Hannah. Mr. Spitzer contributes anecdotes. Vera narrates her mother's interior: its shape, its contradictions, its magnificent and exhausting unreliability.

We learn more about Catherine's love life, or rather her love's absence: Peron, the man she loved, whose neglect she has reinterpreted as a form of devotion too large for expression. His silence was his love. His distance was his tribute to her power. Catherine has constructed this interpretation with great care and considerable creativity, and she has been living inside it for years.

We learn that Catherine does not believe in women's suffrage. She never did. This is not incidental: Young places it here deliberately, in the long meditation on Cousin Hannah's life's work, so that you feel the full weight of the irony. The woman Hannah loved most, the woman whose household she visited, whose memory she haunts: that woman thought the cause was wrong.

And we get Cousin Hannah herself, arriving in this chapter as she always arrives: fully armed, whistling, trailing snowstorms, carrying iron keys and jeweled swords. A figure of myth assembling itself out of Catherine's guilty admiration.

Obtuse and acute

Young gives us, in Chapter 38, a geometric vocabulary for the novel's central contrast. Catherine and Mr. Spitzer are described as obtuse: wide-angled, blunt, unable to cut. Cousin Hannah is acute: sharp, incisive, a finely tempered blade.

These are called, in the text, masculine virtues. Notice that Young says this with some irony. Cousin Hannah's sharpness is called masculine not because it belongs to men but because the culture has assigned it to them: shrewdness, incisiveness, the willingness to press forward without softening the edges. Cousin Hannah claimed these qualities anyway. She did not ask permission to be acute.

Catherine could not admire these traits without feeling their rebuke. Every quality she admired in Hannah was a quality she did not have, could not have, had perhaps chosen not to have by retreating to the bed and the opium and the beautiful, inaccurate dreams. The admiration and the guilt are inseparable. You cannot love someone for what they are without sometimes feeling diminished by the comparison.

Catherine's love, and the dead love that never was

The passage about Peron is one of the novel's quiet heartbreaks, and it deserves to be read slowly.

Catherine loved Peron. Peron did not love her back, or did not express it, or expressed it through neglect, which Catherine has, over years of opium-assisted interpretation, come to understand as a love too great for conventional demonstration. His silence was greater than hatred. His distance was a tribute. The love between them was a “dead love which never was and never would be real,” and was therefore, Catherine reasons, paradoxically eternal. What never happened cannot be lost. It is still there, unchanged, in the place where unrealized things live.

You might want to argue with this. Young wants you to feel both the argument against it and the deep, exhausted human logic that produces it. People do this. They construct the love they needed out of the materials available, which sometimes means constructing it out of absence and silence and the stories silence permits. Catherine is not deluded in any simple sense. She is doing what the mind does when the heart's actual history is too painful to live inside directly.

Cousin Hannah, Young tells us, never loved anyone, or loved only the image of the dead. Two women in the same house, both unable to love the living. One because she gave everything to a cause. The other because the living disappointed her, or frightened her, or simply were not the dream.

Catherine against suffrage

Let's stay with the fact that Catherine did not believe in women's right to vote.

This was not unusual among wealthy white women of her era and class. The arguments they made were various: that suffrage would disrupt the family, that women lacked the necessary political temperament, that doubling the electorate without adding new perspective served no purpose. Some opposed it because of racism, because they understood, correctly, that the logic of universal suffrage could not be contained to white women alone, and they did not want that. Some opposed it out of loyalty to the husbands and fathers and social arrangements that had, in their particular cases, been kind.

Young does not excuse Catherine. But she also does not make Catherine a simple villain for holding this view. She is interested in the specific texture of the irony: that Cousin Hannah devoted her life to a freedom the woman she loved most did not want for herself. That the relationship between them was genuine, complicated, full of real feeling on both sides, and built over this foundational disagreement. That people can love each other deeply across a chasm of this kind, and that the love does not resolve the chasm.

This is one of the places where the novel becomes historical without being didactic. Young is not delivering a lesson. She is showing you a room.

Cousin Hannah as the red cross knight

Chapter 38 reaches for medieval imagery to describe Cousin Hannah: she is a crusader, an armored figure, a knight of the suffrage campaigns riding into battle against the ogres of social arrangement. Young connects her explicitly to the Redcrosse Knight of Edmund Spenser's The Faerie Queene: a figure of allegorical virtue, armored righteousness moving through a landscape of monsters and temptations toward a goal that is always receding slightly ahead of him.

What does it mean to frame a suffragette as a knight errant? It means Young is placing the women's movement inside the oldest literary tradition for heroic struggle, the quest narrative, and insisting it belongs there. Cousin Hannah is not a footnote to the real history. She is the thing the quest was always about: the battle against the forces that would keep people from their full humanity.

And like the Redcrosse Knight, she is not without paradox. She fights for liberation while harboring her secret wish for the domestic life she publicly rejected. She embodies virtue while playing a mean game of cards. The armor has something complicated inside it. That is what makes her a knight worth following.

The music of the spheres, and what Mr. Spitzer hears

Mr. Spitzer contributes to this chapter a meditation on musica universalis: the ancient idea, traced through Pythagoras and Plato to Boethius and Kepler, that the mathematical relationships governing the cosmos express themselves as harmonics, as a music too vast and too perfect for human ears to detect directly.

Mr. Spitzer cannot hear it. He hears everything a minute late, and he hears it off-key. “The music of the spheres, the” harmony that supposedly underlies all of existence, is available to him only as an idea, a concept he can describe but not experience. He is constitutionally cut off from the very order he most wants to believe in.

Young uses this to deepen the portrait of a man who is both the most invested in the idea of order and the least capable of accessing it. His cosmic music plays on without him. He sits in the silence after the last requiem, hearing the absence of what he cannot quite reach.

Zeno's arrow, and the problem of getting anywhere

The chapter engages Zeno's paradoxes: specifically the question of whether motion is real. Zeno argued that before an arrow can reach its target, it must first travel half the distance, and before that half, half again, infinitely, which should make motion impossible. Neil deGrasse Tyson put the contemporary version of this simply: there are an infinite number of steps to a finite destination.

Young is using this not as a puzzle about physics but as a map of her characters' inner lives. Catherine cannot get anywhere from the bed. Not because she lacks the will, exactly, but because each step toward the real world requires another half-step of preparation, and another, and the destination keeps dividing ahead of her. Mr. Spitzer is always in transit, always arriving too late. Even Cousin Hannah, for all her relentless forward motion, was never fully reconciled with peace, always in the next battle, never at rest, the destination perpetually just over the next horizon.

The novel does not offer you a way to solve Zeno's paradox. It offers you three people living inside it.

What to hold onto

If Chapter 38 feels like a great deal of philosophy stacked on top of a simple domestic situation, here is what anchors it: this is a chapter about two women who loved each other genuinely and could not fully reach each other. One because she was always moving toward the next campaign. The other because she was always retreating into the next dream.

They admired qualities in each other they could not embody themselves. They disappointed each other in ways they could not fully name. They shared a household and a history and a disagreement so fundamental it was almost structural, and they loved each other anyway, across all of it.

Young writes about this kind of love (the love that doesn't resolve its contradictions, that carries its irony inside it like a stone) with more patience and precision than almost anyone. Chapter 38 is one of the places where that patience pays off.

guide-14-the-black-coachman:
Chapter 14: The Black Coachman

← Chapter 13 · Guide Home · Chapter 15 →

Research notes: Chapter 14

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer · Vera Cartwheel

Symbols: Horses and Carriages

Philosophy: Astrology, Alchemy, and Esoterica

Allusions: Gambling and Playing Cards · Suicide in History and Literature · The History of Opium

Chapter 14 is the longest chapter we’ve encountered so far, and the most demanding. It asks you to sit inside two minds at once (Catherine’s hallucinatory one and Mr. Spitzer’s bewildered, sorrowful one) for a very long time, as they talk past each other, toward each other, and sometimes through each other in the dark.

If you find yourself losing the thread, that’s fine. You’re supposed to. Catherine loses the thread too. So does Mr. Spitzer. The chapter is partly about what happens to conversation when one person is tethered to reality by the thinnest cord and the other is barely tethered at all.

Stay with it. By the end you’ll know things about Mr. Spitzer that will change how you read him for the rest of the novel.

What actually happens in Chapter 14

Vera is still wandering the estate grounds, and the chapter begins at “the grave of the black coachman”: the old family servant who drove Catherine’s father’s carriage. From there, the chapter pivots into a long reconstruction of Catherine’s obsession with locating the black coachman, her endless interrogations of Mr. Spitzer about where he was buried, what happened to the four white horses, whether her instructions for his funeral were properly carried out.

Around and beneath this obsession, the chapter slowly delivers what we’ve been circling since the novel began: Mr. Spitzer’s brother fell from a tall building. It was not an accident. His brother had a suicidal streak. Mr. Spitzer has been living in the aftermath of that death ever since: wearing his brother’s cufflinks, finding his brother’s cigarette still warm in his coat pocket, being mistaken for his brother on city streets, sometimes not correcting the mistake.

The chapter ends with Catherine still talking after Mr. Spitzer has quietly left the room, addressing his empty chair, unable to register his absence. She will talk until the stars fade and sleep takes her. The night, she says, is the only light.

The black coachman, and why Catherine cannot let him go

The black coachman is not a person Catherine knew intimately. He was a servant: the man who drove the carriage, who knew the roads and the horses and the directions of the winds. He survived everyone in the family, just by a shade. Catherine had arranged, years ago, that he should be buried by the sea with “the carriage and the four white horses,” in his livery and high silk hat, so that he could go on driving under the earth.

Why does this matter so much to her? Young gives us the answer in a single sentence: “If she could find him, she could perhaps find herself, the bewildered passenger.”

The black coachman is Catherine’s figure for orientation. He is the one who knew which way to go, which road to take, how to bring the carriage safely around the long avenue. In a life that has dissolved entirely into hallucination (where even Mr. Spitzer’s reality is uncertain, where time has stopped on the bedside clocks, where the guests are all dead or imaginary) the black coachman is the last possible landmark. Find him, and the carriage stops spinning. Find him, and you know which city you’re in.

She cannot find him. Mr. Spitzer maintains his silence. So she keeps asking, evening after evening, year after year, circling the question the way a carriage circles an avenue with no end.

What we learn about Mr. Spitzer’s brother

Chapter 14 is where Young finally lays out, in full, the story of the twin brothers.

Peron, the brother, was the quick one, the brilliant one, the gambler. He moved in racing circles and shady company. He kept a double life that Mr. Spitzer is still discovering, years later, when strangers on city streets call out to him with debts to settle or old love affairs to resume. He was capable, Young tells us, “of far greater variations on one theme than” Mr. Spitzer, who is cautious and slow and literal-minded and has, in his own assessment, led “the most retired, the most unassuming life imaginable.”

Peron fell from a tall building. There is almost no doubt in Mr. Spitzer’s mind that it was deliberate. He had a suicidal streak. The day of his death was, according to the dream books Mr. Spitzer has been secretly consulting, a lucky day: a great day for new adventures, “an excellent day for beginning a new relationship or ending an old love.” It was, for Mr. Spitzer, the unluckiest day of his life.

And here is the thing Young gives us quietly, almost in passing: Mr. Spitzer had dreamed, long before his brother’s death, that he himself had fallen. He had climbed a rope toward heaven, heard silver trumpets and the fading voices of violins, and then lost his footing and fallen. He woke. He was fine. He was still sitting at Catherine’s bedside, in plain view. And yet; something of Mr. Spitzer died when his beloved brother was buried, he will say later. The clods of earth fell on that other face, and they fell on something in Mr. Spitzer too.

He has been wearing his brother’s cufflinks, double horses’ heads carved in mother-of-pearl, to his brother’s funeral and every day since. He carries his brother’s ivory-headed cane. The cigarette still warm in his coat pocket. The playing card dropping from the sleeve of his brother’s purple dressing gown. These are not supernatural occurrences. They are the texture of grief that has nowhere to go.

The case of Spitzer versus Spitzer

Catherine, in one of her sharpest moments in the chapter, names what has consumed Mr. Spitzer’s entire adult life: “the case of Spitzer versus Spitzer.”

He is both the defense and the accusation. He is the lawyer who has outlived the man he should have been, or who has lived the life the other was supposed to live, and he cannot settle the case. He does not know which brother survived and which one died. He does not know if the thoughts he thinks are his own or his brother’s. He finds things in his pockets that are not his. He is recognized on streets he has never walked. He sometimes does not correct people who call him by his brother’s name, and in not correcting them, he lets his brother live a little longer.

Which is shadow and which is man? Catherine asks this, and it is not a hallucination. It is the most accurate question anyone has ever posed to Mr. Spitzer, and he has no answer.

Catherine as the unexpected authority

One of the most interesting things Young does in this chapter is establish Catherine (the opium addict, the hallucinatory invalid, the woman who has not left her bed in decades) as the person who most clearly sees Mr. Spitzer.

It is Mr. Spitzer who walks about in the world, but it is “my mother who knew, through her absence from the world, the world.”

She knows he has been reading dream books in poor neighborhoods. She knows he sometimes wears another’s high silk hat by mistake and doesn’t realize it’s his own. She knows that his music stopped before his brother died, not after, even though Mr. Spitzer has been telling himself and everyone else that the death was the cause. She knows “he placed a bet on a dead horse” at a parimutuel window without knowing what he was doing. She knows, in Catherine’s precise and devastating phrase, that he is the only living person she has ever found it necessary to doubt, because everyone else in her life is imaginary, and Mr. Spitzer is stubbornly, confusingly real.

The person most disconnected from ordinary reality is the one who sees the real man most clearly. This is one of Young’s great recurring propositions, and Chapter 14 is its fullest demonstration.

What to watch for as you keep reading

Light spoilers: This section hints at what happens later in the novel. Skip it if you want to meet the story fresh.

The black coachman will not be found. That’s not what the search is for. The search is Catherine’s way of insisting that something in her life was once oriented, was once moving purposefully through the world in a known direction. The carriage keeps circling because there is no destination, but there was a coachman, and he knew the roads.

Mr. Spitzer’s relationship to his brother will deepen and complicate across the entire novel. What Young has established here is the basic grammar of it: one quick, one slow; one dead, one surviving; one who took the last chance, one who is still waiting. Every time you see Mr. Spitzer hesitate, fumble, arrive too late, maintain his silence, remember this chapter.

Notice that Catherine sets a place at the table for the dead. She says this plainly, as a domestic fact: the table is “always laid for twelve or thirteen or fourteen guests,” and there is “a place set for the dead.” This is one of the most quietly extraordinary sentences in a novel full of them. She is not being morbid. She is being hospitable. In Catherine’s world, the dead are expected.

guide-18-the-long-night:
Chapter 18: The Long Night

← Chapter 17 · Guide Home · Chapter 19 →

Content note: This chapter strongly suggests that the young Vera has been sexually assaulted, and it shows an adult frightening a child into silence.

Research notes: Chapter 18

Characters: Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Duality and Doubles · Memory and the Past

Symbols: Twins and Doubles

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Chapter 18 is one of the most important chapters in the entire novel, and also one of the most difficult to hold in your hands. It is the night after the revelation, stretched out to its full impossible length, Miss MacIntosh talking and talking in the dark, holding Vera in her arms, talking until dawn.

You may find it overwhelming. That is the point. Vera is overwhelmed. Young is giving you the experience of being inside that room, inside that night, without the mercy of distance or summary.

Read it slowly. Let the proverbs accumulate. Let the voice shift. There are things said in this chapter that the rest of the novel will spend hundreds of pages unfolding.

What actually happens in Chapter 18

The night continues. Miss MacIntosh holds Vera in the crook of her arm, her bald head brushing against Vera’s cheek, and she talks. She talks in two registers, sometimes simultaneously: the familiar Miss MacIntosh of proverbs and schedules and common sense, and another voice underneath, raw and grieving and ancient, crying out about ephemeral life, the missing breast, the hair that was never hers, the kiss that was never given.

She tries to persuade Vera that nothing happened. She promises that by morning, the wig will be back, the red hair gleaming, everything restored to its usual place. She scolds Vera for entering without knocking. She threatens her: “if ever I told what I had seen, she would kill me, for it was nothing another should see.”

By dawn, Miss MacIntosh is asking Vera geography questions again. What is “the chief industry of northern Michigan?” Where is Egg Harbor? Where is the Battle of Shiloh? The night is being packed away.

The chapter ends with Miss MacIntosh rocking Vera toward sleep, whispering that she lost her hair in Vera’s service, that when she came she had her own hair, a thick pale gold mane. “Tempus fugit. Will you believe me when I say that I am not so old as you think?”

The two voices

Young built Miss MacIntosh’s voice in Chapter 18 on two frequencies running at once, and you need to hear both of them to understand what the chapter is doing.

The first voice is the one we know: proverbs, schedules, common sense, almanac facts, moral instruction. It surfaces throughout the night, trying to reassert normalcy. “One dupe would be as impossible” as one twin. “The old ways are best because they have been tried.” We will run a mile and knock down tenpins and say our lessons. This voice is performing recovery, insisting with increasing desperation that what happened can be folded back into the ordinary life of the household.

The second voice breaks through in the long crying passages. “Oh, how ephemeral are we! Oh, how transient were we, my child! The earth has known us not. Our mothers and our fathers never knew us.” God pity the left breast already gone. God “pity us all, for we are” “sinned against more than we are sinning. I can go no farther.” Where is my hair? This is not the Miss MacIntosh of the schoolroom. This is someone much older and more sorrowful, someone who has been carrying something alone for a very long time, and who is, in this one night, in this dark room, with this one child, briefly allowed to put it down.

The two voices are not in conflict. They are the same person. Young has spent seventeen chapters showing you the first voice. Chapter 18 shows you the second. Both are true. Neither is the whole truth.

The secret man and the secret woman

Early in the chapter, Vera arrives at a thought that is one of the most careful things in the novel. She decides that what loomed above her in the darkness was not a “man but only such a man as is hidden in the woman, just as there must also be, in every man, a woman secret and recessive, the forever fading image of the other self.”

Young is reaching here toward something the language of 1965 could barely name, and she does it not by naming it but by making it universal. Every person contains their opposite. The secret self that society will not accommodate doesn’t belong only to Miss MacIntosh; it belongs to everyone, hidden at different depths, pressing differently against the surface. Miss MacIntosh’s secret is simply more visible now, because her wig is on the chair post.

This is why Young cannot be reduced to a simple reading of this chapter. She is not saying Miss MacIntosh is a man. She is not saying Miss MacIntosh is a woman disguised. She is saying that Miss MacIntosh is a person whose inner life exceeded the categories available to contain it, and who spent decades building a persona of radical ordinariness as the only shelter available. The plainness was armor. The proverbs were a wall. And underneath, all her life, that second voice.

The threat and the tenderness

Two things happen near the end of the chapter that seem to contradict each other, and Young puts them almost side by side.

First, the threat: she would kill me if I told. “It was nothing another should see. She had never seen it herself except in a mirror.” This is Miss MacIntosh afraid: afraid with the specific fear of someone whose survival has depended on concealment for so long that the concealment has become the self. The threat is real. It is also the most naked moment of vulnerability in the chapter, because it reveals exactly how much is at stake for her in Vera’s silence.

Then, almost immediately: “she rocked me back and forth in her arms.” She kissed Vera’s eyelids and eyes, her hair, her palms, the soles of her feet. She said she had lost her hair in Vera’s service. That she was no older “than the day she was born.” “Age is the most difficult thing to achieve.”

Threat and tenderness. Concealment and confession. The attempt to erase the night and the refusal, at the same time, to fully let go of it. Young holds these things together without resolving them, because they cannot be resolved. This is what it is to be a person whose secret has been discovered by someone they love.

Memory as the chapter’s frame

The chapter opens and closes with Vera reminding us that she is not sure what Miss MacIntosh actually said. “I am not sure now that Miss MacIntosh did say all I remember her as saying.” “Memory is surrounded by the unknown.” “Memory sometimes provides the one flower more than ever blossomed. Memory sometimes omits the only flower there really was.”

This framing matters. Everything in Chapter 18 is Vera’s memory of a night that happened when she was fourteen, filtered through years of reflection, shaped “by the illumination larger than that of any instant.” The proverbs, the confessions, the geography questions, the rocking and the kissing and the threat: Vera is certain these happened. She is not certain of the exact words.

Young is being scrupulous about the nature of memory while also trusting the emotional truth of it. We may not have the transcript. We have the experience. And the experience left “the heavy, claw-shaped mark of” Miss MacIntosh’s hand on Vera’s forehead, which is the one thing Vera knows was real: “there, that will teach you to remember me.” There, that will teach you charity.

What to watch for as you keep reading

Light spoilers: This section hints at what happens later in the novel. Skip it if you want to meet the story fresh.

Miss MacIntosh will leave. The novel has been telling us this since Chapter 12, when she warned Vera that she might some day retire. Now you understand what departure means for Miss MacIntosh, and what it will mean for Vera. It will not be the retirement of an old nursemaid. It will be the disappearance of the only person who could confirm Vera’s reality.

The wig on the carved chair post. Young places it there and does not take it away. When Miss MacIntosh asks where her red wig is (and then answers that it is on the chair post, in plain sight, while she herself is right here) she is describing the situation exactly. The disguise is visible. The person is visible. They are both present. They are not the same.

“A woman, a wig-maker, and a wild horse are the three things never to be trusted.” This proverb appears in Miss MacIntosh’s mouth in the long night, and it may be the only moment in the novel where she makes a joke about herself. Or it may not be a joke at all. Either way, Young put it there deliberately.

  • The heavy
  • O tempora!
  • Tempus fugit
guide-73-the-stillborn-and-the-fathers:
Chapter 73: The Stillborn and the Fathers

← Chapter 72 · Guide Home · Chapter 74 →

Content note: The Esther Longtree chapters (72 to 81) deal with stillbirth and pregnancy loss, rape, infanticide, racist violence including lynching, and cruelty to children. This chapter describes stillbirths and the hidden remains of infants.

Research notes: Chapter 73

Characters: Abigail Porter · Coleman Bluebough · Esther Longtree · Joe Goldberg · Phoebe · The Chicago Detective · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Duality and Doubles · Identity and the Self · Motherhood, Pregnancy, and Birth · Music, Sound, and Silence

Symbols: Birds · Pregnancy, Birth, and Children · Silence and Deafness · Twins and Doubles · Weddings and Funerals

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Greek Mythology · Pregnancy, Abortion, and Midwifery

Chapter 72 gave you Esther Longtree in her fullness: the little shadow boxer, the defiant hope, the philosophical reach toward the cosmos. Chapter 73 goes deeper into the particular. Into the texture of her loss. Into the faces, or the fragments of faces, of the children she has carried and buried. Into the men who wrote her letters at the end of their lives, asking about children who were never born whole.

This is a chapter about what silence costs, and what it protects.

You should know before you begin that some of what Esther describes here is disturbing: an encounter in a graveyard that was not consensual, a labor that produced nothing, a life of grief conducted almost entirely in secret, inside a body that everyone can see is pregnant and no one can see is also a graveyard. Young does not look away from any of this. Neither should you.

What Actually Happens

Esther continues her account, which is both monologue and meditation, both addressed to Vera (who is presumably nearby, or imagining this, or somehow receiving it) and addressed to no one, to the air, to the stillborn who whisper in her ears.

She describes the children she has carried as fragments: “an eye, an ear, a long gold hair, a fingernail, a cobweb,” a snowflake. Not whole babies, or not always. Sometimes something more nebulous than a baby, something that was almost a child and then wasn’t. She has buried them everywhere: in streams, under snow, in tree stumps, in the autumn leaves. The undertaker has complained that she brings him no business, because she hides the evidence. This is not indifference; it is the opposite. She cannot bear to hand them over to strangers.

She describes the fathers: the traveling men, the salesmen, the transients. Most are weak, sterile in some essential way she cannot diagnose. As they die, they write her letters. They remember her vividly. They ask: did the child live? They want to know they have left something behind. Esther, advised by her old drunken doctor to preserve the dying man’s vanity and peace, does not answer. She keeps their illusions intact. The truth (that there is no child, or that what arrived was a snowflake, a cobweb, a breath of something that did not take) is not something she can give them. It is also not something she can fully bear herself.

The Chicago detective appears, circling. He is investigating something (possibly the disappearance of the stillborn children, possibly other crimes) and Esther fears arrest, fears trial, fears standing before a jury of women who will judge her without understanding her condition. She has done nothing wrong. She has also hidden everything.

And then there is Joe Goldberg.

Joe Goldberg, Champion Featherweight

He is the one father Esther cannot quite remember. This is the novel’s precise reversal: the weak fathers, the sterile salesmen, the men who barely registered in her life; she remembers them clearly. The strong one, the champion, the featherweight boxer who was at the peak of his existence when he knew her; he is lost in clouds, like the weight of a feather in her mind. Young is telling you something here about how memory works: it keeps what hurt least, most clearly, and buries what was most overwhelming. Joe Goldberg wrote her long, anguished letters as he wasted away from tuberculosis. He remembered her as the greatest victory of his life: greater than any fight. He remembered meeting her in a graveyard on a foggy, windy night. He remembered knocking the nose off a stone angel. He remembered taking her against her will. He wrote asking for remembrance, for forgiveness, for confirmation that his child lived. Esther remembers the graveyard. She does not remember him clearly. She cannot anchor his face.

What Young is doing here is both precise and painful. Joe Goldberg assaulted Esther. He knows this; his letter asks for forgiveness, which implies acknowledgment of what he did. He has, in his dying days, turned it into something else in his memory (the “peak of his existence, his greatest victory”) which is what men who have done this often do. Esther cannot remember him clearly because the experience did not belong to her in any way that would make a clear memory. It was done to her. The blur is honest.

She does not answer his letter.

The Birth of Nothing

One of the chapter’s most quietly devastating passages describes a labor: Esther endures all the pain of childbirth (the contractions, the hours, the full physical breaking) and delivers nothing. Her body goes through the complete experience of birth and the child is not there, or is there as a feather, a white drift, something that might be a message from the silence or might be the absence of a message.

She lies alone afterward. She does not call anyone. She does not bring the nothing to the undertaker. She gets up. She goes back to the Greasy Spoon. This is the most extreme form of what Esther carries: not just grief for the children who came and did not live, but the labor itself spent on absence. Her body has done everything right. Everything has gone through the correct motions. And still: nothing. Young refuses to explain this medically or symbolically. It simply happens, the way loss simply happens, without adequate cause or sufficient reason.

The Silence

The old drunken doctor’s advice to Esther is one of the chapter’s key moments of pragmatic wisdom: don’t answer the dying fathers. Let them believe the child lives. What good does the truth do? They are dying. Their belief in the child is all they have. Give them that. Esther follows this advice. She does not answer the letters. She does not confirm or deny. She keeps the stillborn hidden. She carries the truth of her situation inside a body that broadcasts it to anyone who looks (she is visibly, obviously pregnant; she has been obviously pregnant for years) and still no one in the town knows what she actually knows. They have theories. They have suspicions. They have the undertaker’s complaint. They do not have the truth.

This silence is Esther’s great act. It protects the dying. It protects her. It costs her enormously. She is the only one who knows the full inventory of loss (every fragment, every snowflake, every cobweb that was meant to be a child) and she has agreed, by her silence, to be the only keeper of that knowledge. There is no one she can tell. The stillborn whisper in her ears. She listens to them and says nothing outward.

The Accusation

The Chicago detective is, in this chapter, still circling: still a threat rather than a fully materialized presence. But the threat is specific: Esther fears that her hidden stillborn children will be read as evidence of murder. That she will stand trial for the deaths of children she did not kill, that she loved, that she buried with her own hands in places she chose because she could not bear to hand them to strangers.

This is one of the novel’s most quietly accurate observations about how women’s grief is treated. Esther has lost every child she has carried. She has suffered the full physical and emotional catastrophe of this over and over. And the world around her (embodied in the detective, in the undertaker, in the jury of women she imagines judging her) reads her behavior not as grief but as guilt. She has hidden the evidence. She has refused to explain herself. She must be guilty of something.

She is guilty of nothing except surviving.

The Stillborn as Fragments

Young’s most distinctive choice in this chapter is the way she describes what Esther delivers: not always whole babies, but sometimes only their parts. “An eye, an ear, a long gold hair, a fingernail, a cobweb.” A snowflake.

This is, on one level, medically recognizable: very early losses sometimes produce only fragments. But Young is also doing something larger. The stillborn as fragments accumulate into a portrait: if you arranged all of Esther’s losses side by side, you would have, between them, something that adds up to a child. All the eyes, all the fingernails, all the gold hairs. They are dispersed through years and seasons, buried in different places, but they belong together. They are, taken together, the child that Esther has been waiting for all along. The little shadow boxer, still moving inside her, is the one who might be whole.

The Epizeuxis

Beginning in this chapter, Esther’s speech develops a new feature: she repeats words three times in immediate succession. Young, Young, Young. Gone, gone, gone. Baby, baby, baby. This repetition is called epizeuxis in rhetoric, the insistent restatement of a word for emotional emphasis, and it gives Esther’s voice a new quality, something between a stutter and an incantation. It sounds like grief working through language, like a mind returning compulsively to the same unbearable point. It sounds like someone trying to make a word real by saying it enough times. It sounds like someone trying to make something stay. It is also, as To All My Darlings notes, potentially comic in other contexts. Young holds both registers simultaneously: the grief is real, the repetition is also slightly absurd, Esther is both tragic and eccentric, and that combination, not one or the other, is what makes her one of the great characters in this novel.

What to Hold Onto

The stillborn as fragments: an eye, an ear, a fingernail, a cobweb. Each one a child that was almost. All of them together, a child that might still come.

Joe Goldberg’s letters, vivid with a memory Esther cannot share. The strongest father, barely a feather in her mind. The blur is the honest part.

The birth of nothing. Her body going through every motion, the hours, the pain. And then: a white feather, drifting down. She gets up. She goes back to work. The silence she keeps for the dying fathers. The enormous cost of letting them believe. The doctor’s advice: preserve their peace. What good does the truth do?

And the little shadow boxer, still there, still moving. Still two hearts.

guide-76-the-trial-she-welcomes:
Chapter 76: The Trial She Welcomes

← Chapter 75 · Guide Home · Chapter 77 →

Content note: The Esther Longtree chapters (72 to 81) deal with stillbirth and pregnancy loss, rape, infanticide, racist violence including lynching, and cruelty to children. This chapter deals with infant death and abortion.

Research notes: Chapter 76

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Esther Longtree · Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer · Tabitha · The Chicago Detective · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Duality and Doubles · Motherhood, Pregnancy, and Birth · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Angels, Devils, and Myth · Pregnancy, Birth, and Children · Twins and Doubles · Weddings and Funerals

Philosophy: Freud and Jung · Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Greek Mythology · Homer's Epics · Pregnancy, Abortion, and Midwifery · The History of Opium

This is the last chapter devoted to Esther Longtree’s extended monologue. Over Chapters 72 through 76, Young has given her more sustained attention than almost any other character in the novel outside of Vera herself, and what she has given her is not a resolved story but an accumulating one: more loss, more history, more ambiguity, more of the spectral children and the fathers who disappear and the detective who circles.

Chapter 76 brings Esther to a threshold. She has feared the trial the detective threatens. She has hidden everything she could hide. She has kept her silence with extraordinary discipline. In this chapter, she turns. She begins, strangely, to welcome the idea of the trial, not because she expects justice, but because the trial would at least be an acknowledgment that she exists, that what happened to her was real, that the quiet murders, the children who came and did not live, were worth the world’s attention.

She is also tired. Tired of the detective, tired of the fathers, tired of carrying everything alone. And she reveals, in passing, the darkest pocket of her history: she killed her twin sister in the womb.

What Actually Happens

Esther turns over her “successful conceptions” in her mind and concludes they may have been her worst mistakes: “her unfulfilled abortions, her many births.” She is baffled by her last triumphant pregnancy, the “diffused radiance” she feels. She still believes in it. She still feels two hearts. The detective pursues his quiet mysteries: the murders where no bodies are missed, the deaths that go unrecorded, the crimes that only he seems to notice. He uncovers murderers everywhere. He solves everything except his own case. A new loud crime will break, Esther thinks, and the quiet mysteries will remain quiet forever. This is how it always works: the spectacular displaces the invisible. The stillborn children hover around her, robed and bloodless, watching her with innocent smiles, sometimes applauding her act of intercourse as if cheering on the very process that produced them and failed them. This is one of the strangest images in the chapter: the dead children as audience, as witnesses to their own impossible origin.

She killed her twin sister in the womb, she says. She does not explain how, or whether this is literal or metaphorical, or whether she was conscious of doing it, or whether she simply survived and the other did not and she has always carried this as a killing. She notes the question of twins who murder: one twin who kills the other, then accuses the dead one of having done the murdering. She knows this structure. She wonders if she is the twin who killed or the twin who was wrongly accused. The detective’s historical parallel surfaces here: To All My Darlings mentions Robert Ledru, a French detective of the 1880s famous for solving crimes, who discovered through investigation that he was himself the murderer he had been hunting; he had killed while sleepwalking and had no conscious memory of it. The detective who is also the criminal. Young’s Chicago detective operates in this same inverted logic. Esther contemplates the trial with a new quality: she begins to welcome it. Mass infanticide, she supposes, is what she would be charged with. She finds, unexpectedly, a kind of comfort in the cosmic scale of her evidence: her body, nature, her memories, all the things that cannot be produced in a courtroom but that she carries absolutely. Let them try to prosecute what cannot be seen. Let the quiet mysteries finally make noise. She wonders why Cupid has missed her. She has loved. Her heart is broken. The god of love appears to have aimed elsewhere.

She closes knitting and unraveling a black hood: the color of night, the shape of birth, the garment she makes and unmakes because making it is the act of faith she can sustain and the child who will wear it is not yet here to receive it.

The Twin She Killed in the Womb

This is the revelation Young has been withholding for five chapters, and she delivers it with Esther’s characteristic obliqueness, not as confession but as fact, dropped into the middle of Esther’s ongoing meditation on guilt and innocence.

She killed her twin in the womb. This may be literal: vanishing twin syndrome, in which one twin is absorbed by the other early in pregnancy, is real and not uncommon, occurring in an estimated one in eight pregnancies that begin as multiples. The surviving twin has no consciousness of the process. Young gives Esther consciousness of it, or the feeling of consciousness, the retrospective conviction that something was done, that she survived at a cost.

It may also be metaphorical: the twin who did not survive, the self that Esther might have been if the first loss had not happened, the double she has been mourning all along without knowing it. The mud baby. The tall child. The little shadow boxer. All of them may be the twin: the other Esther, the one who did not make it out.

The twins who murder each other, one kills the other and then accuses the dead one of having done the killing, appears as a question Esther poses to herself. She does not answer it. The question is: which twin is she? The killer, or the one who is blamed for a killing she didn’t commit? She has been accused of killing the detective’s children. She has not killed anything. She may have killed her twin. She may have simply survived. She cannot tell the difference anymore, and possibly there is no difference to tell.

To All My Darlings notes that this twin dynamic echoes the story of Joachim and Peron Spitzer: the twin brothers mentioned elsewhere in the novel, where one killed the other and took his identity. The structure of twin-murder-and-impersonation runs through the novel’s mythology: the wrong person wearing the dead one’s face, the guilty party walking free under the innocent one’s name.

The Stillborn as Audience

Young’s most unsettling image in this chapter is the spectral children watching Esther during intercourse: robed, bloodless, hovering, sometimes applauding. They are witnesses to the act that produced them and failed them. They are the audience for the process that keeps generating new versions of them without ever producing a living one.

This image is disturbing and also, in Young’s precise way, logical. The stillborn have nowhere else to be. They cannot be anywhere except in Esther’s consciousness, because that is the only space they were ever given. They did not get a world. They got a mother. So they attend to her life with the complete attention of those who have nothing else.

They watch with innocent smiles. They applaud. They are not accusing her. They are witnessing. This is what Esther has always been unable to give them, a witness, and here they return the gift, imperfectly, from the wrong side.

Welcoming the Trial

The shift in this chapter, from fear of the trial to something approaching welcome, is one of the most significant movements in Esther’s arc. She has spent five chapters afraid of the jury of women who would judge her, the detective who would prosecute her, the public exposure of her hidden stillborn. In Chapter 76, she turns toward it. What has changed? Partly exhaustion: she is tired of the silence, tired of carrying everything alone, tired of being invisible. Partly a recognition that the trial, however unjust, would at least acknowledge that something happened to her: that the quiet murders were murders, that the children existed, that her body was not simply malfunctioning in private but was the site of a history that deserved attention. She also recognizes that her evidence is cosmic and unassailable (her body, nature, memory, the fullness of what she knows) even though none of it is admissible in a courtroom. Let them try to prosecute what cannot be seen. The quiet mysteries will probably remain quiet forever: some louder crime will come along and displace them. But for a moment, contemplating the trial, Esther imagines herself finally, loudly, in the record.

Knitting and Unraveling the Black Hood

The chapter’s closing image is Esther’s most enduring domestic act: she knits a black hood and then unravels it and then knits it again. The hood is the color of night. It is the shape of a beginning: the garment that covers the head at birth, that signals the start of a life.

She cannot finish it. Or she will not. Finishing it would mean the child is here to receive it, and the child is not here yet. So she knits and unravels, knits and unravels: the act of preparation maintained as an act of faith rather than an act of completion. This is Esther’s version of Penelope’s weaving: the work that is done and undone to keep the future open, to prevent the arrival of the wrong ending.

She is wilder than people think, the chapter notes. She runs. She laughs. She endures. Her life is bounded by routine and also marked by moments of freedom that no one from the outside has seen. She is not only what the detective’s investigation reveals. She is not only what the town’s gossip constructs. She is the woman who knits a black hood at night and unravels it at dawn and starts again, because the child is coming and she will be ready.

What to Hold Onto

The twin she killed in the womb, or did not kill, or simply survived: the question she cannot answer, the guilt she cannot separate from survival. The robed, bloodless stillborn, hovering around her, watching with innocent smiles, sometimes applauding. The dead as audience to the life that couldn’t give them a life.

The shift from terror of the trial to welcome of it: let the quiet murders finally make noise. Let the detective try to prosecute what cannot be seen.

Cupid who has missed her. She has loved. Her heart is broken. The god of love appears to have aimed elsewhere.

And Esther knitting and unraveling the black hood. Night, birth, faith, the work that is done and undone to keep the future open. The child is coming. She will be ready.

This is the last chapter that is wholly Esther’s. Carry her with you into what comes next.

guide-75-the-mud-baby:
Chapter 75: The Mud Baby

← Chapter 74 · Guide Home · Chapter 76 →

Content note: The Esther Longtree chapters (72 to 81) deal with stillbirth and pregnancy loss, rape, infanticide, racist violence including lynching, and cruelty to children. This chapter describes the drowning of an infant and hints at incest.

Research notes: Chapter 75

Characters: Esther Longtree

Themes: Guilt, Innocence, and Justice · Identity and the Self

Symbols: Pregnancy, Birth, and Children · Roses and Flowers · The Sea and Water

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft · William James and Pragmatism

Allusions: Fairy Tales and Folklore · Pregnancy, Abortion, and Midwifery

This is the deepest and most disturbing chapter of Esther’s sequence, and it needs to be approached carefully.

The previous chapters gave you Esther in her fullness: her hope, her philosophy, her humor, her grief held in balance. Chapter 75 goes somewhere darker: a particular dead child, the one that keeps coming back. The mud baby. A body thrown into the river by a fisherman who may have been dreaming. A suspicion about the child’s father that Esther approaches and retreats from and cannot quite name. A body bigger in death than it was in life, covered with mud and brambles, returning in dreams “with a funeral wreath hanging from” its navel, its face lit by “awful starlight which was not starlight.”

Young does not soften any of this. You are not meant to feel comfortable. Esther’s story has arrived at its most unresolved and most haunted material, and the chapter holds it all without resolution: the mud baby’s ambiguous paternity, the implied incest, the body in the river, the detective’s accusations, the war coming that will make all of it seem small. Esther survives through it. She always survives. That survival is not peace.

What Actually Happens

Esther’s body swells “like a face under water”: a phrase that gives her pregnancy the quality of something drowned, something submerged and seen through distortion. She wonders whether what is growing inside her is a child or a benign tumor. She has wondered this before. The question is not rhetorical: she genuinely cannot always tell. Her certainty about the little shadow boxer (two hearts, the little shadow foot) exists alongside this uncertainty about the other thing, the growth that may or may not be what she hopes.

The detective comes again. He accuses her, again, of murdering his children. He raped her, she knows; she was already pregnant when he came, the child in her womb already dead. He claims it now as his. His accusation, that she killed what he says he fathered, is one of the chapter’s precise inversions: the man who violated her now presents himself as the bereaved father, the wronged party, the one seeking justice for a death she caused.

There is a particular dead baby in this chapter: the mud baby. Esther gave birth to it, and with the help of a fisherman (a compassionate man who may have been dreaming, who may have been sunstruck, whose state of consciousness is left uncertain) she “wrapped it in a gunny sack” and threw it “into the river above the dam where the current was rapid.” The river took it. The river did not keep it.

It comes back. In dreams, in nightmares, in waking visions. Bigger in death than it was in life. Covered with mud and brambles. “A funeral wreath hanging from its navel.” Walking sometimes, lying in a coffin-like boat at other times, whistling like a policeman. Its face lit by something that is not starlight. It is ugly and beautiful simultaneously: “glass, twigs, brambles, mud, sand, starlight.” It teases her. It will not answer any question.

The child whistles like a policeman. Esther’s father is a policeman. The chapter does not make this explicit connection; it places these two facts adjacent to each other and lets the reader understand what Esther herself cannot fully face: there is a possibility that her father, the night policeman, is the father of the mud baby. She does not confess this. She does not deny it. She has not borne witness against herself, because her father is the policeman, and to accuse him would be to accuse herself in the eyes of a system that would not protect her.

She imagines an eldest son who will not come indoors. She leaves food for him. She calls to him. He does not come.

The chapter closes with Esther’s dark pragmatism: there is “going to be another war soon, killing all the men and some of the children, and one or two old murders should not have mattered so much, especially if it was nothing murdered.”

The Mud Baby

The mud baby is the chapter’s central image, and it is one of the most unsettling figures in the novel. It is a particular dead child, a specific loss from a specific labor, that has taken on the quality of all of Esther’s losses simultaneously. It returns because it was not properly grieved, or because it cannot be grieved properly, or because some of the circumstances of its conception cannot be acknowledged and so the grief has nowhere to complete itself.

Young describes it in accumulation: mud baby, “seed that swelled into a star,” “glass, twigs, brambles, mud, sand, starlight.” It is assembled from what the river gave it and what Esther’s memory added. It is bigger in death than in life, which is the precise description of how unresolved loss works in the psyche. The thing that could not be held grows larger in its absence than it ever was in its presence. It spreads its fingers wide. It will not answer questions.

The “funeral wreath hanging from its navel” is the chapter’s strangest and most perfectly calibrated detail. The navel is the point of connection between mother and child: the umbilical cord’s trace. A funeral wreath hanging there marks the death of that connection, the formal mourning of what the umbilicus joined and then, in death, still joins. The wreath is for the child. The wreath is also for the bond.

The Fisherman

He is the chapter’s only figure of uncomplicated compassion, and he is barely present. He helps Esther wrap the mud baby and throw it into the river. He does this in a state of uncertainty; he wonders if he is dreaming, if he is sunstruck, if what he is participating in is real. Young gives him this uncertainty deliberately: the witness who helps but cannot fully confirm what he has witnessed. He asks no questions. He helps. He goes back to his fishing.

He is the only man in Esther’s story who is present at a moment of her greatest vulnerability and does nothing to compound it. He does not accuse her. He does not claim the child. He does not write her letters later asking for confirmation of a life. He simply helps her carry what she cannot carry alone, and then he goes away.

His compassion is so minimal and so unelaborated that it stands out sharply against the landscape of men in Esther’s life. This is what help looks like in this world: a man who may have been dreaming, who asked no questions, who helped throw a gunny sack into a river, and who did not stay.

The Father Who Is the Policeman

Young places two facts side by side: the mud baby whistles like a policeman. Esther’s father is a policeman. She has not borne witness against herself, because her father is the policeman, and her father is the law.

The implication is incest. Young does not state it directly. Esther cannot state it directly: her father holds authority over her in every sense, legal and familial. To accuse him would be to enter a system where she has no protection and he has every power. The Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination, which To All My Darlings mentions in this context, applies here with a particular bitter irony: Esther cannot testify because the testimony would implicate not only herself but the very figure of authority who surrounds her. Her father is the policeman. The policeman is the law. The law would not believe her.

The mud baby’s whistle, that policeman’s whistle, is the most disturbing detail in the chapter precisely because of its mundanity. It is not supernatural. It is just the sound that a dead child makes when it walks back to its mother in her dreams, and it sounds exactly like her father going about his work.

The Detective’s Accusation

He comes again, and his accusation in this chapter takes its fullest form: he claims the dead children as his, and he accuses Esther of murdering them. This is the complete inversion. He raped her. The children (such as they were, the dead things, the stillborn, the fragments) were produced by his assault. He has now claimed ownership of those deaths and turned them into her crime.

Young gives us the detective’s self-presentation with cold precision: he is a man who cannot solve his own mystery, who comes to Esther repeatedly in disguise, who leaves evidence of his own presence in her body, who then investigates that evidence as if it belonged to someone else’s crime. He has written the crime and cast himself as the investigator. He has fathered the deaths and accused her of murdering them. There is no appeal from this structure. It is sealed.

Esther’s response is what it has been: silence. Stubborn, luminous, unbreakable silence. She will not explain herself unless compelled. She cries only when she is sure no one is near. She faces the detective’s accusations with the same quality she brings to everything: a refusal to be defined by what others have done to her, even when she cannot name what they have done.

The Coming War

The chapter’s closing move is one of Young’s most characteristic: the expansion from the particular to the historical, from Esther’s private grief to the scale of collective catastrophe. There is “going to be another war soon,” Esther thinks. It will kill “all the men and some of the children, and one or two old murders should not have mattered so much, especially if it was nothing murdered.” “If it was nothing murdered”; this is the question at the center of Esther’s legal and moral situation. Were her stillborn children murdered? Were they children? Were they nothing? The law, which has no precedent for Esther’s case, cannot answer this. Esther, who loved every one of them, cannot answer it either. And against the coming war (which will produce deaths by the hundreds of thousands, deaths that will be commemorated and mourned and recorded and justified) Esther’s private losses look, by comparison, like nothing.

This is not consolation. It is the logic of scale that has always been used to make individual suffering invisible. Young gives Esther this thought not to endorse it but to show that Esther has absorbed it, has made a kind of peace with her own insignificance in the larger accounting of death, while remaining entirely, stubbornly, luminously herself.

What to Hold Onto

The mud baby: bigger in death than in life, covered with mud and brambles, the “funeral wreath hanging from its navel,” whistling like a policeman. The fisherman who helped in a state of dreaming, asked no questions, and went back to his fishing. The minimal compassion that is the only kind available.

The policeman’s whistle. The adjacent facts. The thing Esther cannot say because her father is the law.

The detective’s accusation; he claims the dead children as his, and accuses her of killing them. He has written the crime and cast himself as the investigator.

Esther’s final pragmatism: there will be another war. “All the men and some of the children, and one or two old murders should not” matter so much. “Especially if it was nothing murdered.”

And underneath all of it, still: the little shadow boxer, two hearts. She is more hopeful now than she has ever been. Time’s passage helps her. This is not a lie.
